s13-bonus-the-generative-media-shift-scaling-real-time-ai-content-creation-with-sky-yang-founder-ceo-of-imagine-ai

Deposits Before Building: Sky Yang ran discovery calls, mapped ghostwriters' workflows and collected 10 deposits from ghostwriters and agencies before building an AI that drafts posts in a client's voice.

From Voice to Strategy: Matching a client's voice found product-market fit, but the market was small. Imagine AI moved into strategy and ROI by using its own AI to run an agency-like service for B2B companies.

Productizing Manual Know-How: After reaching $1M annual run rate during YC with three people, the team spent December rebuilding the product, baking its LinkedIn know-how into an agent instead of adding headcount for manual work.

Don't Stop Selling: When growth strained capacity again, the team paused go-to-market to focus on R and D and existing customers. Yang calls that a mistake: he should have hired so some people built while others kept momentum.

Data-Driven LinkedIn Content: Imagine AI tracks engagers and CRM stages to steer content toward revenue. Its newest agent has its own computer, makes graphics and creates posts, aimed at companies of about 20 to 200 people.

q: What does Imagine AI do?
a: Imagine AI is a research company focused on B2B growth, with agents that help marketing and growth teams work more efficiently on LinkedIn. As Sky Yang put it, "we have a content agent that focuses on data-driven content" [04:37].

q: How did Imagine AI validate its MVP?
a: Sky Yang did cold outreach to ghostwriters and agencies, held discovery calls to understand their workflows, and asked for deposits before building. "We got 10 deposits from 10 different ghostwriters" [10:00], he said, adding that agencies were among them.

q: How does Sky Yang define product-market fit?
a: Yang describes it as demand so strong that a company must hire or build a more scalable product to survive. In his words, "you have so much demand that your company will literally die" [12:04] if you don't respond.

q: What was Imagine AI's biggest mistake while scaling?
a: Yang says the team stopped go-to-market and selling to go back to R and D, which cost it some momentum. As Yang put it, "I think it was a mistake that we just stopped" [26:51], and he now believes they should have hired more people and kept selling while others did R and D.

q: What has Imagine AI learned about LinkedIn engagement?
a: Yang says the company found that engagement follows a log-normal distribution, with some posts doing very badly and others very well. Rather than expecting every post to be a hit, he said, "what you can do is that you can optimize your posts" [26:14].

s12-e29-fractional-talent-traditional-freelance-marketplaces-fail-enterprise-workflows-and-the-shift-toward-managed-engineering-teams-with-danny-gal-co-founder-ceo-of-proteams

Invite-Only MVP for Pharma: Proteams' first product was an invite-only platform matching senior freelancers to corporates. Early clients were large pharmaceutical companies, and much of the work was people-led alongside the platform.

Two Ways to Deliver: Proteams gives large multinationals access to dedicated freelancers, contractors and experts, or runs end-to-end projects with experts on its team, similar in some ways to a consultancy.

Bootstrapped and Client-Led: Danny says Proteams never took external funding and was profitable from day one. Its roadmap skips 12-month plans, follows client needs and covers service and delivery as well as tech.
Plan 18 Months Out: Rather than thinking three years ahead, Danny focuses on this month, next quarter and the next 12 to 18 months, with a goal of getting 1% better every day.

Seamless Across Client Styles: Some clients want to do everything through the platform, while others just want to speak to a person. Proteams is working on UX, workflows, AI and reporting to serve both.

q: What is Proteams and how does it work?
a: Proteams, which Danny Gal calls the Airbnb of people, helps large multinationals access freelancers, contractors and experts. Clients can work with dedicated people or have Proteams deliver a project, and Danny said of the latter, "we'll deliver that as an end-to-end project similar to a consultancy type model" [03:22].

q: Why did Danny Gal start Proteams?
a: After a corporate career and time in startups, Danny went independent and struggled to scale his own work. As he put it, "teaching people how to scale and I couldn't scale myself" [03:46], and procurement people at big corporates later told him they needed the model he was discussing with his co-founder.

q: How does Proteams decide what to build next?
a: Danny says the biggest input is what customers ask for, alongside a look at competitors, and the roadmap covers both the platform and the service. Contrasting it with typical SaaS planning, he said, "We didn't need 12-month roadmaps and a normal roadmap" [08:02].

q: Is Proteams bootstrapped or venture funded?
a: Danny Gal says Proteams is bootstrapped and has never taken external funding. In his words, "We've been profitable from day one and we've grown organically." [08:39]

q: Why do procurement teams need an external workforce strategy?
a: Danny argues that large enterprises spend billions a year on service suppliers such as consultancies, agencies and freelancers without a plan for it. He said, "no procurement team have a strategy behind that spend" [15:33], and believes using the right supplier for each job would benefit businesses and suppliers alike.

developer-chats-oleksandr-piekhota

Growth Exposed the Platform Gap: A team grew from about 10-15 to 80-90 people in half a year. Without cross-team standards, local development and service integration broke down, and internal testing showed the product couldn't handle the load.

Public APIs Are Contracts: Moving from B2C to B2B, the hardest part wasn't scaling infrastructure. It was backward compatibility, versioning, rate limits and careful naming of endpoints, parameters and errors.
Be Your Own API Client: Building an internal invoicing tool on the new public API surfaced design issues during prototyping, before real clients arrived, while also streamlining an internal workflow.

Open Source Raises the Bar: Piekhota says developers on his team put more care into a component once they know it will be open sourced, because the work becomes public and may become part of their resume.

Maturity Means Wise Trade-Offs: A mature system first makes money and covers customer use cases. Beyond that, it needs a responsible team and an architecture simple and flexible enough to follow business changes.

q: When does an engineering organization need a platform approach?
a: Oleksandr Piekhota saw the need after rapid hiring and a lack of cross-team standards made releases and integration very difficult at a previous company. As he described it, "local development is terrible. It's nearly impossible to run like the whole environment." [05:19]

q: What is the hardest part of moving from a B2C product to a B2B public API?
a: For Piekhota, the challenge in PDFfiller's shift was not mainly infrastructure scale. He said "it was more about contracts and formalizing interface, which you develop." [07:25] Backward compatibility, versioning strategy, rate limiting and endpoint design became much more important.

q: Why is it hard to decide when to stop an R and D experiment?
a: Piekhota warns that after weeks of research, proofs of concept and presentations, engineers are inclined to sell the tool they invested in. In his experience, "when you're trying to do some R and D work, it becomes very emotional." [12:28] Feedback from teammates and a skilled manager can redirect the work or slow it down.

q: How do you recognize a mature engineering system?
a: Piekhota starts with business value rather than code quality or tooling, saying "a mature system is like the system that makes basically money and where customers have their" [20:31] use cases covered. He also stresses balance, with a team that makes wise trade-offs and keeps the architecture simple but flexible.

q: How could AI change software architecture and engineering practices?
a: Piekhota expects that if codebases become largely AI generated, code elegance will matter less and the "shift is going to be is to focus more on tests and contracts." [24:24] He points to stronger CI/CD checks, canary deployments and rollback strategies, and suggests monoliths may regain popularity because agents work better with a single codebase.

s11-e15-passing-telco-infrastructure-costs-to-advertisers-and-scaling-an-all-ip-wireless-carrier-to-300m-downloads-with-derek-ting-co-founder-ceo-of-textnow

Frugality Sparked the Product: Derek Ting built TextNow in college to avoid AT＆T's $20 monthly texting fee on top of calling and data. Unlike other apps at the time, friends didn't need it installed to get his texts.
iPod Touches Revealed the Market: Many early users were on iPod Touches because they couldn't afford a phone plan. That insight widened the goal from free texting to free phone service.

Email Gateways Powered V1: The first version sent texts for free through carriers' email-to-text addresses. It could only send, and building the much harder receiving feature led Ting to recruit a classmate who became co-founder.

Roadmap From Repeated Signals: Early priorities came from patterns in user feedback, not a multi-year plan. Sometimes the response wasn't building anything, but testing price after users said a one-time $5 was too expensive.

Always Have Backups: Working solo and tired, Ting wiped the production database with a typo during a live edit. He rebuilt it with a script that replayed actions from log files, in what he recalls was an all-nighter.

q: How did TextNow get started?
a: Derek Ting was a college student with the first iPhone who didn't want to pay extra for texting. He explained, "TextNow first started as an app that I built to not have to pay for texting" [04:20].

q: How did the first version of TextNow send text messages for free?
a: Ting used carrier email addresses tied to phone numbers, so an email arrived on the recipient's phone as a text, and the app hid that process behind a normal messaging interface. As Ting put it, "lot of these carriers have what they call email gateways" [07:00].

q: What scaling problems did TextNow face early on?
a: Ting said the backend stopped working as usage grew and couldn't handle the load. In the first year, a Christmas morning spike from people opening new iPod Touches took the service down, and Ting recalled, "And it totally crashed our servers" [11:56], leading to all-nighters with his co-founder over the holidays.

q: What does TextNow offer for free?
a: In the interview, Ting described free talk and text through the app, plus a SIM card for cellular coverage where users pay about $5 for shipping. He also said, "we do have a basic free data plan where you can use our app" [18:06] and a few other apps such as email, maps and ride share, while broader data is a paid add-on.

q: What advice does Derek Ting give to startup founders?
a: Ting advises founders to trust their own instinct over the noise from venture capitalists and advisors, since each journey is different. He also said that "grit and persistent is the common thing that will prevail" [21:54].

s11-bonus-p2-the-radical-transparency-framework-eliminating-middle-management-and-running-an-18-year-product-studio-as-a-pure-meritocracy-with-yaroslav-lazor-sergiy-korolyov-co-founders-of-railsware

Craft Alone Didn't Drive Growth: Revenue stayed flat for many years while engineer-led management focused on craft. Growth began when the team decided to push itself to be more commercially successful.

Recruiting Unlocked Scale: Railsware first hired for new roles ad hoc, figuring out interviews on the fly. Building a dedicated recruitment team, and searching beyond Ukraine for engineers, helped it grow.

The $80,000 Calendly Miss: Railsware had borrowed money to invest in clients, then stopped before taking Calendly equity. The founders say that $80,000 stake would now be worth $250 million, and they use it to size later problems.

Studio of Independent Products: Railsware now acts as a mother company for three of its own products, two joint ventures and a consultancy, with increasingly independent teams. The plan is to build at least one billion-dollar business among them.

Validate Before Polishing Pixels: Find out who you're building for by talking to people, even if they reject you. Then check your ideal customer profile, reachable market and realistic conversion rates to see whether revenue could plateau.

q: Why is Railsware's consultancy model hard to scale?
a: Sergiy Korolyov explains that quality software needs very good engineers, and clients used to typical outsourcing shops often start the conversation with rates rather than seeking a technical partner. As he put it, "comparing to the bigger outsourcing shops, which has thousands of people, our model is still unscalable" [05:05].

q: Why didn't Railsware invest in Calendly?
a: Yaroslav Lazor and Sergiy Korolyov say earlier client investments had gone badly, and trying to recover them was tiring and painful, so they declined equity in Calendly. In the founders' words, "we said, let's pull the plug on investments. It just doesn't make sense." [12:13].

q: How did Railsware scale its team?
a: Yaroslav Lazor and Sergiy Korolyov describe searching for talent in countries such as Romania, Spain, Portugal and Brazil, and later creating a team to run the hiring process. As the co-founders put it, "Building a recruitment team was the key point for us" [08:42].

q: What problem is Railsware's Coupler trying to solve?
a: According to Yaroslav Lazor and Sergiy Korolyov, many companies don't understand their P and Ls, marketing or sales numbers, and joining data often requires an expert. The goal is an easy analytics platform with dashboards, reports and AI communication, and as the co-founders said, "Coupler is aimed to bring light into this fog of the data." [18:06].

q: Should a first-time founder hire a CTO right away?
a: Sergiy Korolyov would probably advise working with a product studio first to start the product and validate the idea, then deciding whether to hire a CTO. He has often seen the mistake "that people just think that they need to hire CTO without having any understanding what this role is" [27:36].

s10-bonus-leveraging-kernel-level-ebpf-to-eliminate-sampling-blind-spots-and-track-ai-pipelines-with-shahar-azulay-co-founder-ceo-of-groundcover

Data Stays With Customers: Groundcover has run its databases and entire data plane in customers' environments since day one, which lets it stop pricing by data volume. Shahar sees this as a harder differentiator to copy than eBPF.

A Sensor-First MVP: Within the first three months, Groundcover was installed in a big company. The MVP was mostly an eBPF sensor and a few simple dashboards, with no logs yet, but it worked out of the box and was enough to close the first customer.

Broad Platform Over Niche: Expecting to rip and replace incumbents, the team built log management, infrastructure monitoring and APM very early. A niche eBPF tracing tool, Shahar argues, would never have won organizational buy-in.

Self-Serve for Technical Buyers: DevOps and R and D buyers want to try products before talking to sales. Documented self-install and a live playground keep later sales talks shorter and focused on use cases and migration.

Explain What Feels Obvious: Bring your own cloud felt so intuitive to the founders that they didn't explain or simplify its benefits. It took a few months to a year to fix, and users then responded much better.

q: What is Groundcover and how does it use eBPF for observability?
a: Groundcover is an observability platform for cloud native environments that competes with platforms such as Datadog, Dynatrace and Grafana Cloud. Shahar Azulay describes eBPF as "a technology that allows us to basically turn on the light" [03:22], so teams start getting data without changing their code or environment.

q: Why did Groundcover choose bring your own cloud instead of SaaS?
a: Shahar says the founders felt that starting as SaaS would create technical debt they could never reverse, so the data plane has run in the customer's environment from day one. He acknowledged, "That's a very unorthodox choice for a startup in the SaaS era" [07:50].

q: What did Groundcover's MVP look like?
a: According to Shahar, it was mostly a first eBPF sensor with a few simple dashboards, and it did not yet collect logs or really help users troubleshoot and correlate data. Still, after the first three months, "we already installed Groundcover in a big company" [05:22].

q: Why did Groundcover build a full observability platform instead of a niche tool?
a: Shahar explains that observability is a mature, noisy market, so the team needed logs, infrastructure monitoring and APM to have a chance of displacing existing tools. They had an "early understanding that it's gonna be a rip and replace motion rather than" [09:41] a product living alongside an incumbent as a complement.

q: What mistake did Shahar Azulay make with Groundcover's bring your own cloud approach?
a: Shahar says the approach felt so intuitive that the team did not simplify it or spell out its benefits for users. He described it as a mistake "of not trying to explain that vision to the user" [15:33], and said people reacted much better once the team did.

s10-bonus-the-value-pricing-revolution-overthrowing-the-hourly-hamster-wheel-and-maximizing-profits-for-solo-consultants-with-jonathan-stark-author-of-hourly-billing-is-nuts

Hourly Billing Rewards Junior Developers: Managing about 10 developers, Stark saw that a low-salaried junior could earn far more profit than the firm's best, fastest developer. He traced it to billing by the hour and went solo on January 1, 2006.

Offer Three Options: Borrowing from Alan Weiss's Value-Based Fees, Stark advises putting good, better and best options in proposals. Clients weigh how to work with you, and new value pricers leave less money on the table.
Value First, Scope Last: Don't try to scope a project in the sales meeting. Learn the value, set prices based on it, then decide scope from the desired outcome and the price the client chooses.

Scale by Raising Your Altitude: Stark describes three tiers of client work: maintenance, implementation and deciding what comes next. To scale without hiring, move toward strategic advisory work, selling your brains rather than your hands.
Ruthless Simplicity: Stark sets a yearly theme, works from 15 or 20 recurring daily to-dos and skips nice-to-haves. His Ditching Hourly podcast has no intro music, ads or routine editing.

q: Why did Jonathan Stark stop billing by the hour?
a: While managing developers at a FileMaker consulting firm, Stark noticed that hourly billing made a junior developer far more profitable than a highly skilled one. He said that after puzzling over it, "I finally realized it was because we were billing by the hour" [04:25]. He then went solo to work out an alternative without risking his colleagues' livelihoods.

q: How do you control scope creep on a fixed-price software project?
a: Stark's answer includes a sales-meeting "why conversation" and a mind shift he calls "scope last," where scope is decided after value and price. As he put it, "you do not try and do not even try to scope the project in the sales meeting" [09:41].

q: How can a solo consultant scale without hiring a team?
a: Stark recommends shifting from implementation toward strategic work that helps clients decide what to do next. He explained, "My approach to scaling for myself and the people I work with is to increase the altitude of involvement with your clients." [14:02]

q: What is the hourly trap?
a: Stark describes people who need more money but feel they can't raise their rates, work any more or easily hire help. Of that bind, he said, "So they're trapped in this, I call it the hourly trap." [19:43]

q: How is Jonathan Stark using AI to spread his value pricing advice?
a: Stark has experimented with training an AI on about a thousand hours of recorded community Q and A sessions dating back to 2017, and it points users to the source of each answer. He described it as an "AI bot thing that can do a really good job answering" [25:07], though he noted it isn't perfect.

s10-e8-from-cisco-meraki-and-splunk-to-fixing-privilege-sprawl-why-treating-identity-as-a-static-one-time-login-invites-cloud-catastrophe-with-shashwat-sehgal-co-founder-ceo-of-p0-security

Access Beyond Human Users: P0 Security aims to secure and govern cloud access for every kind of identity, including engineers, contractors, sales engineers, workloads and service accounts, across the lifecycle.

First Deployment Within Months: Starting in late 2022, the team had its first customer deployment by February 2023 and closed that contract by March or April, then sought similar customers and made the MVP work in their environments.

Roadmap Mapped by Segment: Sehgal's team speaks with five to ten customers and prospects weekly, then maps the product gaps between its current best-fit segment and the broader market, revisiting the roadmap regularly.

Scale Without Boiling the Ocean: P0 laid architectural foundations meant to reach hundreds of thousands of identities, but did not over-optimize performance while early customers had roughly 100 to 300 engineers.

Question the Feature Request: A customer may ask for a feature because they haven't considered other ways to solve the underlying problem. Sehgal relies on MVPs and tight customer-to-R and D feedback loops to catch misdiagnoses early.

q: What does P0 Security do?
a: P0 Security focuses on securing cloud access, with a mission of abstracting security away from developers. Co-founder and CEO Shashwat Sehgal says the company aims to "help secure access to a company's crown jewels in the cloud" [05:46], no matter who is trying to access them.

q: Why are non-human identities a cloud security challenge?
a: Sehgal says the number of entities that can take action in the cloud has exploded over the last few years. It is no longer only employees, because "increasingly it's also workloads, service accounts, quote-unquote non-human identities" [03:30].

q: How did P0 Security build its MVP and win early customers?
a: Sehgal says the first deployable version reached a customer within about three months, and that deployment became a closed contract. From there the approach was, in his words, "let's find another customer that looks like the last customer we closed" [00:25] and make the MVP work for their environment.

q: How did P0 Security approach scalability?
a: Sehgal says the team laid architectural foundations intended to scale to tens of thousands of employees and hundreds of thousands or more workloads and machine identities. He also cautions that with smaller early customers, "it's also important to not boil the ocean" [13:23].

q: What does Shashwat Sehgal look for when hiring a startup team?
a: Sehgal looks for intellectual curiosity, high integrity and a willingness to take extreme ownership. On curiosity, he says "you have to go one step beyond and hire not just smart, but also curious or flexible people" [10:26].

s10-bonus-the-founders-for-hire-evolution-moving-past-the-agencies-to-build-early-stage-products-with-custom-venture-studios-with-rob-grazioli-managing-partner-of-bread

Founders for Hire: Bread works with early-stage founders on product, design, engineering, sales motion and go-to-market, operating less like a vendor and more like a partner helping them reach or follow a raise.

Run the Company Like Product: Bread works in six-week cycles, keeps no backlog and makes small to mid-sized bets. It tests growth ideas, such as serving larger legacy businesses, the way it would test a feature.

Automate to Stay Small: Internal tools for staffing, budgeting and forecasting build the reports so operators can focus on decisions. The goal is to scale quality without adding overhead or middle management.
Hire People Who Climb Ladders: Rob looks for experienced, versatile people, such as full stack engineers or designers who code, who can move quickly between the big picture and the details.

A Near-Bankruptcy Lesson: Around 2013, a flimsy book of business, likely R and D overspending and a lost key account left payroll short. Founders skipped their pay, split the team, took on debt and clawed back to profit.

q: What does Bread do for early-stage founders?
a: Bread, where Rob Grazioli is a managing partner, helps founders shape their product, refine sales and go-to-market, and handle design and engineering. Rob describes the model as "less like a vendor and more like a partner or even like a venture fund" [04:12].

q: How does Bread approach product development?
a: Rob Grazioli says Bread works in six-week cycles, avoids backlogs and treats work as small to mid-sized bets, such as validating a feature or design. In his words, "You try to do the smallest thing you possibly can that achieves the outcome" [05:04].

q: What does Rob Grazioli look for when hiring?
a: Rob favors experienced, flexible people who can both see the big picture and solve specific problems, which often means full stack engineers or designers who can code. He loves "people who know when to climb up and when to climb down" [11:12] the ladder between those views.

q: How can a services business scale without adding middle management?
a: Rob Grazioli says Bread first asks why it needs to scale, automates work like reporting, and explores other revenue, including an experimental PE-like function for buying and growing small software products. He explains, "We also don't want to create a middle management layer in our business or for our clients" [12:50].

q: What was Rob Grazioli's biggest mistake as a business owner?
a: At his first services company, Rounded, the team let a bill-paying account end, expecting another project that did not arrive. Rob recalls, "we didn't have enough money to pay our people" [16:40], and calls it a foundational learning experience.

s9-bonus-riding-the-36k-star-black-swan-how-an-impromptu-open-source-fork-saved-the-devops-ecosystem-from-proprietary-lock-in-with-omry-hay-co-founder-cto-of-env0

Lambda First, Then Move: env0 began running customer deployments on AWS Lambda despite its 15-minute limit. When a customer needed longer runs, the team moved to ECS, and later added self-hosted agents and Kubernetes.

A Deliberately Thin MVP: The MVP took a few months. A first customer install failed for lack of SSH key support with Bitbucket; the team returned a week later with it, then built user management when asked.

Vision Plus Repeated Demand: env0 says no to many requests, looking for vision fit and more than one customer asking. Yet a self-hosted agent built for one customer drew many more, and most larger customers now use it.

Multi-Framework by Design: env0 started with Terraform, then added Terragrunt to be an infrastructure as code platform rather than a Terraform one. Omry estimated maybe 30 to 40% of customers use Terragrunt on it.
Hire Before It Hurts: Omry says that by the time you feel you need a marketing, sales or customer success hire, it's already too late. Sometimes env0 needed the person three to six months earlier.

q: What is env0 and what does it do?
a: env0 helps teams manage infrastructure as code deployments, with governance, policies, compliance, cost management, self-service and visibility. Co-founder and CTO Omry Hay describes it this way: "env0 is a platform to manage all of your cloud deployments on top of infrastructure as code." [02:41]

q: How was env0's first version built?
a: Omry Hay says the MVP took a few months, and the company runs mainly on AWS with a mostly serverless architecture and a React single-page front end. On running customer deployments, he recalled, "we started off using a Lambda to deploy the customer infrastructure." [08:40]

q: How does env0 decide which features to build?
a: Omry Hay says the team weighs whether a request fits the product vision and whether more than one customer is asking for it. That discipline means turning things down: "We had to say no to a lot of feature requests" [10:40].

q: What did env0 look for in its early engineering hires?
a: Omry Hay says R and D had no separate front-end or back-end teams, and engineers sometimes helped with things like blog posts, marketing and support. In his words, "we looked for very versatile people at first" [13:47].

q: What technical mistake did Omry Hay's team make early on?
a: An advisor told the team to keep data and application separate, which they did not understand at the time, and coupling the two later caused problems. Omry Hay recalled, "I remember him saying, just separate the data part and the application part." [18:47]

dev-interrupted-assembling-nurturing-engineering-teams

Career Changers Bring User Perspective: Noah hires hungry career-changing engineers who have often seen problems as end users. Senior engineers coach them, and those showing architecture or people-leadership potential are grown to mentor the next wave.

Interview for Collaboration: Senior candidates must prove technical depth, then whiteboard a problem with future teammates. The team watches how they ask questions, take feedback and adapt when the problem changes midstream.

Act Sooner on Poor Fit: Noah kept one early hire about six months too long, costing the team weeks of long hours. Now missed results bring direct feedback, then a week-long project with daily check-ins if problems persist.

Squads as Mini Startups: Variable organizes squads around product lines, led by engineering managers. Engineers act as subject matter experts and co-own roadmaps with the platform team, supported by core platform and core UI squads.

A Failed Product Management Experiment: Adding a product management team put a layer between strategy and engineering, creating bureaucracy and unhappy engineers. Noah eliminated the organization, and says the team went back to thriving.

q: Why hire career-changing engineers?
a: Noah Labhart says they are excited to build, eager to make a name for themselves and bring a user's view of the product. In his words, "They see the world as the end users because they used to be one" [04:21]. Variable pairs them with senior engineers who teach and lead them.

q: How do you interview senior engineers for collaboration?
a: Noah first checks that candidates can architect a good solution, then has them whiteboard a problem with people they would work with. He explained, "what we look for is how they respond to people giving feedback, either" [11:16] positive or negative, and how they adapt when the problem changes.

q: How should an engineering manager handle an underperforming engineer?
a: Noah starts with direct feedback and another project, then moves to a small week-long project with daily check-ins if problems continue, with parting ways as the last resort. Reflecting on an early hire, he admitted, "We kept that person on probably six months longer" [17:49] than they should have.

q: What is the difference between a developer and a programmer?
a: To Noah Labhart, programmers only program and depend on others for requirements, specs and testing, while developers blend programming with design, quality assurance and product ownership. He describes a developer this way: "It's someone who is taking ownership of what they're building" [22:51].

q: Why did Variable eliminate its product management organization?
a: Noah Labhart says the added team got between strategy and engineering, creating extra work and metrics and dictating roadmaps to engineers. As he put it, "The engineering teams were unhappy because they felt like they didn't have buy-in" [28:41]. He removed the product organization, and engineering managers lead the squads.

from-tools-and-weapons-putting-ai-in-the-hands-of-people-everywhere

Platform Over Gatekeepers: Kevin Scott says Microsoft and OpenAI align on building AI that others can create with, rather than leaving a handful of people in big tech to decide how it works, what it's used for and how it's steered.

Predictable Scaling Changed His Mind: Scott was skeptical of rapid progress until meeting Sam Altman's team. Seeing hard problems solved, and capability scaling predictably with compute and data, convinced him OpenAI could do something very interesting.
Turning Scarcity Into Abundance: Scott sees AI as a way to turn hard zero-sum problems, such as education and healthcare where need outstrips capacity, into non-zero-sum ones.

Mission as a Filter: At LinkedIn, teams tested infrastructure, features and products against the mission of making professionals more productive and successful. Scott says that culture helped them question attractive ideas that could pull them off course.

Culture Before Safeguards: Scott wants teams to have already addressed most of what safeguards enforce before products reach them. Clear dangers get firm red lines, while fuzzier questions need real-world exposure to settle.

q: How did Kevin Scott's upbringing in Gladys, Virginia shape his view of AI?
a: Scott grew up among construction workers and other industrious, creative people who solved problems for their community, and he believes people everywhere can do great things with the right tools. Caching Is a Major Cost: GPU compute and in-memory caching are Ntropy's two largest costs. The team weighs how long to store a result against discarding it and recomputing later, especially for odd transactions unlikely to recur.

Test for Consistent Outputs: Ntropy periodically reruns fixed sets of transactions and investigates any changed output. It also aims for stable results when only minor details, like a reference or card number, differ.

Build Human Labeling Early: External labeling quality wasn't acceptable, and Ilia says Ntropy waited too long to build an in-house team. Human labels are essential for training, ground truth and real-time quality monitoring.

q: How does Ntropy run large language models on financial transactions at a reasonable cost?
a: Ilia Zintchenko says Ntropy uses model distillation, layer fusing, quantization, different architectures and caching, reusing earlier computation for very similar transactions. The goal, as he put it, is "how do we bring this performance and reasoning ability of large language models into a stack" [04:18] that processes transactions at massive scale.

q: How does Ntropy measure and maintain model reliability?
a: Ilia explains that the same input should produce the same output, and similar inputs with insignificant differences should too. For live testing, he said, "We have some kind of fixed sets of transactions" [07:49], which are periodically rerun so any changes can be flagged and investigated.

q: Why use language models instead of rules to understand bank transactions?
a: Ilia argues that rules alone won't capture important edge cases, and that Ntropy's approach only became possible with transformer models. In his words, many players are "still pushing this rules-based agenda, which we believe is very performance-capped at a certain point." [11:57]

q: What data sources does Ntropy use to identify merchants?
a: Ilia says Ntropy combines location lookup tables, merchant databases, search engines, APIs, web scraping and the financial data itself. q: What would Ntropy's CTO do differently if he could start over?
a: Ilia Zintchenko would build up human data labeling sooner, saying "if I were to do it again, I would invest more in our labeling data with humans." [16:34] He also would have invested earlier in customer-facing pieces such as documentation and onboarding.

Context Drives Categorization: The same Sweetgreen salad can be an employee expense, business revenue or consumer food spending. Naré says a model needs common sense and context to tell these apart.

A Counterintuitive Early Bet: While banks and providers relied on rules and database lookups, Ntropy built language models, aiming to solve bad transaction data globally, including the long tail, across use cases from payments to lending.

Match the Model to the Task: Sending billions of real-time transactions to a model like GPT-4 doesn't make sense on cost or latency. Teams have to balance precision, latency, cost and privacy for each use case.

Small and Large Models Combined: Ntropy spent millions training its own smaller models on transaction data. It now pairs that stack with large pre-trained models for analytics, natural language queries and text generation.

q: What does Ntropy do with financial transaction data?

q: Why use language models instead of rules to categorize transactions?

q: Can GPT-4 be used to process transactions in real time?

q: How is Ntropy's transaction enrichment used in lending and payments?

[15:51], where bank data, combined with sources such as accounting and sales, helps lenders understand a business and give it access to capital. Scale After Demand Appears: The MVP wasn't built to scale. Postgres limited things like fast page search, so Elasticsearch came later, with freelance help, bringing faster performance, better aggregations and new features.

q: What is Simple Analytics and how is it different from Google Analytics?
a: Simple Analytics is a privacy-focused competitor to Google Analytics, with features such as goals, conversions and data downloads. Adriaan van Rossum explained that "we don't place cookies and it's still a simple, understandable dashboard" [04:23].

q: Why did Adriaan van Rossum start Simple Analytics?
a: As a freelancer building websites, Adriaan was uneasy about adding the Google Analytics script for his customers, and his girlfriend suggested he build his own solution. His concern was that he "knew it was sending all the data to Google Analytics" [03:01] and to Google's ad networks.

q: How was the first version of Simple Analytics built?
a: Adriaan built the MVP in about three months with tools he already knew, including Node.js, Postgres and Chart.js, and offered a very limited dashboard. He credits part of its success to the fact that "the tools that I already knew didn't limit me" [05:39].

q: Can you track sessions without cookies by hashing IP addresses?

q: Why did Eisen's founders decide to tackle escheatment?

Test the Pitch First: Björk iterated on Grafbase's landing page before building the dashboard and product, learning what attracted people and what confused them. He found the pitch harder than expected.

a: Hatchways used its own assessments to find engineers who performed very well, including people who might be screened out on their resumes. Jaclyn Ling said that "because we built a product to vet software engineers, we were able to build our whole initial team through our product." [09:06]

q: What advice does Jaclyn Ling give to new startup founders?
a: Drawing on her first startup, Jaclyn Ling advises founders to find a way to enjoy the process, because making a big impact takes a long time. Before starting again, she told herself to "really learn how to enjoy the process rather than focus on the outcomes" [17:08].

s8-bonus-from-facebook-and-pinterest-data-infrastructure-to-building-the-canva-for-data-with-shawn-cao-of-columns

Data Insights Without Engineers: Shawn saw that getting metrics took pipelines, BI people and technical help. Columns aims to let managers and other non-technical users turn raw data into presentation-ready stories themselves.

Google Sheets Came First: The MVP led with Google Sheets because the live connection keeps stories in sync as data changes. It also meant smaller datasets, fitting a target market of small businesses rather than big companies.

A Roadmap Shaped by Cutting: Early testers said the workflow was too complicated, so the team cut many elements. Today the roadmap is mostly public, and user requests are weighed against the long-term vision of a co-pilot for data storytelling.

q: What is Columns and what does it do?
a: Shawn Cao describes it simply: "Columns is a data storytelling platform." [02:37] It aims to streamline the path from raw data to insights, and then to a polished presentation for your audience.

q: What problem is Columns trying to solve for non-technical users?
a: Shawn observed that getting conclusions from data was a long process that relied on pipelines, BI people and technical staff. He wanted managers to get insights on their own, saying it would be amazing "if they can just do this everything by himself with a little help or no help" [04:02].

q: What tech stack was used to build the Columns MVP?

q: Why did Columns start with Google Sheets as its main data source?

s8-e11-the-firebase-blueprint-for-saas-integrations-delivering-real-time-context-to-ai-agents-with-lauren-long-co-founder-cto-of-ampersand

Code-First Integration Platform: Ampersand helps engineers build, test and manage user-facing integrations with customers' CRMs, ERPs, HR software and more. Lauren likens it to Zapier's connectivity in a developer-first product rather than no-code.
Validate Before Building: The team held over 100 conversations with people who had dealt with integrations, then built a Firebase demo that raised a $4.7 million seed round led by Matrix Partners.

Docs as an MVP: Borrowing a Twilio practice, Ampersand launched full documentation for its UI library, CLI and API before building the product. Design partners then read the docs and helped scope the initial spec.

Scale With a Horizon: Because engineer customers ask about architecture, Ampersand plans for two to three years of scale, choosing tools that can later meet five-to-ten-year challenges without a full rewrite or migration.

Leaving Stealth Helped Hiring: Ampersand couldn't close founding engineer candidates while in stealth. After announcing its seed round and publishing docs, it reached many more interested engineers and was able to close them.

q: What is Ampersand and how is it different from Zapier?

q: How do developers define integrations in Ampersand?
a: Integrations are defined in a YAML configuration file covering the data to read, write and subscribe to, the options exposed to end users, and how data moves into the app. Lauren Long explains, "You can think of it as a terraform for integrations." [09:32]

q: Why did Ampersand launch its documentation before its product?
a: Lauren Long says the team adopted a Twilio philosophy shared by a partner at Matrix: "launch the docs first, because as a developer product, your documentation is really" [07:27] the primary interface. q: How does Ampersand approach scalability as an early-stage developer tool?

a: Lauren Long found that coming out of stealth was much less scary than expected and made recruiting far easier, even though someone had copied the idea while Ampersand was still in stealth. s8-bonus-the-alchemy-of-the-tide-pod-engineering-global-materials-science-and-strategic-partnerships-with-p-scott-bening-former-ceo-of-monosol

Decades to a Mainstream Pod: A water-soluble film laundry product launched in 1962 and failed fast. The technology later gained traction in industrial and institutional use, then auto dish, before reaching mainstream consumer products like Tide Pods.

Chemistry Plus Process Engineering: The film interacts with the product it wraps, with moisture moving until equilibrium, so formulation was critical. So were robust systems able to make hundreds of millions of pods.

Agreements Before Collaboration: MonoSol settled contracts, patent filing and information sharing with partners up front, so people in labs and factories could work together without wondering what they were allowed to say.

Fit Leaders to the Stage: MonoSol grew from about 30 people toward 1,000. Bening says leadership must match the circumstances, and the team running it inside Kuraray differs from the one that owned it before the sale.

Know When to Cut Bait: Terralock, a dust abatement product used by the military, never got named in the U.S. Defense Department budget. Bening says he should have dropped the effort three or four years sooner.

q: What does MonoSol make, and how is it connected to Tide Pods?
a: MonoSol makes the polymer film that encases products such as Tide Pods and Cascade dishwasher pods. Scott Bening describes it as a "film that dissolves in water and disappears" [02:48].

q: What was hard about engineering the water-soluble film used in detergent pods?
a: Bening says organic chemistry and formulation came first, followed by process engineering to manufacture pods at consumer scale. The team focused on "getting the chemistry right because the film has to work with the product it's wrapping" [06:16].

q: How did MonoSol build trusted partnerships with large consumer goods companies?
a: Bening says MonoSol relied on open innovation, personal relationships and joint summits, and anticipated intellectual property hurdles early. As he explains, "we developed the right type of agreements, the legal agreements, the contracts and the understandings up front" [12:39].

q: How did Scott Bening build and change his leadership team as MonoSol grew?
a: He started by breaking down silos in a small team, then added trained professionals who still thought like entrepreneurs as headcount climbed. Bening's lesson is that "you have to customize the leadership team and the people" [17:16] around you to fit the circumstances.

q: What mistake did Scott Bening make with MonoSol's Terralock product?
a: Terralock was a dust abatement solution that Bening considered a great product, but he failed to get it listed in the U.S. Defense Department budget. Bening admits, "It's one of these where I hung on too long and I think that was a big mistake." [24:36]

s8-bonus-bypassing-the-slack-distraction-loop-architecting-real-time-rescheduling-algorithms-and-dynamic-calendar-telemetry-with-matt-martin-co-founder-ceo-of-clockwise

Augment, Don't Replace Calendars: Clockwise shipped as a Chrome extension to avoid asking users to switch calendars. The trade-off was limited screen space and a set-and-forget product that has to work to regain users' attention.
Single-Player Value Fuels Spread: Features like meeting color coding, Slack status sync and personal calendar sync gave individuals a reason to stay long enough for Clockwise to spread to coworkers.

Abstraction Became a Drag: Early backend abstraction gave a small team optionality and speed, but as the company grew, layers of cruft made the code hard to reason about, especially for new engineers.

Paywalls Need New-User Attention: The first monetization worked well on large, already-scaled organizations, but new organizations meeting paywalls were far less successful. It took too long to spot, and the paywall was re-engineered.

Chat for Complex Scheduling: Martin says LLMs, including GPT-4's temporal reasoning, make Clockwise AI possible, letting users ask in chat for hard scheduling tasks, though he doesn't see chat as the be-all, end-all calendar interface.

q: What is Clockwise and how does it optimize your calendar?
a: Matt Martin describes Clockwise as a calendar automation tool that helps individuals, teams and whole organizations get more time for their most important work. It finds inefficiencies, such as a meeting that breaks up a focus block, and as Martin put it, "we'll move them to better times that optimize for your schedule" [03:16].

q: Why did Clockwise launch as a Chrome extension instead of a new calendar?
a: Matt Martin says a new calendar would have added table stakes, friction and switching costs, even though it would have given the team more control over the UI. He explained, "We didn't want to ask users to transition off their existing calendar in order to use Clockwise." [08:21]

q: What tech stack is Clockwise built on?
a: Matt Martin said, "our tech stack, we use Java for services" [06:36], covering everything from auth to crawling. A Node web server in TypeScript with GraphQL serves the clients, which include Slack, a Chrome extension and a web app, built in TypeScript with React.

q: What mistake did Clockwise make when it introduced monetization?
a: Clockwise went to general availability without any payment infrastructure, and Matt Martin says the initial version of monetization, pushed out almost two years later, was wrong. It captured scaled organizations well, but "we didn't pay attention to the new organizations that we were acquiring with paywalls" [00:24].

q: What advice does Matt Martin give to new startup founders?
a: Martin passes on advice from another founder about managing your own psychology through the highs and lows, to avoid burnout and be a better leader. He recalled, "he'd said something that really sticks with me, which is make sure to manage the amplitude" [30:48] of the waves.

s8-e10-from-chrome-extension-to-a-professional-network-for-500k-developers-engineering-content-recommendation-pipelines-with-ido-shamun-co-founder-cto-of-dailydev

Ship the Side Project First: Ido built the first version in about two weeks, using familiar JavaScript and Google Cloud plus a SaaS provider for RSS scraping. He didn't worry about scale; the goal was to see whether it worked.

Three Inputs Shape the Roadmap: daily.dev weighs weekly user interviews, its multi-year strategy and product usage data. A mix of stakeholders, including co-founders, product managers, data analysts and marketing, then decides what comes next.

Hiring From the Community: After raising funding, the founders went fully remote to set an example for daily.dev's global community. The first hires were platform power users or contributors to its open-source projects on GitHub.

q: How was the daily.dev MVP built?
a: Ido built it in roughly two weeks, with a browser extension, an API server and scraping of a closed list of sources, using JavaScript and Google Cloud. In his words, "What I had to build was an RSS scraper" [05:27], and he used a SaaS provider to supply that scraping functionality.

q: How does daily.dev decide what to build next?
a: Ido says the team combines user interviews, long-term strategy and product data, then decides with a mix of stakeholders from across the company. On the first of those inputs, he said, "So we rely heavily on user feedback." [08:47]

q: What went wrong during daily.dev's domain migration?

the-closer-toys-r-us

Built Around Repeat Visits: Charles Lazarus moved from cribs and baby furniture to toys because children tire of them quickly. Exclusive deals with toy makers then made Toys R Us the place to go for certain toys.

The Debt Trap: The 2005 buyout by KKR, Bain Capital and Vornado added about $5 billion in debt. Cash went to servicing it, at one point about $400 million a year, instead of e-commerce or better stores.

Walmart Changed the Game: Walmart and Target could sell toys cheaply to pull shoppers in for everything else. Toys R Us never made its stores magical enough to give people a reason to choose it instead.

A Run on the Bank: News that bankruptcy was being weighed led toy companies to stop shipping, fearing they wouldn't be paid. A filing planned for after the holidays happened within three weeks, with no plan to emerge.
The Last Holiday Season: The company needed a huge holiday season to keep creditors at bay, but rivals slashed toy prices. Liquidation was announced in March 2018, and U.S. stores had closed by June.

q: How did Toys R Us become the dominant toy retailer?
a: Founder Charles Lazarus understood what children wanted and built close ties with toy makers, including exclusives that drew shoppers to his big box stores. Reporter Lauren Hirsch said that "the most special thing about it was its relationship with the toy companies" [06:08].

q: How did the leveraged buyout hurt Toys R Us?
a: The 2005 takeover by KKR, Bain Capital and Vornado loaded the company with about $5 billion in debt, leaving it unable to invest against Walmart or Amazon. In Hirsch's words, "This debt became effectively an albatross on the company" [12:50].

q: Why did Toys R Us file for bankruptcy before the holiday season ended?
a: Hirsch broke the story that the company was weighing bankruptcy, and surprised toy companies stopped shipping for fear of not being paid. She recalled that "the next three weeks were this like complete frenzy where it was effectively a run on the bank" [20:09].

q: Why did Toys R Us liquidate instead of emerging from bankruptcy?
a: The plan was to emerge leaner, but that required creditor support and a very strong holiday season, which price cuts at Walmart and Target made very hard. Hirsch explained that the company "had creditors who basically believed this company was worth more dead than alive" [25:47].

q: Was Amazon or Walmart responsible for the fall of Toys R Us?
a: Hirsch points mainly to Walmart and its ability to compete on price, while noting that other factors, such as lost supplier trust, also mattered. She said people focus heavily on Amazon "and they forget the original disruptor, which was Walmart" [31:53].

s8-bonus-the-nine-figure-legal-tech-exit-turning-millions-of-scattered-slack-and-email-logs-into-instant-legal-evidence-with-andy-wilson-co-founder-former-ceo-of-logikcull

From Dining Room to Cloud: Wilson started Logikcull on a rack of servers in his Washington, D.C. dining room. Around the Great Recession, the company bet on the still-early cloud and pivoted to a cloud-native service anyone could use anywhere.

A Three-Year MVP: The first version let users drag and drop huge data sets, such as a 100GB zip file, and made it all searchable and organized. This mostly backend problem took three years, and the threat of running out of money forced feature priorities.

Listen Beyond the Request: Wilson says 80 to 90% of enterprise software should come directly from customers. The rest comes from active listening, digging into why they ask, which can reveal needs nobody has stated outright.

Hiring Against Sheng: Logikcull assesses talent with an acronym based on co-founder Sheng's name: smart, hungry and humble, empathetic, nimble and gritty. Applicants rate themselves from one to five and give examples.

Distribution From Day One: Self-serve signup and in-product viral loops made the business almost entirely inbound and referral driven. Wilson thinks it could be 10x bigger had he spent one day a week learning distribution earlier.

q: What does Logikcull do?
a: Andy Wilson describes Logikcull as a data discovery service for legal and IT teams handling disputes, investigations or records requests. It uses AI and automation to organize uploaded or synced data and surface what matters, "so that you can cull the noise and find the signal" [03:09].

q: How did Logikcull get started?
a: Wilson had worked at a company that printed email on a massive scale and trucked it to law firms, and he saw a large product opportunity in legal. Before the cloud, he built his own setup at home, and as he put it, "in my dining room. So imagine like a rack of servers and lots of wires" [03:42].

q: How did Logikcull decide which features to build for its MVP?
a: Wilson said the team tried scoring systems such as RICE and ICE. What mattered more was the deadline created by limited cash, since "the biggest motivator was the reality of running out of money" [05:43].

q: How did Logikcull use product-led growth to scale?
a: Wilson said the company removed as much friction as possible from trying and buying, so users could sign up, enter a credit card and get started. Viral loops then let customers spread the product, and "our business is almost entirely inbound and referral driven today" [11:22].

q: What does Logikcull look for when hiring?
a: Wilson said the company codified one of its five core values around co-founder Sheng's name and uses it as a behavioral framework to assess talent. Explaining the acronym, he said "it stands for smart, hungry, and humble, empathetic, nimble, and gritty AF" [09:41].

s8-bonus-pioneering-computational-entomology-converting-wingbeat-light-disruptions-into-real-time-pest-telemetry-with-dr-eamonn-keogh-co-founder-of-farmsense

Hearing Insects With Light: Keogh's prototype used a Radio by Light science toy: an insect crossing the laser disrupts the light, which becomes sound. Unlike a microphone, this optical approach isn't deafened by outdoor wind noise.

Turning Pests Into Data: FarmSense field sensors detect arriving bugs, identify details such as sex and species, and push the data to the cloud. Growers can check a phone or laptop to see where bugs are and act.

Start With High-Value Crops: Rather than tackle every field at once, the team focused on tree nuts like almonds, pistachios and walnuts: high-value, insect-sensitive crops grown close to home. It then expands crop by crop and insect by insect.

A Three-Part Founding Team: Keogh brought AI and machine learning, then added a co-founder with embedded hardware skills and a PhD entomologist who understands both the bugs and how growers work with them.

Proving Demand Before Scaling: 3D printing produced roughly 500 or 600 devices, but could not reach thousands. Paid field trials proved value and helped unlock funding, with injection molding pieces ready for production in China.

q: What does FarmSense do?
a: FarmSense, co-founded by Dr. Eamonn Keogh, makes a field sensor that detects insects and sends information about them to the cloud so growers can take action. As Keogh describes it, "When the bugs arrive at the sensor, we detect them." [03:37]

q: Why detect insects with light instead of a microphone?
a: Dr. Eamonn Keogh explains that even a small amount of outdoor wind noise overwhelms a microphone, while an optical sensor can pick up tiny insects without it. In his words, "if you measure the sound optically you can be completely deaf to" [04:52] external noise.

q: Which crops did FarmSense target first, and why?
a: Keogh says the team started with tree nuts such as almonds, pistachios and walnuts, which are high-value, very sensitive to insects and widely grown in California. The goal was to "solve one crop, one insect, do it very well, prove value to the world," [07:24] and then expand incrementally.

q: How did FarmSense manufacture its early sensors?
a: The company initially built its sensors in California using 3D printing, which Dr. Eamonn Keogh credits with saving them dramatically. "We've been able to 3D print maybe 500 or 600 of these physical devices" [09:53], he said, but scaling to thousands required a move to other production methods.

q: How can insect monitoring reduce pesticide use?
a: Keogh says growers who don't know what is in their fields are tempted to spray everything, which can hurt bees, pollinators, birds and bats. He argues that "Our company, in principle, can reduce the pesticide use dramatically" [11:48] by showing growers what is actually there.

s8-bonus-rewriting-database-physics-engineering-a-hybrid-memory-nosql-engine-for-petabyte-scale-ai-inference-with-srini-srinivasan-co-founder-cto-of-aerospike

Interviews Picked the Beachhead: Srini and co-founder Brian interviewed about 40 industry leaders, concluded ad tech was the place to start, and chose the 2.0 release's features from what they learned.
Rewritten in C: The team took about six months to rewrite the code. C meant building their own tools, but let them engineer the database for its exact purpose without interference from libraries.
Flash Alongside DRAM: Aerospike uses Flash as well as DRAM for real-time data, promising 10x better performance on much cheaper hardware. Its first customer saw a 10x reduction in timeouts.

Too Many Features, Too Fast: After getting funding, Aerospike packed too much roadmap into 18 months around 2013 and shipped incomplete features. Srini says the backlash set the company back at least a year or two.
Raise More, Earlier: Srini's biggest do-over would be bigger funding rounds sooner, to compete on non-technical fronts like marketing. He ranks that above being more careful with new features.

q: What is Aerospike used for?
a: Srini Srinivasan describes Aerospike as a database for real-time decision-making in areas such as ad tech bidding, fraud detection, gaming and e-commerce, where very high uptime matters. As he put it, "Aerospike has been focused on building out a high-performance database" [02:38].

q: How was the first version of Aerospike built?
a: Srini joined co-founder Brian around an existing SSD-based caching effort, then rewrote the code in C over about six months, releasing it as version 2.0. Srini set a condition for getting involved: "but only if we build a true database for the long term." [05:18]

q: Why does Aerospike use Flash storage in addition to DRAM?
a: Srini says using Flash for real-time data lets Aerospike run on far cheaper hardware while still targeting 10x better performance than other solutions. As he explained, "the price per bit for Flash is actually much lower than that for DRAM." [13:44]

q: How does Aerospike decide what to build next?
a: Srini says he and Brian looked for gaps among existing customers and in target markets such as financial services, telcos and e-commerce, then validated new features with prospects and avoided building for just one customer. In his view, product builders must lead, and "We better be the experts in the field" [09:02].

q: What was Aerospike's biggest early mistake?
a: Srini says that after getting funding and more people, the company added features too quickly around 2013 and 2014, and many were not complete. In his words, "We just did too much of the roadmap too fast within an 18-month period." [17:30]

s8-e9-the-death-of-the-separated-bank-and-spreadsheet-automating-solopreneur-taxes-at-the-swipe-of-a-card-with-lilac-bar-david-co-founder-ceo-of-lili
Own the Experience, Outsource Infrastructure: Lili used Galileo for back-end infrastructure and a sponsor bank for its checking account, while controlling onboarding and the mobile experience itself.
Swiping Makes Expenses Engaging: In a Tinder-like flow, users swipe right or left to mark expenses as business or personal. Lilac says it drove engagement and kept owners organized and up to date.
Automate the Tax Set-Aside: Owners were often surprised by IRS bills of $10K or $20K. Lili moves a set percentage of incoming money into a tax bucket, so owners know money is set aside for taxes.

One Account Didn't Work: Lili first tried to serve freelancers' work and life through one consumer account. The community recommended separation, and Lili later built a business account with accounting and tax software on top.
Pair Paid Channels With Education: To scale acquisition, Lili mixed paid channels with brand and community building, investing from day one in blogs, guides and webinars.

q: What is Lili and who is it for?
a: Lili is a banking platform that also offers bookkeeping, invoicing and tax optimization, which began with a focus on freelancers and moved toward small business owners. As co-founder and CEO Lilac Bar David put it, "We are building a platform for small business owners to try to tackle all of their different financial challenges." [02:42]

q: How does Lili's automated tax savings work?
a: When income arrives, Lili moves a portion of it into a separate tax bucket within the account, so owners know what remains in checking is available to spend. Lilac explained, "So whenever an income hits the account, we take a specific percentage." [09:17]

q: How was the first version of Lili built?
a: The mobile-only MVP was a consumer account for freelancers with expense management built in, supported by a sponsor bank and card infrastructure. On the back end, Lilac said, "So we ended up working with Galileo as an infrastructure," [06:13] while the team controlled the customer experience.

q: How does Lili make expense tracking easier and more engaging?
a: Lilac Bar David said the team wanted a banking app that was fun to use, so it created a Tinder-like experience for sorting expenses. In her words, "You have to swipe right or left, whether an expense is business or personal." [07:01]

q: What mistake did Lili make early on?
a: Lilac said the team tried to combine freelancers' personal and business finances in one consumer account, but the community recommended keeping two separate accounts and cards. She admitted, "We were trying to embed everything together. It wasn't successful." [15:36]

s8-bonus-the-rag-playbook-bypassing-data-warehouses-to-build-a-secure-federated-enterprise-ai-search-engine-with-prasad-kawthekar-co-founder-ceo-of-dashworks

A Spotlight-Style MVP: Dashworks' first version took about three months: an Electron desktop overlay with its own keyboard shortcut that searched Google Drive and other cloud apps, using Algolia for fast autocomplete-style results.

Integrations Are a Maintenance Problem: The team planned for building many integrations quickly but didn't anticipate the hours needed to maintain them, and had to go back and rewrite a large part of the system.

From Result Lists to Answers: Dashworks began with traditional search results, then added synthesized answers that combine information from different sources. At recording time, multi-turn chat about internal work data was about to be released.

Retention Before Acquisition: Prasad says prioritizing acquisition over retention was an early mistake. Dashworks moved from enterprise sales to self-service onboarding, which tied its work more closely to the end-user experience.

Pricing for Active Users: Dashworks moved from large upfront enterprise contracts to usage-based pricing where customers pay only for users actively using the product, aligning the team's efforts with customer value.

q: What problem does Dashworks solve?
a: Prasad Kawthekar explains that "Dashworks is essentially solving the problem for helping employees find instant answers to their questions at work." [02:37] The idea grew from his own experience in a previous role, where it took seven email threads and roughly eight weeks to find a document that was just a link on the company intranet.

q: How was the Dashworks MVP built?
a: The MVP took about three months and started as an Electron desktop app with a keyboard-driven overlay, similar to Spotlight on a Mac, that searched cloud apps. Prasad said, "we specifically used a search service called Algolia, which is optimized for these low latency, auto-complete kind of queries." [05:18]

q: What is hard about building integrations for workplace search?
a: Prasad says the team learned that integrations are a maintenance problem as well as a build problem, which led them to rewrite a large part of the system. With the right abstractions they could move quickly, "but maintaining those integrations cost you a lot more time" [06:54] than they had anticipated.

q: What was an early mistake Dashworks made?
a: Prasad said, "One of the mistakes I think we made early on was prioritizing acquisition before user retention." [12:11] The company then focused heavily on the end-user experience, moved to self-service onboarding and adopted usage-based pricing.

q: What is the future vision for Dashworks?
a: Prasad describes Dashworks evolving into a work assistant with a single chat experience that can take actions, such as sending emails or updating Salesforce. The goal is to find answers, "which is what we're doing right now, but also start acting on that information itself" [14:38].

s8-bonus-the-webrtc-blueprint-engineering-ultra-low-latency-video-and-voice-infrastructure-for-ai-agents-with-kwindla-kramer-co-founder-ceo-of-daily

Hardware Came First: Daily's first product was a small hardware appliance for conference room video calls and screen sharing. Early browser WebRTC was unstable, so the team controlled everything from the CPU and GPU up through the UX.

The Pivot to DevTools: Developer experiments gained traction and Safari added solid WebRTC support, opening up iOS. Daily decided around the end of 2018 to end-of-life its hardware and become a developer tools company.

Boring Tech Beat Firebase: Firebase became Daily's biggest DevOps and support pain, and other platforms had similar issues. Kramer spent two weeks over Christmas building Kitchen Sync on a SQL database and HTTP polling.

Hire People Who've Built It: Daily aimed for its first 20 or so engineering hires to have built a version of their work at least once, ideally twice. It scaled with experienced people to roughly 35 or 40.

Native Mobile Came Too Late: Kramer calls this Daily's biggest mistake and takes the blame. For about a year and a half too long, mobile support was mostly a browser experience, costing the company customers and customer discovery.

q: What does Daily do?
a: Daily makes developer tools that help engineers add video and audio to websites and apps, handling networking, latency, scaling and cross-platform issues. Kwindla Kramer said that to investors, the company explains that "we make it easy to add audio and video features to any website or app" [11:00].

q: Why did Daily start with a hardware product?
a: Kramer explained that WebRTC was so new, and browser implementations so unstable, that a reliable experience required controlling the full device. In his words, "we kind of needed to control the whole thing we gave them" [06:16].

q: Why did Daily move off Firebase?
a: State updates backed up and WebSockets disconnected, and the problems persisted even with help from Firebase's team. After prototyping on other platforms, Kramer said, "i built exactly what we needed on top of the most boring technologies we could" [16:42], using a SQL database and HTTP polling.

q: How does Daily balance scalability with shipping quickly and technical debt?
a: Kramer tries to choose tooling, platforms and architecture that can scale, then ship and iterate fast even if technical debt builds up. His approach is to "get the low level choices right and then build quickly on" [13:59] top of them.

q: What was Daily's biggest mistake?
a: Kramer points to being slow to fully support native mobile, even though many interesting use cases are mobile first. He admitted that "it took us a long time to really focus on building native mobile libraries" [19:37].

s8-e8-the-anatomy-of-a-high-stakes-pivot-engineering-a-zapier-for-money-with-gilad-uziely-co-founder-ceo-of-sequence

Why Lance Had to Pivot: Building a neobank on embedded finance tools brought a financial institution's downsides, like chargebacks and fraud, without a real bank's ability to lend against its balance sheet. Users also expected a bank account to be free.

Users Pointed to the Product: Lance's best users loved its end-to-end money automation and wanted it across all their accounts, including 401k, cards and crypto. One even described it as "Zapier for money."

Validate With Real Payments: Landing pages offered early access to the not-yet-built product, then called Money Route, for $200. In five days, 100 people paid, giving the team conviction and a group of design partners.

Simple Pricing as a Learning Tool: Nobody could use Sequence for free, but to move fast, the team opened the whole product at the lowest tier. Within three or four months, this helped them connect pricing to what users actually valued.

Free Doesn't Fix Weak Value: When no one would pay about $12 or $15 a month for Lance, the team made it free and relied on interchange fees. Gilad calls that a huge mistake because it dodged the real problem of not giving enough value.

q: What is Sequence and how does it work?
a: Sequence is a financial router that lets consumers and small business owners manage money across different places using if-this-then-that rules, such as topping up a rainy day fund when it drops below $1,500. As Gilad Uziely explains, "We have them move money from one place to the other," [02:45].

q: Why did Lance pivot away from the neobank model?
a: Gilad Uziely says revenue didn't grow fast enough and the fundraising market had shifted away from rewarding user growth alone. Because Lance relied on a custodial bank and embedded finance tools, he explains that "you get all the downside of being like a financial institution, chargebacks, fraud" [05:07], without being able to make money like a real bank.

q: How did the team validate Sequence before building it?
a: After interviewing Lance users and people who had never heard of Lance, the team put up landing pages asking $200 for early access. Gilad recalls that in five "days hundred people paid two hundred dollars and we got to conviction" [08:00].

q: How does Sequence decide what to build next?
a: Sequence leans on a highly engaged community, including a Discord server that early users started themselves. Gilad estimates that "60 or even 70% of everything that we've built came directly from requests" [12:01] from users.

q: What pricing mistake did Gilad Uziely learn from at Lance?
a: When users wouldn't pay a monthly subscription, the team gave the product away because it still earned interchange fees on debit card use. Gilad says this avoided the real issue that people didn't see enough value, and of giving it away he says, "That's the worst thing that you can do." [17:57]

s8-bonus-the-salsa-dancing-founders-rewriting-b2b-support-eliminating-legacy-tool-sprawl-with-embedded-ai-and-dynamic-slas-with-nooshin-alibhai-eric-klimuk-co-founders-of-supportbench

Built From Frontline Pain: Eric built a tool set to manage large enterprise accounts after the platform his company chose failed. It went viral and took over the company's support infrastructure, becoming the genesis of Supportbench.

Offload Infrastructure to Azure: Eric built in .NET on Azure so the team manages no infrastructure and he could focus on the code base. It still took a couple of years to have enough features to start selling.

Requirement Sheets Shaped the Roadmap: Target support teams arrived knowing their requirements and gaps, and unmet needs stalled deals. The challenge was building features that benefit all customers, not just one buyer.

Hire People Who Know Support: Eric found that developers and support hires who didn't understand support work missed what the product needed. The team now has strong support experience, including frontline enterprise support.

Spending Too Fast Forced Layoffs: After selling property to bootstrap, the founders hired and took office space too soon, then had to let people go. They later pivoted and rehired everyone they had let go.

q: What is Supportbench and who is it for?
a: Supportbench is a premium B2B customer support platform for companies whose support has grown too complex for simpler help desks and a pile of add-on tools. Eric Klimuk said he started building it because "there was nothing really on the market that really focused on B2B" [06:20].

q: What technology was Supportbench built with?
a: Eric Klimuk built the product on Microsoft technology, using Azure as the platform so the team would not manage infrastructure. As Eric put it, "I went straight to my roots and I went straight into .NET." [06:42]

q: How does Supportbench use AI in customer support?
a: Eric Klimuk said there are innovative ways B2B companies can use AI, and pointed to examples inside the product, including automatic knowledge base creation to make KCS easier. His other examples were "CSAT prediction or auto summarizations of problem solution" [20:46].

q: What was the biggest mistake Supportbench's founders made?
a: Nooshin Alibhai explained that after investing their own money, they hired and got office space too quickly, had to shut it down and let people go, and were later able to rehire them. Eric Klimuk's lesson was about money: "I didn't respect cash the way that I respect cash now." [00:21]

q: What does Supportbench look for when hiring?
a: Eric Klimuk looks for people who buy into the vision and understand the market and product, because he saw a big disconnect when hires didn't understand support. He said that "all of our developers and all of our support people all have really strong experience" [13:02] or have worked in support.

s8-bonus-how-an-att-executive-and-a-harvard-ai-engineer-scaled-an-11m-generative-ad-engine-with-hikari-senju-matt-swalley-co-founders-of-omneky
Brand and Data as Moats: In 2018, when AI imagery wasn't yet good enough, Hikari Senju bet on building a brand and gathering data to gain a head start on competitors as the technology advanced.

Analytics Came First: The MVP took two years and launched in January 2020. It ingested Facebook ad data, tagged creative with computer vision, found what lifted click-through and return on ad spend, and offered very early ad generation.

Choosing Winnable Battles: Essentially bootstrapped for three years, Omneky didn't try to out-build Google or Facebook on foundation models. It focused on ad analytics, management and workflow for advertisers.

Consistency Across Channels: Senju argues that each platform's own generative model would push brands toward different local maxima. Omneky aims to keep the brand experience consistent across them, which he says builds trust and ad returns.

Hiring for Energy and Curiosity: Matt Swalley names high energy, great core values and fast, curious learning as must-haves. The founders also scout for people who could fit three months to a year from now.

q: What does Omneky do?
a: Omneky uses real-time marketing data to learn which imagery and copy drive sales for different customer personas, then creates ads for testing at scale. As Hikari Senju put it, "we use generative AI to generate hundreds and thousands of personalized ads" [03:11].

q: What was the first version of Omneky's product?
a: Released in January 2020 after about two years of work, it integrated with Facebook ads, analyzed what performed, and offered early stock image suggestions and copy generation. Hikari Senju said "the very first product that we built was an analytics engine for analyzing content" [06:34].

q: Why didn't Omneky build its own large language model?
a: Hikari Senju said the company had very limited resources and could not compete with Google or Facebook on foundation models, so it focused on ad analytics, management and workflow. He explained that "Omneky was essentially bootstrapped for the first three years" [12:12].

q: Why does brand consistency across ad platforms matter?
a: Hikari Senju compares a brand to a friend, who would seem strange if their personality changed every time you saw them. His view is that "Consistency drives trust. Trust drives higher ROI in ad spend." [08:47].

q: What does Omneky look for when hiring?
a: Matt Swalley described must-have traits that include energy, values and the ability to learn quickly with intellectual curiosity. In his words, "you have to have high energy, you have to have great core values" [14:23].

s8-e7-the-lawyer-who-learned-to-code-turning-unstructured-contracts-into-a-32b-enterprise-workflow-engine-with-jason-boehmig-co-founder-of-ironclad

Workflows Before AI Extraction: Ironclad first looked at AI for contract data entry in 2014, but it wasn't accurate enough for legal teams. It turned to workflows, so contract data was structured from the moment of creation.

Hand-Coded to No-Code: Engineers first hand-coded each customer workflow, then legal engineers configured them in JSON, and finally customers got a no-code designer. Boehmig says those less scalable steps produced secret sauce competitors struggled to replicate.
