Win a Small Market First: Ironclad's first goal was to be the number one CLM in Soma. It got close to local legal teams, even non-buyers, to shape the roadmap. Boehmig says going too broad too quickly has been a repeated mistake.

Deep Interviews and References: Early hires came largely from the founders' networks. Toby, the first hire they didn't already know, got about 48 hours of interviews and slept on an office couch, and the team also dug deep into candidates' references.

AI Speeds Review and Extraction: Some customers now review specific contract types in two minutes instead of 40, with better results. Field extraction from scanned PDFs took eight years to reach about 20 fields, then jumped to 198 within months.

q: What is Ironclad and what problem does it solve?
a: Ironclad is a contract lifecycle management platform that helps companies create business contracts and manage the information in them. Co-founder Jason Boehmig described the goal this way: "We're trying to restore the business contract to be a really simple, easy, clean, and helpful" [02:53] concept for the modern business.

q: Why did Ironclad focus on contract workflows instead of AI at the start?
a: The founders first hoped AI could replace the manual data entry that traditional contract repositories required. Jason Boehmig said they quickly realized AI "in 2014 was not at the level that a legal team could rely on" [06:39], so they built workflows that capture structured information as contracts are created.

q: How did Ironclad build its no-code Workflow Designer?
a: It started with software engineers hand-coding workflows, moved to an internal JSON tool for legal engineers, and then became a no-code interface for customers. Jason Boehmig credits that sequence: "we had first done it in software code, then done it in JSON" [13:40], which led them to the right configurable interface.

q: How is AI changing contract review at Ironclad?
a: Jason Boehmig said global customers are using AI in production on specific types of contracts, with better results than before. They can "review a contract in two minutes where it used to take them 40 minutes" [17:53], though he noted it is still early days.

q: What advice does Jason Boehmig have for early-stage founders?
a: He advises founders to trust their instinct and insight, even when experienced investors have strong opinions. As Boehmig put it, "you know best you're closest to the customer you're closest to the problem" [21:08], and he recalled many early investors telling Ironclad to pick another idea.

s8-bonus-democratizing-entity-graphs-and-data-fusion-with-adam-judelson-co-founder-of-firstprinciples-networknerd
Ship Small, Then Listen: Adam built a basic iOS note app for himself in four weeks with a team in India. A year later, flipping it to free brought a couple thousand downloads in one weekend.

Manual Entry Is the Obstacle: A landing page booked 55 interviews in under 12 hours on about $8.50 of ad spend. People loved the idea but didn't want to type notes, so reducing data entry became the focus of every feature.

Test Talent with Real Work: Network Nerd runs on contractors and agencies. Adam looks for passion for the problem and validates skills through paid experiments that contribute to the product, even though a failed one costs money.

Rebuilding a Brittle Backend: The early stack's MySQL database and old PHP site couldn't handle growth. The team moved to Google Cloud, Firebase and Firestore, and began shifting iOS logic into cloud functions to prepare for cross-platform support.

Ads Before Product-Market Fit: Adam spent tens of thousands of dollars on digital ads and gained very few users. He turned to guerrilla market tests, trying the same features with different audiences such as teachers or MBA candidates.

q: What is Network Nerd and what does it do?
a: Network Nerd is an app Adam Judelson created for keeping notes on the people in your life, such as their kids' names, locations and interests, so you can stay in touch. He describes it as a contact app for your notes, "except that it's powered by a personal assistant that gives you smart reminders" [02:48].

q: How long did it take to build the Network Nerd MVP?
a: Adam hired a team in India and built a very basic native iOS app that let users log in, create a note and store it. He wasn't super proud of it, but he was proud of the speed: "So we put that thing together and launched it in four weeks." [04:58]

q: Why don't people keep notes on their friends and contacts?
a: Adam's user interviews showed that people love the concept and want to track information about their friends, but resist the effort of recording it. As he put it, "the main obstacle to doing it is nobody wants to enter any data" [11:23] manually, which led to features like voice notes and Google Calendar integration.

q: How does Adam Judelson evaluate contractors and agencies?
a: Adam looks for people who are passionate about the problem and likely to become power users themselves. He also tests their skills through real project work, saying that for product disciplines, "not just engineers, it requires an experiment." [14:40]

q: What was Adam Judelson's biggest mistake with Network Nerd?
a: After a cheap ad landed many user interviews, Adam got excited about digital advertising and tried to dial in acquisition costs. He recalled that "before I knew it I had spent tens of thousands of dollars and had driven very few new users" [21:20], which taught him to test markets as rigorously as product ideas.

s8-bonus-the-death-of-hardcoded-env-chaos-unifying-developer-identity-and-secrets-automation-with-vlad-matsiiako-co-founder-ceo-of-infisical

Ship a Narrow MVP Fast: Infisical launched its first version in about two and a half weeks, targeting just .env file management with Node.js and Next.js. Time to value came before performance and scale, but security and cryptography got close attention.

Open Source Builds Trust: Infisical started closed source, then opened up after hearing from users. Self-hosting keeps secrets on a company's own infrastructure, and Vlad says he would now go open source from day one.

Rewriting the CLI in Go: The first command line tool was an NPM package that only fit the JavaScript ecosystem. The team rewrote it in Go so companies could use it regardless of language or operating system.

Hiring From the Community: After its seed round, Infisical plans to hire slowly, starting with open source contributors. Within a few months it had almost 6,000 GitHub stars and over 60 code contributors.

One Source of Truth: Infisical distributes secrets from one place to engineers and services like Vercel, AWS and GitHub Actions. Its Kubernetes operator automatically redeploys containers with new secrets.

q: What is Infisical and what problem does it solve?
a: Vlad Matsiiako, Co-Founder and CEO, describes it simply: "Infisical is an open source secrets manager for developers." [02:34] It helps companies manage API keys and other developer secrets across their infrastructure, both locally for engineering teams and through integrations with third-party services.

q: Why is Infisical open source?
a: Infisical was closed source at first, but user feedback showed that a tool storing such sensitive data needed to earn trust. Vlad said "it makes all the sense in the world to actually be open source" [06:59], and self-hosting means secrets never have to leave a company's own infrastructure.

q: How long did it take to build the Infisical MVP?
a: Vlad said, "we pretty much launched the MVP for Infisical within two or three weeks." [04:11] That first version focused specifically on managing .env files, using Next.js for the frontend and Node.js for the backend.

q: Why did Infisical rewrite its CLI in Go?
a: The first CLI was an NPM package, so it only worked within the JavaScript ecosystem. Vlad explained that the team "had to go back and rewrite everything in Go" [12:18] to make it OS and platform agnostic.

q: What is on the roadmap for Infisical?
a: Vlad said, "We want to create an end-to-end framework that starts with whenever you commit your secrets to" [14:24] Git, where Infisical scans commits and prompts you to move those secrets into the secrets manager. The vision continues through storage, orchestration and easy secret rotation.

s8-e6-the-1b-treasury-lifeboat-engineering-compliance-first-yield-and-business-banking-for-startups-with-bryce-crawford-co-founder-cto-of-meow

Costco for Financial Services: Meow treats bank and treasury accounts as commodities and competes on low fees and transparency, passing more interest back to business customers instead of relying on sneaky fees.

Six Weeks to T-Bills: As interest rates rose, Meow went from considering Treasury bills to shipping the product in about six weeks. The early version was extremely manual, but it got customer feedback and showed there was something there.

Manual First, Automate Winners: Meow tests ideas with a bare-bones UI and manual work behind it, then automates what works. Bryce says the 13-person team manages a little over $1 billion in assets, which only works through automation.

Always Compare Multiple Vendors: Meow got bitten when it adopted one provider without weighing alternatives, then had no backup if that vendor fell short. Bryce now looks at two or three providers for the same solution.

Hire by Being Upfront: In first interviews, Bryce tries to scare candidates away more than pitch them, making clear the work is hard and urgent. He looks for urgency and very high work ethic to compete with much older institutions.

q: What is Meow and what does it offer businesses?
a: Meow gives businesses an interface to manage their treasury and bank accounts, including buying and managing T-bills and a high-yield checking account, through infrastructure and banking partners. Bryce Crawford said, "we really like to brand ourselves as Costco for financial services." [02:50]

q: How long did it take Meow to launch its Treasury bill product?
a: Bryce Crawford said Meow first built a general-purpose B2B suite, including multi-user roles and KYC/KYB compliance, and the MVP took several iterations. The T-bill product itself moved quickly: "thinking about treasury bills to actually shipping the product was really only about six weeks." [05:50]

q: How does Meow test new product ideas quickly?
a: Crawford described building a bare-bones UI around an idea to get it to customers as fast as possible, then automating it once it proves out. Behind that interface is "a whole lot of manual process to make it look like magic on the back end." [06:41]

q: What lesson did Meow learn about choosing infrastructure providers?
a: Crawford said the team got bitten when it picked a single product without considering alternatives, leaving no backup if the provider missed its SLA or failed to deliver. His advice is to "Get two or three vendors for any product you're buying." [14:08]

q: How does Bryce Crawford hire for Meow's culture?
a: Crawford looks for a sense of urgency and an extremely high work ethic, and is candid about how demanding the company is. In a first interview, he said, he is "not trying to pitch them on the company so much as scare them away." [10:55]

1e5c54ba-27ca-4bf9-b967-d4afc0aed3cd
s8-bonus-the-20m-seed-manifesto-unifying-application-code-and-infrastructure-into-one-language-with-elad-ben-israel-shai-ber-co-founders-of-wing-cloud

One Language for the Cloud: Winglang treats cloud services as first-class citizens, so developers can use a bucket much like a file system, while Wing handles many of the manual tasks needed to stitch a cloud application together.

A Deliberately Broad MVP: The team built a language, a standard library abstracting cloud services, a local simulator and a visual console together, keeping each to the minimum needed for an end-to-end experience.

The Gun-to-Your-Head Test: To set beta scope, they keep asking whether they would release Wing without a given feature or bug fix. They accept shipping fewer features so each one is more fully baked and earns developers' trust.
Hiring From Open Source: Elad recruited people he knew from projects like AWS CDK and Projen, and another hire came from Wing's own community. Real pull requests and feedback showed how they work.

The Closed Alpha Miss: Wing gated its alpha behind a signup, so most visitors from a Hacker News spike never saw what the project was about. Shai believes opening it from day one would have brought more feedback and involvement.

q: What is Winglang?
a: Winglang is a programming language that lets developers express an entire cloud system in one language, with cloud services built in. Shai Ber explained that "It treats the cloud as the computer it targets to basically do a lot of those manual tasks" [05:56], freeing developers to focus on business logic.

q: What problem is Winglang trying to solve in cloud development?
a: Developers have to use many tools to define each part of a service and then glue the parts together into a system. Elad Ben-Israel said the team realized "the challenge is that developers don't really have the right tools to express cloud systems" [03:48].

q: How did the founders approach the MVP for a new programming language?
a: They built several pieces at once, including the compiler, standard library, local simulator and visual tooling, because an end-to-end experience required them. Elad Ben-Israel said that in each part they were "really trying to find the minimal set of things that are required" [08:26].

q: How can an open source project help a startup hire engineers?
a: Elad Ben-Israel said working with contributors shows their code style, how they interact and how they react to feedback. In his view, hiring people you have worked with in open source "is the easiest and most certain way to hire someone" [12:46].

q: What mistake did the Winglang team make with its alpha launch?
a: They started with a closed alpha where developers had to sign up before they could access the GitHub repo. Shai Ber called it "a bit of a missed opportunity to get more feedback and more people involved with the project" [20:56].

s8-bonus-cutting-through-the-chatgpt-hype-deploying-practical-profit-driven-ai-strategy-with-andrew-louder-founder-ceo-of-louder-co

Capacity Over Full-Time Seats: Louder Co. found clients were more willing to spend on more consultants at lower capacity, such as four people with capacity instead of two full-time, because they got added brainpower and varied big-company experience.

Fixing the Cobbler's Kids Problem: Near the end of 2021, the team began using AI and other technologies internally, not just for clients. It drove productivity gains and gave them first-hand knowledge of the tools they recommend.

Operating Rhythm for Growth: System and Soul gave the firm quarterly OKRs, annual, three-year and 10-year plans, and a weekly scorecard review. Andrew says doubling in size in just over a year would have been chaotic without it.

Tools That Stretch Capacity: Using ChatGPT and Beautiful.ai helps the team do more with the same people. Andrew says Beautiful.ai has cut time spent on thought leadership presentations by half or more.

Mid-Market Impact Goal: Louder Co. serves companies generally under $150 million in annual revenue and has a 10-year goal of generating $1 billion in economic impact through its clients and the nonprofits it has a hand in.

q: What does Louder Co. do?
a: Louder Co., founded by Andrew Louder, is a business consultancy that helps companies improve operations, leverage AI and increase profits. AI is one tool among several, alongside work like process improvement, KPIs and change management, and as Andrew put it, "And not every solution requires AI." [03:28]

q: How did Louder Co. change its consulting model?
a: Andrew used to try to sell people into projects on a full-time basis, then shifted to offering larger teams with each person at lower capacity. He realized clients would spend more "if we gave them, let's say, more people, but at lower capacity" [08:41].

q: What return can a business get from AI solutions?
a: Andrew says AI tools can save companies hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of dollars, and that Louder Co. helps clients put them in place. Speaking about the savings or revenue generated, he said, "These are 8x, 40x oftentimes their investment for these products" [23:27].

q: How can a consulting firm scale when its product is people?
a: Andrew admits it is very hard, since the firm is still limited by headcount and hours in the day. His team's answer is to "utilize technology to our advantage and also trying to productize what we do as much as we can" [16:11], and at the time of the interview he said a new revenue stream purchasable 24/7 was coming soon.

q: How does Andrew Louder hire his team?
a: Andrew starts with experience, then bakes the core values into a multi-step process: be honest, be human, be purposeful and be growing. He says the decision sometimes comes down to a simple test, "would i love to grab a beer with this person" [15:12].

s8-e5-the-evolution-of-testops-unifying-manual-and-automated-qa-without-the-archaic-tooling-sprawl-with-nikita-fedorov-founder-ceo-of-qase

Born from Ugly Tooling: As an engineering manager hiring QA engineers, Nikita found Excel didn't scale and test management tools looked stuck in the 90s. He built his own with PHP, Laravel, Postgres and DigitalOcean.
Polishing Delayed Real Feedback: The MVP took two years of evenings after his day job. Users liked it but rejected some features, teaching Nikita he should have released much earlier.

Customers Shaped the Roadmap: Qase launched free, and Nikita used Canny to collect and vote on feature requests. Having never done end-to-end testing himself, he relied on what users said they needed.

Freelancers as a Flexible Ramp: Nikita scaled himself with freelancers, starting his first developer at 10 hours a week. Some became full-time staff, and once the team reached five, all new hires were full-time.

Unifying a Fragmented Testing Stack: Nikita cites research showing 500+ testing tools, with an average IT company using 20 to 40 daily. Qase is building an apps marketplace to be a single window into product quality.

q: Why did Nikita Fedorov start Qase?
a: Nikita was an engineering manager who hired QA engineers and needed a test management tool to support them. He found the existing options badly outdated, saying "They were from 90s with big print button." [03:23], so he decided to build his own.

q: How long did it take to build the Qase MVP?
a: It took Nikita two years of work after his day job, using PHP, Laravel, Postgres and DigitalOcean. He considers the extra polishing a big mistake, admitting "I should have released it earlier." [05:45]

q: How did Qase decide which features to build?
a: After launch, Nikita built close communication with customers and used Canny so they could submit and vote on feature requests. He explained that "Qase was built using the feedback from our customers" [06:52].

q: What problem does Qase's TestOps platform solve?
a: Nikita saw that separate tools for manual and automated testing made it extremely hard to understand what was going on. The ambition now goes further, as he put it: "We want to become a JIRA in a software testing world." [13:25]

q: What hiring lesson did Nikita Fedorov learn while scaling Qase?
a: Nikita learned that a manager who can only hire engineers isn't enough when you have big plans, and Qase had to replace that manager with one who could build teams and structure. His rule is that you "have to hire people who will hire people who will hire people." [12:01]

no-priors-jensen-huang-founder-ceo-of-nvidia

Walking the Acceleration Line: NVIDIA made its chips more general to grow its markets and fund R and D, but not so general that they lost their edge over CPUs. Huang calls finding that line one of the company's gifts.

CUDA Was a Long Bet: NVIDIA made every chip CUDA compatible to attract developers, despite very few CUDA customers for the first five to 10 years and gross margins that started out poor and got worse.

Hopper's Two Big Ideas: Huang names 8-bit floating point (FP8) and a transformer engine, a pipeline shaped for training and inference of transformers, as the key architectural advances behind the H100.

A Bespoke Org Design: Huang has 40-some direct reports, with no one-on-ones or career coaching at that level. He argues a company's structure should fit its purpose and leaders rather than copy a generic org chart.

Conviction Plus Agility: Huang tells founders to stay determined without becoming stubborn, believing in their work and that they could be wrong equally hard. Resilience also means forgetting the pain and moving on.

q: Why did NVIDIA invest in CUDA before it had many customers?
a: Jensen Huang explains that NVIDIA wanted a computing platform that would attract developers, which required every chip to be architecturally compatible. He recalls that "for the first five, 10 years, we had very few customers for CUDA" [09:39].

q: When did NVIDIA realize AI would be important to its business?
a: Huang places it around 2012, when researchers including Andrew Ng, Geoff Hinton and Yann LeCun's lab were turning to GPUs for neural networks. NVIDIA saw something bigger than computer vision, and as Huang put it, "we observed that this might be a new way of writing software altogether" [13:37].

q: What makes NVIDIA's H100 (Hopper) different?
a: Huang points to 8-bit floating point and a pipeline designed for learning and inferencing transformers, alongside a very large, fast chip connected at scale. In his words, "the big architecture idea is FP8 and transformer engine" [34:08].

q: How many direct reports does Jensen Huang have?
a: Huang says, "I have 40 somewhat direct reports" [29:15], with no one-on-ones or career coaching at the executive staff level. He reasons that people reporting to a CEO are sophisticated, talented leaders who should require little management.

q: What advice does Jensen Huang have for startup founders?
a: Huang is reluctant to give advice that might discourage founders, but says that if you're determined, don't wait too long. He also believes "ignorance is one of the superpowers of an entrepreneur" [38:27].

s8-bonus-democratizing-the-software-factory-scaling-ai-accelerated-no-code-development-with-george-novik-founder-cpo-of-zerocoder
Two-Week No-Code MVP: Zerocoder built its platform in two weeks, using Bubble as a full-stack visual builder. George favors Tilda or Webflow for landing pages that need fast changes.

Automations Run the Operation: The team uses Zapier and Integromat to connect tools such as Slack, Telegram and Airtable, notifying staff and automating client work. George stresses that no-code tools can also integrate custom code.

Roadmaps Shrink With Scale: George described planning five or six weeks ahead with 10 clients, but only six days ahead with 1,000. He said ChatGPT made the world change 20 times faster for the company, which then had to integrate it.

Test Before You Build: George says his key mistake was testing hypotheses only after building, which cost $5,000 or $6,000. With no-code, he argues, you can launch an MVP in days and run ads to see whether it solves a real problem.
Customers Before Investors: Looking back, George would stop chasing investors before having first customers and product-market fit. He would put that time and money into finding both.

q: What is Zerocoder?
a: Zerocoder is George Novik's company providing software and product development for startups and mid-sized companies through no-code talent. In George's words, "The Zerocoder matches no-code developers and designers with the top companies in the world now." [02:59]

q: How fast can you build an MVP with no-code tools?
a: George Novik says Zerocoder's own platform took two weeks, including a form for tasks and technical proposals and a project chat connecting clients with developers. As he put it, "two weeks we create mvp in two weeks we create our platform in two weeks because we're using" [03:18] no-code.

q: How does Zerocoder decide what to build next?
a: George Novik says the company previously ran without a roadmap, but now builds one around its clients, with a shorter planning window as the customer count grows. He explained, "If you have 1,000 customers, we have a roadmap only next six days because the world is very" [07:46] fast changing.

q: What mistake did George Novik make with hypothesis testing?
a: George described building first and validating with customers afterward, which cost him time and $5,000 or $6,000 before he saw the work needed to be remade. He summed it up as "testing hypothesis after when I build something. So I'm not testing this with yet customers." [12:26]

q: What is Donote, the Chrome extension George Novik is building?
a: Donote is a Chrome extension that lets designers, developers, agencies and freelancers comment on websites and share those notes, replacing screenshots pasted into documents. George said, "Use the R extension where you can note whatever you want and share link for your designer." [14:18] At the time of the interview, he reported 500 users and 12 B2B customers.

s8-bonus-stop-reinventing-the-wheel-dropping-full-stack-collaboration-building-blocks-into-any-app-with-rickard-hansson-founder-ceo-of-weavy

Collaboration as a Feature: Weavy's 2019 bet was that "collaboration is not an app, collaboration is a feature." It offers developers building blocks for chat, feeds, and file and document collaboration to embed in their own products.

Pivoting from Platform to Add-On: Enterprises had little appetite for Incentive, the team's earlier all-in-one collaboration platform. Adding its features on top of existing products like Microsoft CRM drew strong feedback and led to a hard pivot.

A Polished but Flawed MVP: The roughly six-month MVP reused the old product's features in an embeddable form. It looked great to end users but was a terrible developer experience, so the team rebuilt the core in the background.

Developer Experience Drives the Roadmap: From early 2020, the roadmap centered on how developers consume Weavy, including authentication, UI kits, tokens, APIs and webhooks. Rickard regrets not making that shift sooner, as his CTO had expected it to rank last.

Pricing Took Several Tries: Rickard went all in on perpetual licensing because he would want it as a buyer, but customers wanted monthly subscriptions. He says he should have changed his business models faster.

q: What is Weavy and who is it for?
a: Weavy provides building blocks that let developers add collaboration features such as chat, feeds and file collaboration to their own apps. Rickard Hansson describes its promise as being "the fastest possible way to add new features to your product" [02:49].

q: Why did the team pivot from Incentive to Weavy?
a: Rickard Hansson says the team couldn't get growth selling Incentive's all-in-one collaboration platform to enterprises, but got good feedback when they layered its features onto existing products. The realization was that "adding value to something is a way easier sell" [03:51], and they pivoted and rebranded in 2019.

q: How was the Weavy MVP built?
a: Rickard Hansson's team converted their existing .NET product into something that could be embedded in other apps, which took maybe six months. He compares the old product to a Skoda or Volkswagen and says, "We tried to make it a Porsche, like with the exact same components" [04:58].

q: What pricing mistake did Weavy make early on?
a: Rickard Hansson led with perpetual licensing, assuming buyers would prefer to own the technology rather than pay more as they grew. In his words, "I went straight in and like all in on perpetual licensing" [15:35], only to find that people wanted to subscribe and pay monthly.

q: How does Rickard Hansson approach building a team?
a: Rickard Hansson has had the same engineering team for more than 15 years and believes engineering teams should stay small and lean. When hiring, he looks beyond talent and conventional backgrounds, noting that "It's really, really hard to find good people" [10:35].

s8-e4-the-isolation-of-the-tech-c-suite-eradicating-cto-burnout-and-building-communities-of-practice-with-andy-skipper-founder-of-cto-craft

Support Gap Behind Team Problems: As a consulting CTO, Andy found many major company and team issues traced back to CTOs lacking support. Many were first-time leaders with no formal training, so he shifted from filling the role to coaching the people in it.

An MVP With Proven Demand: CTO Craft began with a Slack group, one-to-one coaching and early in-person mentoring circles. Interest existed from day one, so it was low cost, simple and needed no real marketing or growth planning.

Let the Community Steer: Members' feedback drove what came next, including a first conference at the end of 2020. It sold hundreds of tickets but left the two-person team burnt out, so they added people to sustain a twice-a-year target.

Scaling People, Not Technology: CTO Craft is tech light, relying on apps like Slack, Zapier and Mailchimp. Self-funded with no outside investment, its scaling challenge is prioritizing and triaging what the team can manage.

Build Support Before Exhaustion: Andy says he waited too long to build a team, which hurt his energy and health. He would also spend longer looking for a co-founder, since support might have let the company grow faster.

q: What is CTO Craft?
a: CTO Craft is a mentoring, community and events company for technology leaders, offering a Slack group, one-to-one coaching, year-long Circles of 10 to 12 people and conferences. Andy Skipper said that "It's for anyone in a senior leadership position, basically, for technology." [02:53]

q: Why do first-time CTOs often feel isolated?
a: Andy Skipper explains that CTOs sit between the business and the technology, and leaning too far toward one side means missing what matters on the other. As he put it, "It's quite common for especially first time CTOs to get quite isolated because you're essentially" [12:37] at that corner of both.

q: What was the MVP for CTO Craft?
a: The first version combined a Slack group, some one-to-one coaching and early mentoring circles, which met in person rather than over Zoom as they do today. Andy Skipper recalled, "It started with a Slack group, which is still there today." [05:34]

q: How did CTO Craft grow its community?
a: Andy Skipper says growth was organic, with word of mouth working well for roughly the first four years and member feedback shaping new offerings such as the conference. "So we've never done any paid marketing. We've never had any kind of growth plan beyond word" [08:02] of mouth, he said.

q: What advice does Andy Skipper give founders about burnout?
a: Andy advises founders to watch their energy levels, delegate and resist the idea that they must be all things to all people. He stressed, "Your well-being, it's not just important, but it's also fairly crucial to the success of" [18:01] the business.

s8-bonus-the-open-source-launchdarkly-killer-engineering-privacy-first-edge-evaluation-with-egil-sthus-co-founder-ceo-of-unleash

Born From a Developer's Pain: Egil Østhus's brother and co-founder created Unleash around 2014-15 when no tool met his needs. It wasn't meant to be commercial; Egil was introduced to it in 2019 as the open-source project gained attention.

Validate Before Going All In: The founders spent a full year of nights and weekends talking to customers, testing whether others shared the pain, how Unleash differed from competitors and what people would pay.

Open Core, Enterprise Upsell: The core is free and open source. Teams tend to move to the paid enterprise version when compliance needs appear, such as proper single sign-on and role-based access control.

Vision as the Feature Filter: Requests are weighed on whether they help developers work more efficiently, alone and together, and whether they belong in open source or enterprise. A clear direction makes it easier to push back on big clients.

Asia First Was a Mistake: To avoid two major competitors in the US, Unleash targeted Asia but didn't understand the culture or how to sell there. With inbound interest coming from the US, the team dropped Asia and switched.

q: What is Unleash and what problem does it solve?
a: Unleash is an open-source feature management tool that helps developers release software with less risk. Egil Østhus explained the payoff: "we give developers back time to really focus more on being creative and doing what they love the most." [03:44]

q: What is the difference between open-source Unleash and the enterprise version?
a: Developers can start with the freely available open-source version, and the company sells an enterprise version built on top of that core. Østhus said the move comes with compliance needs: "You need to have proper single sign on capabilities or you need to have proper role based access control." [03:32]

q: What tech stack was Unleash built with?
a: Unleash is a Node.js application on a Postgres database, and its first version solved a very simple use case. As Østhus put it, "It's built on top of a Postgres database. It was built in a few weeks." [06:32]

q: How does Unleash decide which feature requests to build?
a: The team checks each request against its product vision, including developer efficiency, teamwork and whether it fits open source or enterprise. Østhus described the test as "does that feature request move the product towards the vision of where we want it to be?" [09:48]

q: What advice does Egil Østhus have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Østhus advises building a team with skills that complement your own, and in particular bringing in a strong salesperson if you don't already have that strength. His starting point: "more than anything make sure you are getting complementary skills to your team" [23:50].

s8-bonus-bypassing-the-staging-queue-hooking-local-processes-into-live-kubernetes-clusters-with-aviram-hassan-co-founder-ceo-of-metalbear-creators-of-mirrord
Staging Was the Bottleneck: Aviram's last team could only see a change's system-wide effect in a shared staging environment, after tests, code review and CI/CD. That pain led to mirrord.

Two MVPs, Two Jobs: A one-month first MVP, split between code and messaging, tested open source traction and led to the first funding round. The real MVP took about six or seven months with six people.
Rough Invites Better Feedback: The team shipped a barely working "skeleton" on purpose, so users felt they could shape it. Strangers responded with use cases that helped prioritize the next MVP.

Remote, Global, and Asynchronous: MetalBear hired for open source experience, communication and self-management. Work runs mainly through Discord, GitHub and Notion with few meetings, and the code is about 99% Rust.

Sell to Companies First: The team spent up to about three months on a paid tool for individuals, then scrapped it. Demand for a paid mirrord showed that converting teams and companies was the better path.

q: What problem does mirrord solve for backend developers?
a: Aviram Hassan describes long iteration times between changing a line of code and seeing how it affected a system of many microservices and data. In his previous company, "only in staging you could really see the effect of your new change" [04:51], and that staging environment was shared.

q: How does mirrord work without a VPN?
a: Aviram explains that mirrord lets you run local code in the context of a remote environment, using low-level techniques. In his words, "It doesn't do any mounts, it doesn't use VPN, it's just on the process level." [11:08]

q: How did MetalBear build the first version of mirrord?
a: The first MVP took about a month and worked like a landing page for the real product, with one real feature plus messaging and documentation. Aviram said the goal was "to build something as lean as possible, like a skeleton of a bicycle" [08:42] and build anticipation for what it would become.

q: Why did MetalBear pivot from selling to individuals to selling to companies?
a: The team first built a paid solution for individuals, but after releasing the mirrord MVP they saw demand that pointed toward teams and companies. Aviram noted that supporting many individual users is hard, while "If you have tens of paying customers and each one is a company, it's way easier to build that" [21:05].

q: What is Aviram Hassan's advice for startup founders?
a: Aviram advises founders to network, ask questions and gather as many perspectives as they can, because advisors rarely have the founder's full context. When it is time to decide, he said, "never do something because someone told you to" [23:46].

s8-e3-the-developer-flight-simulator-simulating-production-melt-downs-and-in-a-safe-sandbox-with-shem-magnezi-co-founder-cto-of-wilco

Manual MVP Before Heavy Building: Wilco's first version took about a month or two: a minimal e-commerce codebase, a fork per engineer, and Shem playing the on-call engineer, manager and colleagues over Slack while reviewing their PRs.

Shortcuts to Test Demand: Rather than spend months building AWS sandboxes for production quests, the team gave each user a new Heroku app, knowing it wouldn't scale. They also considered buttons that did nothing, to see whether people would click.

Keep Plan B in the Drawer: Design reviews asked what happens when scale hits, without pre-building for it. When an influencer's tweet brought thousands of users and hit GitHub's rate limit, the team implemented its backup plan and recovered in about three to four hours.

Building in Public Drove Hiring: Shem and a co-founder tweeted their plans, problems and failures for months. Most of the team later came inbound through Twitter, and interviews stressed connection to the mission and a generalist willingness to stretch.

Think About Buyers Early: Wilco began as a fun, engaging B2C product focused on user happiness. Shem wishes they had considered monetization and sales sooner, including how it brings value to engineering managers, CTOs and VPs of R and D.

q: What is Wilco and what problem does it solve for developers?
a: Wilco, co-founded by CTO Shem Magnezi, puts developers in a fantasy company with a codebase, bugs and Slack-like chat, where they learn by solving quests in a sandbox. It targets the gap between theory and daily work, where, as Shem put it, "you need to open a PR and you don't know how to even create a PR" [04:06].

q: How did Wilco build and test its first MVP?
a: Shem Magnezi's team built a very minimal e-commerce codebase with a UI, back end and database, and gave each engineer on a test team their own fork. Much of the experience was run by hand, and as Shem described it, "the product was me going live with the first team that we tested the product on" [05:34].

q: What tech stack did Wilco choose early on, and why?
a: Shem Magnezi said the team chose React, Node and MongoDB, separated the front end from the back end with an API layer, and avoided complex microservices. A schemaless database suited an undefined product because, in his words, "We really didn't know how the schema would look like." [08:24]

q: How did Wilco handle a sudden surge of users after launch?
a: A few weeks after the public launch, an influencer's tweet brought a few thousand new users within minutes, and Wilco hit GitHub's rate limit. Shem Magnezi said the team already had a solution in mind, so "we opened the drawer, got out the plan B plans" [16:17] and was back up after about three to four hours.

q: What advice does Shem Magnezi give to early-stage entrepreneurs?
a: Shem advises founders to be passionate about the problem and less attached to a specific solution, since the solution will change a lot. As he put it, "Don't pick a solution, pick a problem. And you better be highly motivated about this problem." [21:48]

s8-bonus-the-aws-blueprint-for-consumption-decoupling-cloud-metering-from-billing-architecture-with-puneet-gupta-co-founder-ceo-of-amberflo

Metering Came First: Amberflo spent about its first 10 months building only a cloud metering service, then layered a pricing and billing application on top for customers to build their own pricing plans.
A Longer Road to MVP: Taking a platform approach meant roughly two years of building before alpha and beta customers. Design partners shaped the near-term roadmap once about 70-80% was built.

Scale From Day One: Puneet sees platform and scale as synonymous, since core design choices are very hard to revisit. The team's internal narrative was that it was building a metering service for the world.
Downturns Favor Usage Pricing: When budgets tighten, usage-based pricing lets a vendor offer customers a way to use less and dial back up later, instead of forcing a subscribe-or-cancel decision.
Don't Build in Silence: Puneet wishes Amberflo had built a groundswell or waiting list during its two heads-down years and pushed go-to-market sooner, as the shift arrived faster than he expected.

q: What does Amberflo do?
a: Amberflo helps businesses track and charge on usage as they move to usage-based, or consumptive, pricing. As Puneet Gupta put it, "we provide what we call a cloud metering and usage-based pricing and billing" [03:07] platform.

q: How did Puneet Gupta's time at AWS lead to Amberflo?
a: Puneet joined Amazon Web Services in 2011, where his team launched Amazon CloudSearch and Amazon Elasticsearch and he saw both the technology and the P and L side of usage-based services. He saw how such a model "drives just organic adoption, lowers the friction for user adoption, and just really drives exponential growth" [04:07].

q: How was Amberflo's usage metering and billing platform built?
a: Puneet Gupta's team built the metering foundation first, then added a pricing and billing application on top of it. He said that "for the first 10 months, we did nothing but build out the cloud metering service" [08:19].

q: How can usage-based pricing help SaaS companies keep customers in a downturn?
a: Puneet Gupta says it lets a company respond to a customer's tighter budget with a plan and contract aligned to lower usage, which can be dialed back up later. The message to the customer becomes "Simply dial it down. We don't have to say goodbye." [18:34]

q: What mistake did Amberflo make while building its first product?
a: Puneet Gupta believes the company could have done more outreach during its two-year build, creating a groundswell or a waiting list. Looking back, he said, "we were essentially just silent we you know we were just all heads down building" [16:48].

s8-bonus-the-linux-kernel-maverick-rewriting-sqlite-in-rust-scaling-micro-databases-for-ai-agents-with-glauber-costa-co-founder-ceo-of-turso

Drawing the MVP Line: Turso chose not to push SQLite inside serverless functions via WebAssembly at first. It built a more traditional database, accessed over HTTP and massively replicated, after weighing the options for about a month.

A Two-Month MVP: While Glauber was away after his daughter's premature birth, the team got an MVP to early users in about two months. His co-founder wrote the control plane in Go at a Rust-heavy shop, alongside tools like Fly.io and Vault.

Friction That Revealed the Persona: Private beta applicants had to fill out a form saying what they would use Turso for. Answers from 200 to 300 people clarified the use case and showed which feature requests could safely wait.

Scale by Dimension: Turso was built from day one to add locations and read capacity horizontally, but not to scale everything. Glauber argues that scaling nothing hurts robustness, while scaling everything could delay launch by two years.

Act on the Signal Sooner: Users said for months that the SQLite edge piece of the earlier product, ChiselStrike, interested them most. Glauber's biggest regret is not building a new product around it much sooner.

q: What is Turso and what makes it an edge database?
a: Glauber Costa describes it simply: "Turso is a database for the edge." [02:49] It replicates data to many locations for last-mile latency advantages and is reachable over protocols like HTTP and WebSockets, which suits restricted edge compute environments.

q: Why is Turso built on SQLite?
a: Glauber explained, "the idea was that with SQLite, you can deploy everything locally." [06:10] If the data can then be distributed, developers run the same code locally, in production and at the edge, using a database light enough for resource-limited locations.

q: How long did it take to build the Turso MVP?
a: Glauber said, "It took around two months in total to just get something together, put in the hands" [08:46] of some early users. Work then began on a public release with a free tier that people could sign up for.

q: How did Turso decide what to build after the MVP?
a: Before opening up publicly, Turso ran a private beta with a form asking what people wanted to use it for. Glauber said that with hundreds of people "telling you this is what I want to do with that" [13:57], the use case becomes clear, and feature requests can be judged against that persona.

q: What mistake does Glauber Costa say his company made before Turso?
a: Glauber said one of the big mistakes in the company's previous iteration "was exactly not to jump in this direction sooner." [20:40] In hindsight, he wishes they had sunset the earlier project and built a new product to solve the edge problem from the start.

s8-e2-the-clickops-cure-automating-multi-cloud-infrastructure-discovery-and-code-drift-with-sefi-genis-co-founder-late-cto-of-firefly

Drift Detection With Context: Firefly scans the cloud footprint, analyzes infrastructure as code and finds the disparity between them. Its drift detection shows who made a change, when and how, and can also fix it.
A Two-Month Solo MVP: Sefi built the first version in about two months, covering a few AWS resource types, Terraform code generation and drift detection. It helped Firefly raise its seed round.

Speed First, Refactor After Seed: Working alone, Sefi chose Lambda over his preferred Kubernetes to avoid DevOps work and bought a frontend library to ship fast. After the seed round, the team moved to Kubernetes and rebuilt the front end.

Hire Hustlers for Hard Problems: Sefi looked for people who could crack any challenge, such as working around limits when fetching AWS resources at high scale and building a filterable, searchable inventory.

Move to the Field Sooner: Sefi moved from VP of Engineering to a customer-facing field CTO role and says he should have done it earlier. With strong engineers and architects in place, he saw that Firefly needed him with customers.

q: What is Firefly and what does it do?
a: Firefly is a cloud asset management solution powered by infrastructure as code, aimed at DevOps and SRE leaders who need to govern the cloud and reduce complexity. Sefi Genis explained, "We scan the entire cloud footprint and we analyze the infrastructure as code" [02:40].

q: How does Firefly handle infrastructure as code drift?
a: Firefly continuously monitors drift, which is the disparity between the cloud and the infrastructure as code. According to Sefi, "our drift detection also contains context, it means who made it, when, how, we can also fix drifts" [03:14].

q: How long did it take to build the Firefly MVP?
a: Sefi said, "It took me around two months to build the first MVP" [04:57]. It was deliberately minimal, handling a few types of AWS resources, generating Terraform code and detecting drift, and it helped the company raise its seed round.

q: What were the hardest technical challenges in scaling Firefly?
a: Sefi pointed to fetching cloud resources at scale and building a filterable, searchable inventory. As he put it, "fetching resources from the cloud for AWS is very difficult in high scale" [08:27], and his team built a scalable solution that worked through the limits.

q: What advice does Sefi Genis have for early-stage founders?
a: Sefi advises asking unbiased questions to understand prospects' pains, choosing co-founders as carefully as a marriage partner, and knowing why you are starting a company. On the first point, he said, "you should read the mom test book because asking questions without bias is the key" [14:16].

s8-bonus-the-language-of-money-re-engineering-messy-transaction-data-for-the-era-of-ai-agents-with-nare-vardanyan-co-founder-ceo-of-ntropy

Consumer Product as Data Source: With no access to financial data at scale, Ntropy built a website where people linked bank histories and got manual answers about unfamiliar charges. About 20,000 consented transactions helped train the MVP.

Ship Early, Learn Faster: The team released a model only slightly better than raw bank statement output, returning just the merchant and a label. Real usage would supply the data needed to improve it.

Going Global Improved U.S. Results: Ntropy started early on Latin American transactions to build multilingual models. Training on different languages and diverse data also improved its U.S. product on the long tail.

Generality Over Rule Patches: Rules could have hidden mistakes and helped sign paying customers, but they would have killed generality. Ntropy instead worked through errors with customers and kept retraining its models.

Act Quickly on Hiring Misfits: Naré says delaying hard conversations about a wrong fit is extremely costly. Ntropy set up weekly, two-way one-on-ones to keep asking whether working together still makes sense.

q: What does Ntropy do?
a: Ntropy is building data infrastructure for financial services, turning messy records of what people and companies spend into usable information. As Naré Vardanyan put it, "we're creating a unified layer that will standardize, clean, enrich, categorize this information for the world to use." [04:02]

q: How did Ntropy get financial transaction data to train its first model?
a: Financial data is sensitive and not publicly available, so the team collected it with user consent by answering people's questions about their transactions. Naré explained, "we actually decided to create a consumer product, essentially a website where people" [06:00] would link their bank histories.

q: How did Ntropy decide when its MVP was good enough to release?
a: Naré and her co-founder and CTO went back and forth, then chose to release a version they knew would return mismatches and errors. In Naré's words, "We released something that's not great, but then it gets used and becomes better" [08:46].

q: Why did Ntropy build multilingual, multi-geography transaction models so early?
a: The end goal was to understand transactions from any data source and any location, so the company made a big bet on going global instead of focusing on one geography. Naré said that "even our U.S. product became better because we trained models that" [12:22] parsed different languages and saw diverse data.

q: What is one of the biggest mistakes Naré Vardanyan has made as a founder?
a: Naré says one of her biggest mistakes, which she still makes, is "not reacting to a wrong fit" [16:25] in hiring quickly enough. She says it has cost a lot of time, effort and emotion, and she wants to improve through honest, bidirectional weekly one-on-ones.

s8-bonus-bypassing-the-enterprise-black-box-building-an-extensible-headless-supply-chain-operating-system-with-ronald-richardson-of-fleetbase

API-First MVP: Ron Richardson built the first Fleetbase API in PHP Laravel over about three to four months, with a minimal UI. A demo to hauliers in Malaysia led to a partnership with Port Klang Authority.

The Cost of Headless: Starting API-only was a handicap in logistics. The port relied on EDI and other integration methods, SDKs were missing in needed languages, and users disliked the basic, Stripe-like UI.

Cloud Pricing Didn't Fit: Logistics firms often wanted on-premise software because of data concerns. Fleetbase refactored, built a more modern web console, and began pivoting to open source with dual licensing.

Modular by Design: The refactor split the back end and front end into packages, using Ember Engines for front-end modules. The goal is an ecosystem where outside developers add modules to the console like plugins.

Retainers Over Lump Sums: Early on, loosely structured deals left the team with more work than it could handle. Fleetbase now focuses on retainer-based contracts, which Ron says improve stability and keep companies with them.

q: What is Fleetbase?
a: Ronald Richardson describes it this way: "Fleetbase is a platform and an API for rapidly developing logistics and supply chain applications." [02:47] He adds that it can also be used as an operating system, with features such as a routing engine, service rates and orders.

q: What was the first major project built on Fleetbase?
a: Richardson says Fleetbase partnered with Port Klang Authority in Malaysia, where they "started to develop a freight container marketplace for hauliers" [04:42]. It launched within three months, and he says it has since grown to over 200 companies and helped transport over 52,000 containers.

q: Why did Fleetbase move away from a cloud-only model?
a: Richardson found that standard cloud pricing didn't work because most logistics and supply chain companies wanted on-premise solutions. As he put it, "They're very concerned about their data" [07:58] and where it is stored. At the time of the interview, the company was pivoting to an open source version with dual licensing.

q: How is Fleetbase architected to be modular and extensible?
a: Richardson says the team split most back-end modules and the front end into packages after the initial API, which was not built to scale. On the interface side, "We use Ember and Ember Engines to package the front end into individual modules" [10:58]. The infrastructure is also defined in Terraform.

q: What advice does Ronald Richardson have for founders building a team?
a: Richardson urges founders to make sure that "whoever you decide to put on your team, that you guys are all on the same page" [20:38] and share the same goal. He speaks from experience, naming a misaligned founding team as one of Fleetbase's biggest mistakes.

s8-e1-the-death-of-leetcode-eradicating-whiteboard-anxiety-with-project-based-interview-analytics-with-sargun-kaur-co-founder-ceo-of-byteboard

Interviews That Mirror The Job: Byteboard replaces pre-onsite technical interviews with an anonymized, project-based work sample. It targets skills engineers said they use daily, like communication, trade-off analysis, systems reasoning, and reading and writing code.

Sell Before Building The Platform: Byteboard landed Lyft as its first customer with barely any code. Interviews went out manually as a Google Doc and zip file, and the first 200 candidates went through a process much like that.

Owning Grading End To End: The plan was for customers' engineers to grade interviews, but buyers wanted a complete solution. To save a pilot, Byteboard agreed to grade about 300 candidates in a month, and in-house evaluation became the model.

Scrappy Tools Carry Tech Debt: Apps Script let the team automate the early product, learn quickly and shape the roadmap. Kaur says they likely relied on it too long and are still ripping it out of their infrastructure.

Rushing A New Assessment Backfired: Byteboard skipped its usual research to launch a data science assessment. Beta feedback exposed deep problems, forcing the team to pause it and rebuild the supporting infrastructure.

q: What is Byteboard and how does it change technical interviews?
a: Byteboard is a technical interview platform that Sargun Kaur says "replaces pre-onsite technical interviews with a project-based alternative." [03:07] The interview is a work sample that mirrors what engineers do on the job, and it is anonymized to help reduce bias.

q: Why are whiteboard and algorithm interviews a problem?
a: Kaur argues the industry standard is to "often use these algorithmic riddles that don't actually apply to what you do end up doing on the" [04:56] job. She says this left many capable candidates out, particularly self-taught people and those without industry connections to help them prepare.

q: How did Byteboard build its MVP?
a: Kaur's team researched what engineers actually do, drafted an interview in a Google Doc, and ran it manually before automating with Apps Script. As Kaur put it, "We sold Byteboard to our first customer, which was Lyft, without really having coded barely anything." [06:35]

q: Why does Byteboard grade interviews itself instead of leaving it to customers?
a: Kaur's original idea was for engineers at client companies to do the grading, but prospects wanted something that worked end to end. About to lose a pilot deal, she recalls, "And the call was like, OK, we'll just grade all of them." [10:58] That decision shaped Byteboard's product roadmap and go-to-market strategy.

q: What mistake did Byteboard make with its data science assessment?
a: Kaur says the team rushed it out without its normal research and scalability work, then found beta feedback required deep changes. She explained, "we had to pull it out and put that assessment on pause and completely rebuild the infrastructure to support it." [20:41]

from-tools-and-weapons-connecting-africas-youth-to-the-world

Taking the Monopoly to Court: With only 0.14% of Zimbabweans having a phone, Strive Masiyiwa challenged the state telecom monopoly. The court struck it down on freedom of expression grounds, though he left the country soon after.
Moving Beyond Mobile: Around 2003, Masiyiwa saw that connectivity was the next game. His company has since laid 100,000 miles of fiber and is building data centers in Africa's 10 largest economies.

Skills Unlock the Potential: His philanthropy offers free Microsoft, AI and machine learning courses and broadband for tech hubs. A program with UNICEF and Microsoft hopes to connect up to 10,000 schools.

Money Wasn't Enough for Vaccines: Export bans blocked supply even after funds were raised. Africa secured 300 million single-shot Johnson and Johnson doses, including output from a South African plant that had been headed to Europe.

Food Needs Hard Infrastructure: Masiyiwa says 40% of what Africa produces is lost to spoilage and only 5% of farm output comes through irrigation. He calls for rail, ports, storage, cold chains and private investment.

q: How did Strive Masiyiwa get started in African telecommunications?
a: After a couple of years in state-owned telecom, Masiyiwa started his own company at 26 and later fought the government in court for the right to offer mobile service. He wrote a mission statement that began, "my mission is to provide telecommunications to all the people of Africa." [06:37] On his lawyer's advice that this was a little ambitious, he narrowed it to Zimbabwe.

q: What digital infrastructure has Strive Masiyiwa's company built across Africa?
a: Masiyiwa described a shift from mobile to fiber, saying "we've laid 100,000 miles of fiber across the continent." [09:54] He also pointed to a newly completed route from Angola across the Democratic Republic of Congo to Mombasa, plus data centers being built to prepare for cloud growth.

q: Why was it so hard for Africa to get COVID-19 vaccines?
a: Masiyiwa, appointed to lead the continent's COVID response, found that raising money did not solve the problem because countries around the world had restricted exports to serve their own people first. As Masiyiwa put it, "We thought it was just going to be about money." [24:17] Johnson and Johnson doses and a later partnership with the Biden administration helped carry Africa through.

q: Why does Africa import food, and what would help change that?
a: Masiyiwa pointed to limited irrigation and missing cold chain, distribution and transport infrastructure. He explained that "even what we produce, 40% never leaves the farm gate, as it were, because it's wasted" [29:07]. He wants investment in rail, ports and storage, along with private sector partners who can help open global markets to African food.

q: What does Strive Masiyiwa want to see happen in Africa over the next 10 years?
a: Masiyiwa's priorities are science and technology education, followed by an ecosystem that invests in African entrepreneurs, including homegrown venture capital and deregulation. On the stakes of AI, Masiyiwa asked, "How do we participate if we're not digitally educated?" [32:50]

s7-bonus-the-algorithmic-construction-site-engineering-a-generative-scheduling-engine-with-rene-morkos-of-alice-technologies

Simulating Millions of Build Options: ALICE takes a project such as a bridge, hospital or tower and generates millions of ways to build it, varying things like crane count. Morkos says this can save 17% on duration and 13% on labor costs.

Empty Sites Sparked the Idea: Morkos found only 3% of construction site space is used for construction at any given moment. An algorithm built to fill that space revealed something bigger: it knew how to build, so resources, calendars and cranes could be added.

Ask Customers What Sucks: Customers were too polite to criticize early versions. When the team openly said it sucked and asked why, they would blurt out reasons, which sent the team back to the drawing board.

Process Pain While Scaling: Growing from about six to 18 people broke things without management processes, and was far more painful than going from 18 to 70. Once constraints arrived, the early coders left.

Segment the Market Earlier: Morkos wishes he had defined an ideal customer profile sooner, created value for it, and been brutal about saying no to everyone outside it. He believes things would have moved faster.

q: What does ALICE Technologies do?
a: René Morkos describes ALICE as a construction simulator that explores many ways to sequence and resource a project. He explained that "it can take a construction project like a bridge, a hospital, a tower," [02:19] and generate millions of ways of building it.

q: How did the idea for ALICE Technologies start?
a: Morkos struggled to find the best way to sequence runway repairs in Afghanistan, then noticed during his PhD that construction sites were largely empty. On how much site space is actually used for construction, he said, "And the answer to that question is actually 3%." [04:00]

q: What did the first version of ALICE look like?
a: Morkos said the prototype was written in Java and showed a top-down view of where construction work was occurring. As he recalled, "we literally had a white screen that had these colored squares" [05:29] that would appear and disappear.

q: How did ALICE get honest customer feedback on its product?
a: Morkos said customers were apologetic and reluctant to criticize, so the team told them they knew it sucked and asked why. Customers would then list several reasons, and Morkos said "we'd go take those six reasons," [09:02] return to the drawing board and fix the product.

q: What advice does René Morkos give young entrepreneurs?
a: Morkos passes on what he calls the best advice he has received, from someone a few years ahead of him at a business school presentation. The advice was "don't take the highs so high and the lows so low." [18:32]

s7-bonus-the-death-of-cookies-engineering-995-accurate-device-identification-with-valentin-vasilyev-of-fingerprint
Backend Over Browser Code: FingerprintJS Pro made the browser library an agent that collects signals, while processing moved to a backend because JavaScript is easy to inspect, even when obfuscated.

Accuracy Was the Product Gap: The open source library was about 60% accurate, and roughly 40-45% on iOS. Valentin focused on improving that with twice the signals, a smarter backend and machine learning.

Two Months to Real Traffic: Starting in April 2019, Valentin switched from Ruby on Rails to Go within weeks and had a production MVP taking customer traffic by late May. It wasn't stable, but it worked.

Scaling Early Had a Cost: A queue and worker design on AWS made later scaling as simple as adding instances. In hindsight, Valentin says he should have spent more of that early time on business development.

Hiring Slowly, Even While Growing: Valentin interviewed 70 engineers before making the first offer. He says careful interviews and attention to culture carried through 2022, when headcount went from about 27 to about 100.

q: How accurate was the original open source FingerprintJS library?
a: Valentin Vasilyev says the library tried to give each browser a unique identifier but wasn't really successful. In his words, "The accuracy rate was about 60%." [04:55], and it was even lower on iOS, which led him to focus on accuracy in the Pro product.

q: How does Fingerprint's device identification work?
a: Valentin explains that a script in the browser gathers data and the backend processes it, returning information that is valuable to customers. As he described the design, "the client-side library will be just an agent that runs in the browser, collects signals," [03:46]. The company later added Android and then iOS support.

q: What tech stack was used to build the Fingerprint MVP?
a: Valentin built the client side in TypeScript and deployed to AWS Elastic Beanstalk with DynamoDB, using SQS to connect a web server to workers. He began the backend in Ruby on Rails, but recalls, "I switched to Golang for the backend. And at that time, I didn't know any Golang." [06:49]

q: How did Fingerprint hire its early engineering team?
a: Valentin hired slowly and carefully, with early engineering clusters in Central and Eastern Europe and South America built partly through referrals. He recalls that for the first hire, "our first engineer, I interviewed 70 other engineers" [12:06] before an offer went out.

q: What is next for Fingerprint beyond device identification?
a: Valentin says the company is building a rule and decision engine on top of its identity platform, so businesses can act on risk signals and not just receive an ID. The goal is an "engine customers can utilize without having to write any code." [21:51]

s7-e30-the-architecture-of-infinite-scale-harnessing-vitess-and-database-sharding-with-sam-lambert-of-planetscale
Scaling Down Proven Tech: PlanetScale's backend, Vitess, ran at YouTube's scale. Lambert says the challenge is bringing it to everyone, with a smooth path from no users to billions.
Beta in Under Six Months: Starting with mature Vitess, the team built the cloud product with Friday demos and Monday planning. The stack pairs a Rails API and Next.js frontend with lots of Go.

Database Creation Speed First: After seeing one database company take 24 minutes, PlanetScale made provisioning almost instant. That meant deliberate trade-offs, such as keeping warm pools of machines ready.
Too Much Magic: The UI hid so much, even the word "server," that some users may not sense the product's heft. The team is now working to surface more of what happens under the hood.
Short Roadmaps, Careful Core: Surfaces people interact with are planned quarter by quarter and iterated quickly. Some deeper database work may take a year and demands care and deliberation.

q: What is PlanetScale?
a: Sam Lambert, CEO of PlanetScale, describes it as a cloud-hosted database platform that runs major websites and workloads on a Vitess backend. In his words, "We are known for being able to take databases and the applications that run on those databases" [02:25] to extreme scale.

q: What is Vitess and where did it come from?
a: Vitess is the database technology behind PlanetScale, developed at YouTube and later picked up by companies including Slack and GitHub. Lambert says of YouTube, "They were running it till about two and a half billion monthly active users" [02:37].

q: How long did it take to build the PlanetScale MVP?
a: Lambert says the cloud product reached beta in less than six months, helped by mature Vitess technology, familiar tools and weekly demos. As he put it, "we actually went from first line of code to out in" [04:38] beta in that window.

q: Why did PlanetScale focus on how fast a database can be created?
a: Lambert argues that someone signing up has an idea they want to build, and a long wait gets in the way. He said, "the first thing we did was decide we're going to be the fastest place to deploy a database" [07:02].

q: What mistake did PlanetScale make in its early product?
a: Lambert says the team oversimplified parts of the product and hid too much of what was happening underneath. He admitted that "we made some things a bit too magic" [13:44], and said they have not fully corrected it yet.

From Budgeting App to Infrastructure: Ruben's team began with a budgeting app sold to community banks and credit unions, then pivoted because they were better at building infrastructure than dynamic user experiences.

One Normalized Financial Data Model: Quiltt offers a unified API over providers like Plaid and MX, normalizes their data and supplements it with other third-party data, so builders can skip stitching schemas together in-house.

The Front End Mattered Too: Quiltt assumed the backend was the hard part. Beta showed customers wanted integration problems solved, so it built the Quiltt Connector, added with a single copy-and-paste line of code.

Hire People Who Surpass You: The lead engineer, hired from Chime, started deleting most of Ruben's code and replacing it with better code. Ruben sees building a team better than him as his first job as CEO.

A No-Code to All-Code Spectrum: Quiltt aims to open financial data to non-technical builders through a Zapier app, its Connector and eventually drag-and-drop workflows, while engineers can still drop deeper into code.

q: What is Quiltt and what does it do?
a: Ruben Izmailyan describes Quiltt as a way to connect customer accounts, stitch financial APIs together and release intelligent workflows and user experiences. At its core, he says, "we're a unified API for multiple different types of APIs and data providers" [18:38], including Plaid and MX.

q: How was the first version of Quiltt's product built?
a: Ruben spent at least a year building the MVP in Ruby on Rails with Postgres, hosted on Heroku, while learning as he went. It connected bank accounts through Plaid, and he chose accessible tools because, as he put it, "I didn't know what a load balancer was. I wanted somebody else to figure that out for me" [05:44].

q: Why did Quiltt pivot from a budgeting app to financial data infrastructure?
a: Ruben saw many entrepreneurs and companies locked out of new financial tooling by how much they had to build in-house. He also recognized the team's strengths, saying "We were better at building the infrastructure than building, you know, really dynamic user experiences." [06:46]

q: What is the Quiltt Connector and why was it built?
a: Ruben explains that Quiltt had not prioritized the front end, even though configuring providers involves real UX trade-offs. "So what we ended up doing is we effectively dogfooded our own API and built the Quiltt Connector." [21:16] It handles the logic and configuration for the most common scenarios, and customers can still build a custom front end.

q: Is Quiltt a no-code or a developer platform?
a: Ruben wants it to serve both engineers and people who don't code, with parts of the product requiring less and less code over time. "We like to think of it as like a no-code to all-code spectrum." [25:38]

the-new-notification-stack-for-developers-drew-youngwerth

Patterns Become the Product: Courier was founded on seeing software companies rebuild the same notification systems, adding channels and features like localization until they needed an entire engineering team.

Digests as Drag-and-Drop Nodes: Automations reduces work like batching and digests to a few visual nodes, so e-commerce cart events can feed one end-of-week message instead of a notification for every item added.

Too Simple Was Too Restrictive: An earlier version of Automations focused on non-technical users and only allowed sequential steps, such as send, wait five days, send again. The rebuild aims to scale across skill levels and use cases.

Borrowing from Game Editors: The flow-based design draws on visual programming in LittleBigPlanet, which Drew used in eighth grade, and node editors in Blender and Unity, applied to notification workflows.

Building on Existing Foundations: The team used the open source React Flow library for the visual editor, plus AWS Step Functions, Lambda, Dynamo and S3. Drew said a good portion of the time went into researching what already existed.

q: What problem does Courier solve for developers?
a: Drew Youngwerth explained that software companies kept building the same notification systems, which grew in channels and features until they needed dedicated engineers. In his words, "Courier was built on those patterns so that Courier could be that notification engineering team" [03:39].

q: How can Courier Automations avoid sending too many notifications?
a: Drew described using batching or digests so a shopper doesn't get a message every time they add a product to their cart. Customers building this "can do something as simple as drag over the batching or the digest node" [07:00].

q: Can Courier Automations schedule time-based notifications?
a: Yes, Drew called scheduling one of the big use cases and said there is a schedule trigger designed for it. On its design, he said "we took inspiration from the event creation in Google" [05:31] Calendar.

q: Why did Courier rebuild its Automations product?
a: Drew said the earlier version only supported sequential steps, and it was difficult to go beyond them. The team behind it "focused on the non-technical to the point that it made what you could deliver with automations very restrictive" [08:30].

q: What technology was used to build Courier Automations?
a: Drew said the team used AWS Step Functions, Lambda, Dynamo and S3 and pieced them into a scalable product. For the visual editor, "we did find a really great library on the front end called React Flow" [10:38].
