Automate, Don't Digitize the Clipboard: Manik's earlier company, CoInspect, replaced paper checks with mobile apps but struggled to gain traction. Users didn't want to check temperatures at all, which led to Therma's sensors.

A Stripped-Down Hardware MVP: Therma spent about nine months building its own sensor, shipping in early 2020. It cut fancy dashboards and reporting for a simple mobile app and bare-bones website, which made customers easier to win.

Deepen the Core Customer: Therma explored cold storage warehouses and transit, then chose to focus on restaurants, convenience stores and food service, moving beyond monitoring to control that targets their energy bills.

Test Controls Manually First: Before building the software layer, the team installed off-the-shelf hardware and had people switch refrigerator compressors on and off by hand, then checked the results on utility bills.
Cooling Timed to the Grid: Knowing the temperature inside lets refrigerators pre-cool and run when energy prices are low or the grid needs it most, aiming to cut both costs and emissions.

q: What does Therma do?
a: Therma monitors and controls refrigeration and cooling equipment to reduce energy use, product spoilage and maintenance costs, along with the related emissions. Manik Suri described using a "combination of sensors, controls, and data science to turn essentially dumb assets into" [03:04] intelligent loads.

q: How did Therma get started?
a: Therma grew out of CoInspect, Manik Suri's earlier company, which used mobile apps to replace pen-and-paper workflows in the food industry. Manik realized that automating temperature checks with sensors was a better answer, saying "We were replacing a clipboard with a digital clipboard." [05:31]

q: What was in Therma's first MVP?
a: The MVP was an in-house sensor about the size of half a deck of cards, paired with an app for labeling sensors and setting thresholds. Manik said that instead of a feature-rich dashboard, "we went for a very simple out-of-the-box experience with a mobile app and a bare-bones website." [10:28]

q: How can smarter refrigeration lower energy costs and help the utility grid?
a: Lucas Tepman explained that many large refrigeration units cycle without regard to energy prices or utility demand. With temperature monitoring in place, he said, "we can do things such as pre-cool the refrigerator to actually make it run" [07:36] when prices are low or the grid needs it most.

q: How did Therma test refrigeration controls before building the software?
a: Lucas Tepman said the team installed off-the-shelf hardware with technicians at a few McDonald's locations and had people respond to alerts around the clock. They controlled the "compressors of the refrigerators, turning them on and off manually and seeing the results on the" [19:32] utility bills.

s7-bonus-architecting-the-dark-warehouse-scaling-autonomous-mobile-robots-with-tapan-pattnayak-of-addverb

Central Intelligence for AGV Fleets: Addverb's AGVs lack their own perception and take direction from a fleet management server, which handles routing when robot paths collide across fleets that can run to thousands.

Consumer Electronics as Cost Benchmark: Tapan contrasts industrial robots with cameras and lidar that can top $10,000 with a $350 iPad carrying both, and aims to cut robot costs sharply while increasing safety.

Control the Entire Chain: After vendor deliveries slipped amid supply chain constraints, Tapan designed an in-house alternative that worked. His lesson: fundamentally new innovation requires control of the whole chain.

Character Before Everything Else: Tapan screens for character, excellence and perseverance alongside very tough technical interviews. He admits this has made hiring slow, even after going through thousands of resumes.

Basics and Passion Over Pedigree: Drawing on Henry Ford's autobiography and Tesla, Tapan argues that strategy gets rediscovered along the way, and that passion plus basic physics, chemistry and math can beat long experience.

q: How do Addverb's automated guided vehicles work?
a: Tapan Pattnayak explains that the AGVs move in a barcode-based system, carrying items such as those a cobot picks from a conveyor to a chute bound for shipping. The intelligence sits above them in a fleet management server, and as Tapan put it, "if the path collide, then you have to take intelligence to pass one" [07:01].

q: What engineering challenges go into building low-cost AGVs?
a: Tapan describes three areas: calculating optimal routes, managing power and recharging, and keeping cost low while meeting safety needs. Underneath all of them, Tapan said, "at the center of all these things was all pure basics PID, control systems." [07:33].

q: How can robots become affordable enough for mass adoption?
a: Tapan believes it takes progress in safety, control, and mechanical and electrical design, following the way consumer electronics were commoditized. He expects a point "where the robots will become not only retail, not only warehouse, but will go to every" [08:48] aspect of our life.

q: What did Tapan Pattnayak learn from supply chain delays?
a: Tapan had relied on a vendor's delivery promises, and when the parts did not arrive, he came up with an in-house design that solved the same problem. His conclusion was that "unless you have a control on the entire chain, you cannot build new" [15:47] things.

q: What does Tapan Pattnayak look for when hiring engineers?
a: Tapan looks for character first, including a drive for excellence over short-term money and perseverance, and he also holds a very high technical bar. As Tapan put it, "If your character is in the right place, everything else follows." [11:35].

A Quarter of Work at Google: Maria says integrating Google Home with internal notification infrastructure took about a quarter with two or three engineers, and the team still had to plan and build its own preferences system afterward.

From Categories to Subscription Topics: The older categories feature required code changes to pass a category with each send call. Preferences Center lets teams drag templates into subscription topics, set defaults, and publish a hosted page.

Protecting the Send Pipeline: Courier added preference checks to its core send pipeline incrementally, defining which unsubscribe rules take precedence and logging when and why a notification was blocked.
Choose Your Level of Control: Developers can use Courier's hosted preferences page, embed its React component and override the styles, or skip the UI and work directly with the APIs.

Required Alerts, Flexible Channels: For crucial messages like password resets, a product can block opt-outs while still letting users choose the channel, such as text instead of email, if custom routing is enabled.

q: Why is building notification infrastructure in-house so time-consuming?
a: Maria Irizarry recalled that at Google Home, the work covered send timing, notification design and opt-outs, even with an internal notification infrastructure available. She said "that project actually took around a quarter to build with two or three engineers" [03:51], and the preferences work came after that.

q: How quickly can developers set up a preferences page with Courier Preferences Center?
a: Maria explained that teams design subscription topics in the web app, publish, and get a hosted page they can link from their notifications. Users can "click into that URL and see that beautiful page in a matter of literally 20 minutes." [08:28]

q: What was the biggest technical challenge in adding preferences to Courier?
a: According to Maria, it was building preference checks into the send pipeline, Courier's core infrastructure, through incremental changes. As she put it, "we have to be very, very careful with not breaking the send pipeline" [09:27].

q: Can users opt out of critical notifications like password resets?
a: Maria described how Courier customers can restrict opt-outs for crucial messages while offering custom routing. For end users, "they can't necessarily opt out of those crucial notifications, but they can select" [18:31] the channel they receive them through.

q: Can Courier's preferences component be customized to match your brand?
a: Maria said the hosted page uses the brand you have already set up in the Courier web app. With the React component, "you can override the styles to make it look how you want." [16:01]

s7-e28-the-elixir-stack-behind-a-5b-payments-engine-scaling-vertical-saas-with-sean-stavropoulos-of-boulevard

Consumer Idea, Business Product: Boulevard set out to make booking easier for consumers, then found salon and spa back-end software couldn't power that experience. The team shifted to building software for the businesses themselves.

Scheduling Couldn't Stand Alone: The team tried to avoid building payments and shift management, but separate card processing meant totals didn't add up. The MVP took about a year and a half to run a six-person Santa Monica salon.

Model for National Chains Early: Though the first customer was a single small salon, Boulevard's data model supported 100-plus location chains from day one, because that jump would have been very costly to make later.

Where the Tech Debt Landed: Point of sale wasn't in the original plan, so checkout and the commerce engine needed overhauls, including messy sales tax logic. Sean advises vetting early decisions with domain experts.

Break Up With Poor Fits: Early on, Boulevard sold to nearly any appointment business, from exotic race car driving studios to float tank franchises. Some became distractions, and parting ways helped the team focus.

q: What is Boulevard and who is it for?
a: Boulevard serves appointment-based self-care businesses such as salons and spas, with tools including online scheduling, text messaging, card processing and inventory management. Sean Stavropoulos said, "we describe as a client experience platform built for appointment-based" [02:06].

q: Why did Boulevard shift from a consumer booking app to business software?
a: Sean was frustrated that he still had to call his hair salon to book, but the team found that existing salon back-end systems couldn't support a better consumer experience. As Sean explained, "we had to begin by providing better software directly to the businesses." [04:55]

q: How long did it take to build the Boulevard MVP?
a: Work began around 2015, and the first paying customer arrived in early 2017. Sean said, "it took a good year and a half for us to get to a place where Boulevard was full-featured" [06:19], enough to run a six-person hair salon.

q: Was Boulevard built to scale from day one?
a: Sean said some areas were, while others became challenges as the company grew. The team prioritized data modeling for large multi-location chains because, as he put it, "It's easier to make some of those early data model changes at the beginning" [14:27].

q: What did Sean Stavropoulos learn about choosing customers?
a: Sean said Boulevard signed some early customers it didn't serve well, and they often distracted the team. His advice is "don't be afraid to break up with customers that you learn you might not be the best fit for" [18:01], as long as it gives you the focus to keep growing.

s7-bonus-cutting-customer-acquisition-costs-turning-ticketing-data-into-viral-referrals-with-ashley-cline-of-ice-cream-social

Born From Client Need: Ice Cream Social came from TicketSocket, a white label ticketing platform, where Ashley Cline was helping clients sell more tickets without spending more on marketing. The answer was to gamify bringing friends and family to events.

From Share Button to Rewards: The first version simply asked ticket buyers to share the event on social media. It grew into challenges offering refunds, free merchandise or gift cards for bringing five friends, which required far more tracking and analytics.

Compliance Over Early Virality: The team chose to run the tool as GDPR compliant in every location. That took priority over other work and meant finding new ways to create a viral factor in place of some early features.

Automate Rewards, Amplify Channels: Merchant processor integrations automate refunds and gift cards so clients avoid a full-time task. Marketing stack integrations let referrals fuel channels like Facebook ads, email and SMS rather than replace them.

Break It to Stop Fraud: Because referral rewards invite gaming, the team keeps trying to hack its own tool to prevent fraud. Cookie changes, privacy updates and new iOS releases make accurate tracking ongoing work.

q: What is Ice Cream Social?
a: Ice Cream Social is a referral and word of mouth marketing tool that also collects first party data on consumers and their friends. Ashley Cline describes it as "a widget that can easily be bolted on to any website or checkout flow" [02:07].

q: Can referral marketing lower customer acquisition costs?
a: Ashley Cline says many client case studies point that way when referrals are compared with other marketing channels. In her words, it "is coming out to be the lowest cost for acquisition when you're comparing it against" [02:40] those channels.

q: How did Ice Cream Social get started?
a: It grew out of Ashley Cline's marketing work with clients of TicketSocket, the parent company's ticketing platform. As Cline put it, "It was born out of a need that already existed for clients." [04:08]

q: What did the first version of Ice Cream Social do?
a: Ashley Cline says the first iteration was very simple and asked ticket buyers to share the event with friends on social media. She explained that "someone would buy a ticket. They'd see a small call to action" [04:40], and the team later added challenges and rewards.

q: How does Ice Cream Social handle referral fraud?

Capture the Front End: Reprise captures any UI that loads in a browser so it looks and behaves like the real product. Evan Powell likens it to a Western movie set: the saloon front exists, but there's nothing behind it.

Paid Checks Prove Viability: The first version had no login, and Brian Stevenson handled work manually behind the curtain. Sam Clemens counted it viable once three customers wrote checks for it, guarding against false-positive praise.

q: What problem with software sales demos led to Reprise?

q: How did Reprise build and validate its MVP?
a: The earliest product centered on capturing and rendering an app, with no interface a customer could log into and some work done manually. Sam Clemens said the test of viability was payment: "will someone write us a check for this awful raw thing?" [07:28].

q: How did Reprise prepare its product for enterprise customers?

Notifications Are an Iceberg: Sending one SMS is simple, but a great experience needs multi-channel delivery, preferences, tracking, provider failover, templates, branding and workflows.

q: Why is it hard to build product notifications in-house?
a: Seth Carney says a simple send is manageable, but reliability and engagement require channels, preferences, tracking, failover, template design and more. As Seth put it, "I think you can look at notifications and say, it's an iceberg." [09:30]

a: As a destination, Courier uses Segment events for profile capture and automations, and as a source it pipes Courier activity back into Segment. For teams already collecting data in Segment, Seth said, "Segment is probably the fastest way to get up and running with Courier." [10:51]

Born From Print-on-Demand: Patterson's team spent about three years building in-house Google Shopping bidding tech for its own print-on-demand marketplace. A big revenue uptick for an investor's client helped convince them to take it to market.

Bidding at SKU Level: Instead of grouping hundreds or thousands of products under one bid, Bidnamic built campaigns around individual SKUs, reflecting differences in margin, average order value, repeat rate and lifetime value.

Search Intent Matters Too: Beyond product data, Bidnamic models what shoppers type. Broad queries like "men's shoes" rarely convert, while exact models, sizes and colors convert far better, so bids account for both product and query.

Senior Specialists Over Juniors: The gap proved too wide for early-career hires on this technical product. Bidnamic relies on a small team of experts, including PhD researchers who pass a clear roadmap to engineering.
Read the Metrics Sooner: When COVID hit, Bidnamic held back on growth despite keeping all its staff. Patterson says it was slow to see the e-commerce boom and lost momentum for around six months.

q: What does Bidnamic do?
a: Bidnamic, led by CEO Liam Patterson, uses machine learning and AI to help e-commerce retailers manage Google Shopping advertising. Patterson says the technology handles something beyond human capability, "which is predicting exactly how much to pay for a single click" [03:01].

q: How did Bidnamic get started?
a: Liam Patterson's team was running a print-on-demand marketplace that relied heavily on Google Shopping, and found off-the-shelf tools lacked the granularity they wanted. They built their own, as Patterson put it, "in-house for about three years, which really became our secret to success" [05:41] before taking it to market.

q: How does Bidnamic handle retailers with millions of SKUs?
a: Liam Patterson says the technology has scaled pretty linearly, but a marketplace with millions of SKUs across many countries created challenges around Google Ads API limits on changes and account partitions. The team had to work out "how we dissect and work with such a large inventory" [14:58] while keeping product intelligence at the individual SKU level.

q: What data assets does Bidnamic use to build new products?

q: What advice does Liam Patterson give new entrepreneurs?
a: Patterson advises identifying and tracking the metrics that drive the business, such as customer acquisition cost and lifetime value, then benchmarking them and working to close the gaps. His starting point is to "think about the metrics that really matter behind this product" [26:55].

Save Now, Buy Later: Walletifai uses machine learning to predict future expenses and automatically detect essential ones, helping Canadians and Americans make room for savings goals as an alternative to credit cards.

Test Manually Before Building: Roya would swap the first mobile app for a few hundred lines of code run on a sample group's banking data, sharing results by email, paper or Excel to learn whether they were valuable.

Two Jobs During Lockdown: When the pandemic hit, saved commuting time helped the founders work their nine-to-five jobs, which self-funded the startup, while building Walletifai as a second full-time job.

Forecast Revenue Early: The team believed it had to show customer growth before thinking about revenue. Roya calls skipping proper financial forecasting a mistake, one that incubator advisors helped fix quickly.

a: Roya Kachooei learned the hard way that building the mobile app first was a mistake. Her advice from that experience: "You probably want to test out your idea in the market before building it" [06:14], by doing it manually for some people first.

s7-e25-from-a-philosophy-phd-to-creating-helm-and-the-next-wave-of-serverless-with-matt-butcher-of-fermyon

Frustrations Became the Roadmap: At Microsoft, Butcher's team heard of problems they couldn't solve with VMs or containers, including slow startup and costly pre-warmed images for serverless. That search led them to WebAssembly.

Density and Speed Gains: Butcher says an extra large AWS VM might run 30 to 40 containerized apps, while Fermyon's open beta ran 900. Cold start, targeted at around 100 milliseconds, is now under one millisecond.

Culture Takes Deliberate Work: Fermyon brought in organizational psychologist Adam to coach conflict and feedback and help interview for its values: curiosity, humility, inclusivity and passion. He now works 30 hours a week with the company.

q: How did Fermyon get started?
a: Matt Butcher's team at Microsoft explored WebAssembly during research time, but their internal pitch drew little interest, and conversations with VCs showed him a larger opportunity. After the team agreed to start a company, Butcher said, "we turned in our notice at Microsoft, all 10 of us on the same day." [10:07]

q: What is Spin, Fermyon's open source tool?

[13:21] After its March 31 release, it trended on Hacker News and drew what he recalled as roughly 1,100 GitHub stars over the weekend.

The Hidden Push Pipeline: A basic push means getting a device token, storing it in your database, retrieving it to send a message, then making the notification actionable in the app. Miller says the sending step usually doesn't go well.

Stale Answers, Bad Prompts: Push has changed on iOS and Android, so many answers found by Googling are old. Miller suspects copied snippets are why some apps ask for push permission before users have even tried them.

Silent Payload Failures: Data sent to a push token must be structured precisely. A message can appear to send successfully yet never arrive, and the problem can be very difficult or impossible to debug.

One Engineer Can Start: Courier's SDK syncs push tokens automatically and can send test pushes without a backend. A single mobile engineer can prove it out, then hand the send request to the backend team.

Days Down to Hours: Miller estimates the integration takes around 50 lines of code or fewer and a couple of hours, replacing many days of digging through potentially outdated Apple and Google documentation.

q: What are common mistakes when adding push notifications to a mobile app?
a: Mike Miller points to asking for permission at an awkward moment, such as the first time an app opens, and to badly structured message data. On the latter, he warned, "You can send the message and have the message go through successfully, but you won't receive it." [05:52]

q: How does Courier's mobile SDK handle push notification tokens?
a: Mike Miller explains that the SDK syncs tokens to Courier automatically, so developers don't have to worry about whether a token is valid. In his words, "you don't have to manually sync push notification tokens." [07:27]

q: Can you test push notifications without setting up a backend?
a: Yes, according to Mike Miller, with no backend work or raw HTTP calls needed. He described a function in the SDK "that allows you to send a test message out to yourself." [08:25]

q: How much code and time does Courier's mobile SDK save?
a: Mike Miller says developers can get up and running within a couple of hours and save code on both the mobile app and the backend. He estimates the integration at "less than 50 lines of code or around there and saving many, many days." [12:14]

q: Which platforms does Courier's mobile SDK support?
a: Mike Miller says the SDKs support both Apple Push Notification Service and Firebase Cloud Messaging, with documentation at docs.courier.com. On the options available, he said "there are four SDKs. We have an iOS, Android, React Native, and Flutter SDK." [10:19]

Accrual Accounting Drives SaaS Metrics: A prepaid annual contract counts as only one twelfth revenue in the first month. If the deferral isn't booked correctly, the ARR and MRR that stakeholders care about will be wrong.

Full Versus Assisted Automation: Assisted automation still has an accountant downloading reports and uploading templates. Full automation sees a deal close, invoices the customer and books entries in the correct periods.

Payroll Needs Granular Booking: Many payroll providers book only summary entries to QuickBooks Online. FinOptimal typically has clients turn those integrations off and builds its own, so spend can be analyzed by person, department or city.

API Gaps Hinder Accounting: Some data appears in a web UI but not the API, forcing manual report downloads. Deletions are another problem, though Jesse praised QuickBooks for its change data capture endpoint.

Flat Fees Reward Automation: Jesse argues hourly billing gives accounting firms no incentive to automate. FinOptimal charges a flat fee and combines three roles: accountant, coder and thought partner.

q: Why should startup founders care about accounting?
a: Jesse Rubenfeld says founders need it to talk about their business with investors, employees and customers, and that SaaS metrics like ARR and MRR depend on booking deferred revenue correctly. In his words, "accrual accounting is the language of business. And you need to speak it" [04:41].

q: What is finance automation?
a: Jesse defines it as using software to automate back office finance and accounting tasks, such as charging customers, paying bills, booking entries and reporting. In his example of full automation, a closed deal triggers software that sees "that status change, invoices the customer automatically, and it calculates the entries" [07:28].

q: What are the limitations of native QuickBooks Online integrations?
a: Jesse says third-party developers often treat them as an afterthought or build them only to a minimally viable level. Payroll is a key example, where he says you may need to go further and "book the payroll by person so that you can see the spend" [13:42].

q: Why does combining engineering and accounting matter?
a: Jesse has seen implementations where each side struggled to specify what was needed, leaving integrations with the wrong fields. As he put it, "Engineers don't know enough accounting to know what to offer." [09:48]

q: How is FinOptimal different from a traditional accounting firm?
a: Jesse says FinOptimal replaces the billable hour with a flat fee and brings together accounting, coding and thought partnership. He summed up the pricing difference by saying "it's flat fee. The optimization's on us" [23:29].

Maps That Link to Maps: Next up is product-led growth, including a "Wikipedia black hole of maps" where a point shows other maps featuring it. Better consumer discovery follows once there's a critical mass of users.

q: What is Proxi and what is it used for?

a: Chelsey Roney's co-founder Melinda turned a Facebook thread of trick-or-treat addresses during the first COVID Halloween into a crowdsourced map that went viral. Optimize Beyond the Website: For longer, multi-session journeys, FunnelEnvy ties experiments to qualified leads, pipeline, revenue and free-to-paid conversion, not just website leads or signups.
Test the Offer, Not Cosmetics: Arun estimates 80% of the value for lead gen and SaaS businesses lies in testing the offer, its framing, proof and exchange method, and aligning them to visitor intent.

Hypothesis Quality and Speed: Optimization comes down to creating strong, evidence-backed hypotheses and testing and acting on them quickly. Doing so takes strategy, engineering and data working together.
Break Down Data Silos: Web analytics, CRM, product and marketing automation data often sit apart. Arun advises unifying them, and sees GA4's BigQuery sync as a chance to move past built-in reports.

Decouple Experiments From Product: Product engineers are expensive and used to roadmaps with assumed value. A separate growth engineering capability can test uncertain ideas quickly without incurring a lot of technical debt.

q: What does FunnelEnvy do?
a: FunnelEnvy, founded by Arun Sivashankaran, helps companies convert more of their paid, content and SEO traffic into leads, customers and revenue, with the aim of lowering acquisition costs. As Arun put it, "we work with lead gen and SaaS businesses to optimize their inbound" [02:03] funnels.

q: What is the difference between conversion rate optimization and revenue funnel optimization?
a: Arun Sivashankaran says conversion rate optimization traditionally starts and stops with conversions on the website, which can work for short e-commerce journeys. When revenue comes after the first visit, he says "we need to go beyond traditional conversion rate optimization to consider the full revenue funnel." [04:43]

q: What should B2B and SaaS companies A/B test on their websites?
a: Arun recommends focusing on the offer itself, including its headlines, positioning, copy, proof and how visitors take advantage of it, all matched to their stage in the journey. Superficial tweaks like button colors are not enough, as he explained: "For our customers, cosmetic changes just won't do it." [06:11]

q: Why do siloed analytics hurt funnel optimization?
a: Arun Sivashankaran explains that when web, CRM, product and marketing automation data are separate, there is no consistent view of the customer from first awareness through retention. He urges teams to integrate it into "a single source of truth, because ultimately that siloed data is going to impede" [15:09] the team's ability to get answers.

q: Why can't growth teams run funnel experiments with their internal product engineers?
a: According to Arun, marketing and growth teams often lack dedicated technical talent, while product teams are not necessarily good at investing based on uncertain, risk-adjusted returns. Pulling them onto experiments "has huge opportunity costs because those engineers are expensive. They should be building product," [20:42] he said.

s7-e24-from-scaling-frank-and-oak-to-engineering-decentralized-brand-communities-with-ethan-song-of-rarecircles

Onboard Users Before Building: To beat the cold start problem, RareCircles spent months on interviews and market discovery, onboarding potential users so they were ready to test. Analysis took about six months, with three to six months of building in parallel.

Show and Tell Roadmap: About half the roadmap comes from the team's own research and ideas, half from surveys and customer conversations. Items are stack ranked by highest impact and lowest development cost.

Speed Over Early Scale: In a new market, Song expects early scaling bets to be wrong, so the team accepts tech debt. Every couple of months, it devotes a sprint or two to refactoring before things break.

Passion Beats Market Size: RareCircles onboarded some customers who weren't ready, making useful feedback hard to get. The lesson was to find the most passionate users, even if that means starting with a smaller market.

Hustle and Referrals First: For early hires, Song favored willingness to work hard, experiment and fail fast over five or ten extra years of experience. Referrals saved months of getting to know each other.

q: What is RareCircles and what does it do?
a: RareCircles is a B2B product that uses Web3 technology for memberships, serving customers such as brands, sports teams and gaming studios. Ethan Song said the company started "with the intent of creating a product that helps to deepen engagement" [03:09], and eventually to help businesses generate more revenue from that community.

q: How did RareCircles solve the cold start problem when launching its MVP?
a: Before launching, Ethan Song's team did interviews and market discovery so they had users with an existing relationship ready to give rapid feedback. In his words, "before launching a product, we spent quite a bit of time doing interviews, doing market discovery" [03:58].

q: How does RareCircles decide what to build next?
a: Ethan Song said the roadmap is split between the team's own ideas and competitive research, and input from surveys and customer conversations. He explained, "we basically stack rank them based on what gives the highest impact" [06:26] and the lowest development cost, favoring features with faster turnaround.

q: Should an early-stage startup in a new market build for scale from day one?
a: RareCircles chose not to, prioritizing experimentation and speed while refactoring as it grows. Song, who sees the company as building a fairly new market, said "it's very hard to build for scale at early on because you're most likely going to be wrong" [09:36].

q: How does Ethan Song think brand marketing and customer relationships will change?
a: Song argues that rising acquisition costs, harder targeting and weaker email and SMS performance are making transaction-based marketing less effective. He said, "our perspective is that everything is going to shift from the transaction to the individual" [15:02], with community driving business success.

Outcomes as a Subscription: Faisal's early MVP delivered IT services as outcomes that customers could subscribe to and scale up or down. His current one applies that idea to cybersecurity and compliance for businesses where security isn't a core expertise.

Recovery Is Part of Security: Calian's managed detection, threat hunting and response offering (MDR/XDR) goes beyond spotting attacks. IT engineering and architecture teams help customers respond, restore systems and recover data after a breach.

Think Like the Attacker: When a technology like ChatGPT draws excitement, Faisal's team asks how bad actors will use it, such as writing malware without coding skills or drafting convincing phishing emails despite poor English.

Know When to Exit: Faisal invested heavily in a backup-as-a-service product with a company that went bankrupt, then saw Amazon, Google and Microsoft in the space. He says he saw the signs and should have taken his chips off the table.
Narrow the Focus: Looking back to the early 2000s, Faisal would stop trying to be a lot to a lot of people and say no to bad deals and bad customers, even if focusing shrinks the addressable market.

q: What does Calian do?
a: Faisal Bhutto describes Calian as a publicly traded company headquartered in Canada with four business units: health, advanced technologies, consulting, and IT and cybersecurity. q: How does Calian's managed detection and response offering help after a breach?

a: Faisal focuses on culture, encouraging new ideas, accepting mistakes and giving people time to learn through conferences, user groups and subscriptions such as Gartner. He also believes mediocre "people don't want to work with exceptional people. If you hire wrong, fire fast." [11:32]

q: What mistake did Faisal Bhutto make with backup as a service?
a: Faisal invested a lot of money in a backup-as-a-service product with a company that went bankrupt, and then Amazon, Google and Microsoft were in the market. Reflecting on the signs he saw, Faisal said, "I should have probably exited and taken my chips off the table." [16:10]

s7-e23-the-45-million-combination-problem-why-human-cognition-fails-precision-oncology-and-the-rise-of-knowledge-based-medical-ai-with-navid-alipour-co-founder-ceo-of-ai-med-global

From Space Weather to Mammograms: Scientists who had detected space weather anomalies for NASA applied AI to breast cancer. Curemetrics got a first-of-its-kind FDA clearance in 2019, which Navid cites at 99% accuracy from a mammogram.

Earlier Detection Proved the MVP: Early algorithms trained on mammograms from a hospital in Mexico. On images going back years, Navid says they found the known cancers and caught many earlier, by up to four years.

One Mammogram, Two Diseases: Cardiologist investors helped the team see it could also score breast arterial calcification, an early sign of heart disease. That heart disease product was still pending FDA clearance.

Matching Beyond Human Cognition: Curematch takes a tumor's next-generation sequencing report and recommends drug combinations. With over 4.5 million possible three-drug options, it supports the oncologist's decision rather than replacing it.

Hire Slow, Fire Fast: Navid hired someone against his gut, and that person brought a toxic work culture, even in a remote environment. He admits that in one or two cases the company hired too fast and fired too slow.

q: What is AI Med Global and what do Curemetrics and Curematch do?
a: AI Med Global is the umbrella company Navid Alipour leads for Curemetrics, which detects anomalies in mammograms, and Curematch, which recommends cancer drug combinations. Speaking of Curematch, Navid stressed that it is not there to "replace a doctor. It's there to empower them to take better care in helping fight cancer." [05:04]

q: Why is choosing combination therapies so hard for oncologists?
a: Navid Alipour explains that every cancer differs at the molecular level, and a three-drug combination can involve more than four and a half million options. As he put it, "So it's beyond human cognition." [04:54]

q: Can AI detect heart disease from a mammogram?
a: Navid Alipour says Curemetrics can detect and score breast arterial calcification on the same mammogram used for cancer detection, though FDA clearance was still pending. He describes it as "calcification in the arteries, which is early onset to heart disease." [03:45]

q: How did Curemetrics build its technology to scale?
a: Navid Alipour says the company was on Amazon's cloud from day one, so it can ramp processing up or down and keep startup costs lower. In his words, "the beauty of what we build is we're 100% cloud-based" [06:19].

q: What hiring mistake did Navid Alipour make?
a: Navid made a hire against his own gut feeling, and the person brought a toxic work culture. Reflecting on the rule of hiring slow and firing fast, he said, "in one or two cases, we hired too fast and fired too slow." [18:58]

s7-bonus-the-real-time-arcade-engineering-instant-leaderboard-micropayments-with-joe-de-pinto-of-haste-arcade

A Leaderboard That Pays: Haste Arcade players earn a fraction of each later play for as long as they stay on the leaderboard. Payouts hit their wallet instantly, and the game's developer gets a share too.

Idea to Players Within a Week: Dan Wagner coded the first tap-the-dot game in an hour or two, with HandCash wallet sign-in and plays from a penny to $100. After a tweet, it reached a couple thousand people within a day or two.

Money Changes Game Security: With cash on the line, a hacked scoreboard matters, so games must be server authoritative. That is new to many hyper-casual developers, which makes a strong SDK and documentation essential.
Micropayments Need Massive Scale: Micropayments from a couple thousand players could not cover eight full-time salaries. Joe says profiting from them takes massive scale.
Follow the Demand: Take It, an NFT marketplace where the price rises 30% with each take, matched the arcade's revenue in about six months. The team chose to build it out as a standalone platform.

q: How does Haste Arcade's instant leaderboard payout model work?
a: Joe De Pinto explains that players pay a small amount to play, and those on the leaderboard earn from the people who play after them, with higher spots earning more. In his 25-cent arcade example, "you're gonna get a fraction of their 25 cents." [02:53]

q: Why does Haste Arcade use Bitcoin SV (BSV) instead of other blockchains?
a: Joe says the arcade needs hundreds of transactions per second at very small amounts, and the team could not find that elsewhere after looking into chains including Solana and Ethereum. In his view, "BSV is the only blockchain that actually scales to the levels of global adoption." [18:48]

q: How long did it take to build the first version of Haste Arcade?
a: Joe says co-founder Dan Wagner programmed the very first test version in an hour or two, followed by a few days of UI cleanup. As Joe put it, "it was definitely less than a week idea to proof of concept." [08:38]

q: Why do games with real-money leaderboards need to be server authoritative?
a: Joe says few people care if someone hacks the scoreboard of a typical hyper-casual game, because nothing is at stake. Of Haste's games, he said, "Well, now that money's on the line, it does matter." [19:39]

q: What advice does Joe De Pinto have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Joe's advice is to be persistent, especially on days when people don't seem to get your idea, and to find something productive to do in the next 10 minutes. Through hard times and moments when you feel like quitting, he said, "you just have to keep going forward." [30:02]

growthmode-on-zach-fragapane-growthmatch

Managed, Not Just Matched: GrowthMatch is an actively managed marketplace that assembles cross-functional teams of freelancers and micro agencies into packaged growth services, then manages the relationship for best practices, transparency and outcomes.

Senior and Fractional First: Zach urges founders to put experienced people over revenue, product and customer discovery, even if paid fractionally or in equity, and to consider pre-vetted fractional specialists before defaulting to full-time hires or agencies.

Human Video Cuts Through: As AI-written text floods audiences, Zach says B2B companies should focus on short videos featuring in-house experts, usually leaders. Salespeople can share those clips in follow-ups to lift response rates.

Reporting Before Experiments: Don't start a growth experiment until you've built the reporting that shows success or failure. The advanced step, which Zach admits he hasn't reached, is committing in advance to what you'll do for each outcome.

A Three-Person Content Team: The thought leadership package pairs a content strategist, a short-form video marketer and a social media manager. A 30 to 60 minute interview becomes video clips and text posts, with dashboards to track performance.

q: What is GrowthMatch and who is it for?
a: GrowthMatch offers packaged growth services to digital or tech-enabled companies such as B2B SaaS firms, professional services businesses and marketing agencies. Co-founder Zach Fragapane describes it as "an actively managed marketplace of supremely talented growth specialists, usually freelancers or micro agencies" [03:32].

q: What is a fractional growth team?
a: Zach Fragapane explains that fractional simply means part-time, and describes the team as "a cross-functional group of part-time people" [05:09]. Its mix of skills depends on the growth engine or one-time boost being pursued, the customer being sold to and the solution category.

q: What kind of content should B2B companies be creating?
a: Zach says every business that intends to grow should create content consistently, and that B2B companies should focus on video. He recommends "short video content that features the humans in the organization who are the subject matter experts" [20:08].

q: How do you accurately measure growth experiments?
a: Zach advises writing your experiments down as bets toward your goals and setting up measurement before launch. In his words, you don't start "until you've built the reporting that will tell you if it's a success" [26:46].

q: How does GrowthMatch's thought leadership content package work?
a: Zach says of the package, "we've assembled a fractional growth team that only does this and it consists of three people" [29:23]. A strategist interviews the company's expert, a video marketer cuts the recording into short clips and a social media manager writes the posts, which the client can edit and approve before publishing.

s7-e22-the-instagram-of-building-maintenance-engineering-a-photo-first-facilities-engine-with-paul-mccarthy-of-snapfix
Cut the Scope in Half: McCarthy designed what he thought was the simplest property tool, then halved its scope. Early PowerPoint viewers said it had too much; they just needed to take a photo.

Design Before Heavy Coding: Before the prototype, Cathal, now SnapFix's CTO, wrote a statement of work of about 50 pages with screen mock-ups, screen transitions and the business rules underneath them.

Tap-to-Prove Fire Checks: NFC tags on fire doors let staff tap their phones during fire walks, recording who attended which door and when. This replaced paper checklists that offered no verifiable proof.
Architect for 10x: Cathal designed for ten times the target customer count, such as 1,000 when aiming for 100. It cost somewhat more in monthly AWS bills but supported a global system from day one.

Going Wide Too Early: After COVID hit its hotel niche, SnapFix sold as far as Australia, Africa and Alaska, with demos at midnight and 5am. It now focuses on hotels, primarily in the UK, Ireland and the US East Coast.

q: What is SnapFix and how does it work?
a: SnapFix is a photo-based maintenance platform that Paul McCarthy modeled on the principles of WhatsApp, with photos, messaging and information sharing. As McCarthy explained, he "overlaid it with a red, yellow, green traffic light system" [03:02], where red means something needs doing, yellow means in progress and green means completed.

q: How did SnapFix find the right team to build its MVP?
a: Paul McCarthy met about 10 software companies, most of which didn't grasp the idea, before meeting Cathal, who is now SnapFix's CTO. McCarthy's lesson was that "choosing the right person on day one to build your prototype is really, really important" [04:38].

q: How does SnapFix verify that hotel fire safety checks are done?
a: SnapFix added a checklist feature integrated with NFC tags that can be fixed to fire doors and doorframes. McCarthy said the engineer walks at a good pace and "they just tap their phone on the tag" [08:47], creating proof of presence with the date and time.

q: How did SnapFix approach scalability from the start?
a: McCarthy credits Cathal with always architecting the system for ten times the current target. He recalled that "if we were targeting 100 customers he had it architected for a thousand" [10:59], even though this added somewhat to the monthly AWS bills.

q: What mistakes did SnapFix's founder learn from?
a: After COVID hit hotels, SnapFix went very broad and talked to prospects around the world, which McCarthy found exhausting and stretched things too thin. He said, "I think on mature reflection, that was a little bit of a mistake" [13:00]. He also learned that desktop access matters, after initially planning a mobile-only product.

Start With Upload and Serve: Piñata's MVP took about a month: a simple IPFS node on something like a DigitalOcean droplet, a basic API and a simple dashboard. The team focused on uploading and serving content well rather than piling on features.

Education as a Feature: When the roadmap turned toward blockchain use cases around 2020, the work was mostly messaging. Piñata treated blogs teaching developers how to build with IPFS and blockchain as product features.

Scaling Through Daily Fixes: In 2021 the system had hard outages seven months in a row. Methodical daily improvements and better human processes helped Piñata handle scale, and it now moves petabytes of data per month.

Don't Price on One Opinion: Piñata adopted usage-based pricing largely because one early user asked for it. Kyle believes it was the wrong long-term decision and says the company still sees the scars.

Betting on App NFTs: Kyle sees NFTs moving beyond art and images toward managing permissions for full applications. In that model, holding an NFT in your wallet grants access to content and data, instead of logging in to an account on every site.

q: What is Piñata and what does it do for NFTs?
a: Piñata, co-founded by CEO Kyle Tut, is a home for NFT media, where projects upload the files their tokens represent and then manage, serve and display them. As Kyle put it, "we help NFT companies, NFT projects, marketplaces to manage their media" [02:06].

q: How was Piñata's first MVP built?
a: Kyle Tut says it took about a month, with co-founder and CTO Matt doing the building, and users were asked to pay to pin content. Kyle explained that "all we did is we took a simple IPFS node, which is the desktop node" [04:19] and spun it up on a cloud server.

q: What scaling problems has Piñata faced?
a: Kyle Tut says Piñata was not built for scale from day one and has repeatedly hit new walls as usage grew. The roughest stretch came in 2021, when "our system fell down seven months in a row, where we had just like a hard outage" [14:23].

q: What is token gating in the NFT space?
a: Kyle Tut describes token gating as serving content based on whether a person owns a particular NFT, a feature Piñata found by talking to customers. In his words, "If they own an NFT, you'll serve the content" [11:07], and if they don't, the content isn't served.

q: What are Piñata's dedicated IPFS gateways for?
a: Kyle Tut lists dedicated IPFS gateways among the newer features, aimed at getting stable content to end users who won't tolerate long waits. He said they are "all about making content serving as fast and efficient as possible" [10:38].

s7-e21-democratizing-enterprise-code-engineering-ai-no-code-apps-for-regulated-markets-with-nanxi-liu-co-ceo-of-blazetech

Born From Internal Bottlenecks: At Nanxi Liu's last company, non-technical teammates kept waiting on engineers for internal tools. After the acquisition, she and the same co-founders built Blaze to let them build those tools themselves.

Alpha Customers in Three Months: Blaze started in January 2022 and had alpha users by March. The early product connected to databases for create, edit and delete work, and founders gave tutorials on live calls.

Paying Customers Shape the Roadmap: Requests from paying users moved work up fast. A Stripe integration was built when asked for, and basic data visualization shipped although it wasn't in the year-one plan.

A Reunited Team Moves Faster: The first nine people all came from the last company. They already knew Angular and each other, which spared recruiting and training time and helped get an alpha out within three months.

Higher Prices, More Customers: Very cheap early pricing made some doubt Blaze's quality. Raising prices brought more leads and customers, and Liu says she would approach pricing differently from day one.

q: What is Blaze.tech and what can you build with it?
a: Nanxi Liu describes it this way: "Blaze.tech is a no-code platform where we enable people to build custom software" [02:10]. Her examples include internal tools such as a custom CRM admin panel or inventory management software, built through a visual drag-and-drop interface.

q: How did Blaze.tech build and launch its MVP?
a: The company started in January 2022 and began getting alpha customers in March, many through Liu's network and a LinkedIn post. She said the lesson from her last company was to "roll things out as quickly as possible and just get customer feedback" [04:26].

q: How did Blaze.tech approach SOC 2 Type 2 compliance and scalability?
a: Liu said getting SOC 2 Type 2 certified had taken about two years at her last company, so Blaze prepared from the start. As she put it, "we just set up the internal controls and our security and data privacy" [14:22], and the platform also had to handle millions of rows of data for some customers.

q: What would Nanxi Liu do differently with Blaze.tech's pricing and onboarding?
a: Liu said very low prices made people question whether the product was serious, and noted, "When we actually increased our pricing, it got us more leads and more customers" [23:01]. She would also have offered hands-on implementation help earlier instead of leaving new customers to figure out the platform alone.

q: How does Blaze.tech interview and hire new team members?
a: Candidates meet multiple people and take a skills test that mirrors the job, such as answering sales objections or solving engineering case problems. Even with a strongly recommended candidate, Liu said, "We always still make sure we put them through a pretty rigorous interview process" [16:44].

s7-bonus-making-the-operating-system-multiplayer-from-a-13m-collaboration-engine-to-openai-with-alex-embiricos-of-remotion

Built Into macOS: Remotion went native so it would feel like part of the operating system, with a dock for teammates. The cost was years spent building a team that was truly excellent on the platform.

Waitlist as Research Tool: When retention and signups stalled, the team shut off self-serve signups and got on a call with each new person. They learned people wanted a social team culture, not just frictionless calling.

Overestimating Product-Market Fit: Acting for almost a year as if they had fit led to unneeded hires, small layoffs and wasted building. A hard look showed deep value in engineering teams getting work done, not socializing.

Buy Scale, Don't Build It: Remotion runs on Firebase and Google infrastructure, with audio and video on top of Zoom's. The choice was initially painful, but it means the team doesn't have to worry about scaling video servers.
Polarizing Recruiting Works: Emails asking "are you passionate about macOS native apps and remote work?" put off most people, but drew candidates who cared about both and normally ignored recruiters.

q: What is Remotion and what problem does it solve?
a: Alex Embiricos describes Remotion as a video chat tool for engineers who need to solve technical problems together remotely, as though sitting side by side. In his words, "We are basically building a better Zoom for engineers." [02:06]

q: Why did Remotion build a native macOS app?
a: Alex said the team believed it would win by building the best product, and wanted talking to a teammate to feel like glancing over at them. From basically day zero, the idea was an operating system upgrade: "Remotion should not feel like an app." [08:06]

q: Why does Remotion use Zoom's audio and video infrastructure?
a: Alex explained that Remotion picks services that handle scaling, so the team doesn't have to scale video servers itself. Of building on Zoom, he said "that's a super intentional and initially painful decision but it also means that if and as we scale" [16:57] they don't have to worry about it.

q: What was Remotion's biggest mistake?
a: Alex said the most impactful mistake was "overestimating our amount of product market fit about a year ago" [20:08] and operating as though they had it. The result was hiring people they didn't need, a small round of layoffs and time spent building the wrong thing.

q: What advice does Alex Embiricos have for founders?
a: Alex advises caring about your customers as people, a lesson from an earlier gaming company that lasted less than a year. Before investing years in something, he would "make sure I care about the person whose problems I'm trying to solve." [25:52]

s7-bonus-the-ai-cto-democratizing-app-development-for-underserved-founders-with-sydney-davis-of-nixcode

Typeform as MVP Signup: To avoid AWS costs from free accounts, Davis used a Typeform (about $30 a month) to collect app requirements, estimate cost and take the first monthly payment before sending users to the backend to build.

AI Beyond No-Code: NixCode uses AI to answer app development questions, inform tech stack, plugin, workflow and business model choices, and advise founders after publishing, such as what to change when bounce rate is high.

Roadmap From Active Users: Davis builds the roadmap around what the highest paying, most active users say they need. Demand for monetization led to in-app purchasing and a plugin marketplace that outside builders could contribute to.
Pick a Niche Sooner: Davis says trying to serve everyone made the road to success longer. Looking back, she would have set a formal go-to-market strategy, chosen one niche up front and stuck with it.

Initiative Over Permission: After team turnover, Davis looks for resilience, vision and people who act without waiting for permission, try ideas, fail fast and apologize later. She also avoids C-suite titles in favor of functional roles.

q: What is NixCode and what problem does it solve?
a: NixCode is a no-code app development platform, founded by Sydney Davis, where users pick a template, add plugins and customize content, with AI guidance for the roadblocks that remain. As Davis put it, "Product development is not easy no matter what tools you use" [03:39].

q: How did NixCode handle user signup in its MVP on a tight budget?
a: Davis delayed building a self-service signup because free accounts could have driven up AWS costs. She said she "shortcutted the signup version of my MVP with a Typeform" [07:36], using its logic to produce requirements and a cost estimate and to trigger onboarding.

q: How does NixCode decide what to build next?
a: Davis relies on data, surveys and feedback, giving weight to the users getting the most value from the product. She explained, "When I say highest paying users, people are using it often." [11:49]

q: What would Sydney Davis do differently with her go-to-market strategy?
a: Davis says her early approach was to serve everyone and see who floated to the top. She believes she would have had a shorter road to success "had I just picked one niche up front and stuck with it" [18:53].

q: What AI features is NixCode planning next?
a: Davis wants users to enter keywords or requirements and get a generated app that they can then modify in the control panel. In her words, "our AI would match it with our plugins in the marketplace and organize them" [19:52].

s7-e20-engineering-a-1b-graphql-data-federation-engine-real-time-db-queries-with-tanmai-gopal-of-hasura

Two Jobs Inside Every API: Tanmai's team reduced API work to data mapping and transformation, plus domain-specific authorization. Hasura has developers declare models and security rules, then automates the API.

A Compiler and Web Server: Hasura was written in Haskell because it had to compile domain configuration into data source queries while serving low-latency, highly concurrent traffic. Configuration changes apply at runtime, with no rebuild.

Existing Data Over Greenfield: Hasura chose not to host the database, focusing on APIs over data companies already had. The team accepted losing some users to reach mission-critical production use faster.

Performance Earns Behavior Change: Tanmai said automation alone wasn't enough; in production it had to beat hand-built work by experts. He claims Hasura APIs run 5x to 100x faster than hand-built ones.

Cutting to the Data API: At launch time, the team saw that other pieces of its platform, though loved by developers, were getting in the way. Within a week it killed them and moved forward with only the data API.

q: How does the Hasura GraphQL Engine automate API development?
a: Tanmai Gopal explained that developers define their data models and security rules, and Hasura provides the API from that configuration. His team started from the insight that in any API service, "there's essentially just two pieces of work that you're doing" [04:09]: mapping and transformation, and security and authorization.

q: Why was Hasura built in Haskell?
a: Tanmai said the system had to translate a description of a domain into upstream queries while also serving requests with low latency and high concurrency. As he put it, "what we were essentially building was a compiler that was simultaneously a web server" [06:02]. He also said the choice let a small team write robust code and move quickly.

q: Does Hasura host your database or work with existing data?
a: Tanmai said the team made an opinionated call not to host the database, so that companies could use data they already had. In his words, "It's a data API for your data, for existing data, right?" [10:26].

q: Why did performance matter so much for Hasura's adoption?
a: Tanmai said Hasura asks developers to change behavior, which is hard, so saving time was not enough on its own. He said that "in production, when you're running this, it needs to be 10x better than what an expert would have built by hand" [15:31]. He credits that focus with winning early mission-critical adoption.

q: What would Tanmai Gopal do differently if he started Hasura again?
a: Tanmai would treat go-to-market as measurable and hypothesis-driven from the start, while still letting early product work be instinct-driven. He said "GTM is science from day zero" [24:35], and believes learning this earlier would have put the company where it is today two years sooner.

s7-e19-from-uber-data-analytics-to-an-hbs-dropout-scaling-a-19m-workflow-engine-with-ken-babcock-tango

Prototype Before You Build: Tango's earliest MVP was Figma mockups, then a bare-bones proto.io prototype, used for seed financing and shown to department leads. The hook was people asking whether it actually worked.

Choose Where to Be Exceptional: Tango copied proven patterns for things like notifications and put its creative energy into one core need: giving users confidence and trust that their process was being captured accurately.
Roadmap by a DVF Score: The team ranked work by desirability and viability relative to feasibility, meaning engineering investment, to find quick wins with high value and ROI.

Time to Value Drives Scale: Tango measures the time from account creation to a user's first piece of documentation, then at five minutes. Being a Chrome extension reduced friction and offered built-in distribution.
The Cost of Chrome-Only: Tango took almost a year to accept that users needed to capture steps outside the browser. Once it added a desktop app, engagement and paid conversion rose.

q: What problem does Tango solve?
a: Tango creates step-by-step how-to guides automatically as someone goes through a process, so teams can scale what their high performers do. Ken Babcock said the barrier was "that no one's scaling it is because documentation sucks." [03:38]

q: How did Tango build its first MVP?
a: Ken Babcock and his co-founders started with design mockups focused largely on the documentation output, then used proto.io to make a very basic prototype that looked like it worked. In Ken's words, "Like we were literally in Figma designing what the product could look like." [05:19]

q: How does Tango prioritize its product roadmap?
a: Ken Babcock described using the DVF framework, weighing customer desirability and business viability against the engineering investment required. He said, "we were pretty ruthless about each of those parts of that equation" [10:11].

q: Why did Tango build a desktop app in addition to its Chrome extension?
a: Research showed most workflow activity happened in the browser, but users said core parts of their processes lived outside it, which broke their workflows. Ken Babcock admitted, "It took us almost a year to come around and say, you know what, we actually need to have a desktop application," [17:50].

q: What advice does Ken Babcock give to new entrepreneurs?
a: Ken advises admitting what you don't know and balancing conviction with curiosity, even if that means asking a dumb question. He said this vulnerability helps "to reinforce a culture for your team of like, we don't all know what we're doing." [25:08]

s7-bonus-whats-new-with-materialize-arjun-narayan-co-founder-ceo
Rebuilt for the Cloud: Materialize moved to fully hosted SaaS and re-architected the product rather than just hosting the old one. Users no longer carry the management or operational burden.

Storage and Compute, Separated: Ingested data is stored permanently on S3, while compute clusters run in containers on EC2 and scale independently. Users spin one up with a SQL command, create cluster.
Isolation With Shared Data: Instead of running many separate Materialize deployments, teams can share data under one control plane. Independent clusters keep dev work from taking down production.

Streaming Joins in Plain SQL: Joining streams like web events and transactions means managing large, fast-changing state. Materialize handles it through a materialized view, with Drizly's abandoned cart notifications as an example.
Batch ML Moving Real-Time: Narayan sees many users go on to move batch machine learning pipelines to real time, running training and prediction as a continuous closed loop in SQL.

q: What is Materialize?
a: Materialize is a database purpose-built for fast-changing data, aiming to be as easy to use as a familiar database like Postgres. Arjun Narayan, its Co-founder and CEO, explained that you can take any query, turn it into a materialized view, and it "will continue to stay up to date, updating incrementally in the background" [07:10].

q: How is Materialize's cloud architecture built?
a: Narayan said the team broke apart what had been a tightly co-located deployment into parts that users can scale independently, with data stored on S3 and shared across compute clusters. In his words, "we built a storage engine for storing all of your streams of data" [10:53] and separated it from the compute engine.

q: Does moving Materialize to the cloud increase latency?
a: Narayan said it isn't much of a problem, since most users were already running Materialize on AWS and much of the latency comes from moving data between systems. He noted that you can bring it down "by co-locating your Materialize right next to your Kafka cluster" [08:49].

q: How does Materialize handle joins across data streams?
a: Users write the join in SQL as a materialized view, just as they would in another SQL database. Narayan said of the underlying work, "we take care of that streaming data flow, incremental updates, state management problem for you" [16:44].

q: Do you need an existing data pipeline to try Materialize?
a: No, although Narayan said most users connect existing sources such as Postgres or Kafka. If you have nothing set up, "You can start with some fresh empty tables and start inserting the events yourself." [20:27] At the time of the interview, access was through an early access sign-up with a waitlist.

s7-bonus-whats-new-with-pulumi-joe-duffy-co-founder-ceo

Deployments Built on Automation API: Pulumi Deployments, launched in October, takes code from a Git repo to the cloud. It runs on the Automation API, which turns infrastructure as code into an embeddable library and is used by over 80% of enterprise customers.

Customer-Driven Integrations: Early on, Pulumi added an integration only when a customer needed it for real production use. That has grown to roughly 150 integrations, including seven languages and over 100 cloud providers.

Open Source Feeds SaaS: Most people find Pulumi through its Apache-licensed open source, which can run entirely offline. Two thirds of open source users choose to pair it with the Pulumi SaaS for easier team collaboration, security and reliability.

Templates Beat the Blank Page: Pulumi shipped about 25 to 30 getting-started templates covering common architectures, such as microservices, static websites and Kubernetes clusters, so new users pick more than just a language and cloud.

Win a High-Impact Beachhead: Joe says Pulumi works with customers to start with a business-critical project, then move other infrastructure over. At Snowflake, Pulumi was essential to hitting a data cloud deadline tied to the IPO.

q: What is Pulumi Deployments and how does it work?
a: Pulumi Deployments hosts the compute and workflow that deploy your infrastructure, so you no longer have to run it manually or configure it all in your own pipeline. As Joe Duffy describes it, you "just point us at your Git repo and we'll take care of all the heavy lifting" [07:11]. He says the same foundation opens the door to things like drift detection, remediation and scheduled workloads.

q: What is the Pulumi Automation API?
a: The Automation API lets you embed infrastructure as code inside a larger system, such as a custom SaaS product, portal or tool. Joe Duffy explains the idea as "what if Infrastructure as Code was a library instead of being a command line?" [05:21]. It also underpins Pulumi Deployments.

q: How is Pulumi different from Terraform and CloudFormation?
a: Joe Duffy says CloudFormation relies on YAML or JSON, while Terraform uses a domain-specific language that makes complex things very complicated. Of Pulumi's answer, he says, "We tackle that problem by saying, hey, bring your favorite language" [18:13]. Pulumi pairs that expressiveness with declarative, provisioning-based infrastructure as code.

q: Is Pulumi open source or a paid product?
a: It is both: the open source technology is Apache licensed, and there is a commercial SaaS service that is free for individuals and has a generous free tier for teams. Joe Duffy notes that "you can use our open source entirely offline if you want" [10:26]. He says the SaaS makes things much easier in a team setting.

q: How did Snowflake use Pulumi?
a: Snowflake used Pulumi for its data cloud effort, which had ambitious deadlines ahead of its IPO, writing infrastructure in Go, a language it already used. Joe Duffy says that from experience with other tools, Snowflake knew "they weren't going to be able to get there with those tools" [15:45]. He says the company has since expanded its use of Pulumi to other systems.

Cash Offers Within 24 Hours: OpenStore gives Shopify merchants very large cash offers within 24 hours of engagement, and most can complete the offer flow in under 15 minutes.

q: What is OpenStore and what does it do for Shopify merchants?

q: How fast does OpenStore make an offer for a Shopify store?

q: How did OpenStore build its MVP?
a: Jeremy recalls that "the real original MVP was probably hacking together with spreadsheets" [04:43]. His engineering work then turned that into a slightly automated version, built in about a month or two, that gathered what was needed from merchants and prepared analysis for operators.

q: How did OpenStore approach scalability in its early architecture?

q: Why did OpenStore switch from Remix to Next.js?

s7-bonus-the-death-of-data-sampling-shifting-observability-left-to-catch-anomalies-at-the-source-with-max-lukichev-of-telmai

Beyond Rules-Only Data Quality: Max says rigid, hand-set expectations stop scaling as data sources and volumes grow. Telmai automates detection as much as possible while still letting users define their own expectations.

No Sampling, Scale First: Cloud scale for any data volume, no sampling and self-service without heavy configuration were foundations from the start. The first real POC tested this with a table of 100 million records and 8,000 attributes in JSON.

A Lego-Box MVP: The first version chained Google Dataflow, BigQuery and Data Studio. It wasn't yet a monitoring system, but it showed customers how much garbage was in their data and opened conversations about what they needed.

Validation Before the Real Build: Once customers strongly validated continuous monitoring, the team went full throttle, replacing the Data Studio dashboards with backend analytics, alerts and a React UI that presents evidence clearly.

Beware False Signals: The team went too deep, too soon on features for one customer who never converted. Max advises asking whether a request applies broadly, playing devil's advocate and changing course early.

q: What is Telmai and what does it monitor?
a: Telmai is a data monitoring platform that connects to databases, data warehouses and data streams, tracking volume, timeliness, schema and the quality of the values themselves. Max Lukichev explained that "it can monitor data anywhere in the pipeline, left side of the pipeline or the delivery" [02:15].

q: How is Telmai different from rule-based data quality tools?
a: Max Lukichev says the classic approach of setting rigid rules or expectations becomes non-scalable as data grows. Telmai still accepts user-defined expectations, but as he put it, "We really focus on making possible to detect problems in the data without relying on the rules only" [03:13].

q: How was the first Telmai MVP built?
a: The team used Google Cloud, with a simple Dataflow pipeline delivering data into BigQuery and Data Studio dashboards on top. Max Lukichev described it this way: "It was a solution built from the kind of Lego box, trying to combine those" [04:35] three tools.

q: Why did Telmai decide against data sampling?
a: Max Lukichev treated cloud scalability for any data volume as a foundation that wasn't up for debate, drawing on his prior experience of seeing these technologies work at scale. In his words, "We are not going to do sampling." [06:55]

q: What mistake did Max Lukichev make early on at Telmai?
a: He says the team built some things too early and went too deep for one customer who didn't convert, though they recovered quickly with little harm done. Max described the mistake as "building stuff too early until you have a very solid validation" [13:37].

s7-e18-the-99-speedup-architecting-real-time-disability-underwriting-for-the-gig-economy-with-hadi-radwan-of-asteya

Licenses and Filings Come First: Hadi says Asteya couldn't test demand with a quick MVP. State-by-state licensing took around a year, and pricing, filing and winning regulatory approval for products took another, while the team built the technology.

Automate What Sells First: Quoting, underwriting and policy issuance were treated as essential to selling. Billing, accounting and reporting could initially lean on manual, offline work, even though that wasn't the most efficient route.

Partners and Underwriters Shape Roadmap: Asteya sells through licensed brokers, agents and managing general agents. Their requests, plus underwriters' new products and compliance needs, drive priorities on a pipeline that usually extends three to six months.
Two Sprint Speeds: Small features that can go live quickly run on one-week sprints. Longer, more complex ones run on two- to four-week sprints, so weekly deployment and testing don't delay delivery.

No HIPPO Culture: Asteya avoids deferring to the "highest paid person with an opinion" and wants junior people able to bring Hadi ideas and challenges. He counts some wrong hires, with their hidden opportunity cost, among his biggest mistakes.

q: What problem is Asteya trying to solve with income insurance?
a: Hadi Radwan says many people live paycheck to paycheck and more than half don't know disability insurance exists, leaving families exposed if work stops. As Hadi put it, "one out of four people get disabled due to an unforeseen circumstance during their career" [02:47].

q: Why does it take so long to build an insurtech MVP?
a: Hadi explains that Asteya needed licenses in each state, plus priced and filed products approved by regulators, before it could sell. In his words, "you cannot sell a policy if you don't have licenses" [05:07].

q: Does Asteya sell disability insurance directly to consumers?
a: No, Hadi says Asteya works through licensed brokers, agents and managing general agents, and asks them which platform features matter most. He explained, "we do not sell directly to the end consumer we partner with distribution" [09:45] partners.

q: What trade-offs did Asteya make in its first product?
a: Hadi's team prioritized quoting, underwriting and policy issuance, while weighing each feature against the company vision, team capacity and complexity. Of billing, accounting and reporting, Hadi said "you need those, but you can actually do some manual interventions" [08:02].

q: How did Asteya architect its insurance platform to scale?
a: Hadi describes a modular platform with APIs that let modules across the insurance value chain talk to external providers, with deadline shortcuts revisited through refactoring. One test he applies to new products is "can we onboard that product within a few days" [14:54], compared with a few months in the original version.

s7-bonus-hacking-the-platform-building-a-global-no-code-extension-for-squarespace-with-nick-ippolito-rowan-findlay-of-squarekicker

A Weekend Prototype Changed Plans: The team planned to sell code snippets until Rowan spent a long weekend, roughly 40 to 50 hours, building a button that generated code inside the Squarespace editor. They then doubled down on SquareKicker full time.

Cutting the MVP Down: With a runway of roughly five to eight months, the team shipped an MVP in about five months with only a few tools: text tweaks, button colors, and rotating, hiding and shifting blocks. Planning the tools was harder than coding them.

Foundations Before Advanced Features: Basic text and image controls came first because blog and gallery tools depended on them. Common requests from the Squarespace Circle community helped shape what came next, including animations and scrolling effects.

Selective Scaling by Design: Data storage and servers were built to scale early, while some tools were built quickly because they could easily change. Generated code lives mainly in Squarespace's code injection area, with backups, which Rowan said helps them scale.

Hiring for Fit First: Nick said the team weighs how well people get along above coding ability or degrees, since coding can be taught. Rowan said he cares more about what makes someone tick than their past accomplishments.

q: What is SquareKicker and how does it work with Squarespace?
a: SquareKicker is a no-code design and animation extension that writes custom code and saves it in your Squarespace custom code area. Nick Ippolito described it as "a no-code visual builder that the user gets the ability to drag and drop certain sliders" [02:49], with real-time feedback on the design.

q: How did the idea for SquareKicker turn into a prototype?
a: Nick Ippolito and Rowan Findlay were working on code snippets during the pandemic when Rowan got curious over an Easter long weekend. Rowan recalled that after what was probably 40 or 50 hours, "I came back to Nick and Hannah with a prototype" [06:48].

q: What tech stack was used to build SquareKicker?
a: Rowan Findlay named Netlify, which they started with, along with MongoDB, Heroku, GitHub and Squarespace itself, plus a more React-based dashboard for subscription management. For the interface inside Squarespace, he said "Vue.js is mostly what we're using for the actual UI" [09:18].

q: Was SquareKicker built to scale from day one?
a: Rowan Findlay said the answer is both, and that scaling was part of the team's conversations from the start while they still had to move fast. On any parts that don't scale, he said, "I believe that's a choice we made based on a compromise." [16:32]

q: What advice do SquareKicker's builders have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Nick Ippolito advises shipping fast and often, staying lean and continuing to iterate: "If you've shipped a product that is perfect, then you've shipped it too late." [27:11] Rowan Findlay adds that you can't do it alone, so surround yourself with people you trust and respect.

s7-bonus-the-aws-of-fintech-engineering-a-multi-processor-payment-orchestration-layer-with-casey-kipfer-co-founder-of-justifi

Three Pillars of Platform Payments: Kipfer says platforms need a sub-account architecture, an orchestration layer and an experienced team. Most already use some form of sub-accounts but lack in-house people who have been through it before.
