Own Versus Rent: JustiFi decided early what it had to own and what it could rent, aiming to spend most time and resources on the former. Renting helped it go faster, with some pieces likely to be revisited later.

Narrowing the Market: JustiFi's seed pitch highlighted multiple verticals, but solving for each was too hard. Focusing made some earlier work unusable, yet let the team move much faster where the product was hitting the mark.

Trusted Early Hires: Probably the first 10 hires were previous co-workers and more, which built trust and cut ramp time. As the company grew, it hired to core values as much as or more than to resume-style skills and experience.

q: What does JustiFi do?
a: JustiFi provides white-labeled payments and fintech technology, plus team support, to vertical platforms and marketplaces. Co-founder Casey Kipfer said, "we exist to accelerate potential, specifically the payments and fintech potential that exists" [02:06] within those businesses.

q: What is a payment orchestration layer?
a: Kipfer describes it as "the ability to leverage multiple partners to be able to strategically offer products and route transactions" [03:33] or experiences to the best partner for a given user, platform or ecosystem. He says it addresses platforms becoming single-threaded or building up a poorly planned spaghetti mess over time.

q: How long did it take JustiFi to build its MVP?
a: Casey Kipfer said, "Our MVP, you know, really probably took about two to three quarters to build." [04:37] The scope was large because it needed multiple partners, onboarding and underwriting, and money movement ready for the first customer.

q: What early mistake did JustiFi make?
a: The team had identified several markets when it went out to raise its seed round, and solving for all of them was going to be very hard. Kipfer said that "what we needed to do was actually focus on, you know, one of, say, the four areas" [15:25] it had highlighted.

q: How did JustiFi build its early team?
a: Kipfer said probably the first 10 hires were people the founders already knew, including as previous co-workers, which brought a great deal of trust. He explained that "when everybody starts on the same page, it's a lot easier to go fast." [09:56]

s7-e17-the-human-side-of-system-failure-engineering-sociotechnical-resilience-with-nora-jones-founder-of-jeliio

People and Coordination First: Jeli.io coordinates live incidents and analyzes them afterward, surfacing whether the right people, service owners and on-call schedules were in place, and whether people were paged at night.
Annotation Tool as MVP: The early product hooked into Slack, PagerDuty and Workday so teams could highlight key moments from incident conversations. It landed three customers right at the outset.

Unlearning SRE Instincts: Nora's team pushed back on engineering early for upper limits. Hitting one would mean people were using the product, so they separated what was foundational from what could wait for validation.
Culture Built From Best Teams: Early hires described the teams where they did their best work and were happiest. Nora still reviews those results with every new hire during onboarding.

A Holiday Release Lesson: Nora and engineering decided to ship a feature just before the holidays to avoid losing context. An incident followed, touching teams across the company and prompting a spirited, openly discussed review.

q: What is Jeli.io and what makes it different from other reliability tools?
a: Jeli.io is an incident management platform that helps teams coordinate during incidents and analyze them afterward. Nora Jones says its biggest difference is that "we really focus on people and coordination" [03:58].

q: What did the first version of Jeli.io do?
a: The early product was an annotation tool that connected to Slack, PagerDuty and Workday so teams could mark important moments from incident conversations. Nora Jones said it was "akin to reading a book in school and taking a highlighter and writing on the margins" [05:49].

q: How did Jeli.io approach scalability when building its product?
a: Scaling was handled as the company grew, even though SREs on the team were inclined to build for it early. Nora Jones questioned engineering for upper limits too soon, reasoning that "if we hit this upper limit, it means that people are actually using the product" [14:22].

q: What is Jeli.io's Learning Center used for?
a: Learning Center shows metrics and patterns across incidents, helping people make a case for needs such as headcount or more time on a service. Nora Jones said these are "things like that you should have data on to help you tell your story" [16:14].

q: What advice does Nora Jones give to new startup founders?
a: Nora Jones advises founders to choose something they will stay excited about for a long time and to understand what makes them happy. She also urges them to make sure "you are finding a solution to a problem rather than trying to find a problem to fit your solution" [23:46].

s7-bonus-the-algorithmic-recruiter-automating-global-tech-vetting-and-remote-scaling-with-alex-svinov-co-founder-ceo-of-insquad

Look Where Others Aren't: After spending two or three months to hire any decent developer, Svinov went remote. Insquad vets engineers from Africa, Latin America, India and Eastern Europe and matches the best with mostly US startups.
A Deliberately Small MVP: The first version took about three months, used external tools such as authentication and ran on AWS. It let developers join and start taking tests, but had no admin panel.

Treat Tech Debt Like Features: Svinov meets weekly with his CTO and CPO to pick releases that need limited tech debt. He now takes debt as seriously as new functionality, having seen it spiral at an earlier startup.
Test People With Real Work: After interviews on hard and soft skills, new people get simple tasks on day one to reveal behavior. Svinov says teams need technical, management and people leadership.

Scale by Adding Teams: Rather than adding two or three people to a strong team of five to seven, Insquad prefers to build a standalone team beside it, sometimes seeding it with a few experienced engineers.

q: What is Insquad and how does it work?
a: Insquad is a talent platform that matches remote software engineers with startups, predominantly in the US, with some European clients. Alex Svinov explained that candidates go through lots of tests so Insquad can select "the best of the flock, and then we get them matched with the startups" [02:37].

q: Why did Alex Svinov start Insquad?
a: At his last startup, Svinov struggled to hire qualified developers because the strong candidates seemed to get rich offers from wealthier companies. He concluded that "hiring developers shouldn't be that hard" [03:35] and that the answer was to look remotely, not where everyone else was looking.

q: How did Insquad build its MVP?
a: Svinov says the MVP took about three months, relied on external tools such as authentication, and was hosted on AWS. It covered the basics of getting developers onto the platform to take tests, and Svinov recalled that "it was very, very simple with absolutely no administrative panel" [04:54].

q: How should a startup scale its engineering team?
a: Svinov said, "In my experience, software engineering only scales in teams." [13:57] Once there is demand and financing, he prefers to build a separate team next to a successful one, because simply adding people can damage team spirit.

q: What management mistake did Alex Svinov learn from?
a: Svinov says micromanaging limited how large the team and product could grow, made people feel distrusted, and cost him one of his first CTOs. His lesson about great people was that "you have to give them the space to develop and to grow and to build something good" [19:44].

s7-bonus-return-to-komodor-andrey-pohkilko

Beyond Troubleshooting Kubernetes: Komodor is expanding from a troubleshooting platform into a broader place for day-to-day Kubernetes operations, including deployments, application state and seeing who changed what and when.

Open Source Without Lock-In: Komodor's open source tools work without being a Komodor customer. Andrey sees enterprise needs like authentication, SSO and role-based access as where commercial value can sit.
A GUI for Helm: Helm Dashboard shows installed charts, repositories and revision history in a UI. It replaces what can take five to eight commands for a single pass of root cause analysis.

Helm First, Not Platform First: Some existing Helm visualizers sit inside heavy Kubernetes platforms that take time to set up. Komodor built a tool where Helm is the main concern and extras like Checkov and Trivy scanning are secondary.
Marketing Matters in Open Source: Great code goes unnoticed if no one hears about it. Komodor announced Helm Dashboard at KubeCon North America, gained many GitHub stars and then saw organic sharing.

q: What is Helm Dashboard by Komodor?
a: Helm Dashboard is an open source UI for Helm, the package manager for Kubernetes, that lists installed applications, connects repositories and shows chart history. Andrey Pokhilko says it saves time on investigations where the manual answer "is five different commands in the command line, sometimes even eight different commands." [22:39]

q: How is Helm Dashboard different from other Helm visualization tools?
a: Andrey Pokhilko explains that most alternatives are tied to a larger Kubernetes management platform that takes significant setup before you can reach Helm. Komodor took a different approach, and as Andrey put it, "So we created something that is Helm first." [24:10]

q: Why does Komodor invest in open source?
a: Andrey Pokhilko says open source lets Komodor quickly turn ideas outside its commercial product into tools people can use, which also builds reputation. q: How do you make an open source project successful?
a: According to Andrey Pokhilko, a project has to deliver on its promise, and people need to hear about it in the first place. He stressed that "For open source projects, the marketing, the promotional activities actually matter a lot." [09:47]

q: How can I contribute to Helm Dashboard?
a: Andrey Pokhilko points contributors to the project's GitHub repository, where they can ask questions, request features or pick up existing issues and write code for review. He noted that "It's already a contribution if you just create the feature request or you ask the question." [25:41]

s7-e16-the-opentable-for-creative-spaces-engineering-a-saas-enabled-marketplace-with-gabriel-isserlis-of-tutti

No-Code Marketplace First: After failed attempts with HubSpot, Squarespace and others, Gabriel launched on ShareTribe in hours in 2018. At £150 a month, it carried Tutti to 1,000 customers and let the team test what people would pay for.

A Higher Bar for MVP: When rebuilding in its own code, Tutti integrated payments through Stripe Connect despite an advisor saying it wasn't needed. Gabriel set the roadmap by what he considered the base level for a booking platform.

Building Through the Pandemic: The rebuild didn't go seamlessly, and the first version wasn't what Gabriel had asked for. With in-person spaces mostly unused from April 2020 to March 2021, he and two developers in India built full-time.

Scalable in Theory: Engineers strong in JavaScript had no AWS experience, and the site crashed repeatedly mid-pandemic until outside help stepped in. Speed is still a fight, and Gabriel says he'd now probably pick React over Vue.

Treat Decisions as Reversible: Borrowing Jeff Bezos's idea of one-way and two-way decisions, Gabriel views almost everything in the business as reversible. He decides quickly, tries it, and rolls it back if it doesn't work.

q: What is Tutti and what problem does it solve?
a: Tutti is a marketplace where creators search for, request, book and pay online for physical spaces for shoots, rehearsals, recording and performance. Gabriel Isserlis explains, "So it is essentially Airbnb for creative spaces" [03:37], with the wider goal of cutting the admin that takes creators away from creating.

q: How did Tutti build its first MVP without developers?
a: Gabriel used ShareTribe, a white label, no-code marketplace platform that supplies the back end so founders can add their own branding and customers. Recalling the launch on Halloween 2018, he said, "We had an entire marketplace that we hadn't had six hours ago" [05:45].

q: How did Gabriel Isserlis decide what belonged on Tutti's product roadmap?
a: In the early days, Gabriel chose features based on what he personally saw as the base level for a booking platform, including integrated payments. Pushing back on arguments for doing much less, he said, "there's workable and then there's just crap" [10:40].

q: What scaling problems did Tutti run into after leaving ShareTribe?
a: Gabriel's engineers had no AWS experience, and what he believes was a caching issue crippled the site until external help sorted it out. As Gabriel put it, "In the middle of the pandemic, we had the site crash over and over again." [14:41]

q: What advice does Gabriel Isserlis give to early-stage founders?
a: Gabriel advises founders to "be careful who you take advice from" [21:24], since some advisors haven't really been down the road themselves. He also urges them to make sure customers are willing to pay and to stay focused until the first product is working well.

s7-bonus-from-importing-coconut-water-to-running-a-global-500-agent-support-engine-with-nathan-yap-of-supportzebra

A Physical MVP: SupportZebra's first version was a leased 20-seat office, an operations manager and an initial team. To avoid paying for a big generator, they asked the hospital across the street to let them tap into its power.

Guerrilla Recruiting at Scale: Once referrals couldn't keep up, the team enlisted a local DJ, handed out flyers at malls, ran its own university job fairs and sent a jingle-blasting zebra mobile through busy areas.

Narrowing to Two Verticals: After taking any paying client across roughly 10 industries, SupportZebra focused exclusively on SaaS and e-commerce, so tech stack and process lessons could carry across the whole client base.

Culture Over Experience: After hiring several thousand people, Nathan calls experience overrated. He looks for hunger and willingness to learn, digs into references, and would rather leave a role open than rush a poor culture fit.
Letting Go to Scale: Nathan was burnt out in years four to six. Building a stronger leadership team and ceasing to micromanage brought the biggest strides in top and bottom line growth.

q: What does SupportZebra do?
a: Nathan Yap's company builds and manages outsourced customer service programs, including playbooks, metrics, training content, hiring and performance management. In his words, "SupportZebra does white glove outsourced customer service for fast-growing SaaS and e-commerce companies." [02:08]

q: How did SupportZebra get started?
a: Nathan says they fell into outsourcing by accident: their coconut water import business had a back office in the Philippines, and friends and family began asking them to add people. The MVP was physical, which Nathan described as "signing a lease for a 20-seat office. We built out the cubicle." [04:57]

q: How did SupportZebra recruit without a big budget?
a: Nathan's team started with friends, family and referrals, then turned to guerrilla marketing once that network could no longer support their scale. As he recalled, "We canvassed the malls and handing out flyers, went to universities" [06:23].

q: What does Nathan Yap look for when hiring?
a: Nathan puts culture fit ahead of experience, looking for people who are hungry, willing to learn and open to change. He would rather leave a gap than "be rushed to fill a hire that is not 100% culture fit." [16:20]

q: How did SupportZebra approach rising employee attrition?
a: Nathan says spending more money did not fix the problem, which pushed the company to double down on culture, engagement and a fun work environment, and not to keep toxic team members even if they perform. He learned that past a certain point, "money and salaries starts to become diminishing returns" [17:15].

A Narrow, Year-Long MVP: Coalesce took close to a year to ship an MVP, started at the beginning of the pandemic with an offshore team. The goal was to build a simple DAG and generate code on Snowflake.

The Data Ingestion Detour: An early first customer asked for data ingestion, and the team built toward it. Satish calls it a mistake: the space was crowded, the work was heavy and it was outside their vision, so they corrected course.
Skipping the Built-In Scheduler: For the MVP, Coalesce chose not to build a scheduler. Open source options were plentiful, and prospects for the founders' previous tool had wanted to use their own.

Hiring for Passion Over Pedigree: Early hires included boot camp graduates chosen for passion, intelligence, willingness to learn and collaboration. The team has grown from two founders to 40-plus people, mixing veterans and newer engineers.

Architect First, Stress Test Later: The founders laid an architecture meant for scale but did not stress test it at the very beginning. Performance work came as the product matured, and it now scales along with Snowflake underneath.

q: What is Coalesce and what does it do?
a: Coalesce is a SaaS product that turns raw data into a meaningful form so businesses can run analytics and make decisions. As co-founder and CTO Satish Jayanthi put it, "it primarily deals with data transformations." [02:16] The team built it from the ground up on cloud technologies and applies automation to the transformation work.

q: What was in the first version of Coalesce?
a: The MVP took about a year and focused on building a simple DAG and generating code on Snowflake. q: What mistake did Coalesce make in its early days?
a: Satish says the team spent time on data ingestion because their first customer asked for it, even though their goal was transformations. Of that decision, he said, "We just thought that was an easy path, and it was not." [13:41] The space was already crowded and was not their primary background, so they corrected course.

q: How did Coalesce build its engineering team?
a: After starting with an offshore team, the founders brought on a very experienced person in the U.S., which Satish says changed everything. They hired people who were intelligent and wanted to learn, including boot camp graduates, and Satish said "more important to us was that passion that willingness to learn and the collaboration" [10:17].

q: What advice does Satish Jayanthi have for new founders?
a: Satish advises founders to follow their gut and to find a co-founder with complementary skills who agrees on vision, hiring and how to run the company. "But my advice is, if it's possible, don't go solo." [19:04]

s7-e15-from-dot-com-exits-to-celebrity-backed-logistics-the-future-of-corporate-food-tech-ghost-kitchens-with-jeff-grass-of-hungry

Ghost Kitchens Change the Economics: Hungry partners mainly with top local chefs cooking in incubator and ghost kitchens, and its own team handles delivery and service. Grass says this supports high quality, variety and affordable pricing.

Spreadsheets Before Software: The pre-MVP ran on highly complex Google Spreadsheets, letting the team iterate fast on its model. The first core elements of Hungry OS, built with React, Ruby on Rails and SQL, then took about a year to a year and a half.

Innovating Through COVID: When millions in sales evaporated in March 2020, Hungry launched new service lines to keep its team together. Grass says it was profitable within six months and ended up tripling in size during COVID.

Know When to Partner: Scaling last-mile delivery to 1.5 million meals a month in New York, Hungry struggled to build dispatcher UI/UX in-house. It ultimately kept its platform for part of the work and partnered with WorkWave for the rest.

Invest in Product Sooner: For a long time, business staff talked directly to developers, who acted as the product interface. Grass says building a strong product organization sped up development, and he wishes he had done it earlier.

q: What is Hungry and how does its office catering model work?
a: Jeff Grass describes Hungry as a platform connecting companies with local chefs and restaurants for office catering, snacks and events, with Hungry's own team handling delivery and service. He explained that "cooking out of Ghost Kitchens gives us a significant economic advantage versus sourcing food from a restaurant" [02:35].

q: How did Hungry build its MVP?
a: Before writing its platform, Hungry worked out its operating model in spreadsheets, then built the first core elements of Hungry OS with React, Ruby on Rails and a SQL database. Grass said the pre-MVP "was actually building a lot of how we operated in Google Spreadsheets." [03:54]

q: How did Hungry's tech stack change as the company scaled?
a: Grass said that with growth from one city to 14 major cities, "Ruby on Rails just wasn't fast enough." [09:31] Hungry shifted to a microservices architecture, kept React and React Native on the front end, and moved more of its data to Mongo, plus some graph databases.

q: How did Hungry survive the COVID-19 pandemic?
a: Grass said the company tried to hold on to its people and innovate its way through, rolling out new service lines built on its technology, operations and chef network. He recalled that within "Six months, we turned the business profitable with revenue from service lines we'd never started to work on pre-pandemic" [13:34].

q: What startup advice does Jeff Grass give about pivoting?
a: Grass advises founders to stay committed to the bigger vision while remaining flexible about how to get there, and to listen closely to customers. Reflecting on his second company, he said, "We were unwilling to really clearly hear what the market was telling us and to pivot and change." [24:10]

s7-bonus-the-offboarding-architecture-weaponizing-cancellation-flows-to-save-saas-revenue-with-rob-moore-co-founder-cto-of-churnkey

Engineering as Retention: After spending about $20-25K on an outside agency that didn't move the needle, Rob's team built its own cancel flow at Waave. It collected cancellation reasons and offered pauses, discounts or priority support.

Zero Margin for Billing Bugs: Handling other companies' subscription and billing data meant even the MVP needed a first-class cancel flow and no billing bugs. It also had to clearly beat what a company could build in-house in a couple of weeks.

Narrow the Market First: Churnkey launched for Stripe only, waiting over a year to add Chargebee, Paddle and Braintree. Advanced dashboard analytics were also cut, so early users exported data to spreadsheets.

Score Features by ROI: The bootstrapped team scores ideas on build effort and return potential, including market expansion, conversion and expansion revenue. This curbs extraneous work but can push longer-term builds down the road.

No Silver Bullet Tools: Rob says committing too much time to engineering as marketing was a mistake. Tools like a Stripe-connected churn audit still needed heavy marketing to drive traffic and could become a distraction.

q: How did Churnkey get started?
a: Churnkey began as an internal tool at Waave, a podcast marketing product whose growth stalled because new customers couldn't keep up with churn. Rob Moore said of the fix, "The first thing that we did was, and most effective to date, was building out a cancel" [03:12] flow. After selling Waave in March 2021, the founders focused on productizing the tool.

q: How can a cancellation flow reduce SaaS churn?
a: Rob Moore describes a flow that learns why people are canceling and then makes an offer, such as a temporary subscription, discount, pause or priority tech support. His team stopped seeing cancellation as black and white: "There's this huge gray area where customers might still want to use the product," [03:47] but the timing or full price doesn't work for them.

q: Should you build a cancel flow in-house or use a tool like Churnkey?
a: Rob Moore says building in-house is a major alternative companies weigh when evaluating Churnkey. That shaped the MVP, which the team wanted to be significantly better "than what somebody could do in-house in a couple of weeks." [06:02]

q: How does Churnkey decide what to build next?
a: Rob Moore says the team collects feature ideas in a Notion table and talks through each one. As he describes it, "we score them for their level of effort to build and how much ROI potential it has." [08:06]

q: What would Rob Moore change about Churnkey's tech stack?
a: Rob Moore would move the billing data from MongoDB to SQL, saying, "I would have put that in a SQL database for faster querying and the built-in capabilities there." [18:23] He would also use TypeScript on the back end instead of the front end, though he says these choices have had very little day-to-day impact.

s7-bonus-from-commodore-128-self-taught-coder-to-building-an-ai-map-engine-with-juan-soberanis-of-beacon

Privacy as the Position: Beacon moved from navigation sharing to privacy-first location sharing, aiming to be to location what Signal is to messaging. Juan says encryption means even he can't read location data in the database.

Firebase Cut the Burn: Needing to pivot fast and spend less, Juan moved from AWS to Firebase. Engineering went from three people to one, and the app developer could also handle server work. The 1.0 MVP took about three months.

Quality Was the Trade-Off: To experiment without overinvesting in features that might be thrown away, the team accepted usability glitches, missing animations and a bug backlog, while keeping stability reasonably solid.

Pivot Sparked Growth: Weak traction on 1.0 led to a significant pivot and a 2.0 about three months later. At recording, Juan reported about 30% week-over-week growth and 5,000 monthly active users on a small ad budget.
Focus Means Saying Not Now: Juan advises founders to target a specific customer, say "not now" or no to the rest, and hold on to their why while staying flexible about how they get there.

q: What is Beacon and how does it protect location data?
a: Beacon is a location sharing product for finding family and friends, which Juan Soberanis says uses end-to-end encryption so location data can't be sold, tracked or abused. As Juan put it, "even me with access to the database, I can't see people's location data" [02:41].

q: Why did Juan Soberanis move from AWS to Firebase?
a: Juan needed to reduce burn rate and pivot quickly, and found AWS powerful but complicated for that goal. Firebase let him shrink the team because "the app developer, me, could also do the server development" [05:15].

q: Was Beacon built to scale from day one?
a: Yes, Juan says it was built to scale from the start, and serverless technology means the team doesn't worry about server downtime or signup surges. He explained that when they "switched to Firebase, it was a conscious choice for scalability, but also for its ability to sync" [11:15] data between server and mobile apps in real time.

q: How does Beacon decide what to build next?
a: Juan draws on traction numbers, market research, conversations with advisors and business contacts, and feedback from a user community the company is starting in Facebook groups. Describing that community, he said, "our mission is to delight 100 customers" [09:03].

q: What mistakes did Juan Soberanis learn from while building Beacon?
a: Rather than naming one incident, Juan describes the search for product-market fit and the right early adopters as a learning curve, which led to a sharp focus on families with tweens and teens. In his words, "The whole journey up to this point has been a series of mistakes" [13:22].

s7-e14-the-royalties-exchange-engineering-a-fractionalized-music-investment-engine-with-olga-stern-cto-of-tangy-market

Royalties as an Asset Class: Tangy Market lets anyone with the app invest in music royalties, while songwriters, recording creators and artists get an advance instead of waiting years for radio and streaming payouts.

Cut Non-Essentials to Launch: The team went from first Git commit in September to launch in March. It shipped without password reset, added it a month or two later, and nobody had asked for it in the meantime.
Serverless for Speed and Scale: The back end runs on AWS Lambda with queues and SAM. A new feature can be a new function plus an API route, though heavier load testing still exposed some odd bugs.

Culture Add Over Culture Fit: Olga's team looks for people who bring missing viewpoints, plus strong communication skills. A culture clash with a summer data hire taught them to discuss expectations during hiring.

Start Cheap, Then Refactor: Olga would resist building the elegant solution on the first try. She struggled with AWS documentation early on, although that work left them with easy-to-deploy development and production environments.

q: What is Tangy Market?
a: Tangy Market is a marketplace for music royalties that also lets music creators get an advance on their work. As CTO Olga Stern describes it, "Tangy Market is an online marketplace where anyone can invest in music royalties." [02:07]

q: How do music creators benefit from selling royalties on Tangy Market?
a: Instead of waiting year after year for radio and streaming income, creators can receive money up front and reinvest it; Olga Stern says some artists have hired producers or bought a synthesizer. She explains that "you can get it in one chunk, and that way you can make an investment" [04:16].

q: How long did it take to build the Tangy Market MVP?
a: Olga Stern recalls a first Git commit in September and a launch in March, after the team mapped user flows and sketched screens in Figma. Cutting features was key, and she points to "things that you remove that actually let you launch your product kind of on time." [07:20]

q: What tech stack does Tangy Market use to scale?
a: Olga Stern says everything runs on AWS, with a serverless back end built on Lambda functions, queues, an API and the Serverless Application Model (SAM). On handling growth, she says, "Everything is serverless, everything is functions, so basically we just have to flip a switch" [16:26].

q: How does Tangy Market decide what to build next?
a: Olga Stern says user feedback is an important source for the roadmap, alongside studying other investment apps and considering what potential investors would see as smart steps. The team made a communication channel a high priority at launch, figuring that "if it's easy for them to get in touch, then they'll let us know" [09:33].

s7-bonus-author-nick-donofrio-if-nothing-changes-nothing-changes

Change Something to Get Something: The book's title comes from Donofrio's father, who never finished 10th grade. His point on the front porch: if what you've been getting isn't what you want, stop doing what you've been doing.

A 1.1 That Changed Everything: As a new manager, Donofrio scored 1.1 on IBM's opinion survey, where 1 was worst. He told his team he had been doing their jobs rather than managing them, and promised to become their advocate and enabler.

Betting on FET Chips: At IBM, Donofrio designed two of the three key chips in a new semiconductor memory subsystem. His early bias toward FET over bipolar technology proved right, and he says it saved his job twice.

Family Decisions Need Voices: Writing the book, Donofrio concluded he hadn't given his family a real say in IBM relocations, including three moves in about two and a half years. He says he probably wouldn't do it that way again.

Graduate, Don't Retire: Donofrio urges people leaving a first career to say "graduated," build a network and decide what truly interests them. At 77, he says he still sits on 10 boards and helps enable women and people of color in technology.

q: Why did Nick Donofrio write If Nothing Changes, Nothing Changes?
a: Donofrio wanted to tell his own story and help readers draw out leadership traits he believes are probably already in them. He described "documenting my life before somebody else decides that they want to tell the story" [01:00], a project that took six years with Mike DeMarco.

q: Where does the phrase "If nothing changes, nothing changes" come from?
a: Nick Donofrio got the phrase from his father during a front porch conversation in his high school years. Donofrio recalled his father asking that if you aren't getting what you want, "why do you keep doing what you've been doing, son?" [06:54].

q: What did Nick Donofrio work on at IBM?
a: Donofrio started as a co-op student in 1964, working on ferrite core memory and other System 360 assignments, and later designed chips as IBM moved to semiconductor memory. "I was fortunate enough to have designed like two of the three chips that mattered" [13:11], he said of the new memory subsystem.

q: What is Nick Donofrio's management philosophy?
a: Donofrio centers it on teams, collaboration and enabling people to do their best, with less concern about who gets credit. After a poor opinion survey, he told his team, "I will enable you to do your job as well as you could have ever imagined" [16:39].

q: What advice does Nick Donofrio give people retiring from their first career?
a: Donofrio advises changing how you describe it, then building a social network and deciding what you really want to engage in. As he put it, "you have to stop using the word retired" [25:40], and say you have graduated instead.

s7-bonus-the-integration-bottleneck-reclaiming-50-of-rd-capacity-with-michael-zuercher-co-founder-ceo-of-prismatic

Built From 600 Integrations: At his law enforcement software company, Zuercher's team built 600 productized integrations for a couple thousand customers, a burden that weighed on onboarding and sales and led him to start Prismatic.

MVP as Conversation Prop: Prismatic built just enough to test key parts of its thesis with private beta customers, guarding against the founders over-indexing on their own experience and limiting what they'd throw away if wrong.
A Roughly Half-and-Half Roadmap: After the MVP, about 50% of the roadmap was sequencing the original vision. The other 50% came from new lessons as more customers used the platform.

Build Order Matters: Zuercher says key pieces of the platform could have been built more simply in a different order. Missing a bit on the overall vision early cost the team a few months of wandering.

Capitalize Once You Have Fit: Looking back, Zuercher says his previous company had product-market fit but was undercapitalized, and should have stopped bootstrapping and taken institutional capital a couple of years sooner.

q: What is Prismatic and who is it for?
a: Prismatic helps software companies build, deploy and maintain integrations for their customers. Michael Zuercher describes it as "an integration platform that is focused on helping software companies provide integrations to their customers" [02:10].

q: Why did Michael Zuercher start Prismatic?
a: Integrations remained a significant challenge at his previous law enforcement software company, and he found no platform focused on the problem. After selling it, he teamed up with his former CTO and one other person and, in Zuercher's words, set out to say "we're going to build the thing we wish we always had." [04:33]

q: What tech stack is Prismatic built on?
a: Zuercher describes it as a fairly traditional software stack that grew more complex on the way to version one. He listed "Node and TypeScript, and it's built on top of AWS and has Python in the back end" [05:43], along with a PostgreSQL database.

q: How did Prismatic approach its MVP?
a: The team focused on proving the most important parts of its thesis and checking that its view of the problem reflected a real market. Zuercher said they were focused on "building just enough to kind of act as a prop almost in conversations" [07:04] with early beta customers.

q: What advice does Michael Zuercher give early-stage founders?
a: Zuercher advises focusing on the product, seen through the customer's eyes, and ignoring much of the outside noise. He believes that "if you focus on solving a real problem for a real customer, a lot of other things just take care of themselves." [20:10]

s7-e13-from-fake-ai-to-60000-organizations-unlocking-product-market-fit-with-krish-ramineni-of-firefliesai

Validate Before Writing Code: Before building any automation, Krish and co-founder Sam had real people join meetings, take notes and email them afterward. Customers paid for it for a couple of months, proving the demand.

Driving Down Transcription Costs: Transcription once cost a dollar a minute, or $60 for a one-hour meeting. Fireflies worked toward $10 to $20 subscriptions covering fully automated transcripts and summaries.

Rebuilding for Scale: After a 2019 seed round, the team grew from three to 10, scrapped the off-the-shelf beta and rebuilt from the ground up to handle thousands of simultaneous meetings at lower compute cost.

Flat Pricing Over Metering: Per-minute pricing made users worry about overages. A flat monthly price proved far more successful and simplified buying, despite early fears that heavy users would abuse the platform.

Take a Stand on Advice: Conflicting advice on enterprise sales, verticals and being in Silicon Valley had the team running in circles. Krish estimates not taking the wrong advice would have saved easily six months.

q: What does Fireflies.ai do?
a: Krish Ramineni describes Fireflies as an AI meeting assistant that joins calls on platforms like Zoom, WebEx, Microsoft Teams and Google Meet. As he explains, "it records, transcribes, and generates notes from those meetings" [02:21]. It also analyzes sentiment, speaking time and topics discussed.

q: How did Fireflies.ai validate its idea before building the product?
a: Krish and his co-founder Sam started with a manual service in which a real person joined meetings, took notes and emailed them afterward. Krish said that before writing any code, "we would build a human in the loop system" [04:11]. People paid for it, which showed the problem was worth automating.

q: How did Fireflies.ai prepare its platform to scale?
a: The team rebuilt the platform from scratch, moving away from off-the-shelf tools and working to cut compute costs. Krish described planning for the point when there are "10,000 simultaneous calls that are happening? So we had to build for scale" [09:20].

q: What did Fireflies.ai learn about SaaS pricing?
a: Because the technology was expensive early on, Fireflies charged based on usage, which left people worried about overages. Krish said that "our product was way more successful when we said" [19:03] there was a flat price with a set allowance. He noted the allowance was more than enough for 95% of customers.

q: What does Krish Ramineni say about taking startup advice?
a: Krish said contradicting advice left the team running in circles when they should have taken a stand and proved things out faster. In his words, "advice is subjective and you have to do things your own way and figure it out" [24:24].

s7-bonus-from-counter-terrorism-network-analysis-to-mapping-workplace-connection-with-shawn-ramirez-of-mystery
Dates to Remote Teams: Mystery began by orchestrating surprise dates. When COVID hit, it moved to virtual events and found they created positive outcomes for remote teams, which became its focus.

Scores Must Be Believable: The MVP had to score connection for teams Mystery had never met. Since employees could see themselves marked as poorly connected, the team had to be able to stand behind the data.
Context Changes the Reading: Mystery started with calendar data, then added HR data. A CEO probably shouldn't be closely connected to everyone, while someone in product may connect with many teams.

Roadmap by Levers and Data: Mystery weighs the ROI of potential levers, such as peer awards or employee resource groups, then plans the data sources and engineering work needed to make them effective.

Research the Customer's Tools: In hindsight, Ramirez would talk to people leaders first about what they already use, such as Lattice, and use that to decide which integrations and levers to prioritize.

q: What does Mystery do?
a: Mystery builds surprise events for teams and measures how connected employees are, then arranges experiences to bring people together. Shawn Ramirez, its VP of Data Science, describes it simply: "Mystery is a company that is creating happiness at work." [02:18]

q: How did Mystery pivot from surprise dates to team events?
a: Mystery started out as something close to a dating service, planning surprise dates, until COVID made that model a poor fit. Ramirez explains that the company moved to virtual dates, and then "they started to realize that actually virtual events create really positive outcomes for remote teams." [03:29]

q: How does Mystery measure workplace connection?
a: Mystery infers connection from digital footprint data, beginning with who employees meet, when and how often, and adding HR data for organizational context. Ramirez said, "So we started with calendar integration, thinking that's the easiest way to measure" [13:11] connection.

q: How does Mystery decide what to build next?
a: The roadmap is split between choosing which levers for workplace happiness to build and which data will make them effective. Ramirez said one way Mystery scopes it is by "isolating and doing the ROI or calculating the ROI on these potential levers." [12:31]

q: What mistake did Shawn Ramirez make when approaching connection data?
a: Ramirez says she underestimated the problem at first, doubting that data could show whether people were really connected. After scoping it further, she concluded that connection is multidimensional and dynamic: "It's more like a fabric of connection than like a connection score." [21:23]

s7-bonus-the-first-benefits-placement-system-engineering-a-shared-architecture-for-a-150b-industry-with-shaheeb-roshan-co-founder-cto-of-threeflow
Sell the Prototype First: Rich and Ryan built a clickable InVision prototype, and it was used to capture ThreeFlow's first four accounts. A Rails and React app on a tiny Heroku dyno followed.

Splitting the Early Monolith: Combining Rails and React meant any UI change redeployed the whole app, and performance suffered with only tens of users. The team separated a backend API service from a series of frontend apps.

Senior Specialists Before Full Stack: The founding engineering team favored deeply specialized front-end and back-end engineers, with at least seven to eight years of experience, to shape the architecture and mentor later hires.

Refactors as Investments: Shaheeb says the two significant refactors were driven by new insurance lines and workflows, not meltdowns. Making time for tech debt takes buy-in from non-technical teams at sprint and quarterly planning.
Get Management Help Earlier: Pushing to rescue a slipping project in 2021 worsened team burnout. The lesson led Shaheeb to build support around himself, including VP of Engineering Brett Carter.

q: What problem does ThreeFlow solve in employee benefits insurance?
a: Shaheeb Roshan explains that brokers and carriers have largely worked through phone calls, emails, PDFs and spreadsheets, which can lead to errors that surface during claims. In his words, the business "historically has been transacted with rather poor modern tooling" [03:23].

q: How did ThreeFlow build its first MVP?
a: After using an InVision prototype to land four accounts, the team built a monolithic Rails and React single-page application and deployed it on Heroku. Shaheeb recalls a "tiny dyno that would fall over every time you had more than like, you know, five users" [07:07].

q: Why did ThreeFlow move away from its monolithic architecture?
a: Shaheeb says front-end bloat and back-end strain made certain interactions unusable as more users came on. The team learned it had two full-featured layers "that each needed to be optimized separately from the other" [09:47], so it split them into an API service and front-end applications.

q: How did ThreeFlow hire its founding engineering team?
a: Shaheeb says the founders deliberately chose deep experience, hiring specialists who could lay the architecture and draw other strong engineers from their networks. He explains that "our early founding engineering team would bias more towards senior engineers" [16:20] rather than full-stack generalists.

q: What mistake did Shaheeb Roshan make while managing a growing engineering team?
a: During a 2021 growth period, Shaheeb focused on getting a lagging project back on track and missed the burnout one of his managers was trying to surface. As Shaheeb put it, "What I was actually doing was just like shoveling coal onto that fire." [25:01]

s7-e12-the-finops-revolution-turning-cloud-chaos-into-unit-economics-with-roi-ravhon-co-founder-ceo-of-finout

From Cloud Bills to Unit Economics: Finout takes usage-based costs from cloud providers and tools like Snowflake and Datadog, breaks them down, and assigns them to teams, features and products, so customers can see spend per event, click or transaction.

Design Partners Shaped the MVP: Roi's team gathered as many design partners as it could for constant feedback during development. It built on AWS, Kubernetes and managed services, putting time to market first.
Speed With a Testing Floor: Finout accepts some technical debt to ship before money runs out, but holds a firm line: no feature is released, and no pull request approved, without tests.

DevOps, Not Finance: Finance leaders liked the pitch but lacked the organizational influence to drive adoption. Shifting to DevOps engineers, who field finance's cost questions and want fast integration, sent conversion soaring.

Get an Office Sooner: Looking back, Roi would go all in on a dedicated office as early as possible. Moving from shared WeWork space to Finout's own Tel Aviv office immediately changed how the team worked together.

q: What problem led Roi Ravhon to start Finout?
a: As an engineering director at Logz.io, Roi faced finance questions about cloud spend, customer costs and feature pricing that existing tools couldn't explain. Roi said, "We felt that we should have the answers to those questions that were supposed to be trivial." [02:51]

q: How does Finout allocate cloud costs?
a: Roi explains that Finout collects usage-based costs, cleans and enriches them, and breaks them into granular units using technologies such as Kubernetes, Spark and RDS. In Roi's words, "we can help customers assign the cost directly to their respective team, feature, product, whatever that they're running on." [03:39]

q: How was the Finout MVP built?
a: Roi says the team built on AWS and Kubernetes with as many managed services as it could, using Node.js and Python, while design partners gave constant feedback. Roi said, "You know, we prioritize time to market more than anything." [05:25]

q: What was an early mistake Finout made?
a: Roi says the team first aimed the product at finance, whose leaders were receptive but lacked the influence to get organizational buy-in. "So I think very early on, we focused the product on the wrong persona." [11:28] Roi said that shifting to DevOps engineers brought a dramatic improvement.

q: What is the long-term vision for Finout?
a: Roi argues that traditional systems break down when instances are billed by the second and queries by the gig. According to Roi, "the way that we envision Finout is to be that next generation of ERP systems" [13:36] for cloud-native technologies, serving as the system of record for cloud spend.

eb87e5db-0a9d-42ea-9df3-f4c2950b81f9
s7-bonus-the-death-of-static-credentials-architecting-hardware-attested-device-identity-with-mike-malone-founder-ceo-of-smallstep

Authentication Before Authorization: Smallstep began with a custom policy language for service-to-service authorization. Prospects said they couldn't yet verify which service was calling, which led the team into certificate management.

Launching Without Billing: The commercial MVP took roughly three to six months and shipped without billing. The team figured the 30-day free trial gave them time to build it before anyone's trial ended.

Architect for Scale First: Malone accepts implementations that can't yet handle full scale and iterates on them later. He works harder to avoid APIs, interfaces or features that inherently can't scale.

The On-Prem Cost of Microservices: Smallstep's Kubernetes dependency and service-oriented architecture have complicated on-premise deployments. Malone also calls writing the first iteration of the technology in Haskell a mistake.

Desire Over Language Experience: Malone hires for intelligence and passion that overlaps with the work, plus a culture gut check. Wanting to learn the team's programming language matters more to him than already knowing it.

q: What does Smallstep do?
a: Smallstep helps large organizations manage certificates for their internal infrastructure, positioning itself as production identity for DevOps and cloud native environments. As Mike Malone put it, "our core technology does certificate management." [02:23]

q: Why did Smallstep move from authorization to certificate management?
a: Mike Malone's team first built a programming language for authorization policies between services, but prospects lacked a consistent authentication layer. He explained that "any policy on top of that inter-service communication is sort of useless because we don't know who's making the call." [06:17]

q: What is ACME device attestation, and how does it relate to SCEP?
a: Malone describes it as an open standard, implemented in Apple's newly announced zero-touch secure enrollment technology, for enrolling devices such as iPhones and laptops in enterprise IT. He said it is "replacing seeing" no older protocol lightly, calling SCEP an "older school, really insecure, crappy protocol called SCEP" [18:45].

q: How does Smallstep decide what to build next on its roadmap?
a: Mike Malone prefers to feel a pain firsthand, so the team dogfoods and adopts technologies its customers may be using. Listening to others comes second, and he said "The best way in my experience to develop roadmap is to experience a pain yourself" [10:18].

q: Did being open source help Smallstep recruit engineers?
a: Yes. Mike Malone said the company has hired from its own community, and some engineers see public open source work as a perk that helps their careers. In his words, "being open source is a huge advantage." [13:31]

s7-bonus-the-spatial-applied-math-engine-building-geospatial-ai-for-franchise-growth-with-kateryna-sytnyk-co-founder-of-fract-cto-doctor

Geospatial AI for Territories: Fract helps brands decide where in the physical world to target customers, such as which zip codes make up a franchise or marketing territory, and predicts revenue using geospatial AI.

The Cost of a Fast MVP: Fract's first version was built on Drupal because the team knew it and could ship right away. The near-total rewrite, moving to Node.js, MongoDB and Vue.js, slowed them down by probably half a year.

Manual Work Behind the MVP: Early on, the team put the user experience first and uploaded some data files by hand, deferring the automation needed to import, export and process large volumes of Excel data.

Roadmaps From Sales Calls: Feature ideas came from sitting on sales calls. The team rated each for customer value and estimated complexity in Fibonacci points, then planned the next few months in sprints.

Complex Models, Simple Answers: Kateryna is proud that Fract turned heavy data processing into plain-sentence insights, such as telling an eyelash extension store that nearby high sales of bodywork services matter for placement.

q: What is Fract and what does its geospatial AI do?
a: Fract is a product Kateryna Sytnyk co-founded that predicts revenue and helps define franchise or marketing territories. As Kateryna put it, "it's helping brands figure out where in the physical world is best to target their customer" [02:21].

q: Why did Fract have to rewrite its product?
a: Kateryna Sytnyk says the first version was built on Drupal for speed, even though it was not the best tool for the job. The team pretty much had to rewrite "the whole product over and it did slow us down for probably half a year" [14:45].

q: How did Fract decide which features to build next?
a: Kateryna Sytnyk's team gathered needs directly from customers, then rated features by value and complexity before splitting the work into sprints. Describing the early days, she said "it was just being on the sales calls" [07:04] and figuring out what would make customers' lives easier.

q: What is CTO Doctor and who is it for?
a: CTO Doctor is Kateryna Sytnyk's company that builds MVPs and provides fractional CTO support to women founders of early-stage startups without a technical co-founder. Of the search for one, she said, "finding a technical co-founder, I find that a lot of them struggle" [16:39].

q: What should early-stage startups look for when hiring engineers?
a: Kateryna Sytnyk looks for technical skill combined with ownership, initiative, low ego and strong teamwork. She also values engineers who grasp the customer's needs, saying that "if they can understand also the end user problem, that's where the magic happens" [09:18].

s7-bonus-the-80-software-problem-eradicating-boilerplate-code-with-micro-app-architectures-with-john-rush-founder-of-marsx

Modifiable Blocks Over Fixed Ones: MarsX assembles projects from reusable microapps such as payments, search and user profiles. Block-based building isn't new, John says; the difference is making each block easy to modify when custom needs arise.

Manual Work Behind the MVP: Built in three months of evenings and weekends, the MVP cut almost everything about UX. A project creation form simply emailed John, who set up each project himself and sent back the URL.

Users Became the Builders: John triaged repeated requests and bug reports, then made it simple for any user to contribute fixes. He estimates that after about five months, 90% of the code came from developers using the platform.

Rebuild Instead of Carrying Legacy: The second version was written from scratch in six months and wasn't compatible with the first. John's team helped port users' projects, and did the same for the third and fourth versions.

Hiring From the Contributor Community: After a year as the only team member, John offered full-time roles with equity to top contributors. He also says growing the team too late was a mistake, since programming took 90% of his time.

q: What is MarsX and how do its microapps work?
a: MarsX lets developers and non-developers build projects from ready-made blocks of functionality called microapps, which developers can sell through a marketplace. John Rush stresses that "it's really important that the blocks are modifiable, that you can actually change the block" [03:10].

q: How did John Rush build the MarsX MVP in three months?
a: Working alone on evenings and weekends, John used traditional tools for the first month, then built MarsX on itself. He also handled some features by hand, such as project creation: "I get an email and I just go and do it myself very quickly" [08:13].

q: How did MarsX get its users to contribute code?
a: John built the platform so that anyone using it could easily fix bugs or add the features they needed, and developers who fixed others' problems earned likes from their peers. By John's estimate, after about five months "90% of the code was coming not from me" [11:07].

q: Should the first version of a product be built to scale?
a: John Rush believes building something unscalable is usually the least wrong choice, though he says it carries risk and can depend on the project. Of the first version of MarsX, he said, "I knew that the first version has to be so crappy that I have no feelings for it" [14:26].

q: What advice does John Rush give to young entrepreneurs?
a: John advises founders to work on a problem they personally experience and to love the users they are serving, rather than chasing a trend. In his words, "do not try to build something you don't care about" [27:20].

s7-bonus-bypassing-the-zoom-fatigue-building-threaded-on-screen-contextual-video-pipelines-with-tom-medema-of-bubbles

Slack Meets Zoom, Asynchronously: Bubbles lets teammates record themselves or their screen and share a link, and others reply with video when it suits them. You keep tone of voice, facial expressions and screen sharing without meeting live.

A Four-Week Proxy MVP: After spending years on earlier products, Medema scoped Bubbles' first version to about four weeks. It let users screenshot and annotate a website, a proxy for the bigger product that validated demand and brought early traction.
Skip Billing and Login First: To ship faster, the team initially left out billing and authentication. Videos were kept private by making each one accessible over a secret, unguessable URL.

Remote Pain Improved the Product: Medema first tried building a local team in San Francisco, then went fully remote. Local talent was hard to find, and using Bubbles to work through remote friction helped the team build a much better product.

Confidence in Async Replies: User research showed people worry that async messages won't get timely or serious responses. Bubbles' planned features aim to give teams confidence an answer will arrive within a window such as eight or 24 hours.

q: What is Bubbles and how does it work?
a: Bubbles is an asynchronous video collaboration tool where you record yourself or your screen and send it to teammates, who can respond with video when convenient. Tom Medema describes it this way: "Imagine Slack and Zoom having a baby." [02:09]

q: How long did it take to build the Bubbles MVP?
a: Medema deliberately narrowed the scope to a first version that let users take a screenshot of a website and annotate it. He said, "I thought of an MVP that only took about four weeks to build." [04:49]

q: How did Bubbles keep videos private without authentication?
a: The team postponed authentication and billing so it could release much faster. Instead, Medema explained, every video "will be accessible over a secret, unguessable URL link." [06:24]

q: Why did Tom Medema move Bubbles to a fully remote team?
a: He initially believed a founding team in a San Francisco office was necessary, but found local talent very difficult to hire. Medema also learned that "by actually embracing those issues around remote work, we are able to build a much better product." [12:37]

q: Does asynchronous work mean slower responses?
a: Not necessarily, according to Medema, although a reply may not come within five minutes. He said "asynchronous doesn't mean that you're not going to get a response quickly" [14:19], and Bubbles is focusing on giving teams confidence that answers will arrive in a timely manner.

s7-e10-the-low-code-boom-bringing-devops-and-git-to-enterprise-data-pipelines-with-raj-bains-of-prophecy

Trade Market Risk for Execution: After his machine learning studio failed with analysts, Raj Bains pivoted to production data engineering, targeting replacement of legacy ETL as companies moved to the cloud, where he knew the market existed.

Migration Work as Product Research: Bains took a contract to build an automated translator from a very large company's old ETL product to Spark. It exposed its complex pipelines and what a replacement would minimally need.

Composable Blocks for a Changing Product: Prophecy was built as microservices made of small libraries, so pieces could be reassembled or fixed with limited damage. Code only had to be okay while product-market fit was unproven.

Core Tech Work Attracts Talent: Unable to compete for Bay Area hires, Bains grew engineering in India, paying well and offering core technology work, not the secondary work often sent there. That drew very smart engineers.

Get to Users Sooner: Bains says he spent too long building and would now ship a really small product early. Going straight to enterprise was painful, though he believes it avoided architectures that couldn't scale.

q: What is Prophecy and who is it for?
a: Prophecy is a low-code data engineering product that Raj Bains says lets people build data pipelines without being experts in PySpark, Scala or even SQL, including business users who know the data. As Bains put it, "what we provide is software that makes it super easy, right? It's visual drag and drop." [03:21]

q: Why did Raj Bains start Prophecy?
a: Bains came from compilers and CUDA, then became product manager for Apache Hive at Hortonworks, where he saw customers struggling with hard-to-use tools for building data pipelines. Looking at the tooling, he concluded that "we're still in the stone age we can build something way better" [04:39].

q: How was the Prophecy MVP built?
a: Bains moved back to his parents' house in India, spent six or seven months teaching himself cloud and Kubernetes programming, and built with Scala, React and a couple of contract UI developers. For flexibility, his choice was to "build the product as microservices and even within microservices as the small libraries" [08:28].

q: How did Prophecy hire strong engineers as an early-stage startup?
a: Bains lacked the Bay Area network and found salaries there very high, so he hired in India and offered engineers the chance to work on core technology. He recalled his pitch: "we are going to build a core tech company and going to build a core tech in India" [13:00].

q: What advice does Raj Bains have for startup founders?
a: Bains advises founders to stay in the game, because they keep learning and give luck a chance to swing their way. As Bains put it, "if I could give any advice is stay long enough in the game." [22:59] He credits being relentless with carrying him through his mistakes.

s7-bonus-the-blueprint-for-a-1b-product-launch-automating-gtm-silos-with-derek-osgood-founder-of-ignition

Push Information to Teams: Ignition modularizes launch plans and sends each team only the relevant pieces by email or Slack, so groups like sales don't have to adopt a new tool or dig for information.

An MVP Built to Learn: The first version was mostly customizable text documents plus basic email sharing. Templates and research tools were cut to learn what goes into users' launch plans and how they share them.

Table Stakes Don't Differentiate: Derek says the team spent too long overhauling core documentation, burning a couple of months. They should have focused on the automation and tooling that set Ignition apart.

Get Dollars Before Building: Many early would-be customers changed jobs midway through the alpha, and feedback evaporated. Derek would now collect money up front, even if fully refundable, to keep them engaged.

Avoid Unneeded Market Risk: Ignition's category creation approach means there's no existing budget line, so more people must buy in. Derek advises selling into an existing budget when possible, as with payroll tools at Rippling.

q: What is Ignition and what does it do?
a: Ignition is a go-to-market platform from co-founder and CEO Derek Osgood that combines project management, documentation, asset management and launch workflows. As Derek put it, "Ignition's basically at its core a platform for managing go-to-market processes," [02:16].

q: Why did Derek Osgood start Ignition?
a: Derek had been through hundreds of launches, at companies ranging from PlayStation to small startups, and found the process fragmented and inconsistent. Of those launches, he said, "They were just always dumpster fires." [04:37]. After trying to build the process in many tools that didn't work for it, he started his own company.

q: What was the first version of Ignition like?
a: Derek and his co-founder wrote their first line of code in March 2021, shipped an alpha that July and a beta the following January. Describing that first incarnation, Derek said, "It was basically just modular documentation." [06:25], paired with tools for sharing pieces of it by email.

q: What mistake did the Ignition team make while building the product?
a: Following customer feedback, the team did a significant documentation overhaul between the first and second versions. Derek admitted, "We definitely spent too much time revamping the kind of core documentation." [18:28], when differentiating automation features deserved more focus.

q: What advice does Derek Osgood have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Derek advises shipping fast and keeping what you build as narrow as possible. He also warns founders, "don't take market risk if you don't have to," [26:47], and suggests selling into an existing budget where possible.

s7-bonus-the-tipping-protocol-normalizing-mobile-payments-for-home-services-with-justin-clegg-founder-ceo-of-allset

Tipping Was the Wedge: Allset's MVP was SMS-based tipping, with an average tip of $25 and about a 16% conversion from text sent to tip received. It later grew into a full payments and communications platform.

Text Beat the App: Allset built an app that busy tradespeople didn't want to download or learn. That pushed the team to SMS, with automated messages running in the background so owners could set it and forget it.

Passing Along Card Fees: Business owners see about 3 to 4% in card processing fees. Allset helps them pass those fees on to clients compliantly, alongside text payments, review and referral capture, and automated messaging.

Freemium for a Tough Market: Because busy trades businesses can balk at paying upfront for a subscription, Allset has spent time building a freemium model that earns from on-platform transactions, a revenue stream in addition to SaaS.

Don't Hire from Desperation: Justin says some early hires were made out of need rather than quality. His lesson is to wait for the right person, and when a hire misses, act quickly and give them a soft landing.

q: What is Allset and who is it for?
a: Allset is a payments and communications platform for home service businesses such as plumbers, HVAC, roofers, painters, cleaners and outdoor care providers. Justin Clegg says it "is designed to run in the background for these professionals" [02:51], helping them accept payments by text, capture reviews and referrals, and automate communication.

q: How did Justin Clegg come up with the idea for Allset?
a: A handyman did work at Justin's home, and Justin had no way to pay him. Justin recalled, "I offered to pay him with Venmo and he didn't use Venmo" [03:44], and that handyman later became Allset's first merchant.

q: What was Allset's first MVP?
a: The early product centered on SMS-based tipping, which business owners liked at a time when retaining employees was a challenge. Justin said the team found that "when prompted through text, Americans will leave an average $25 tip" [04:58].

q: Why does Allset use text messages instead of relying on a mobile app?
a: The team did build an app, but Justin says that "as it turns out, no one wanted to download because tradespeople are busy" [07:55]. SMS let Allset send automated messages for them without requiring them to learn a new interface.

q: How does Allset decide what to build next?
a: Justin says the go-to-market team talks with customers by phone and in person at trade shows to learn their biggest pain points, and that feedback informs the roadmap. When the same need keeps coming up, "then it really becomes a prioritized feature" [09:50].

s7-e9-the-evolution-of-mlops-rebranding-gridai-and-building-modular-ai-platforms-with-william-falcon-ceo-of-lightning-ai

From Research Code to Platform: PyTorch Lightning began in Falcon's undergrad around 2015 on Theano, later TensorFlow, then was largely rewritten in PyTorch. Enterprise production problems like fault tolerance and cluster scaling led to Lightning, once also known as Grid.

MVPs Measured in Years: PyTorch Lightning took about four to five years to reach a stable MVP around fall 2019. The current platform's MVP took roughly another two years because it handles infrastructure and compute for full businesses.

Selective Tech Debt: Falcon will take on debt to ship products, but not in platform foundations that everything else is built on. Deciding when to pay it down has been one of the team's hardest trade-offs.

Underbuild, Then Scale: Rather than designing for millions of users upfront, Falcon pushes the team to build for 100, let it break, fix the cause, then target 1,000. This limits overbuilding and makes unsuccessful products cheaper to kill.

Hire for Company Stage: Falcon says some early mistakes were hiring executives who were excellent but wrong for the stage. A public-company CTO or an overly rigorous big-tech engineer may not suit a small startup.

q: What does Lightning AI let developers build?
a: Lightning helps developers build machine learning products, including training and deploying models and connecting pieces such as data labeling and user interfaces. William Falcon said it "lets you build machine learning products, like machine learning SaaS products" [04:08].

q: How is Lightning AI related to PyTorch Lightning and Grid.ai?
a: PyTorch Lightning is a framework Falcon created to scale deep learning training, and its enterprise adoption exposed production problems that led to the company. On the naming, Falcon said "At the time, it was also known as Grid, so a lot of rebranding." [04:04]

q: How should startups think about technical debt?
a: Falcon argues that startups should put shipping the product ahead of perfect code, while keeping infrastructure foundations strong. In his words, "your goal isn't to have pristine code, your goal is to actually build the product" [07:11].

q: Should you build a product to scale from day one?
a: William Falcon advises against it, preferring to add scale as real usage reveals where the product breaks. "So you should not be building for that. Build for 100 users" [12:49], he said, before moving on to the next milestone of 1,000.

q: What hiring mistakes has William Falcon made as a founder?
a: Falcon said some of his earlier mistakes were hiring the wrong executives, along with the risk of hiring for skills the company didn't yet need. Of those executives, Falcon explained that "It's just they're wrong for the stage of company." [15:23]

s7-bonus-from-post-berlin-wall-business-architecture-to-scaling-irish-tech-culture-with-conor-carmody-of-furthr-festival

Free Support, Founders Keep Equity: Furthr doesn't charge entrepreneurs, relying on commercial funds and government agency support. It works with about 150 companies a year, probably 25 of which get funded, and asks them to pay it back with their time.

Test Demand Before Committing: The Silicon Stroll, which took entrepreneurs to meet multinationals, tested whether large firms and startups wanted to connect. Strong interest led the team to commit resources and book Dublin's convention center.

Depth Over Headcount: Carmody doesn't want a 4,000 or 5,000 person event that loses its informality. For him, scale means deeper engagement and collaboration that could continue for six to nine months after the one-day festival.

An Annual Product Release: The team rebuilds the festival each year using feedback and reviews. Past speakers refer new ones, and conversations with experts reshape themes, such as steering "sustainable cities" toward smarter sustainable cities.

Summer Planning Squeezes Timelines: Planning an October event after lockdown meant chasing Europeans over summer and squashing three months of work into about five weeks. The festival returns to May next year, with a burst of work starting in January.

q: What is Furthr and why doesn't it charge entrepreneurs?
a: Furthr, previously called Dublin BIC, is a Dublin organization that helps entrepreneurs shape their businesses, meet funders and get to a seed round. Conor Carmody says it doesn't charge because at the early stage "they need to hold on to their equity. They shouldn't be giving that away" [03:59].

q: What problem does the Furthr Festival solve?
a: The festival connects large companies with startups and scale-ups, and also brings in government and academia. Carmody explains that "both parties want to talk to each other but they don't know how to talk each other's language" [06:26].

q: How does the Furthr Festival team decide what to change each year?
a: Carmody compares it to an annual product release cycle, driven by feedback, reviews, referrals and conversations with experts, with the focus on content and speakers. Each year starts with "taking the learnings from the previous iteration and then trying to rebuild again" [12:00].

q: How does Conor Carmody think about scaling an in-person event?
a: Carmody isn't aiming for thousands more attendees, since he thinks that would cost the event its informality and atmosphere. In his view, success and "scalability looks like the depth that we can go to into the future" [18:07], including follow-up and collaboration after the day itself.

q: What advice does Conor Carmody have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Carmody advises founders to enjoy the experience, recognize their own and their team's work, and bring their people with them. His "advice to anyone who's on that journey who's in the thick of it enjoy the ride" [26:13].

s7-bonus-why-correlation-lies-engineering-true-gtm-accountability-with-mark-stouse-founder-ceo-of-proof-analytics

Analytics as Navigation: Once automated data flows were connected, Proof's models behaved like a phone's GPS, showing the gap between forecast and reality and what to change, and when, as outside conditions shift.

Two Equal User Experiences: Proof serves both analysts and everyone else. Stouse likens the first three years of development to boring a tunnel from both sides of a mountain, with the two experiences having to meet and sync.

APIs Came Last: Version one accepted only flat file uploads so anyone could build a model and get to value fast. APIs followed for scaling, and a key ongoing lesson is what to build natively versus integrate.
An All-Contractor, Virtual Team: Proof has no employees and has been virtual from day one. New people start on a targeted, well-paid project and earn further contracts by delivering.
People Are the Long Pole: Stouse says his biggest mistakes involve hiring and firing, especially giving people too many chances, which in some cases created near-death experiences for Proof.

q: What problem is Proof Analytics trying to solve?
a: Mark Stouse built Proof to make data science usable in day-to-day business decisions, including by people who are not trained data scientists. He explained, "The problem has been historically that data science has been very slow" [02:23], and also described it as complicated, expensive and hard to understand.

q: How does Proof Analytics work like a GPS?
a: Stouse said that when automatic data flows were hooked up, "the model started behaving exactly like a GPS on your phone" [04:59]. It plots a route toward a goal and shows when a delta develops between the forecast and reality, for example when the economy changes or a competitor makes a big move.

q: How was the first version of Proof Analytics built?
a: The first version used flat file uploads only and was designed so anyone could create and explore a model quickly, with APIs added later. Stouse said the team's method means "you start with the business question and you just reverse engineer" [09:12] down to the data, which is specified last.

q: How is the team at Proof Analytics structured?
a: Mark Stouse said the company has been fully virtual from day one and is made up of contractors, stating, "So there are no employees of proof." [12:53] He said this removes a costly layer of administration, gives flexibility in team makeup, and that Proof generally pays above market.

q: What advice does Mark Stouse give young entrepreneurs?
a: Stouse urges founders to invest in strong legal work, noting that marketers and salespeople in particular "typically really undervalue great legal." [19:39] He estimates a good starting set of agreements costs $50,000 to $100,000 and views it as insurance.

s7-bonus-no-code-edits-for-real-code-solving-the-developer-capacity-bottleneck-with-jake-vacovec-co-founder-of-flycode

No-Code for Real Code: Flycode connects to a customer's codebase through a GitHub application so non-technical teams can edit web apps without relying solely on engineers, and without integrating a new API or SDK.

Proving Feasibility First: Before finding a CTO, the founders took specs to a handful of third-party development agencies. The months-long process showed the idea was feasible, surfaced the challenges and shaped the initial scope.

Hard-Coded Text Held the Value: Flycode first edited copy in resource files, which was easier but limited its value and pulled it toward localization. Supporting hard-coded text was much harder, but opened doors, especially with larger enterprises.

Customers Shape the Roadmap: A self-serve, low-integration product let Flycode take a product-led approach, with users guiding next steps such as image editing and editing from Netlify deploy previews.

Raising Less Money: Jake calls raising a couple million dollars from angels a mistake. He thinks half would have been perfect and would have changed how the team approached the problem and used its resources.

q: What is Flycode and what does it do?
a: Flycode, co-founded by Jake Vacovec, makes web apps editable so product managers, marketing teams and other non-technical people can make changes without solely relying on engineers. Jake explained that it works by "connecting directly to your code and enabling editing on top of the code base" [03:24].

q: How did Flycode validate that its idea was technically possible?
a: Jake Vacovec and his co-founder did not know whether a bespoke, complex codebase could quickly be made editable. Jake said "we started to talk to a handful of third-party development agencies" [04:36], which helped them understand the challenges, confirm feasibility and define an initial scope.

q: What trade-offs did Flycode make when building its first product?
a: The team started with React, which meant it could not support companies using Vue, Angular or PHP, and it began by editing product copy in resource files. Jake later noted that "the higher value was in the hard-coded text because that was even harder to change" [07:20].

q: What fundraising mistake did Flycode make early on?
a: Jake Vacovec said the company raised a couple million dollars from angels, which was much more than it needed at the start. Reflecting on the amount, Jake said, "So I think half the amount would have been perfect" [16:14].

q: What would Jake Vacovec do differently if he started Flycode again?
a: Jake would spend more time finding early design partners and validating exactly where in the workflow the problem was before investing in an initial product. He encourages anyone thinking of starting something to "just spend more time talking to the customer" [22:48].
