s7-e8-the-tech-enabled-empire-scaling-a-3x-founders-financial-engine-with-waseem-daher-co-founder-ceo-of-pilot

Sell the Service, Not Software: Pilot does the accounting itself, pairing customers with full-time experts. About 95% of the software it has built is invisible to customers because it serves the internal accounting team.

A Hands-On MVP: Waseem and co-founder Jeff did friends' books in QuickBooks Online while co-founder Jessica watched and wrote Python to automate the tedious, error-prone steps, fully or most of the way.

Build on QuickBooks, Not Over: Pilot chose QuickBooks' APIs over building its own accounting system. It accepted less flexibility and API constraints so engineering could focus on eliminating manual bookkeeping work.
Time Tracking Drives the Roadmap: Pilot tracked time spent per customer and per step of the accounting process, then automated the costly steps, much like reading a code profiler's output.
Scaling Breaks Processes First: At around 2,000 accounting customers, the biggest breakages were less about database performance and more about processes that had lived in one person's head.

q: What is Pilot and who is it for?
a: Pilot provides finance, accounting and tax services, principally for high-growth startups from pre-seed to Series D, with software built to support its in-house experts. Waseem Daher describes that software as "the Iron Man suit for our accounting team, software that lets us work more accurately, more reliably, more efficiently" [02:37].

q: How did Pilot build its MVP?
a: Waseem Daher and co-founder Jeff did the bookkeeping for friends' startups in QuickBooks Online while co-founder Jessica looked over their shoulders. Waseem said she "started to write the first lines of Python code to take the most mechanical and tedious and" [05:16] error-prone parts and automate them.

q: Why did Pilot build on top of QuickBooks instead of creating its own accounting system?
a: Waseem Daher said QuickBooks already existed, had users and was known in the ecosystem, so Pilot focused its engineering on eliminating manual work. He acknowledged the trade-off: "you're never going to get the level of kind of flexibility with what you can do" [06:26] compared with building your own system.

q: What broke as Pilot scaled?
a: Waseem Daher said transaction volume brings real technical challenges, but the bigger problems were operational ones in Pilot's mix of people and software. Describing what had to be revisited, he said "we didn't have a process for doing this thing because it was fine" [14:07].

q: What is the long-term vision for Pilot?
a: Waseem Daher wants Pilot to expand beyond accounting and tax into areas such as HR, legal, IT and business insurance. He explained, "what our customers really want is for us to run the entire back office for them" [17:33].

s7-bonus-shattering-the-data-breadline-building-the-connected-spreadsheet-layer-for-dbt-and-snowflake-with-ryan-buick-co-founder-of-canvas

Spreadsheets for Non-SQL Teams: Canvas is a no-code, spreadsheet-like analytics tool for product, operations, finance and marketing teams that would otherwise wait days on a data team or stitch CSV exports together.

Engineering for Spreadsheet Scale: The team set out to handle a billion rows in the browser, using Rust, WebAssembly and WebGL to build a fast, collaborative canvas that Ryan likens to Figma for data.

Partner on the Plumbing: After taking a few turns at building integrations themselves, the team partnered with Snowflake, Fivetran and dbt so it could focus on the core technology that would set Canvas apart.

Sell Before You're Ready: Pitching an early prototype separated polite interest from real demand. The right customers agreed to buy and let requested features come later instead of making them a blocker.

Don't Force Growth: After raising money, the team got a little too excited about spending to grow. Months later it went back to basics: talking to people, building relationships and improving the product.

q: What is Canvas and who is it for?
a: Canvas is a no-code analytics platform that Ryan Buick says is sold primarily to B2B SaaS startups and non-technical users such as product, operations, finance and marketing teams. As Ryan described it, "It really looks and feels like a spreadsheet interface connected to all of your data sources." [02:12]

q: Why did Ryan Buick start Canvas?
a: As an early product manager at Flexport who didn't know much SQL, Ryan took a data analytics course on nights and weekends and realized millions of others couldn't do the same. He said, "We started Canvas really to help out the 90% of the organization that isn't technical," [03:45].

q: How was Canvas built to handle large datasets in the browser?
a: The team used Rust, WebAssembly and WebGL, and designed the product to be both performant and collaborative. Ryan explained that they asked, "how could we build essentially a spreadsheet that could handle a billion rows of data in the browser?" [08:13]

q: How does Canvas work with Snowflake, Fivetran and dbt?
a: Ryan described partnering with Snowflake for data warehousing, Fivetran for moving SaaS data into the warehouse and dbt for modeling it. He said this let the team "not have to focus on integrations, but rather focus on the core technology" [09:19].

q: How can founders tell if they are solving a real problem?
a: Ryan Buick says some people will take a call and ask for more features first, while those with a real need will buy and join the journey before everything is built. In his words, "You're solving such an immense pain for them that they don't need to" [12:30] wait for the rest of the features.

s7-bonus-bypassing-confusing-vendor-proposals-building-a-mintcom-style-portal-for-vertical-transportation-assets-with-ashleigh-wilson-of-auditmate

Contracts Become Data Points: AuditMate turns an elevator contract into data points, then manages and audits vendor activity such as maintenance, testing and insurance certificates so customers get what they pay for without overpaying.

A Manual First Version: The MVP, built on Salesforce, was a polished front end with humans running the math behind it. Wilson estimates it held about 15% of the algorithm the company ran at the time of the interview.

Roadmap Driven by Two Questions: AuditMate prioritized what would matter most to clients, including maintenance delivery and savings, and what was consuming the most company time, such as audits that took an hour of pulling and comparing data.

Automating Too Early: The team invested too much in emails, dashboards and graphs that people didn't care about as much as expected. They pulled back on email and notifications and got closer to clients.

Trust Your Gut Sooner: A non-technical founder who now leads most of the company's innovation, Wilson wishes she had shaken off imposter syndrome faster, learned the software and relied less on others' judgment over her own.

q: What is AuditMate and what does it do?
a: AuditMate is elevator and escalator auditing and management software founded by Ashleigh Wilson. As Wilson describes it, "it's a software that takes essentially a legal document, turns it into data points" [02:30], then manages and audits the vendor's activities against it.

q: What problem do building owners have with elevator maintenance contracts?
a: Ashleigh Wilson says owners and managers receive on average only about half of the elevator services they should, and have no real checks on how vendors explain, price or perform work. In Wilson's words, "elevator contracts are intentionally vague and confusing" [02:16].

q: How was the AuditMate MVP built?
a: Ashleigh Wilson's team built it on Salesforce with basic data point connections between the contract and the vendor's activities. Wilson said, "It was a really pretty face on humans behind the scenes running" [05:11] some math.

q: How did AuditMate decide what to build next?
a: Ashleigh Wilson says one factor was what was taking up the most time inside the company. The other, as Wilson put it, "was what is most impactful to the client and the negotiations" [07:47], including getting clients their paid-for maintenance and savings.

q: What advice does Ashleigh Wilson give new founders?
a: Wilson advises founders to trust their gut, absorb input from mentors and specialists, keep what fits and discard the rest. Wilson's reasoning is that "No one will run your business like you do." [17:24]

s7-e7-the-cost-of-code-smell-quantifying-and-conquering-technical-debt-from-inside-the-ide-with-alexandre-omeyer-co-founder-ceo-of-stepsize

Cut Down to What Worked: Stepsize had a broader product for quantifying technical debt costs, but users valued the editor feature for creating issues linked to code. The team dropped the rest and built a VS Code extension in about a month at most.

Size Debt to Plan It: Alex sorts tech debt into small fixes done on the spot, medium tasks that go through sprint planning, and large projects that can take a quarter or more. That progression shaped the roadmap.

Issue Trackers Create Team Visibility: Medium-sized debt had to enter the team's normal process, so Stepsize integrated with Jira, GitHub, Linear and others. This let engineering and product leaders see it when allocating sprint capacity.

Fix Scaling Problems as They Come: Short on resources, the team dealt with problems when they arose rather than optimizing early. Refactoring happened when needed, with the focus kept on customer value.

Positive Feedback Isn't Product-Market Fit: Early products excited the team and sometimes drew praise, but people weren't buying in droves. Alex wishes they had recognized this sooner, learned faster and moved on to the next build.

q: What does Stepsize do?
a: Stepsize helps software engineers document and fix issues directly in their code base, using editor extensions and a web app. Alexandre Omeyer says a key use is helping "engineers to turn meaningless to-do comments into actionable issues that are kept in sync" [02:32] with trackers such as Jira or GitHub Issues.

q: How was the Stepsize MVP built?
a: The idea came from one popular feature of a broader technical debt product: selecting code and creating an issue linked to it. Alexandre explained, "We got rid of everything else and focused on building an extension in VS Code" [05:48], which took about a month at most.

q: What are the different types of technical debt?
a: Alexandre Omeyer groups technical debt by size rather than by the categories you might traditionally hear about. He said "the only types of tech debt that mattered for us were whether it was small, medium or large" [07:39], ranging from on-the-spot fixes to projects lasting a quarter or longer.

q: How did Stepsize approach scalability as an early-stage startup?
a: Alexandre says the team dealt with scaling challenges as they grew, adding tooling and refactoring when needed while focusing on customer value. In his words, "you tend to deal with problems when they become problems as opposed to trying to optimize all that stuff too early" [14:54].

q: What advice does Alexandre Omeyer give to entrepreneurs with a new idea?
a: Alexandre advises getting started and building momentum, even if that means learning new skills or building a smaller version before you have funding. As he put it, "You don't need to wait to have someone on your team who's got the skills that you need" [24:12].

b7cdcb4d-9e67-41b5-bab9-b1615fa7ba8e
s7-bonus-from-script-to-screen-deploying-ai-to-automate-hollywoods-pre-production-bottleneck-with-ruslan-k-co-founder-cto-of-filmustage

Automating Script Breakdown: Filmustage analyzes an uploaded screenplay PDF with AI and extracts breakdown details in minutes instead of weeks, replacing work often done with pen and paper or spreadsheets.

Cutting the MVP Down: The original idea included instantly showing suitable filming locations. The team cut it, since connecting location providers was far harder than launching online, and sold script breakdown alone.
Built to Scale Early: Ruslan made scalability his top priority, launching on Google Cloud with Kubernetes and Docker. He says the team can now go from 10 machines to 100 with a single button.

Customers Shape the Roadmap: Early subscribers became the team's most important resource. Listening to what they need and would pay for guides the roadmap, which has expanded into scheduling, budgeting and visual prototyping.

Measuring Hires Carefully: After some hiring mistakes, Ruslan stresses clear performance metrics and test periods. If someone can't finish the work they have to do, you end the contract and find someone else.

q: What is Filmustage?
a: Ruslan K, Co-Founder and CTO, describes it simply: "Filmustage is a smart movie or video preproduction platform." [02:04] Its first feature was AI-powered script breakdown, and Ruslan says users can now also create schedules and budgets and prototype a film's visual aesthetics.

q: What is a script breakdown, and why automate it?
a: It is the pre-production step of pulling cast, locations, equipment, props, sound effects and other needs out of a screenplay. Ruslan explained the manual process: "break it down with pen and paper or spreadsheets into some smaller entities" [04:09], which the team saw as a good task for machine learning.

q: What did the first version of Filmustage do?
a: Users dragged a PDF of their screenplay onto the platform, where algorithms and AI analyzed it. Ruslan said the breakdown arrived with the information extracted "in a couple of minutes instead of a couple of weeks." [05:34]

q: How was Filmustage built to scale?
a: Ruslan says building a scalable solution was his number one priority from the very beginning, using tools such as Kubernetes and Docker containers. On the choice of cloud provider, he said, "I chose to launch everything on Google Cloud" [10:17], which he finds more useful and predictable than AWS.

q: How does Filmustage decide what to build next?
a: Ruslan says the team talks with customers, listens carefully to what they need and would pay for, and builds the roadmap around their requests. He admitted it took some time to realize that "your early adopters, your early customers are your gold, actually." [07:25]

s7-bonus-distributing-the-most-valuable-content-through-whatsapp-with-max-koziolek-of-spectrm

Hacking Toward an MVP: WhatsApp's policies didn't allow businesses on the platform, so the founders hacked in with code from Stack Overflow, built their own sending infrastructure, and curated content from Google Alerts, at first by hand.

Designing for the End User: Spectrm is effectively B2B2C, with brands like Ford, Groupon and Zalando using it to engage their customers. That shapes the roadmap and the team's promise to never launch a bad experience with a customer.

Scale After Product-Market Fit: Spectrm wasn't built to scale and went a long stretch without a customer-facing release to fix it. Max advises tackling scalability after finding product-market fit, then doing it rigorously.

Who Let the Dogs Out: Poor separation of staging and production sent a test picture of two dogs to every user in the system. Spectrm apologized to customers, and a two-dog Slack emoji still reminds the team never to repeat it.

Standardize What Isn't Unique: Max would move faster by not reinventing processes like remote work policy or customer onboarding from first principles, saving that effort for problems where the company can uniquely add value.

q: What is Spectrm and what does it do?
a: Spectrm is a conversational marketing automation platform that helps large companies market through messaging channels. As co-founder and CEO Max Koziolek put it, "we help large companies to use WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger," [02:16] as well as Instagram DMs and Google Business Messages.

q: How did Spectrm build its first MVP on WhatsApp?
a: The first version tested whether people wanted to receive journalism on WhatsApp, using a hacked connection, homegrown sending infrastructure and largely manual curation. Max Koziolek recalled that "The connection to WhatsApp was Stack Overflow that we had to rework this later" [06:41].

q: When should a startup focus on scalability?
a: Max Koziolek says Spectrm didn't build for scale from the start and felt real growing pains as customers, users and the underlying platforms changed. His view is that "focusing on scalability is something you should do after you find product" [13:58] market fit, and then to do it rigorously.

q: What does Spectrm's Max Koziolek look for in a good hire?
a: Max Koziolek urges founders to spend a lot of time on hiring, especially early on, rather than rushing to fill roles. His number one indicator of a good hire is speed to contribution: "we still look out for is time to get running." [11:49]

q: What advice does Max Koziolek have for new entrepreneurs?
a: Max advises founders to treat time seriously, prioritize rigorously and recognize the cases where time actually works in their favor. In his words, "Without urgency, everything falls apart." [22:21]

s7-e6-rethinking-the-mvp-spending-25-years-in-stealth-to-build-a-maximum-viable-product-with-jon-darbyshire-founder-of-smartsuite

Maximum Viable Product: SmartSuite spent two and a half years building before letting its first customer use it, believing a minimal product would not solve the problem and would be just another tool in the mix.
Field Types as the Core: SmartSuite built 44 field types with built-in validation for data such as emails, phone numbers and IP addresses, because bad data in means bad data out in reporting.

Revenue-Weighted Roadmap: Customers vote on features in Canny, and the team sees the revenue tied to each request. Large amounts guide decisions, but a $10,000 feature can still win if it could grow in value.

Start With More Developers: Jon's biggest mistake was keeping the early team small. The core group of about 15 could easily have been 35 to 40 in month one, which would have brought the product to market faster.

Partners Drive Growth: With no paid advertising, SmartSuite offers affiliates 50% of first-year revenue for introductions. Consulting partners receive 40% of first-year and 30% of second-year revenue.

q: What is SmartSuite and what does it do?
a: SmartSuite is a no-code work management platform where teams use drag and drop tools and templates to build workflows for sales, marketing, HR, product development and more. Founder Jon Darbyshire says it "helps any organization manage processes and projects on a single platform" [02:02].

q: Why did SmartSuite build a maximum viable product instead of an MVP?
a: Jon Darbyshire felt a minimal product would not solve the customer's problem from start to finish and would leave SmartSuite as just another tool. He described the launch version as "really our maximal viable product of what our customers" [05:52] needed to solve it.

q: What tech stack is SmartSuite built on?
a: Jon Darbyshire says the front end is React and React Native, with Python among the other technologies, and it took four to five months of testing to settle the stack. On the data side, "We use two or three different databases on the backend" [09:48], chosen by the type of data being pulled.

q: How does SmartSuite decide which features to build next?
a: Jon Darbyshire describes a customer-centric roadmap where requests are posted and voted on, then weighed against the revenue tied to them. Before the team writes requirements or starts development on a feature, "we start with just designs" [14:35] and share them with interested customers for feedback.

q: How does SmartSuite handle scalability and tech debt?
a: Jon Darbyshire says there is always tech debt, so part of each two to three week sprint is devoted to it. New features are also judged on their performance impact, and as he put it, "So we treat scalability as a feature." [21:13]

s7-bonus-the-empathy-bot-engineering-psychological-safety-and-burnout-analytics-in-slack-with-andrew-zhou-co-founder-cto-of-kona

Failure Before Validation: Kona's founders first built a personality-test product with no user research. Of 1,200 people brought on, only about 50 used it weekly, and the team kept convincing themselves it was working.
Dig Until Relationships Surface: In October 2019, the team interviewed remote managers and kept asking why. Complaints such as time zones traced back to the difficulty of building relationships.

A Simple Daily Habit: Kona asks teammates a daily red, yellow or green "How are you feeling?" check-in. The non-anonymous tool depends on psychological safety and on coaching managers to be vulnerable and supportive.

Unscalable, Repeatable, Then Scalable: Andrew calls scalability a "yacht problem." Kona ran manual experiments and custom builds, then created an onboarding playbook, and only then turned to changing whole organizations.

Slack Security Limits Bottom-Up Growth: Kona spread to what Andrew estimated was 60% or more of Oyster, but Slack tools need company-wide installation. That security hurdle means adding a top-down strategy alongside bottom-up adoption.

q: What is Kona and how does its Slack check-in work?
a: Andrew Zhou explains that "Kona is a tool that helps companies empower their managers to build better cultural habits." [02:11] Today that takes the form of a daily red, yellow, green check-in with an optional emoji, supported by work on building trust and coaching managers.

q: Why did Kona's first product fail?
a: The team built a personality-test product meant to help people bond, without doing validation or user research first. Andrew says "We started with an idea that nobody wanted." [05:18], and the team later had to admit its usage numbers were low and scrap it.

q: How did Kona research the problems remote managers face?
a: Before COVID, in what Andrew believes was October 2019, the founders interviewed remote managers and repeatedly asked why their challenges were hard. Andrew says they "realized that every single thing came down to the relationship." [07:14]

q: What does Kona look for when hiring engineers?
a: Andrew Zhou says Kona wants former founders or former product managers, and screens for signals such as learning speed and willingness to push back. The reason is that "we want people that have an incredible amount of autonomy and can take incredible ownership." [13:46]

q: How should early-stage startups think about scalability?
a: Andrew treats scalability as a problem you only have once you succeed, while noting it is very case by case. He warns that "if you try to solve for scalability too early, you won't even find the product market fit" [15:53], so Kona starts by doing things manually.

s7-e5-the-real-time-creative-studio-engineering-collaborative-ad-infrastructure-for-distributed-teams-with-vicki-duben-co-founder-ceo-of-viewst

Born From Turned-Away Work: While building rich media ads, Duben's team sometimes rejected peak-season requests for lack of designers. Research showed no affordable tool for display ads, leading to a Canva-like product built for them.

Focus Would Have Saved Time: The MVP took about 10 months while Duben kept working on the first project. She says she should have stopped that work or hired one or two people separately for the new idea.

Ship Ugly, Then Listen: Viewst's first public version looked ugly and had only a couple of features. Launching it brought immediate feedback on bugs, needs and challenges, which helped reveal the ideal customer.

Pivot Toward Professional Teams: Viewst began as a simple banner factory for small businesses and solo marketers. As more professional teams joined, it shifted about a year after launch toward project management for advertisers.

Share Bad News Early: Duben says fear of missing goals led her to tell investors about problems late, making support harder to get. Being open with investors and the team lets both help when the company is behind plan.

q: What is Viewst and what problem does it solve?
a: Viewst is a B2B SaaS tool that Vicki Duben describes as bridging creative and media teams to cut delays in launching digital ad campaigns. It offers a shared cloud space for collaboration, approvals, versioning and asset organization, which Duben says is designed "to actually bring designers and marketers together" [02:35].

q: How did the idea for Viewst come about?
a: Duben's team hit production limits on an earlier rich media ad project and found no affordable tool for display ads, which have specific features and technical requirements. As Duben explains, the idea was "to basically build something similar to Canva," [03:49] but for digital display ads.

q: How did Viewst pivot after its public launch?
a: Viewst first targeted small businesses and solo marketers, but more professional teams with different challenges began joining. About a year after launch the team changed direction, and Duben said "we are building kind of project management tool for advertisers." [11:02]

q: Can a solo founder build a startup like Viewst?
a: Vicki Duben is a solo founder on Viewst and has heard from investors and potential partners that this is too risky. She says "it's hard but it's doable and same with the team you know my biggest support is my team" [12:18].

q: What did Vicki Duben learn about communicating with investors?
a: Duben says that on her first project she was scared to tell investors she was behind, and raising problems at the last minute made their support harder to get. Her lesson is that "you don't have to be afraid to communicate the reality" [19:47].

s7-bonus-whats-new-with-harperdb-jaxon-repp-head-of-product

Fit Developers' Existing Skills: Repp saw rank-and-file developers resist his IoT startup's drag-and-drop platform. HarperDB instead uses pieces developers already know while tackling scale and speed to market.

Index Everything by Default: HarperDB builds on the LMDB key-value store to index all fields without data duplication, so apps stay performant as needs change and developers avoid constant index maintenance.

Balancing Reads and Writes: The team believes RocksDB may write faster, but chose LMDB for its read/write balance since user workloads were unknown. More write speed can come from adding nodes to a cluster.

Custom Functions Reshaped the Roadmap: An API layer with direct, no-latency access to data let the team answer customer requests with quick proofs of concept, shifting focus from packing features into core to making that platform flexible.

Rebuilding Clustering for 4.0: HarperDB is replacing WebSockets with NATS JetStream for exactly-once delivery. No customer had reported lost data, but delivery assurance was the remaining theoretical gap.

q: What problem does HarperDB solve for developers?
a: Jaxon Repp says HarperDB addresses scale and speed to market without forcing developers to abandon the skills they have built. As he put it, "we're not asking you to reinvent the wheel" [04:40].

q: How does HarperDB handle database indexing?
a: HarperDB indexes all fields, using the LMDB key-value store underneath its data model to do so without duplicating data. Jaxon Repp described running into poor indexes elsewhere: "I found myself in a position where my indexes weren't optimal, and HarperDB indexes everything" [07:13].

q: Why does HarperDB use LMDB instead of RocksDB?
a: Jaxon Repp says the team wanted to support hybrid transactional and analytical work without knowing exactly what users' use cases would be. While RocksDB may write faster, "LMDB has an exceptionally good balance of read versus write" [08:48].

q: How does HarperDB's horizontal scaling affect cost?
a: Jaxon Repp contrasts vertical scaling, which he calls an exponential cost model, with adding nodes, which scales cost linearly. In his example, "one node of HarperDB and that costs you $50 a month, then you can handle 20,000 users" [14:58] for $100 a month, up from 10,000 users on one node.

q: What is new in HarperDB 4.0?
a: Jaxon Repp says the upcoming release rebuilds clustering on NATS with JetStream in place of WebSockets, along with performance tweaks. He highlighted JetStream's "persistent streams that allows exactly once guaranteed delivery" [16:53].

s7-bonus-the-software-leadership-playbook-from-engineering-director-to-25000-tech-subscribers-with-luca-rossi-founder-of-refactoring

De-Risk the Habit First: Luca saw publishing weekly as a bigger risk than the tech. With only about an hour to an hour and a half for his side gig, he chose managed Substack, which also brought subscribers through recommendations.

Publish More to Beat Perfectionism: Anxious about each piece, Luca forced himself to publish more often and found details mattered less than he thought. Some pieces he hesitated over became big successes.

Grow Beyond the Weekly Issue: Reader ratings, suggestions and questions help guide the roadmap. Alongside the newsletter, Refactoring added a curated library of 200+ pieces, a private community and tool discounts.

Hire to Get Unstuck: As a solopreneur, Luca hires out of necessity, for work that eats his time or that others do better. His community helper was already a paying, engaged member doing much of it for free.

Know What Won't Scale: Writing a newsletter takes similar daily effort at 100 or 100,000 subscribers. The community does not: it has taken time comparable to writing and needs more resources as it grows to keep quality up.

q: What is the Refactoring newsletter?
a: Refactoring is Luca Rossi's newsletter and membership product, with a content library, private community and tool deals alongside the weekly writing. Luca describes it as "a newsletter for engineering leaders and anybody who cares about building great engineering teams." [02:03]

q: How did Luca Rossi build the MVP of Refactoring?
a: Luca spent weeks investigating options, from fully custom builds to Ghost and Substack, while still working a full-time job. He chose Substack so he could focus on writing, explaining, "So I went for a technical stack that was completely managed" [05:28].

q: How can writers overcome perfectionism and publish consistently?
a: Luca's answer was to increase output, because a public commitment to produce more leaves less time and energy to obsess over details. As he put it, "I figured out how to cure it, I think, by forcing myself to publish more frequently." [15:57]

q: How is hiring as a solopreneur different from hiring at a VC-backed startup?
a: Luca says funded founders hire proactively to grow faster, while bootstrappers and solopreneurs hire to free up their own time. In his words, "what I found is that you hire by necessity, right?" [10:26]

q: Is a newsletter business scalable?
a: Luca considers online writing highly scalable, noting that "your daily job is not much different if you have 100 people who are subscribed or 100,000." [13:04] He cautions that the community side of Refactoring scales less well and needs more resources as it grows.

s7-bonus-securing-the-software-supply-chain-fixing-open-source-trust-after-log4j-with-dan-lorenc-co-founder-ceo-of-chainguard

Born From a Release Problem: While releasing Minikube at Google, Dan Lorenc found no good, secure way to build a binary the community ran as root, and ended up installing Jenkins on Mac Minis under his desk.

Open Source Gave a Head Start: Chainguard's founders had open source projects with adoption and a community before starting the company, which made experimenting with products around them much easier.

Guess, Ship, Then Listen: When design partner feedback stalled because customers didn't know the answers, the team leaned on its own expertise and built products to get into users' hands. Mocks and demos weren't enough.
Speed Over Massive Scale: Build and software metadata workloads are far smaller than production traffic, so Chainguard's scaling challenge is keeping things fast and interactive for developers.

Headquarters Address Matters: The founders used one of their houses as headquarters, then learned the state affects things like available health care plans. That home also receives about 45 compliance posters.

q: What does Chainguard do?
a: Chainguard, co-founded by CEO Dan Lorenc, focuses on securing the software supply chain, including code, dependencies and the build process, not physical supply chains. Lorenc said the "goal and overall mission is to help make the software" [02:16] supply chain secure by default.

q: How did Dan Lorenc get into software supply chain security?
a: Lorenc worked at Google for about nine years and started on Minikube, a way to run a Kubernetes cluster on a laptop. Releasing it exposed the lack of a secure build process, even though "People were just grabbing this 80 meg binary off of GitHub and installing it." [03:21]

q: How did the SolarWinds attack affect software supply chain security?
a: Lorenc explained that an attacker used a compromised SolarWinds build system "to insert malware into their product that they were building and shipping." [04:07] The breach led to new regulations and a Biden administration executive order, and he saw it as a good time to try a startup.

q: How did Chainguard build its product roadmap when customer feedback stalled?
a: Lorenc said the roadmap shifted from features to whatever would produce the next round of feedback, which meant building products people would install. In his words, it became "how do we get the next set of feedback that we need from the next set" [07:46] of organizations.

q: What advice does Dan Lorenc give to early founders?
a: Lorenc advises getting started early and showing your work as often as possible rather than keeping it hidden. He urged founders, "don't keep secrets just start getting feedback start showing everything you're doing to" [15:24] the world as early as you can.

s7-e4-building-in-a-crisis-launching-a-zero-access-data-observability-engine-with-yuliia-tkachova-co-founder-ceo-of-masthead-data

Selling Before the Back End: Masthead validated its idea with an animated Figma UI and nothing behind it. Customers seeing mock data asked to install it right away, before the product could actually run.
Privacy Without Shortcuts: Masthead analyzes logs and metadata instead of querying client data. That choice means the team has to be really good at parsing logs and unpacking SQL queries.
Trade-Offs for a Solid Backend: The team accepted tech debt and ran early installations through the terminal. At recording, a version deployable from the UI in five clicks was due to roll out soon.

An Advisory Board Steers Priorities: Without product-market fit or core customers to guide the roadmap, Yuliia formed a customer advisory board of data professionals whose feedback helps prioritize the backlog.
Hesitation Costs More Than Bugs: Yuliia's biggest regret is not moving faster and starting the back end earlier. In her view, tech mistakes can be fixed, but time lost to hesitation cannot.

q: What is Masthead Data and what does it do?
a: Masthead Data is a data reliability platform that catches anomalies in data warehouses in real time and alerts data engineers or analysts, with column-level lineage to show which data consumers were affected. Co-founder and CEO Yuliia Tkachova describes it as a platform that "catches anomalies in data teams' warehouses before they cause harmful downstream effects" [02:11].

q: How can Masthead Data monitor data quality without accessing client data?
a: Masthead works from logs and metadata, which are processed on its side, rather than querying the client's data. Yuliia Tkachova calls this the main differentiator: "Masthead Data doesn't need direct access to clients' data, meaning we don't query clients' data." [03:33].

q: What problem led Yuliia Tkachova to start Masthead Data?
a: As a data product manager, Yuliia was tagged on her second day in an email chain warning that a major client was at risk because her product was not performing well. The data was sometimes erroneous or missing, and she recalls that "the worst part was that the client get to know about it from their dashboards" [05:17].

q: How did Masthead Data build and validate its MVP?
a: The team started with a front end only, giving the impression of a fully functional product to test whether customers would convert. Yuliia Tkachova explains that "to validate the idea, initially, we used Figma, you know, to animate the whole UI" [07:27].

q: What mistake would Yuliia Tkachova avoid as a first-time founder?
a: Yuliia says she hesitated too much and should have iterated, gathered feedback and developed faster instead of staying with front-end mock-ups. Looking back, Yuliia says, "We should have started building the back-end earlier." [16:46].

s7-bonus-the-twilio-for-pdfs-converting-messy-business-documents-into-developer-apis-with-josh-lewis-co-founder-ceo-of-sensible

White Glove Before Self-Serve: Sensible launched API-only, asking customers to share documents and delivering an endpoint in a week or two. It had two paying customers about two months after starting to build, while developing its query language behind the scenes.

Parallel by Design: Each PDF extraction is isolated with no shared state, so Sensible built on API Gateway, Lambda, S3 and DynamoDB to scale horizontally. The snag has been rate limits from third-party OCR services, handled with smarter exponential backoff.

Golden Extractions Catch Breakage: Alongside unit and end-to-end tests, the team checks core engine changes against hundreds of PDFs with known outputs. Lewis treats outages as process failures rather than one person's programming error.

Exploration Has a Cost: Beta document generation found little commercial traction, and a validation layer demoed well but may see limited use. Lewis calls these product mistakes, while accepting that a company can't skip exploration entirely.

Timing Enterprise Features: Building enterprise features before product-market fit risks wasted effort. Still, with dozens of customers and a push to fill the funnel, Lewis says he might go back and pull work like SSO and other enterprise needs forward.

q: What is Sensible and how does it extract data from PDFs?
a: Sensible is a set of developer tools that turns PDFs into structured data, primarily through an API that takes a PDF and returns JSON. Josh Lewis explained, "the approach that we've taken to it is by building a query language for documents" [02:33].

q: Why did Josh Lewis start Sensible?
a: At Newfront Insurance, Lewis saw account managers spending a lot of time on data entry from carrier documents and expected to find an existing tool. He recalled looking for "the Twilio for PDFs and solve this in a week. And we really didn't find that." [03:57] His team built its own, and about two years later he still didn't see the product he had wanted to buy.

q: How did Sensible build its MVP and land its first customers?
a: The first version was an API with no UI, and the team onboarded each customer's documents as a white glove service. Lewis described the offer as "in a week or two, we're going to give you an API endpoint" [06:48]. It took about two months to go from starting to build to having two paying customers.

q: How does Sensible scale its PDF extraction platform?
a: Lewis said every extraction is independent of the others, which makes the problem task parallel. That meant Sensible "was completely horizontally scalable out the gate" [15:18], using API Gateway in front of Lambdas backed by S3 and DynamoDB.

q: What advice does Josh Lewis give to technical founders?
a: Lewis urges builders to pay attention to sales and marketing, get experience with them, and find partners and mentors in those areas. His advice is "don't sleep on the soft side of building a company or building a product" [30:12].

Conversation Turned Into Software: TeamPay's first flow took the back-and-forth of asking a manager to buy something and made it a chatbot with four steps: request, approve, pay and reconcile. Approved purchases could get a purpose-built virtual card.

Prototype Before Spending: Hoag hacked together the prototype himself in Python over a couple of months, with people able to act as chatbot or manager. Keynote demos and customer validation came before the team had spent a dollar.
Same Product, New Market: After launching free to very small companies, usage fell flat. Around April 2017, TeamPay charged a 100-employee company and usage took off, with the product unchanged.

Values Become Interview Questions: The early team defined what it meant to work at TeamPay and turned that into interview questions. Curiosity is tested by asking where candidates taught themselves something on their own.

q: What is TeamPay and what problem does it solve?

s7-e3-the-supplier-data-blueprint-fixing-the-fragmented-vendor-master-and-scaling-to-acquisition-with-stephany-lapierre-founder-of-tealbook

Hidden Manual Work Nearly Hurt: One person had been manually handling customer data, which surfaced as customer volume grew and that person left. Stephany says waiting a quarter to change the team's leadership and approach cost three months.

s7-bonus-the-family-operating-system-engineering-zero-trust-cloud-architecture-for-lifes-vital-data-with-nat-robinson-founder-ceo-of-trustworthy

Pitch Deck Before Product: Trustworthy's first iteration was a pitch deck used to raise seed money. Robinson calls it a "minimum viable marketing" product: people got excited enough about the idea to write checks before there was anything to touch.

Beyond Dumb Containers: Research with about 30 families found DIY systems left them doing every update themselves. Existing tools had no context, routinely struggled with time-based sharing, and often lacked sufficient security.

Opinionated Over Infinitely Flexible: Trustworthy chose to put families "on rails" rather than offer a blank page. Some customers want to customize everything, but the team stayed the course, likening it to Salesforce asking businesses to fit the software.

Unscalable Onboarding Pays Off: At first, the only way into Trustworthy was a concierge onboarding session. Those sessions taught the team about members, and guided onboarding converts at more than double the self-service rate.

Rehearse Before Tier-One Investors: In its Series A raise, the team practiced its pitch in valuable investor meetings. The pitch was far better 15 or 20 versions in, and Robinson wishes they had done many more dry runs first.

q: What is Trustworthy's Family Operating System?
a: Nat Robinson describes it as an online service that helps families protect, organize and optimize important information, including IDs, money, property, insurance, passwords, legal documents and emergency instructions. On sharing, he said, "We help you share it across what we call your trust graph with your loved ones and trusted professionals." [02:51]

q: How is Trustworthy different from DIY tools for organizing family documents?
a: Robinson says families had cobbled together analog and digital systems that they had to manage and update entirely themselves. He said, "All of the tools that we saw were pretty much what we call dumb containers," [04:27] meaning they had no context about the information and couldn't offer value back based on it.

q: What product trade-off did Trustworthy make when building its platform?
a: Nat Robinson's team chose a guided, opinionated approach over unlimited flexibility, knowing it would be limiting for some people. As he put it, "we knew this was going to be a big trade-off is that we were going to kind of put people on rails" [07:12]. He says most families actually prefer it.

q: Why does Trustworthy offer concierge onboarding if it doesn't scale?
a: Robinson says the sessions helped the team learn what members needed while searching for product-market fit, and they more than double the conversion rate compared with self-service. He explained, "we purposefully do things that we know are not scalable, that won't scale." [13:10] The plan is to move those learnings into the product in more automated ways.

q: What fundraising mistake did Nat Robinson make during Trustworthy's Series A?
a: Robinson says the bigger mistake was not doing enough dry runs before pitching tier-one investors; the team also started right before the Christmas holiday. He admitted that "we were practicing our pitch on some very valuable conversations" [17:09], though the company ultimately received multiple term sheets and chose an investor.

s7-bonus-from-fractional-cto-to-seed-backed-cybersecurity-founder-implementing-practical-searchable-encryption-with-dan-draper-of-cipherstash

Encryption Without Losing Queries: Field-level encryption protects database records but breaks lookups, partial text matching and sorting. CipherStash adds a searchable encrypted index on top of an existing application and database to restore encrypted search.

Research Into Working Product: Dan Draper spent about three years working out how to apply order-revealing encryption to B-trees and inverted indexes. After four or five attempts, he had a working prototype in 2020 and raised funds off it.

Three-Way Design Trade-Off: CipherStash weighs security, performance and query capability. Early free text search was accurate and fast to query, but ingest was abysmal, which pushed the team into further R and D.

Plug Into Existing Stacks: Asking developers to change how they worked was a major early mistake. Most didn't want to switch technologies, so the roadmap shifted to integrations shaped by how customers want to use CipherStash.

Scale Designed From Start: Using indexes and B-trees keeps query time sublinear. Draper's example: a query over a million records can take 20 milliseconds, and at 10 million it might take only 22 or 23.

q: What is CipherStash and what problem does it solve?
a: CipherStash addresses the loss of search, range queries and sorting that comes with encrypting individual database fields. Dan Draper describes it this way: "CipherStash is what we call a searchable encrypted index" [03:30]. It sits on top of an existing application and database so developers can run encrypted searches.

q: Why did Dan Draper start CipherStash?
a: While Draper was CTO at Expert360, large corporate customers asked for proof of how their data was being protected, and he was never fully satisfied with the answers. The team wanted to encrypt the data, but found that once they did, "we were not able to query it" [04:35].

q: What technology was used to build the first version of CipherStash?
a: Dan Draper's prototype was based on PostgreSQL with custom extensions written in C, with application layers written in Elixir. He explains that "The underlying cryptography library was originally written in C, nowadays it's written in Rust." [06:10]

q: Can searchable encryption perform well on large datasets?
a: Draper says it is relatively easy over a few thousand records, and the hard part is millions or billions of rows. CipherStash applies order-revealing encryption to indexes and B-trees, and as he puts it, "a query of a million records can take 20 milliseconds" [13:57].

q: What was a major early mistake CipherStash made?
a: Dan Draper says one major mistake "was trying to get developers to come to us" [16:18], expecting them to change how they worked for an unfamiliar product. The lesson was to find how developers already protect sensitive data and plug into that.

s7-e2-from-learning-to-code-to-700-paying-customers-scaling-a-timeboxing-product-via-twitter-with-marie-ng-of-llama-life
Timeboxing Over Longer Lists: Llama Life puts a countdown timer on each task, helping people focus on one thing at a time and work through their to-do list rather than just add to it.

A Learning Project Gained Traction: About four months into learning to code, Marie posted a basic to-do list on Twitter and someone said they wanted it. Timers came later, and she had not initially planned to build a business.

Mission as a Feature Filter: Marie weighs requests against calm, focused productivity. Rather than becoming a project management tool, she is focusing on integrations with tools like Asana, Jira or Trello.

Scale When It's Needed: Llama Life is sticking with Firebase because nobody has complained about speed. A database restructure can wait while the team works on product-market fit, retention and marketing channels.

Freemium Is a Long-Term Bet: Adding a free tier led more paid users to cancel than expected. A month in, Marie was watching engagement and other metrics, betting that wider reach would eventually mean more revenue.

q: What is Llama Life and how does its timeboxing work?
a: Llama Life is a productivity tool from founder Marie Ng that helps people focus and work through their to-do lists. As Marie explained, "you can essentially set a timer for every single task that you have" [02:47], and the timer counts down to create a positive constraint.

q: How did Marie Ng come up with Llama Life?
a: Marie was making her third attempt at learning to code, this time with YouTube videos and a real project. She recalled, "I built a very basic to-do list and I put it on Twitter" [04:45], and the early interest grew into a following. Having ADHD, she also built in features she wanted but couldn't find in a single tool.

q: What tech stack was Llama Life built with?
a: Marie used HTML, CSS and JavaScript, picked up frameworks like React, took a JAMstack approach and chose Firebase for the database. She was in no rush to switch, noting that nobody had "complained about the speed of the product, how fast it loads" [09:51].

q: How does Llama Life decide which feature requests to build?

q: What happened when Llama Life added a free plan?

Marie said of the cancellations, "We did expect that that would happen, but we didn't" [19:50] expect it to that degree. s7-bonus-the-github-integration-playbook-breaking-down-the-wall-between-devs-and-executives-with-aaron-upright-co-founder-of-zenhub

Start Where Developers Work: Engineers lived in GitHub and rarely updated the project management tool. Zenhub's first prototype, a Chrome extension, injected task boards into GitHub so product managers could see priorities and progress.

Speed Created Backend Debt: Facing heavy demand, the team put much of the product's logic in the front end. Performance and reliability issues followed, and they stopped new feature work to rewrite the backend, moving from Node.js to Ruby.

Plan Beyond the Platform: Building on GitHub was a strong launchpad, but Aaron says they stayed focused on its ecosystem too long. Requiring GitHub logins also cost them control of their funnel with people who had no GitHub account.

Software Is a Team Sport: Zenhub moved from a GitHub-centric task board toward a productivity solution with reporting and a real-time roadmap, aiming to welcome non-developers such as product marketing and design.

Pace Over Top Speed: Aaron worked 10 to 12 hour days early on and found two or three years in that it wasn't sustainable. His advice is to take stock of what gives and drains your energy, then shape your lifestyle accordingly.

q: How did Zenhub get started?
a: Aaron Upright's team struggled to share project updates because engineers worked in GitHub and had little incentive to update a separate project management tool. Their answer was a Chrome "extension that injected some project management task boards into GitHub" [03:21].

q: Why did Zenhub rewrite its backend?
a: Aaron explains that the team built much of the product's logic into the front end to move faster, which later caused performance and reliability issues. At one point they had to halt new functionality "to completely rewrite our backend and move things from Node.js over to Ruby" [07:15].

q: What are the risks of building a startup on top of GitHub or another platform?
a: Aaron says a platform can be a powerful way to start and scale, but Zenhub's reliance on GitHub, including its login, cost the company control of its funnel. His lesson: "eventually you need to have a strategy beyond that to decouple from that dependency" [22:09].

q: What does Aaron Upright look for when hiring?
a: Aaron looks for self-motivation, natural curiosity, a great attitude and a bias towards action. On attitude, he said, "I love working with people that just have, you know, a great attitude" [11:27], and he rates it pretty highly over experience.

q: What advice does Aaron Upright have for young founders about burnout?
a: Aaron compares building a company to a race where "it's really all about your pace and it has very little to do with your top speed" [23:32]. He recommends slowing down, focusing on yourself and noticing what gives you energy and what takes it away.

s7-bonus-bypassing-data-brokers-generating-real-time-phantom-phone-numbers-emails-and-credit-cards-with-arjun-bhatnagar-of-cloaked

A Weekend Extension, Scrappy Backend: Arjun's brother built a form-filling browser extension in a weekend, while Arjun set up email and text relaying in one big Python file. The priority was getting the experience right, not the code.

Familiar Tools Over Exciting Ones: Arjun considered Rust and Go but chose Django and Python, with React on the front end, so hiring would be easier. His rule is to make decisions you can come back to later.
One Database Per User: Cloaked's main architectural bet was separating user data from the main database, giving every user their own. Arjun says nearly everything else stuck to familiar choices.

Scale for the Near Term: Arjun advises building for current scale plus 6 to 12 months of forecast. A QA engineer's infinite loop later sent 16 million test texts to the team in seconds, showing the server scaled well.

Founders Can't Step Away: After raising money, Arjun hired smart people and stepped back from product to focus on the business. He later reversed course, saying early founders must stay in customer calls, product talks and design reviews.

q: What is Cloaked and how does it work?

Arjun Bhatnagar says these are not burners, and describes Cloaked as "a platform that helps you create identities on the fly" [02:38].

q: What inspired Arjun Bhatnagar to start Cloaked?

q: How was the Cloaked MVP built?

q: How does Cloaked separate and store user data?

q: What mistake did Arjun Bhatnagar make after Cloaked raised funding?

s7-e1-killing-the-feature-factory-rebuilding-a-legacy-giant-from-scratch-with-ian-small-former-ceo-of-evernote

Going Quiet to Fix Debt: Ian Small's biggest decision was for Evernote to go quiet for 18 to 24 months and treat tech debt as foreground work, because there was no background left in which to pay it down.

Align All Three Constituencies: Before a long stretch of shipping very little, Small explained the intent and reasoning to employees, investors and customers. If any one of them isn't bought in, he said, it won't work.

Build the Roadmap from Misuse: Over 40% of users took meeting notes in Evernote, and 40% tracked to-dos despite no task management support. Those behaviors drove the push into tasks and calendar integration.

Re-Architect Without Users Noticing: Evernote moved from a sharded Java monolith to a microservices-oriented architecture with horizontal cloud storage, migrating millions of users with the goal of no downtime or hiccups.

Betas Can Miss Ugly Bugs: The new clients launched with bugs unseen in six months of beta. Small noted Apple's 10,000-user beta cap can hide rare problems, and said the team could have better communicated how much would change.

q: How did Evernote tackle years of technical debt?
a: Ian Small decided the work had to be a foreground task and told users the company would not be shipping much while it fixed the underlying problem. In his words, "the biggest single decision that we made was to go quiet as a company for somewhere between 18 and 24 months." [06:24]

q: Why was Evernote stuck when Ian Small joined in 2018?
a: Small says accumulated product and technical debt had stalled innovation, with infrastructure that was costly to maintain and product definitions that had diverged across platforms. He described having "five products running on five platforms with five different feature sets and five different UXs." [21:11]

q: How did Evernote decide what to build next?
a: The team used surveys, one-on-one conversations and anecdotal evidence to profile what users were already doing with Evernote, then turned that into a focused roadmap around tasks and meetings. As Small put it, "Sometimes the most interesting thing in a roadmap is how are users misusing your product?" [12:32]

q: How did Evernote change its architecture to scale?
a: Small says the team re-architected both the client and the cloud during 2019 and 2020, removing single points of failure and migrating the running service. In the cloud, "we moved from a sharded Java monolith" [16:45] to a microservices-oriented architecture with horizontal cloud storage.

q: What is Evernote's mission now?
a: Small explains that Evernote expanded its focus from helping people remember to helping them act and get things done. The company moved to "a five-word mission, which was remember everything and accomplish anything." [09:57]

s6-bonus-killing-security-alert-fatigue-building-developer-first-appsec-with-harshil-parikh-of-tromzo

MVP Feature by Feature: Tromzo had its first design partner a month after starting. With three partners lined up, it built what they had in common first, then iterated, treating each new capability as its own MVP.

Delay Non-Differentiating Work: Customers expected self-service integrations, but Tromzo built them much later because they wouldn't block customers' work or win deals early on. Focus went to differentiating capabilities.

Three Roadmap Buckets: Work was prioritized as customer-reported bugs, requested features that fit the product direction, and differentiators nobody had asked for that build a technical or functional moat.

Lean, Senior Early Team: With no time or resources for micromanagement, Tromzo hired only senior people who could make their own decisions, handle shifting priorities and ship rough MVPs knowing the debt would come due.

Start Distribution at Founding: Parikh says the pull to build an awesome product is consuming. Looking back, he would have worked on distribution from around day one, letting it shape hiring, product and target customers.

q: What does Tromzo do?
a: Harshil Parikh, CEO and co-founder, describes Tromzo as a way to make security a core part of software development instead of a separate function. In his words, "we're building an operating platform for cybersecurity" [02:52].

q: How did Tromzo build its MVP?
a: Parikh says there was no single version they called the MVP; they worked with three design partners who could tolerate bugs and missing features. He explained, "we took the approach of building MVP features rather than thinking about the whole product as an MVP" [04:28].

q: How did Tromzo decide what not to build early on?
a: Parikh's team focused on differentiating capabilities and put off the self-service integration interface, even though customers expected it. Their reasoning, as he put it, was that "no customer will choose us saying hey these guys have really easy" [06:36] to use integrations, at least early on.

q: Did Tromzo build its product to scale from day one?
a: Not for every case: Parikh says the team knew its ideal customer profile would not introduce certain scale challenges, so it waited until such customers were in view. He cautioned that skipped problems don't vanish, saying "you have to be very mindful of those decisions" [13:21].

q: What is Harshil Parikh's advice for startup founders?
a: Parikh advises founders to figure out how they will sell and get the product to the people who need it, because information overload and more startups make buyers hard to reach. He cited a common startup phrase: "first-time founders focus on product second-time founders focus on distribution" [19:58].
