tutelage-of-treehouse-jason-gilmore-treehouse
From Due Diligence to CEO: A 2018 consulting request from Xenon Partners to help vet DreamFactory led Jason to become its CTO. After Xenon acquired Treehouse in late 2021, he moved into the CEO role.

People Behind the Numbers: Jason first saw Treehouse in terms of scale. A tweet from someone who went from about $9 an hour in construction to a six-figure software engineering job, thanks in part to Treehouse, reframed his thinking.

Learning Beyond Video: Videos are reinforced with interactive quizzes, auto-graded code challenges and web-based Workspaces, so students can practice on library or school laptops without installing anything.

Widening Access Through Partners: Because not everyone can afford a subscription, Treehouse works with libraries that fund patron access, nonprofits such as Operation Code, and schools, including one in Florida using it in grades 6 through 12.

Student Success Is Personal: Jason has personally reached out to people who canceled to ask where Treehouse went wrong. Tech degree students get Slack support from the success team and instructors, plus Zoom calls if they're still stuck.

q: How did Jason Gilmore become CEO of Treehouse?
a: Jason was consulting when Xenon Partners asked him to help with due diligence on DreamFactory, which led to a stint at Xenon and a role as DreamFactory's CTO. When Xenon acquired Treehouse in late 2021, his education background made the move natural, and he said "to be perfectly frank, it's a dream come true" [04:22].

q: How is Treehouse different from learning to code on YouTube?
a: Jason points to learning reinforcement, depth and practicality of instruction, and a strong focus on student success. For tech degree students who are still struggling after a Slack conversation, he said "we'll jump on a Zoom call. Good luck doing that on YouTube." [16:35].

q: How does the Treehouse learning process work?
a: According to Jason, "We employ a strategy of learning through video and then learning reinforcement." [13:27]. That reinforcement includes interactive quizzes, code challenges checked by an automated grader, and Workspaces, which are virtual coding environments in the browser.

q: How does Treehouse help people who can't afford a subscription?
a: Jason said the team recognizes that "not everyone has the wherewithal economically to sign up for Treehouse" [08:39]. Treehouse partners with libraries that fund access for their patrons, and also works with nonprofits and schools around the United States.

q: Does Treehouse hire its own graduates?
a: Yes, Jason said a fair number of staff are Treehouse graduates, including tech degree graduates in student success and a technical evangelist. Students who consistently exceed expectations or complete multiple tech degrees stand out, and he noted that "we have several such individuals on the team" [11:41].

s6-e25-why-webhooks-are-broken-building-the-twilio-for-webhooks-with-tom-hacohen-of-svix

Validate by Asking for Payment: A friend's webhook question led Tom Hacohen to ask whether she would pay if he built it. She said yes, someone else in a group chat did too, and another person offered an introduction.
Protect the API, Defer Everything: The two-day V1 had no UI or signup, and users got encrypted API keys. Tom was willing to take on technical debt almost anywhere, but aimed never to break the API.
Scale as the Business Grows: Svix tried to re-architect early for 100x its size, which slowed the team down. Tom says planning for about 10x would have been the better call.
Turn Rejections Into Referrals: When a candidate turned Svix down, or Svix passed on them, the team asked for an introduction to someone else. One of its best hires came from that.

Take Excuses Off the Table: Tom applies YC advice about investor updates more widely: either hit the target or plainly admit you failed and learn. Explaining why you failed can give you a pass to fail.

q: What is Svix and what does it do?
a: Svix helps companies add webhook sending to their services, with webhooks acting as a kind of server-to-server push notification. Tom Hacohen describes it this way: "You can think of it as like SendGrid or Twilio," [02:20] but for webhooks.

q: How did Tom Hacohen validate the idea for Svix?
a: A friend wanted an easy way to send webhooks from her service, a problem Tom recognized from his own company at the time. Tom recalled, "I just told her like, hey, if I build it for you," [03:41] and then asked if she would pay, which she agreed to do.

q: What tech stack was used to build the Svix MVP?
a: Tom, a sole founder, built a raw first version in about two days with no UI and no signup, just a basic API for creating messages. On the tools, he said, "We used FastAPI, Postgres, Docker, TypeScript and React." [04:47]

q: What scaling mistake did Svix make?
a: The team saw its growth rate and tried to scale far ahead of it, aiming for 100x, which slowed them down and later meant changing the architecture again. As Tom put it, "One thing that I think we did, which was a mistake, we prematurely scaled things." [11:26]

q: How does Svix decide what to build next?
a: Tom says the roadmap is based on what customers need or what the team thinks they will need. The team may anticipate a request, but Tom said they "wait for real signal from like a few customers before we" [07:19] do it.

s6-bonus-from-oracle-aws-aurora-to-cto-of-mongodb-scaling-document-databases-with-mark-porter

Layers of the Onion: Security, durability, correctness, availability, scalability and operability come before shiny features. At MongoDB, anyone at any level can raise an inner layer over an outer one.

Quarterly Planning, Bottom-Up Ideas: Developers can write initiative briefs. Product reviews the roadmap in the first half of each quarter, engineering then sizes what's feasible, and the last two weeks bring everyone together to set next quarter.

Scale With Sharding Day One: MongoDB holds a tenet that everything it writes works with sharding out of the gate. Porter calls forcing a rewrite to scale 10 or 100x a betrayal of product managers and customers.
The RDS Lesson: Porter says he pivoted too slowly to operational excellence at AWS RDS, where uptime relied on human toil. When he did pivot, he lost almost 60% of the group over the next year.

Teams Sized for Trust: Porter applies Conway's Law and Dunbar's number, shaping the org around the product and keeping teams small enough to match the trust needed to work efficiently, which he says limits approvals, escalations and politics.

q: What makes MongoDB different from other databases?
a: Mark Porter says MongoDB was founded to scale writes, and that the document model later made things easier for developers. In his words, "It is a distributed system that performs database transactions as opposed to a single system that tries to be distributed." [04:04]

q: What are Mark Porter's "layers of the onion" for prioritizing engineering work?
a: They are security, durability, correctness, availability, scalability and operability, and all of them come before new features. Porter built into MongoDB's culture that "anyone can raise the card of an inner layer of the onion," [06:46] over an outer one.

q: How does MongoDB build its product roadmap?
a: Porter describes a quarterly cycle that mixes bottom-up and top-down initiative briefs, with input from both product and engineering. Long-term roadmaps exist, but as Porter put it, "we don't delude ourselves that we know what's going to happen three quarters from now." [09:11]

q: How does MongoDB approach database scalability?
a: Porter says scalability has to be built into the product as a feature rather than treated as an afterthought. Sharding is how MongoDB clusters scale out, and he describes "a foundational belief in the organization that every single thing we write works with sharding" [15:19] from the start.

q: What mistake did Mark Porter make while running Amazon RDS?
a: Porter says the team kept shipping features while its databases didn't stay up. Porter recalled, "I was yelled at by customers, and it hurt. And my mistake was not pivoting fast enough" [20:10] to operational excellence.

s6-bonus-from-bmw-deep-learning-to-virtual-cities-training-autonomous-systems-with-maria-meier-of-phantasma-labs
Modeling the Human Factor: Phantasma Labs uses reinforcement learning to model how people move in traffic, as a plug-in that makes existing self-driving and delivery robot simulations more realistic.

Agents Learn in a Game Engine: Rather than supervised learning on a dataset, a human-like agent learns to walk inside a 3D game-engine simulator, with some Python and C++ and many training runs in the cloud.

Start With One Pedestrian: The MVP was one person learning to cross one road with no car. Modeling a standard human, such as a young person, came before covering elderly people, kids and people with disabilities.
Experiments Make Planning Hard: The team defines experiments and model goals every week, but results can't be forced. Some weeks they don't go as expected, which makes roadmap planning challenging.

Hire for Learning Ability: With few candidates experienced in their tech, Maria shows applicants part of it in a take-home or technical interview and watches how they learn it. Salary expectations also hint at whether they grasp early-stage life.

q: What does Phantasma Labs do?
a: Phantasma Labs, a Berlin company co-founded by CTO Maria Meier, uses reinforcement learning to model how people move in traffic, for testing self-driving cars and delivery robots. Maria says existing simulations fall short because "in a typical simulation, they tend to only walk on the sidewalk." [03:02]

q: How do you simulate realistic pedestrian behavior for autonomous vehicle testing?
a: Maria Meier explains that Phantasma Labs trains a human-like agent with reinforcement learning inside a 3D simulator built on a game engine. She notes it could look like a video game, but "we care about the physical parts being consistent with reality" [05:36] and about realism.

q: What was the Phantasma Labs MVP?
a: The first version was deliberately small: a single agent learning to cross a road in a human-like way, including walking at a typical speed. Maria described "an MVP, which would look like one person and one road, no car at all in the scene" [06:44].

q: Why is roadmap planning harder for machine learning products?
a: Maria Meier says her team works through weekly experiments, and some weeks the results are nothing like what they expected. In contrast to typical software engineering, she says, "you cannot force an experiment to do what you want it to do" [08:34].

q: How does Maria Meier hire engineers for an early-stage machine learning startup?
a: Maria looks heavily at behavior, including whether candidates understand early-stage work and can learn on the job. Because most applicants haven't used the company's more unusual technology, she says, "the only thing I can test for is learning ability." [12:08]

notifications-north-star-stephanie-griffith-marketing-expert

Segment by Buying Behavior: At Bath and Body Works, with about 26 million subscribers, Stephanie's team led each email with the category a shopper favored, such as candles or body care, and cross-promoted other categories below.

Better Beats More: Brands chasing engagement by sending ever more messages add to the overload. Stephanie warns that as people tune out, even priority or emergency notifications will struggle to break through.

Let Promotions Be Promotions: Marketers shouldn't fight Gmail's promotions tab. Stephanie argues promotional email belongs there, and that sorting makes brand deals easier for consumers to find and engage with.
Inaction Is a Signal: Focus on what users actually do on your site. Skipping a SaaS feature or a product category can signal disinterest, or a need for more education about it.

Pick Channel and Timing Deliberately: Decide who gets each message, on which channel and when, including legal windows for texts. Then ask whether you would engage, ignore it or unsubscribe if you received it.

q: Does sending more emails improve customer engagement?
a: Stephanie Griffith argues it does not, and that piling on messages leaves people overloaded and likely to tune out. She criticizes brands for believing the fix "is just sending more and more and more communications rather than stopping and sending better communications" [09:39].

q: How did Bath and Body Works segment its email marketing?
a: Stephanie says the analytics team used purchase data so that, for example, frequent candle buyers saw candle offers in the hero of the email. The aim was that when messages went out, "at least they were going to an audience we were confident" [04:43] wanted to receive them.

q: Should marketers try to avoid the Gmail promotions tab?
a: Stephanie says no: a promotional email belongs in that tab, and it is actually better for the brand. As she put it, "that is where your email is supposed to go because the consumer is telling you" [08:37] where they want branded emails.

q: What user data should brands use to make notifications more relevant?
a: Stephanie recommends focusing on the actions people take on your site or product, which she describes as zero-party and first-party data. She also notes that "a lack of action is just as much of a signal as an actual" [15:37] behavior.

q: What does a good multi-channel notification strategy look like?
a: Stephanie says marketers aim for the "right message to the right person at the right time" [17:11] but have not done it very well. That means deciding what to send, when, on which channel and sometimes to which device, rather than blasting everyone across all channels.

s6-e24-killing-the-feature-request-black-hole-engineering-product-feedback-systems-with-matt-young-of-uservoice

No Dates on Roadmaps: UserVoice's roadmap product deliberately doesn't allow dates. Young argues they tie product managers to commitments and take away their ability to change plans when they learn something new.

Research Before Building: A survey of about 2,000 B2B software users, followed by what Young thinks were nearly 100 interviews, showed people want quick feedback, plain language and proof something will happen with their input.

Limit Scope With Opinions: Rather than let customers ask anything about roadmap items, UserVoice offers a canned set of questions it considers safe and valuable, avoiding ones that are hard to answer or yield misleading results.

Delete the Backlog: The team wiped a backlog of about 6,000 items and uses Shape Up, picking work the week before each six-week cycle. Young says adoption of new software is way higher than under two-week Scrum sprints.

Buy What Isn't Unique: Young calls building non-core functions in-house a repeated mistake. After moving homegrown billing to a third-party system, he realized how blind he had been to customers expanding and contracting subscriptions.

q: Why doesn't UserVoice's roadmap tool include dates?
a: Matt Young says dates leave product managers feeling tied to a commitment, even after they learn something that should change the plan. Despite many requests, the team held firm: "we had a lot of people asking us to be able to put dates, and we just said no" [12:04].

q: How did UserVoice research its roadmap product before building it?
a: Matt Young says the team started with a survey of about 2,000 B2B software users, then ran interviews and built prototypes. One finding was that people care about giving feedback only on certain products, and as Young put it, "Their time is short, so they want to be" [09:32] able to do it quickly and efficiently.

q: How does UserVoice decide what to build next?
a: Matt Young says the team uses Basecamp's Shape Up method, writing problem-focused pitches and choosing among them just before each six-week cycle. To stay focused, they cleared out a backlog "which had been built up to about 6,000 things, and we deleted it, all of it." [14:14]

q: What tech stack and infrastructure does UserVoice use?
a: Matt Young said of the roadmap product, "We built it all using Ruby on Rails Go and React, which are our standard stack." [10:39] The company also moved from bare metal to containers in the cloud with Kubernetes orchestration, which made testing, scaling and EU hosting much easier.

q: What advice does Matt Young give founders about building a new product?
a: Matt Young advises vetting the problem thoroughly and being able to explain clearly why it is worth solving, instead of focusing on the solution. When a product or feature misses, he says, "it's because it was a tool that you could build rather than a tool that you needed to build." [27:37]

s6-bonus-building-a-hyper-converged-console-zero-trust-rmm-infrastructure-with-tyler-rohrer-of-remotely
Twelve Consoles Into One: Remotely found enterprise admins juggling about 12 tools or tool sets, with maybe 20 truly useful functions among them. Compressing those into one product became the MVP.

Making Real-Time Affordable: To inspect up to 100,000 machines every few seconds without overwhelming Cosmos DB, the team staggered check-ins and tiered data, keeping higher-priority data in the more expensive tier.

Zero Trust From the Start: The app runs in Azure as Docker-based microservices. Each is a security object with minimal ingress and egress, scales on its own, and sits in an architecture that assumes it must withstand breaches.

Customers Reshaped the Roadmap: Asking bluntly what the team was doing wrong surfaced a gap beyond Windows PCs. Early testers wanted phones, tablets, watches and wearables brought into the security and support fabric.

Unmake Wrong Decisions Quickly: Rohrer's team went deep on one CRM, to the point of internal demos, then reversed course. He welcomed the candor, saying Remotely pays for speeding tickets but not parking tickets.

q: What does Remotely RMM do?
a: Remotely RMM is a cloud platform, run on Azure, that helps large organizations support and secure remote users at scale. Tyler Rohrer explained, "help observe, act, and automate the management and security and support of remote users" [02:05].

q: How did Remotely decide what to include in its MVP?
a: Tyler Rohrer and his CTO, a former customer, walked through a day in the life of a modern admin and examined the roughly 12 tools or tool sets involved. Rohrer found that across those consoles "there were maybe 20 things that actually were truly useful" [05:10], and compressed them into the product.

q: How does Remotely monitor up to 100,000 machines in near real time without huge database costs?
a: Rohrer said reading and writing to Cosmos DB in real time is expensive, so the team spread out machine check-ins and tiered its data. As he described it, "the key is, from an architectural standpoint, we built in a stagger" [07:24].

q: How is Remotely built for zero-trust security and scale?
a: Rohrer said the application runs in Azure as an orchestration of microservices in Docker containers, each built to scale individually. He noted that each one "is a security object with a minimal path of ingress and egress" [14:39].

q: What advice does Tyler Rohrer have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Rohrer advises founders to trust themselves, take both good and bad feedback to heart, and expect much less time to convey value to a customer or prospect. His advice is to "trust yourself, get to the point quickly" [27:18].

s6-bonus-trading-while-you-sleep-building-a-247-algorithmic-engine-with-andrew-salvadore-of-coinrule

Automation for a 24/7 Market: Coinrule lets users trade crypto with no-code rules, such as buying $50 when Bitcoin drops below 40k. Rules can also use technical indicators and relations between coins.

From Four Hours to Seconds: When Andrew joined, releasing one component took four hours. Dockerizing the environment and running it on Kubernetes helped bring most releases to about 30 seconds with no downtime.

Ship Small Slices to Production: A rule engine version sat unreleased for six months while aiming for goals like 100% test coverage. Andrew pushes small iterations, even behind feature switches, and accepts nothing until it's in production.

Quarterly In-Person Roadmapping: The fully remote company meets every three months to debate priorities, bringing data to back arguments. Ideas are then validated by talking to customers and studying the market.

Scaling the Rule Engine: Workers pick up rules from a queue and execute trades. The team is moving them from physical machines into containers, partly so different plans can offer different execution-time SLAs.

q: What is Coinrule and how does automated crypto trading work on it?
a: Andrew Salvadore, CTO of Coinrule, compares it to Zapier for coins: you define conditions, such as a price drop, and the action to take when they are met. As Andrew put it, it "fundamentally allows you to automate your trading." [02:55]

q: How did Coinrule speed up its software releases?
a: Andrew focused first on CI/CD, Dockerizing the environment to run on Kubernetes, though some legacy components remain in how applications are rolled out and back. He said "now we do releases, I don't know how many times per day" [05:42], with most taking about 30 seconds.

q: How does Coinrule's rule engine work and scale?
a: Andrew describes a set of workers drawing from a big queue, where "workers pick up the work out of the queue, they execute something and then they update" [12:00] stats and databases and make trades. The team is working to move this from physical machines into containers so it can scale further and support different SLAs.

q: How does Coinrule decide which features to build next?
a: The team gathers in person every three months to debate a quarterly roadmap, weighing customer requests and future direction. Andrew explained, "We try to come to the meeting with as much data as we can" [07:32] to back up their arguments.

q: What advice does Andrew Salvadore have for new startup founders?
a: Andrew urges founders to seek validation and talk to customers, while not trusting all feedback completely because many people don't know what they want. His starting point: "I would say get this in front of as many people as you can" [22:14].

de3d120b-c4bd-4bee-a3fb-f8ccb92a5dc8
notifications-north-star-troy-goode-courier
Notifications Are Part of UI: Troy argues notifications are the part of your UI that users engage with most frequently, yet too few companies treat them as a first-class citizen of the product.

Channel-Agnostic Sending: Courier's vision is that developers shouldn't have to care whether a notification goes to email, Slack, SMS or push. That means the quality bar has to be high on every channel.
Closing the Mobile Gap: Troy's email background and the team's SMS and chat insight shaped a strong platform, but customers said mobile fell short. Elevating push became a big focus in 2022.
Product-Market Fit Before Growth: Founded in April 2019 and funded early, Courier went heads down on product. After finding fit, it built a go-to-market team, then sought more capital to fuel growth.

Investors With Domain Expertise: Troy puts partner over firm, but also wants expertise and connections in communication APIs. Google Ventures added a link to push, alongside SendGrid, Twilio and Slack as investors.

q: Why did Troy Goode start Courier?
a: Troy Goode is an engineer who has led startup engineering teams and wanted a better way to handle product notifications. He describes the work as "Building, candidly, the product that I wished I had and the reason why I started Courier." [01:46]

q: What notification channels does Courier aim to support?
a: Troy discusses email, SMS, workplace chat such as Slack, and mobile and web push. He says "part of the vision is they shouldn't have to care about whether it's going to email or Slack or SMS" [05:41], with push included as well.

q: Why should notifications be treated as part of the user experience?
a: Troy says notifications extend your product into the user's pocket and inbox, and are often what brings people back to an application. As he put it, "one of the things we talk to customers a lot about is thinking about notifications as part of your UI." [07:08]

q: How is Courier educating the market about product notifications?
a: Troy says it is something Courier is still navigating, including by sharing how companies like Slack and LinkedIn, which invest heavily in notifications, build them. The goal isn't to get companies to start messaging, since in his words "we're not going out and trying to convince anyone to start sending messages to their users." [09:07]

q: How did Courier choose Google Ventures as an investor?
a: Troy points to a long relationship with his partner there, who understood the space, plus Google's position as the largest provider of mobile and web push notifications. On choosing investors, Troy said "the common shared advice that I certainly stand behind is it's partner over firm." [02:51]

s6-e23-engineering-global-mobility-building-a-b2b-saas-for-cross-border-teams-with-franzi-low-of-localyze

Follow the Paying Customer: Localyze first built talent features like local sports and kindergarten guidance, but companies wanted visa help. The team shifted to HR features, then could return to the talent experience once HR saw the value.

From R Prototype to Rails: Löw, whose background was statistical engineering, built a first MVP in R to pitch investors and accelerators. The first version sold to customers was built in Ruby on Rails, which still powers the back end.
Experiment, Then Throw Away: As COVID left HR teams unsure what they needed, Localyze built at least three MVP-style features it later discarded because customers didn't really use them.

Hiring Evolves With Stage: Early hires were independent developers who could ship MVPs with little guidance. Later, Localyze sought more experienced people to own code quality, while still wanting pragmatic, customer-focused engineers.

Ask for Help Earlier: Löw spent nights wrestling with AWS setup, and the server was down a day before a customer presentation. Someone suggested Heroku, which the team still used at recording time without a DevOps hire.

q: What does Localyze do?
a: Localyze is HR software that helps companies relocate international employees and manage global mobility, with a personalized to-do list for the person relocating. Franzi Löw described it as a place "where the HR department can manage and track all the employees" [02:48].

q: How was the Localyze MVP built?
a: Franzi Löw first wrote a prototype in R to show investors and accelerator programs what the team wanted to do. She explained that "the real first mvp was built in ruby on rails and this was also the thing that we moved to the market" [05:15].

q: What did Localyze learn from its first customer pitches?
a: Franzi Löw said the team led with an app showing relocating employees what they could do in their new city, but companies cared more about immigration logistics. She recalled their response as "Please just help us with like everything related to visa and all those kind of things." [07:10].

q: What does Localyze look for when hiring engineers?
a: Franzi Löw looks for people who can write quality code but stay focused on creating value for customers and users, and she also cares about building a diverse team. One question she raised about candidates is "Do they have a pragmatic mindset?" [11:29].

q: Why did Localyze move from AWS to Heroku?
a: Franzi Löw had no DevOps experience and struggled to set up and debug servers on AWS until someone suggested Heroku. Looking back, she said, "I could have made my life a bit easier" [24:10] by moving sooner.

s6-bonus-scaling-edtech-infrastructure-de-siloing-the-digital-classroom-with-shaunak-roy-ceo-of-yellowdig

Social Mechanics for Learning: Yellowdig is a SaaS platform for community-based learning, bringing a social media-style experience to courses so students can share ideas, ask questions and help each other. Roy says it works with over 100 universities.

Rebuild Soon After Traction: Yellowdig spent a couple of years growing its MVP, but it started failing as clients expanded from a few courses to whole institutions. A complete rebuild was built in 2018 and launched in 2019.

Learning Outcomes Filter the Roadmap: User feedback carries the most weight, followed by product philosophy. Yellowdig will likely decline a requested feature, even a useful one, if it doesn't drive the right learning outcome.

In-House, Mission-Driven Team: Replatforming came with a shift from fully outsourced developers to a dedicated team. Roy values refining features over just building new ones, and looks for fast learners who care about the problem.

Client Success Was Underestimated: After the 2019 relaunch, some clients tried the product and didn't see its value. Understanding each client's context and guiding adoption turned client success into a strength.

q: What is Yellowdig and what problem does it solve?
a: Yellowdig is a SaaS platform for community-based learning that is licensed to academic institutions. Shaunak Roy saw that coursework was largely one-directional, saying "There is a big missing piece in terms of actually building learning communities where people can" [02:42] share ideas, ask questions and help each other.

q: Why did Yellowdig rebuild its platform from scratch?
a: Shaunak Roy says the MVP wasn't built to scale, and problems surfaced when enterprise clients wanted to expand its use. As he described their plans to take "it from a few courses to our entire institution. That's when the product started failing." [07:43] The team chose a full rebuild over refactoring, with a new database and new front-end frameworks.

q: How does Yellowdig decide which features to build?
a: Shaunak Roy says users and clients are the biggest voice, and ideas are then checked against the product's philosophy and its goal of better learning. In his words, "we try to prioritize that way, which is our users comes first, and then our philosophy comes second." [12:35] Needs such as scalability and security follow.

q: Should a startup design its MVP to scale from day one?
a: Shaunak Roy believes an MVP should test whether the idea works and whether people will use it, rather than optimize technology choices. His view is that the right move "is to focus on the user and the value prop" [16:32], then shift quickly to scalability once the problem and solution are well understood.

q: What mistake did Yellowdig make after launching its second version?
a: Shaunak Roy says that even with a much better product, some clients didn't understand how to get started or why it was better than what they already used. He admitted that "one of the things that we underestimated was the value of client success what i mean by that is" [20:57] helping clients through adoption, which new hires later built processes and systems around.

notifications-north-star-vatasha-white-courier
Customer Turned Courier Engineer: Vatasha White first used Courier as a customer while at LaunchDarkly. She's now a senior software engineer at Courier.

Approval Alerts Across Channels: LaunchDarkly needed customizable notifications whenever an approval came through. Courier automations let the team reach email and Slack without building separate sending logic for each channel.
Building Automations in Code: Rather than using templates at the time, her team used the Go SDK to call the API and construct automation steps. Step types included send, delay and cancel.

Giving Users Retention Control: White is working on how long Courier stores messages and event logs. The plan is to let users set a retention window via the API, including keeping sensitive messages out of dashboards and logs.

Customer Conversations Leave a Mark: As a customer, White got on a Zoom to work through her automation questions and get unblocked. Talking to customers is a core Courier value that she appreciates as an engineer.

q: What is a Courier automation?
a: Vatasha White describes an automation as orchestration of how you send notifications, with room for complex logic and steps such as send, delay or cancel. Speaking about Courier's channel support, she said it "really gives you that functionality out of the box" [02:49].

q: How did LaunchDarkly use Courier for notifications?
a: White's team needed to notify people through different channels, such as email and Slack, whenever an approval came through. They built the automation in code, and White explained that they "called the API directly to construct different steps inside of an automation" [03:53].

q: How is Courier approaching data retention for messages and logs?
a: White is working on controlling how long messages and event logs are stored, with a planned way to set the retention window via the API. Giving the example of a sensitive message a user never wants to appear in their dashboard or logs, she said "then we won't retain it" [05:27].

q: What tech stack change did Vatasha White face at Courier?
a: White predominantly used Go at LaunchDarkly and has had to adjust to a different approach at Courier, which she calls a whole shift in paradigms. As she put it, "I'm shifting from using Go to using TypeScript and then also doing everything serverless" [05:44].

q: Should you build product notifications from scratch or use Courier?
a: White, who now works at Courier, recommends using the product, citing its flexibility and the ability to schedule messages such as a weekly digest. In her words, "you don't have to worry about a lot of the complex knowledge that you would have to bake inside of your application" [06:22].

s6-e22-stop-over-provisioning-automating-kubernetes-finops-with-machine-learning-with-matt-provo-of-stormforge

Pivot Right After Series A: StormForge first applied its machine learning to energy use in HVAC and manufacturing equipment. About seven or eight weeks after a Series A board meeting tied to that product, Matt Provo's team saw it needed to pivot.

Developers Stay in Control: StormForge bet that developers know their apps and it doesn't. Users set how much autonomy the platform gets, from set-and-forget to close control over its recommendations, with explainable AI shaping the design.

Beyond Load Tests: The product began as pre-production only and heavily dependent on load and performance tests. The team has since added data inputs and APM and testing integrations, and worked to close the loop between pre-production and production.

Enterprise Scale Exposed Limits: Large enterprises asked about supporting 85,000 containers and 5,000 Kubernetes applications. The core machine learning could cope but the product often couldn't, forcing changes to the backend and core APIs.

Beware Contractual Release Dates: StormForge committed to a May 1st feature release, in some cases contractually. The delay blocked business-critical objectives for customers, and Matt says any future contractual commitments will be very intentional, if made at all.

q: What problem does StormForge solve for Kubernetes users?
a: Matt Provo says organizations typically trade off cost against performance, either tuning applications by hand or over-provisioning to keep them running. In his words, they are "spending 50, 60, 70% more than they need to." [04:50] StormForge uses machine learning to optimize how those resources are consumed in both pre-production and production.

q: How did StormForge pivot to Kubernetes optimization?
a: The company's first application tuned how HVAC servers and large manufacturing equipment consumed electricity, but it ran into challenges with the diversity of IT infrastructure. The team, then using Docker Swarm, moved to Kubernetes, and Matt says, "It was in this lift and shift that we really unlocked the problem that we solve today." [04:21]

q: Does StormForge take developers out of the resource tuning process?
a: No, Matt describes a deliberate decision to keep developers empowered while automating the ongoing tasks they don't want to do. As he put it, "We bet that developers know their app and we don't." [09:41] Users choose how much autonomy to give the recommendation engine.

q: Can StormForge work with both the Kubernetes VPA and HPA?
a: At the time of the interview, Matt said two-way intelligent scaling was due within the next month or so. He described recommendations "for the VPA and the horizontal pod autoscaler, the HPA, also in the same platform." [13:45] He said the capability came mostly from talking to customers and users.

q: What advice does Matt Provo give early-stage founders?
a: Matt advises going slow and steady, working to reduce unknowns quickly, and finding advisors willing to put in time early. He also warns against following the Silicon Valley formula by default: "So you don't immediately need to go get into an accelerator" [28:29].

s6-bonus-solving-the-legal-relocation-bottleneck-scaling-fintech-infused-legaltech-with-temilola-adebayo-of-humansquad

Two-Week WordPress MVP: HumanSquad built its first version in two weeks with WordPress and third-party plugins, then ran on it for about a year to validate product-market fit before investing in a custom platform.

Manual Work Informed Automation: Adebayo processed bookings herself, coordinating time slots between clients and consultants by email. It was slow, but it taught the team about the product and customers and shaped what to automate.

Customer Pain Drives Roadmap: Requests for school admissions help and for resume reviews to Canadian standards pointed to new products along the immigration value chain, each weighed internally before being built.

Automating Too Soon Backfired: A new cloud portal drew about 4,000 signups in under a week, along with bugs and complaints. The lean team decommissioned it, returned to WordPress and went back to the drawing board.

Canada as the Blueprint: HumanSquad started in Canada, where the founders live and which Adebayo says has over 80 immigration pathways, with a model meant to be repeated in other immigration-friendly countries.

q: What is HumanSquad and what does it do?
a: HumanSquad is an immigration technology company that Temilola Adebayo likens to an Uber for immigration, with the aim of reducing fraud by pairing people with regulated professionals. As Adebayo explained, "We connect them to licensed and regulated consultants." [02:26]

q: How did HumanSquad build its MVP?
a: The team used a small WordPress website with third-party plugins to validate the idea without spending heavily, handling many orders manually behind the scenes. Adebayo said, "So our MVP actually took us two weeks to build." [04:10]

q: How does HumanSquad decide what to build next?
a: Adebayo says recurring customer requests, such as help with school admissions or resumes, point the team toward new products, which they then evaluate before building. In Adebayo's words, "I'd say really our customer's journey actually informs our roadmap." [09:45]

q: What mistake did HumanSquad make when automating its platform?
a: Adebayo says the team built a cloud portal too quickly and was not ready for what followed, including bugs and customer complaints that led them to decommission it. She recalled that "in less than a week, we already had like 4,000 signups to the portal." [18:03]

q: How does HumanSquad plan to scale beyond Canada?
a: The plan is to work out the blueprint in Canada and repeat it in other immigration-friendly countries, with Adebayo citing a goal of scaling into five other countries in three to five years. According to Adebayo, "the Human Squad model is repeatable in any country." [15:21]

s6-bonus-the-api-for-everything-scaling-a-175m-universal-communications-engine-with-christine-spang-of-nylas

Cache Over Proxy: Nylas chose to sync and cache entire mailboxes rather than proxy requests to providers. It cost more and scaled poorly, but was the simplest way to focus on a fast, powerful API design.

A Year to Revenue: The open source version launched in June 2014 and the hosted platform in October, with the first paying customer around January. Microsoft support at launch didn't really work, but most testers tried Google accounts first.

Dropping the Email Client: Nylas first saw its API as a step toward its own extensible email client. That proved a very bad product direction, so the team spun it off as open source and bet the business on infrastructure.

Rewrites Come With Scale: Spang's rule of thumb is that each 10x brings some part you'll likely have to replace. Nylas has been decoupling a "distributed monolith" and rewriting some core components from Python to Go for performance and cost.

Customers Shape the Roadmap: Watching what early builders attempted led Nylas from email into calendars and scheduling, then contacts and drop-in front-end components such as schedule views and an email composer.

q: What is Nylas and what does its API do?
a: Nylas connects applications to communications data such as email, calendars and contacts, and helps people act on it. Christine Spang explained that "Nylas is a software platform that makes it easy for developers to build apps that can connect to communications data" [02:15].

q: What problem led to the creation of Nylas?
a: Spang's co-founder tried to build a customized email client and found that accessing and working with email data through the old IMAP protocol was far harder than expected. As Spang put it, perhaps others weren't building on email because "just the barrier to development and to entry was too high." [05:21]

q: How did Nylas validate its idea and launch its first product?
a: The team released a minimal open source integration and sought press coverage, including TechCrunch, and attention on Hacker News to test demand. Spang recalled that making the GitHub repo public did nothing by itself: "Literally nothing happened after we made it public." [09:55]

q: Why did Nylas move some core components from Python to Golang?
a: Spang said Python was a sound early choice because it let the team iterate quickly and use its many libraries, but the company's scale now demands more performance. She said that rewriting some core components in Go "just really gave us a ton more performance and allowed us to make the product a lot cheaper." [29:13]

q: What advice does Christine Spang have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Spang's advice is that showing up is half the battle and that founders have to keep trying. In her words, "If you just refuse to quit, you're eventually going to figure out something that works." [45:19]

notifications-north-star-patrick-malatack-matrix-partners

Time to Hello World: At Twilio, Patrick's team focused on how fast a new signup could get a first text message. The goal was to get messaging into developers' tool belts and trust them to find uses for it.

Notifications Are a Meta Layer: Good notifications mean the right message, channel and time. That takes orchestration across channels, such as not buzzing a phone during a live laptop session, or sending a digest instead.

Big Companies Built Their Own: Twilio customers like Uber and Airbnb almost all had internal notification teams owning push, email, SMS and in-app. Twilio was just one piece of the problem those teams were solving.

Betting Before the Product: Patrick invested in Courier with only Troy and a partial pitch deck. Whiteboarding complex notification problems convinced him that Troy understood the space even better than he did.

The Switzerland Opportunity: Patrick sees notifications as an enduring, increasingly fragmented multi-vendor space. That makes being small and independent an advantage over big platforms pushing their own agendas.

q: What is time to hello world, and why did it matter at Twilio?
a: Patrick Malatack describes it as the time from signing up for Twilio to receiving a first text message, which he calls a magical moment. The question his team asked was "how long does it take until you get that first text message" [04:02].

q: What makes a good product notification experience?
a: Patrick says blasting users on every channel may lift engagement for a while, but people then uninstall the app or turn notifications off. The products that last are those where "you give the right notification in the right channel at the right time" [08:53].

q: Why did Matrix Partners' Patrick Malatack invest in Courier before it had a product?
a: Patrick had seen the unmet need among Twilio customers, then worked through complicated notification scenarios on a whiteboard with Troy. He came away confident that "Troy understood it, not just as well as I did, but better." [12:00]

q: What is a Switzerland startup opportunity?
a: It is Patrick Malatack's term for a market where not being tied to a big vendor helps you build a better product, and he believes notifications is one. In his words, "the fact that you're an independent is an advantage in the type of product that you're" [13:14] building.

q: Should a startup build its own notification system or use a tool like Courier?
a: Patrick, who invested in Courier, calls it the sensible default for notifications of any complexity and says early startups don't want to staff a full notifications team. He warns that "any calories you're spending on something that isn't your core business model" [16:19] can be spent in the wrong direction.

s6-e21-the-code-first-data-stack-bringing-devops-best-practices-to-data-pipelines-with-douwe-maan-of-meltano

Narrowing the End-to-End Vision: Meltano first tried to replace a team's whole data stack. The turnaround came from focusing on extract and load: the glue code that made Singer connectors work well together and with dbt.
A Website Change as Test: Douwe repositioned Meltano around Singer-based extract and load without touching the product. It took hours, and the numbers climbed throughout 2020.

Investing in the Singer Ecosystem: A better runner for Singer connectors wasn't enough, so the team built an SDK for creating taps and targets and Meltano Hub, a central catalog of 300-plus connectors.

Over-Communicate After Working Solo: After being a one-person team for all of 2020, Douwe found that sharing the vision once let new hires' views drift. The fix was regular alignment and deliberately repeating himself.

Open Source First, Hosting Later: The MIT-licensed project is free. The plan is to monetize through managed hosting, with enterprise features like role-based access control, single sign-on and audit logs.

q: What is Meltano?
a: Douwe Maan, Meltano's founder and CEO, describes it by its tagline: "it is the open source data ops operating system" [02:13]. It brings software development practices such as version control, code review and end-to-end testing to data teams' pipelines and platforms.

q: Why did Meltano's original end-to-end data platform struggle to gain adoption?
a: Douwe says the project, then inside GitLab, took on too much by trying to cover everything from integration to analytics. The catch for users was that "It kind of expects you to throw away any data stack you have today" [08:13].

q: How did Douwe Maan turn the Meltano project around?
a: Left as the only person on the project in 2020, Douwe shifted the positioning toward extract and load with Singer, which was what community members had come for. As he put it, "It was just a matter of changing the framing on the website." [12:02]

q: What is the Meltano SDK for Singer taps and targets?
a: It is a software development kit Meltano built to strengthen the Singer connector ecosystem, and many existing connectors have been ported to it. Douwe said it is something "which makes it easier than ever to build new connectors" [14:18].

q: How does Meltano plan to make money from an open source project?
a: Douwe explained that "the primary way in which we will monetize it is then by making the hosting story easy as can be" [37:27]. At the time of the interview, he hoped for a private beta of managed hosting by the end of the year and expected to start selling it early the following year.

s6-bonus-from-zencoders-exit-to-a-170m-twilio-for-video-platform-engineering-low-latency-video-apis-at-global-scale-with-jon-dahl-of-mux

Opposite MVP Approaches: Zencoder used pragmatic Ruby on Rails to move fast with a small team. Mux built Go microservices, multi-region and multi-cloud, which likely slowed it early but has paid off with scale.

Live and On-Demand Together: Zencoder added live video two or three years in, which was challenging. Mux designed for live and on-demand from day one, taking longer but allowing seamless movement between them.

Strategy Built on Barriers: Drawing on Seven Powers, Dahl wants advantages competitors struggle to copy. For Mux, the two main ones are scale and product stickiness from deep integration into customer workflows.

Two Hard Products, Ten Engineers: Building both video streaming and analytics left about a year with few new features. Mux responded by narrowing priorities, raising money and growing toward 50 engineers.
Customers Don't Separate Video Types: Mux saw real-time video as technically distinct from streaming, but customers kept asking for it. Democratizing video meant expanding into real-time too.

q: What is Mux and what does it do?
a: Mux handles the hard parts of streaming video online through cloud APIs and open source SDKs, which Jon Dahl likens to something like AWS for video. In his words, "Mux is a video infrastructure platform for developers." [02:00]

q: What inspired Jon Dahl to get into video technology?
a: In 2007, while running a small dev shop, Jon Dahl was hired to build a video website and had to create a transcoding backend without knowing what transcoding was. He wished there had been a product "that I could have bought instead of building it myself." [02:52]

q: How was the Mux Video MVP architected?
a: Jon Dahl said the team set out to build the system it would want at high scale, using well-factored microservices written largely in Go. As he explained, "we built in a way to be multi-region and multi-cloud from day one." [05:25]

q: Why did Mux expand into real-time video?
a: Jon Dahl initially saw Mux as a streaming platform, since the technology behind Zoom-style calls has very little overlap with live or on-demand streaming. Repeated customer requests showed him that "our customers don't know the difference." [17:52]

q: What advice does Jon Dahl give young founders about customer feedback?
a: Jon Dahl warns that people will nod and say nice things about a demo, so founders should look for real passion and stay self-critical. His advice is to "Make the customers convince you that what you're doing is the right thing." [25:24]

notifications-north-star-eric-koslow-lattice

Notifications Drive Product Usage: When a bug led Lattice to shut off weekly update notifications for about three weeks, usage dropped by almost 50%, even among people who had been doing the activity almost every week for months.

Enterprise Deals Forced New Channels: Lattice built Slack notifications itself to meet Slack's requirements as a prospective customer. When another prospect asked for the same on Microsoft Teams, Koslow went looking for an outside service and found Courier.
Two Users, Two Preference Layers: Lattice lets employers choose which channels employees can opt in or out of, then lets employees pick how they're notified. Courier's APIs handle the routing.
Customer Branding Without Extra Work: Courier templates use a brand ID, and Lattice lets customers set some brand variables, such as email header color, so each company can match its own style.

Lists Handle Creator Subscriptions: For Vstream, subscribing adds a user ID to a creator's Courier list. One send to that list covers preference matching, channel routing and retries when a creator goes live or uploads.

q: How much do notifications affect product usage in HR SaaS?
a: At Lattice, a bug that sometimes triple emailed people led the team to turn off weekly update notifications for about three weeks. Eric Koslow said that in that time "we saw usage drop by almost 50%" [03:00].

q: Why did Lattice start using Courier for notifications?
a: Lattice had already built Slack notifications itself when another prospect asked for Microsoft Teams instead. Koslow wanted to avoid repeating that work for each new channel, saying, "I don't want to have to rebuild all of our notification infrastructure all over again." [05:39]

q: How does Lattice manage notification preferences for employers and employees?
a: Lattice built a customized preferences panel with two levels, since companies and their employees can want different things. Koslow explained that an employer can say, "these are the mediums that I want my employees to be able to opt in or opt out of" [06:43], and employees then choose among them.

q: Can B2B customers customize the branding on Lattice notifications?
a: Yes, Lattice lets customers set some brand variables, such as making email headers match their company color, and passes Courier a brand ID with the message. Koslow said, "we don't have to do any of that work to customize those emails." [07:46]

q: How does Vstream notify subscribers when a creator goes live or posts a video?
a: Eric Koslow described using Courier's Lists API, where each content creator has a list and new subscribers' user IDs are added to it. Vstream sends one message to the list, and as Koslow put it, "Courier will be the ones that will go through it, will match against everyone's" [10:54] preferences.

s6-e20-eliminating-the-flaky-test-engineering-ai-driven-low-code-qa-with-izzy-azeri-co-founder-of-mabl

QA as the Bottleneck: After calling old Stackdriver customers and hundreds of engineering leaders, the founders found developers shipping multiple times a day while QA still relied on Selenium, a tool about 20 years old.

A Deliberately Narrow MVP: The first product, the mabl Trainer, was a Chrome extension for recording low-code tests, built in about three months. The team chose Chrome first and no injected scripts or code at the start.

Auto-Healing Fixes Broken Tests: mabl collects about 35 locators for every step of every test. When a page change would break a test, it uses them to find the new element and rerun the test, fixing in seconds.

The Technical Moat: Replacing Selenium meant writing a domain-specific language that non-coders could use and developers found flexible. Azeri says it took far longer and cost much more than expected.
From Product-Led to Enterprise Sales: mabl began with a salesless, e-commerce motion, but enterprise clients wanted hands-on proofs of concept. Azeri says he would move to enterprise sales earlier.

q: What problem does mabl solve for software teams?
a: mabl is a SaaS platform for quality engineering that helps development teams keep bugs from reaching their customers. Izzy Azeri found that QA had become a bottleneck as developers sped up, noting that "QA was still using decades-old products to solve their challenges" [04:46].

q: What was the first version of mabl?
a: The first thing built was the mabl Trainer, a Chrome extension that took about three months to get out the door. Azeri described it as a tool "which allowed you to basically record tests in a low-code method" [05:21].

q: How does mabl's auto-healing reduce test maintenance?
a: mabl observes the page elements each test interacts with, keeps a history of changes, and uses other locators to repair a test that would otherwise break. Azeri said fixing a test takes mabl seconds "but takes about 80% of the time of a QA engineer on a day-to-day basis" [12:41].

q: What was the hardest part of building a low-code alternative to Selenium?
a: The team had to write its own domain-specific language, make it easy for non-coders yet flexible for developers, and make sure tests weren't flaky. Azeri admitted that "we underestimated how big of a technical problem this thing was to solve" [14:20].

q: Why did mabl move away from a purely product-led sales model?
a: mabl originally expected people to try and buy the product on their own, but enterprise customers wanted to go deep before committing. Azeri explained that "these enterprise clients, they want a hands-on proof of concept" [15:26], so the company brought in experienced salespeople and technical engineers.

s6-bonus-from-elite-triathlete-to-stanford-bioinformatics-automating-longevity-with-george-georgallides-of-basis-health

Wearable Data Meets Your Calendar: Basis Health uses AI on data from devices like Apple Watch, Oura, Whoop and Fitbit, and reads your calendar, to help fit health recommendations into your actual day.

Validation Before Software: George first published insights from his own data, including a five-day water fast, then did two to three months of customer interviews before an iOS developer built an MVP in three weeks.

Cutting a Successful Feature: Glucose tracking was selling and had a high net promoter score, but users came for a month or two or delayed until they felt healthier. George cut it because it didn't fit his long-term vision.

Users Vote on Features: After shipping features that barely moved engagement or acquisition, George hired a user researcher. The team now reviews findings weekly, identifies two features and lets users vote on what goes in.
Paid Tests for Hiring: George put early contractors through multiple paid tests to check fit and commitment. He also learned to move quickly when talented people don't fit the culture.

q: What is Basis Health and how does it work?
a: Basis Health is a product for people who already have a wearable, combining that data with their calendar to guide daily health decisions. George Georgallides said "BASIS is using artificial intelligence to build your optimal day." [02:11]

q: How did Basis Health validate its idea before building an app?
a: George analyzed his own data and published what he found, including results from a five-day water fast, to see what people responded to. He described this validation as "Just doing that without having any software built from the get-go," [07:10] and followed it with customer interviews.

q: Why did Basis Health remove its glucose tracking feature?
a: Users were excited about it, but George saw them using it for short-term information instead of getting better over the long term. "So I had to cut a very successful feature from my product" [10:49], George explained.

q: How does Basis Health decide which features to build next?
a: George learned that features he was excited about could have little to no impact, so he brought in a user researcher and now reviews findings with his team every week. In George's words, "We identify two features and we let our users vote for what's going to go in." [09:22]

q: Did Basis Health build its product to scale from day one?
a: No. George said the AI parts are built to scale, but the team still handles onboarding and support by hand to learn from users while it looks for product market fit. As he put it, "For example, we still do manual onboardings." [14:16]

s6-bonus-from-corporate-lawyer-to-building-an-enterprise-ai-powerhouse-with-sarvarth-misra-of-leah-ai-formerly-contractpodai

Six-Month Bootstrapped MVP: The team gave itself six months, hired developers in India and launched in Amsterdam before the end of 2014, with a configurable, cloud-based SaaS product and the mindset that if they failed, they would fail faster.

Build Versus Repurpose: Rather than become an e-signature shop, the team integrated electronic signatures out of the box. It also committed to Microsoft technology and used Azure's cognitive search instead of building a search engine from scratch.

Betting on Legal Buyers: Sales and procurement mostly bought contract software, and lawyers were said to lack budget. The founders still designed for legal departments, betting that the people who write contracts would gain a say in the technology.

Big Bang Plus Iteration: Misra's roadmap pairs founder-led leaps customers may not yet see, such as an end-to-end contract platform instead of point solutions, with incremental changes driven by customer feedback.

Cost of Late Fundraising: Bootstrapping 12 to 24 months longer than usual left room to pivot the business model, but also widened the operational gap when scaling around 2018 and 2019 and stretched teams more than necessary.

q: What does ContractPodAi do?
a: Sarvarth Misra describes it as an enterprise SaaS legal technology platform for legal departments, leading with contract lifecycle management that covers drafting, reviewing and negotiating contracts. In his words, "The full end-to-end cycle of contract management from a technology perspective is what we support" [02:50].

q: How long did it take to build the ContractPodAi MVP?
a: Misra says the bootstrapped team put a design together, hired developers in India and got to market on schedule before the end of 2014. He recalls that they "gave ourselves six months to build the MVP" [05:05].

q: How did ContractPodAi decide what to build and what to integrate?
a: The team focused its own work on where it could add value and reused existing technology elsewhere, such as electronic signatures and Azure search. Misra explains that "step one decision making is what are you going to build versus what do you repurpose?" [09:54].

q: Why did ContractPodAi build contract management software for legal departments?
a: Misra, a former corporate commercial lawyer, thought it made no sense that the people writing contracts and designing the process had no say in the technology bought for it. He describes the product as "software designed by lawyers in many ways for lawyers in mind" [12:02].

q: What does Sarvarth Misra look for when hiring executives?
a: Misra looks for three qualities that he admits are very hard to find together and that take some trial and error. He names them as "low ego coachability and high level of competence" [14:53].

s6-e19-turning-chaos-into-order-building-a-media-graph-for-unstructured-data-with-kirk-marple-of-unstruk-data

Born From Repeated DIY Builds: After seeing company after company try to build unstructured data tooling from scratch, Kirk Marple started Unstruk on nights and weekends, initially building a knowledge graph from podcast data.

Serverless and Event-Driven: Unstruk runs on Azure as an event-driven serverless platform, using Azure Functions and managed Cosmos DB. Marple says they kind of overdid scalability from day one, expecting customers might dump 100,000 files into it.

Foundation Before Sellable Product: The team pushed some machine learning work back to focus on ingesting, viewing and searching data. The private preview took about six months but was still light, leading to a Q1 2022 push on core features.

Fixing Product Handoffs: Rough handoffs between UX, design and product were the biggest wall. Explicit roles, mock-up reviews and clear feedback checkpoints cut rework and stopped people being pulled between features.

More Customer Conversations: Marple wishes he'd had 10x more conversations the previous year. As a self-described introverted engineer, he sees go-to-market and customer discovery as the area he would most change.

q: What does Unstruk Data do?
a: Unstruk Data, founded by Kirk Marple, is an unstructured data platform that helps companies get business insights from data such as video, audio and 3D files, and run machine learning on it. Contrasting it with the SQL-based modern data stack, Marple called it "a parallel universe of all the other kind of data" [02:26].

q: Why did Kirk Marple start Unstruk Data?
a: While at General Motors and later as a CTO or VP at other companies, Marple repeatedly saw teams trying to build this kind of media data tooling themselves. Years later, he concluded that "this still doesn't exist in the market I mean I should go build it" [04:06].

q: What tech stack is Unstruk Data built on?
a: The back end is written in C#, ported from .NET Framework to .NET Core, with a React front end and a graph API on Azure Cosmos DB. Marple explained that "it's all Azure cloud native it's a serverless platform basically" [05:05], with an event-driven design.

q: What mistake did the Unstruk Data team make early on?
a: Marple said the biggest struggle was process rather than technology, including knowing when to give feedback. He recalled that the "handoffs between user experience and design and product was really rough at first" [16:27], which the team fixed with explicit roles and review checkpoints.

q: How could Unstruk Data make machine learning more accessible?
a: Marple pointed to auto-tagging images and finding a particular vehicle across all of them without writing code, opening machine learning to a new class of users. He said "Those kind of no code auto ML solutions, I think, are pretty mind blowing" [15:18], though he noted this was not yet fully achieved.

s6-bonus-from-first-line-of-code-at-hootsuite-to-building-a-network-for-tech-talent-with-beier-cai-of-commitdev

Revenue Before Software: Commit started with email and spreadsheets. It hired engineers as employees, matched them manually with seed-stage startups, and let them try different companies for a few months before picking one.
Migration Is a New Product: Moving off Airtable, Notion and Typeform, the team treated it as a technical migration. Users and internal stakeholders resisted the new software, costing several cycles.

Mapping Problems Into Priorities: Beier talked to over 100 engineers, gathered almost 200 problems and organized them in an Opportunity Solution Tree, which gave the team three to six months of visibility.

Open Source as Infrastructure: Senior engineers in the community helped create Zero, open source cloud infrastructure for early-stage software. Commit builds its own platform on it, which makes the system scalable.

Depth Over Headcount: With about 2,000 engineers applying to the waitlist, Beier and co-founder Greg repeatedly chose not to open up further, focusing on deep value for the over a hundred people who love the product.

q: What is Commit.dev?
a: Beier Cai, CTO and co-founder, describes it this way: "Commit is a private professional network for remote startup engineers." [04:29] It focuses on three areas: intelligent peer support, personalized learning and development, and helping engineers find the right career opportunity.

q: How did Commit build its first MVP?
a: Beier says the first version was essentially email plus a spreadsheet, with manual matchmaking between engineers and startups. Describing that start, he said, "With literally no software at all, right? Just kind of put them all together." [07:03] Tools like Notion, Airtable, HubSpot and Typeform came later, once the Engineer Partner Program matured.

q: What should startups know before migrating from no-code tools to custom software?
a: Beier says Commit rushed its migration, and users were reluctant to leave the no-code setup for software that didn't offer exactly the same experience. His lesson is that "you really have to look at it as an overall product, not a technical migration." [20:48] He would do more research and validation if he did it again.

q: How did Commit decide what to build next?
a: Beier focused on customer problems rather than feature ideas, explaining, "So I was able to talk to over 100 engineers." [11:08] He organized the problems with an Opportunity Solution Tree, and the team usually keeps only a two to three month roadmap, with maybe six months at a very high level.

q: What is Zero, the open source project from Commit?
a: Zero came out of work by a few senior engineers in Commit's community, as a toolkit for early-stage startup engineers. Beier calls it "A scalable infrastructure on the cloud that you can build any software on top of" [15:34] in a matter of minutes. He says it includes components such as Docker, Kubernetes, a CI/CD pipeline, auto scaling and load balancing.
