s6-bonus-the-fractional-cto-fallacy-move-beyond-fragmented-freelance-code-and-build-a-dedicated-entrepreneurial-product-engine-with-patrick-bryant-co-founder-ceo-of-codetrust

Merging Teams to Build Capacity: A shared job opening led Patrick Bryant and partners to combine two dev teams instead of duplicating hires. The new team could serve their own products, including a third, Crewmama, as well as outside clients.

A Tightly Defined Agency MVP: Code and Trust set clear targets for client count and size up front. Its first year brought 12 client products through phase one, all just under $20,000, before it pursued much bigger clients.

Build Less, Then Learn: Clients often arrive wanting far more than they need. Code and Trust helps them launch just enough to learn from employees or the market, which may drop planned features or send the product in a new direction.

Engineers Who Think Like Entrepreneurs: Developers are empowered at stand-up to suggest changes as users would, such as moving a button or saving data. Bryant says this is probably more important than being really good at code.

Refunding a Poor-Fit Client: When a client's resistance left software carrying Code and Trust's name looking like it was failing, the team returned the money and walked away. Bryant says the hard call strengthened the culture.

q: What does Code and Trust do?
a: Code and Trust, co-founded by CEO Patrick Bryant, develops software for entrepreneurs and for corporations starting something new, from planning the first MVP to scaling up a team for heavy production and deployment. Bryant summed up the philosophy this way: "We think that code is a commodity, but products are opinionated." [03:27]

q: How was Code and Trust started?
a: Patrick Bryant and a partner were discussing a job opening when Sam, their partner in Event.Gives, overheard and suggested sharing the position. Bryant said that by the time they left that night they had worked out "the vision for the company, the position that we were going to hire." [06:52]

q: How does Code and Trust help founders decide what to include in an MVP?
a: Patrick Bryant said the team helps clients pick a piece that is just enough to learn from employees or the marketplace, then iterate using that data. He described telling clients, "look, you don't need to build out the entire thing right now." [10:45]

q: How does Code and Trust develop its software engineers?
a: Patrick Bryant said the company creates opportunities for interns and junior developers to learn from senior lead talent, while leads are pushed to keep learning too. He explained, "Well, we think of ourselves as a teaching hospital" [15:45].

q: When should a software agency walk away from a client?
a: Patrick Bryant shared an early case where a client pushed back on everything and would not let the team take over a particular piece, making the software appear to be failing. Code and Trust gave the money back and ended the relationship, with Bryant saying, "We've got to go in a different direction." [24:12]

s6-e18-never-rebuild-permissions-again-engineering-full-stack-authorization-and-policy-as-code-with-or-weis-of-permitio

Five Rebuilds Sparked Permit: At Rookout, Or Weis rebuilt access control five times in under three years. A Cisco request for its own back office meant the existing architecture would have to be thrown out.

Three Parts of Full-Stack Permissions: Permit combines authorization infrastructure (a microservice and SDK), a back office for stakeholders, and customer-facing tools such as user management, API keys and audit logs.

OPAL Grew From a Bottleneck: OPA's focus on Kubernetes didn't match the faster pace of application-layer changes. The team built event-driven updates, then open sourced that layer as OPAL, which sped up market feedback.

Developers Lead the Sale: Early talks showed CISOs cared but weren't the decision makers; R and D was. Permit chose product-led growth, using open source and self-service to get developers hands-on early.

Overbuilding for Scale: Weis says Permit was built for scale too much and could have been simpler. He still backs microservices, monitoring and elastic cloud services like Fargate or Lambda from the start.

q: What is full-stack permissions in Permit.io?
a: Or Weis describes it as authorization infrastructure, a back office and customer-facing interfaces that you bake into your software once. The goal is to "have it make your software elastic enough to meet the demands that come down the road" [04:50].

q: Why did Or Weis start Permit.io?
a: Weis had built access control many times and found it especially painful at his previous company, Rookout. He says he "ended up rebuilding access control five times for a company that wasn't even three years old" [02:59].

q: What is OPAL and why was it built on top of OPA?
a: OPAL, the Open Policy Administration Layer, is an open source project that updates the OPA decision engine in real time in an event-driven fashion. Weis explains that "when you take this to the application layer, the pace of change is a lot faster" [08:38].

q: Why does Permit.io use product-led growth to reach developers?
a: Weis says developers dislike having tools imposed by managers, and adoption works better when they bring a product to the decision makers themselves. In his words, "They want to pick their tech stack on their own." [11:19]

q: What go-to-market lesson did Or Weis learn from Rookout?
a: Weis rejects the idea that a great product will bring customers on its own, and says he should have distinguished and communicated two kinds of fit earlier. He stresses there is a reason "we talk about both product market fit and go-to market fit" [29:48].

a8fd39a1-aab6-42fa-a8cb-d2f301509c0d
s6-bonus-swipe-right-for-a-job-engineering-mobile-first-recruiting-and-winning-over-richard-branson-with-stephanie-florio-of-swob

Swipe to Apply: Swob job seekers enter their location, swipe left to pass or right to apply, and can reuse the same resume throughout their search. The free app borrows a gesture people already know from dating apps.

Prototype Before Launch: Coming from marketing and advertising, the founders worked with a prototype agency and ran focus groups to test whether people needed the app and could use it without explanation.

Let Repeat Feedback Lead: Swob prioritized requests heard more than once. Employers first thought screening questions were enough, then asked for resumes; later the questions were removed because resumes often already answered them.

Radio Was Costly: Swob spent on radio ads while trying to get its name out and got nothing in return. Florio's lesson is to research where your audience is, and she sees clickable digital ads as a better fit for a tech product.
Focus Before Expanding: Looking back, Florio says Swob sometimes expanded into areas too quickly. Her advice for a small team is to win one area before trying to take on several.

q: What is Swob and how does the swipe-to-apply job app work?
a: Swob is a job search platform where candidates see jobs in their location, swipe right to apply and swipe left to pass. Stephanie Florio explained that the name blends the two ideas, saying "the sw in swipe and the ob in job so we combine the two" [03:39]. She said it is aimed at hourly wage roles rather than more professional ones.

q: How did Swob validate its idea and build the first version?
a: Florio and her team worked with a prototype agency to create the first version and test whether it was easy to use and needed in the market. As Florio described it, "we worked with the prototype agency and we held a ton of focus groups" [06:22]. She said the feedback was very positive, with participants asking when they could download it.

q: How does Swob decide which features to build next?
a: Florio said the team looks for feedback that repeats and asks whether a change benefits employers and job seekers, such as by leading to a faster interview or hire. In her words, if something was coming up "more than once, then yeah, that's definitely something that you should pay attention to" [10:34]. Resume uploads were added after several employers asked for more information on candidates.

q: What marketing mistake did Swob make early on?
a: Early on, with tight budgets, Swob advertised widely without understanding where its target audience was, including running many radio ads. Florio said, "Radio ads are not cheap and we got nothing in return from doing that" [19:19]. Her advice is to take the time to do the research properly.

q: How did Swob win over Richard Branson?
a: Florio said that in 2018 Swob became the first Canadian company to win Branson's Pitch to Rich contest, which she described as validation of the idea. She recalled that "out of thousands of entries across Canada he personally selected" [23:54] Swob. She also said she looks up to his willingness to take risks.

de7b672c-ba4b-45ce-8ea3-af66a57df050
s6-e17-the-real-time-smoke-alarm-engineering-automated-evidence-collection-and-grc-architecture-with-girish-redekar-of-sprinto

Audits Before Customers: Sprinto deliberately worked with more auditors than customers, getting itself audited about a dozen more times after the first. The team did audits manually while building the software, spending 12-plus months on the first version.

Monolith While Learning the Domain: After a big internal debate, the team chose a monolith over microservices until the core building blocks were clear. That let them move fast and meet auditor and customer requirements during the MVP stage.

Three Buckets for Roadmaps: Girish sorts ideas into game changers, table-stakes deal breakers and everything else. Early-stage time goes to game changers first, then deal breakers, then the rest if bandwidth remains.
Scaling the Team, Not Traffic: Girish worried less about serving millions of users than about whether, say, 50 developers could work on the code base at once, a bottleneck he had hit before.

Hiring for Problem Breakdown: Early developers were assessed on turning fuzzy problems into small, executable pieces, such as a slice delivering about 80% of the benefit, and on having a bias to action over analysis paralysis.

q: What is Sprinto and what does it do?
a: Sprinto connects with systems such as cloud providers, version control and identity tools to automate much of the manual work of running compliance controls. Girish Redekar describes it as "a software platform that helps other SaaS companies obtain security and privacy compliance 10x faster" [02:06].

q: How did Sprinto build its MVP?
a: Rather than rushing a product out, Girish Redekar's team learned what auditors look for by repeatedly getting audited, and spent 12-plus months on the first version they could show others. He said they were "doing these audits manually while we were building a product that would help us go through these" [05:21].

q: Did Sprinto start with a monolith or microservices?
a: Sprinto started with a monolith because the team was still learning the domain and didn't yet know what the basic components would be. Girish explained, "we deliberately made a choice that we're going to be a monolith until it's very clear to us" [06:39] what the building blocks were.

q: How does Girish Redekar decide what to build next on a product roadmap?
a: Girish puts every idea into one of three buckets: game changers that set the product apart, deal breakers that are table stakes, and everything else. In his approach for early-stage startups, "game changers are more important as compared to deal breakers" [09:46].

q: What did Sprinto look for when hiring its early team?
a: Girish Redekar looked for the ability to break a fuzzy problem into smaller pieces that can be executed quickly, along with a bias to action. "we truly believe that a mediocre plan that can be executed today" [11:23] is better than a beautiful one executed tomorrow, he explained.

s6-bonus-the-ubiquity-of-opentelemetry-standardizing-global-cloud-observability-with-austin-parker-of-lightstep

One Standard Instead of Two: OpenTracing, which LightStep helped found, competed with the Google-backed OpenCensus, leaving library authors waiting for a winner. The two efforts merged into OpenTelemetry, using a third-party mediator to set rules of the road.

Fresh Data as a Priority: LightStep focused on shrinking the gap between an event and seeing it, aiming for users to know within 15 seconds. Parker contrasted this with the five or 10 minute lag possible in AWS data.

Governance Before the Crisis: OpenTelemetry set up enhancement proposals, elections and bylaws early, accepting more deliberation to scale gracefully. The downside: decentralized documentation confused new users until parts were centralized.

The Last 20 Percent: A month-long prototype by two people looked about 80% done, which led to an overly aggressive first-year roadmap. The project answered the reputational risk with far more detailed status reporting.

Vision Over Constant Shifting: Parker warns that chasing every request can feel like agility but is really a lack of focus. LightStep tests feedback against one mission: making it easier to understand what changed in a system.

q: Why was OpenTelemetry created?
a: Austin Parker explains that proprietary agents locked users into vendors, and the competing OpenTracing and OpenCensus standards left library authors unsure which to support. The need, as he described it, was "to have a standard that everyone could agree on" [07:04].

q: What problem does LightStep solve?
a: LightStep is an observability platform built to bring technology for monitoring Google-scale systems to everyday developers. Parker said its mission is to make it "easier to understand what changed in your system." [17:29]

q: How did OpenTelemetry prepare to scale as an open source project?
a: According to Parker, the project introduced OpenTelemetry Enhancement Proposals (OTEPs) and formal governance with elections and bylaws from a very early point. He said skipping this risked "some crises that could have been prevented if we had thought about those questions" [27:18].

q: What mistake did the OpenTelemetry team make with its roadmap?
a: Parker said a prototype built by two people in about a month led the team to set an unreasonably aggressive first-year timeline. The lesson he cited is that "that last 20% takes 80% of the time" [35:27], and the project responded by communicating status in much finer detail.

q: What advice does Austin Parker have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Parker values the story of what you are trying to do, including how it touches people's lives and who it is for. For him, LightStep's story of giving engineers their time back resonated, and he advised, "That's what you should focus on, right? Figure out that story," [46:36].

s6-bonus-the-algorithmic-rebalancer-engineering-deep-learning-ensembles-and-automated-downside-protection-with-stephen-mathai-davis-of-qai

Interviews Exposed the Real Gap: After interviewing close to 4,000 investors, the team found the pain wasn't picking or trading stocks. It was position sizing, diversification, and knowing when to take profits or cut losses.

Manual Operations Behind the MVP: The MVP took about six months and integrated Apex Clearing and Plaid, while the team traded and moved money by hand. Most of their assumptions proved wrong once real users went live.

Scoring the Product Roadmap: Q.ai ranked features with an internal quantitative tool, weighing product-market fit, legal and compliance, confidence in user requests, and effect on funded accounts, its North Star metric.

Cheap Servicing Fuels Growth: Stephen says negligible per-customer servicing costs yield gross margins north of 90%, leaving room to spend on customer acquisition and absorb wrong cost estimates without hurting operating margin.

Cutting a Founder's Pet Feature: Investor archetypes tested well, but once 100 users were on the app they were confused and some were angry. Though it was Stephen's "baby," the team pulled it quickly.

q: What investor problem is Q.ai trying to solve?
a: Stephen Mathai-Davis says Q.ai aims to give average investors the kind of money management that high net worth individuals get. Interviews showed that people "had a lot of issues figuring out how much to buy of something, how to build a diversified portfolio" [04:07], which he recognized as institutional portfolio management.

q: How did Q.ai build its MVP?
a: It took about six to seven months to get the product into real users' hands, with Apex Clearing as broker-dealer partner and Plaid for linking bank accounts. Much of the back end was handled by hand, and Stephen recalled, "We were manually withdrawing and depositing funds" [06:53].

q: How did Q.ai decide which product features to build first?
a: The team gathered pain points through one-on-ones and a Discord community, then scored the possible features to set priorities. Stephen explained, "we did that by using a quantitative management tool" [08:35] that they had built internally, and many features pushed to the back of the backlog turned out to be unwanted.

q: What was a major product mistake Q.ai made?
a: Q.ai assigned users investing archetypes, an idea that initial studies and user tests suggested people would love. Stephen said that in the live app "they were confusing personalities with investing strategies" [17:49], so the team removed the feature.

q: What is the future vision for Q.ai?
a: Stephen wants to expand beyond investment management into areas such as credit, Buy Now, Pay Later experiments, and personalized finance experiences. He described the goal as building "the first, you know, natively digital 21st century financial services firm" [19:21].

s6-e16-engineering-the-4x-revenue-engine-building-an-ai-powered-renter-fintech-network-with-jimmy-jacobson-of-stake

Cash Back Beats Free Rent: Stake pitches rent cash back to properties as cheaper and more effective than a month free, helping them lease faster, support renewals and reduce delinquency. Renters earn it by paying on time.

Manual Before Automated: Early on, Jimmy ran scripts for renter ACH details while co-founder Roland sent the money from their bank, probably 100 times. In hindsight, Jimmy would automate after 5 or 10 repetitions, not 25.
From Payouts to Banking: To make a once-a-month transfer app stickier, Stake added FDIC-insured checking, a debit card and direct deposit through Unit, a banking-as-a-service provider.

Workarounds for Legacy Software: When property software vendors ignored Stake's emails, the team built manual parsers for rent roll spreadsheets emailed in daily. Building full API integrations took a year and a half.

Features Over Automated Tests: Stake chose user-facing progress over comprehensive automated testing. Jimmy calls it a mistake and tells engineering candidates about it upfront, asking how they would cope.

q: What is Stake and how does its rent cash back work?
a: Stake partners with property owners and operators to give renters cash back when they pay rent on time. Jimmy Jacobson explained that "we partner with owners and operators of multifamily, single family, student housing" [02:20], and the offer helps a property stand out to people looking for a place.

q: How can rent cash back be used for revenue management?
a: Jimmy gave the example of renovated units that have sat vacant, where existing revenue management tools may suggest a big price drop. Instead, asset managers can offer "a bigger cashback amount for a few weeks using Stake" [04:18] to lease those units quickly.

q: What tech stack did Stake use to build its MVP?
a: Jimmy inherited mobile apps from an outside development shop, written in Java and Swift, and spent about five months working solo to make them usable. He said "Our initial version of the web dashboard was just vanilla JavaScript, HTML and CSS with a Node.js backend" [07:31], and it has since been rebuilt in React.

q: How did Stake get resident data before it had property management software integrations?
a: Rather than ask customers to upload every lease to another system, Stake had rent roll spreadsheets emailed in. Jimmy described how 35 of these files "of a rent roll get dropped into an email inbox like every day. And we've built manual parsers" [16:44] to add resident records to Stake.

q: What would Jimmy Jacobson do differently if he started Stake again?
a: Jimmy would plan more, including setting aside time to remove launched features that go largely unused. He would also do fewer things that don't scale, saying he "would do less of that. Frankly, I think I would try to automate things a little bit faster" [24:00].

s6-bonus-the-b2b-revenue-matrix-how-dreamdata-automates-complex-algorithmic-attribution-at-scale-with-lars-grnnegaard

Born from a 200% Problem: At Trustpilot, product, sales and marketing heads each claimed revenue contributions that added up to about 200%. Lars found no product to fix it, built a solution in-house, then built Dreamdata around that experience.

Segment as an MVP Shortcut: The team sought prospects already using Segment, which supplied tracking history and ETL into BigQuery. That let them hand-build data models and Google Data Studio dashboards without first building tracking or ETL infrastructure.

Scale to the Next Milestone: Dreamdata built for the next stage, such as 10 paying customers, not full scale. When Google Cloud credits ran out, inefficient SQL mattered, and cloud costs at 50% of revenue had to come down.

Self-Service for CRM Quirks: Each customer's CRM stages and pipelines needed small tweaks. As onboarding approached 10 to 15 customers a month, data engineers were swamped, so the goal became letting customers or customer success configure them.

Drifting from the ICP: Taking inbound companies that weren't B2B SaaS or Segment users forced Dreamdata to build much more product, including its own ETL. It slowed learning and go-to-market, and Lars says he would now turn them away.

q: What is Dreamdata and what does it do?
a: Dreamdata is a B2B revenue attribution platform that ties go-to-market tactics to prospect behavior and business results such as pipeline and closed business. Lars Grønnegaard said his earlier company had plenty of data but lacked a model "that would glue all those data points together in a meaningful data model" [04:32].

q: How did Dreamdata build its MVP?
a: The team used Segment to bring tracking, CRM and advertising data into BigQuery, hand-built the data models, and put Google Data Studio dashboards on top. Lars Grønnegaard explained, "we actually went deliberately looking for customers that were using segment.com" [06:05].

q: How did Dreamdata approach scalability?
a: Lars Grønnegaard described scaling in stages, building only what the next milestone required, from a handful of customers to 10 and then toward a few hundred. As he put it, "I think we have a philosophy of not building to scale too early." [12:38]

q: What mistake did Dreamdata make with its ideal customer profile?
a: The company drifted from venture-backed B2B SaaS by accepting interested inbound companies that were different and didn't use Segment, which meant building much more product. Lars Grønnegaard reflected, "If we had stayed more focused on our ICP, I think we could have moved faster." [18:54]

q: What is Dreamdata's long-term vision beyond attribution?
a: Lars Grønnegaard calls the vision revenue automation, where attribution is just one analysis on top of the data and insights can be turned directly into actions. He said the aim is "enabling companies to automate as much of generating" [09:37] revenue as possible.

s6-bonus-the-evolution-of-a-14b-unicorn-modernizing-the-soc-leading-to-an-exit-to-databricks-with-jack-naglieri-of-panther-labs

Born From SIEM Pain: Naglieri's incident response work showed him legacy SIEMs were slow, expensive and cumbersome at scale. Panther treats security as a data problem, using cloud services and detections as code written in Python.

Third Iteration, Not Zero: StreamAlert, the serverless open source project built at Airbnb, was effectively the MVP. Naglieri says he overcorrected with microservices in early Panther, then pulled everything into a single repo that was easy to deploy.

Why Panther Closed Source: Open source built awareness, but maybe one early enterprise customer at most came from it. Closing the source in 2021 ended the split between open source and enterprise development.

Cloud Native From Day One: Panther relies on cloud services to scale rather than conventional software on virtual machines. In a 2020 load test, one engineer fed about 50 terabytes of data per day through it.

Rapid Team Growth: Headcount went from three in 2018 to six in 2019, 26 in 2020 and 106 in 2021. Naglieri says a CEO should build a great executive team, give up responsibilities and focus on company direction.

q: What problem with traditional SIEMs was Panther Labs built to solve?
a: Jack Naglieri found that traditional SIEMs struggled to scale and were slow, expensive and cumbersome for security teams. In his words, "The designs of those architectures didn't innovate fast enough" [03:37] to keep up with the growth of data.

q: What is StreamAlert and how did it lead to Panther?
a: StreamAlert was an open source, serverless data analysis framework that Naglieri's team built at Airbnb, backed by AWS Lambda. Naglieri explained, "You would feed it data, it would automatically scale" [05:11], and its adoption, along with his experience querying a data warehouse, inspired him to build Panther.

q: Why did Panther move from open source to closed source?
a: Naglieri saw that open source did little to bring in enterprise customers, while maintaining it alongside the enterprise product created heavy engineering overhead. As he put it, "open source was really great for awareness and for people to kick the tires" [10:08], but it was not a strong way to enter the market.

q: How did Panther build its security platform to scale?
a: Naglieri said scale was a core goal from the start, helped by early hires with similar experience. "And the way we approached it was just by going cloud native" [17:12], he said, relying on cloud services to manage and scale the system.

q: What would Jack Naglieri do differently if he started Panther again?
a: Naglieri would focus more on security outcomes and the customer journey, and less on just building cool technology. He said that "putting more of an emphasis on solid product management early on would have made a huge difference" [00:30], including by hiring a product manager early.

s6-e15-mastering-day-2-kubernetes-chaos-building-autonomous-ai-sres-and-raising-67m-with-itiel-schwartz-of-komodor
Change History as Backbone: Komodor's MVP put an agent in the customer's cluster to report changes such as new images, replica counts, CPU limits and config maps, then turned them into a timeline.

Cutting a Third to Ship: With quality poor near release, the team tried briefly to fix the system-wide change view, then dropped it to protect the other two screens. It was added a couple of months later.

Good Enough Over Perfect Architecture: Schwartz pushed R and D to ask what would hold for about a year, often with far fewer components. The team also dropped Elasticsearch for Postgres alone, which helped it move faster.

Hire for Comfort With Uncertainty: Early developers came largely from Schwartz's past employers. Some were quite young, but could move fast, work with little guidance and switch direction without fear.
Make the MVP Even Smaller: The first customer was using Komodor after about three months. In hindsight, Schwartz would aim for two months or even one, because customer use taught the team far more.

q: What does Komodor do for Kubernetes troubleshooting?
a: Itiel Schwartz describes Komodor as a platform that helps DevOps and developers detect and solve Kubernetes issues by showing what changed and possible root causes. It integrates with tools like Datadog, Prometheus and New Relic rather than replacing them, and Schwartz says "those tools are doing a great job telling you the symptoms" [02:54].

q: How was the first version of Komodor built?
a: The MVP ran on Kubernetes and tracked how a customer's cluster changed over time, presenting those changes as a timeline. Schwartz explained, "we installed an agent for our customers running as part of the cluster" [06:23].

q: What trade-offs did Komodor make to ship its MVP?
a: The team was building three screens at once, but the high-level view of changes across the system did not work as well as expected, so they released without it. Schwartz recalled that "back then it was hard, like, killing a third of your product" [09:39], though he thinks it was the right decision.

q: Why did Komodor drop Elasticsearch for Postgres?
a: Komodor first used both Postgres and Elasticsearch as main backends, but Elasticsearch was not that valuable and supporting two databases consumed knowledge, time and resources. As Schwartz put it, "we simply decided to ditch Elasticsearch and use Postgres alone" [15:14].

q: What advice does Itiel Schwartz give new founders about validating an idea?
a: Schwartz advises understanding the customer, how acute the problem is and how it is currently solved, and he mentions that his team read The Mom Test to run better interviews. He warns that it is tempting to see a problem "and try to solve it without understanding how acute is it" [24:33].

s6-bonus-scaling-the-technical-mindset-from-self-taught-dev-to-engineering-leadership-with-todd-larsen-of-tech-leaders

Why and What Before How: Todd says many people jump straight to how to solve a problem. His team's framework weighs the why and what first and anchors decisions in the business case, keeping engineering tied to product.

From Micro SaaS to Consultancy: After leaving Digit, Todd built a micro SaaS on a best-in-class stack and hit $1,000 MRR in 30 days. That sparked helping clients build MVPs, then training other leaders to do the same.
Fractional Work as Hiring Pipeline: Tech Leaders plugs subject matter experts into projects part-time and hourly, giving just-in-time expertise. Many then choose to come on more full-time.

Context Is Critical in Handoffs: Todd's first replacement tech lead lacked enough context, which led to avoidable technical debt and a feature not yet needed. New leads now shadow existing ones during transitions.

Lean Into What's Different: Todd's regret is not leaning into what made his approach unique sooner. He had taken its decision-making and product strategy for granted until talks with clients and partner agencies showed how different it was.

q: What is Tech Leaders and what does it do?
a: Tech Leaders is Todd Larsen's effort to scale his experience as an early-stage founding engineer by training and recruiting other technical leaders to help startups build products and teams. Describing the model, Todd said, "It's like productized engineering is the best way to think of it." [06:38]

q: How should startup engineering teams make better technical decisions?
a: Todd Larsen advises discussing the why and the what before settling on the how, with every decision anchored in the business case. Of the why and the what, he said "those are much more critical to consider as inputs to the decision" [00:15].

q: How did Tech Leaders get started?
a: After leaving Digit, Todd Larsen wanted to build something from scratch and launched a micro SaaS, saying "I hit a thousand dollars MRR in 30 days of launching it." [05:52] He then began helping clients bring their MVPs to life, and when he reached his capacity, he turned to training and recruiting other technical leaders.

q: What can go wrong when handing off a tech lead role?
a: Todd Larsen described a replacement tech lead who made a decision without a full enough picture, creating technical debt that didn't need to be taken on. He explained that "it came down to not having ramped up enough context to that technical leader." [14:56] His team now focuses much more on shadowing and onboarding.

q: What advice does Todd Larsen have for early-stage entrepreneurs?
a: Todd Larsen urges founders to focus, niche down and decide exactly who they will serve, even if it feels uncomfortable. He said "the power of focus and power of niching down and doing just one thing is" [18:56] incredible, and that it should happen as early as possible.

s6-bonus-from-aws-s3-to-multimodal-ai-engineering-the-search-for-everything-engine-with-marin-smiljanic-of-omnisearch
A Two-Week, Bare-Bones MVP: The first OmniSearch took about two weeks. It ran speech-to-text on videos at public S3 URLs, exposed a queryable API, and was demoed with Postman and JavaScript snippets.

Education as the Beachhead: After starting too general, OmniSearch focused on online education, where people were excited and willing to try an untested startup. That market then drove support for PDFs, Word documents and presentations.
One Prospect Isn't a Roadmap: The team built features for a prospect whose deal never converted. They now prioritize common pain points with broad appeal and are more willing to say no.

Simple Stack, Informed Instincts: The founders avoided over-engineering and mostly tackle scaling as traction grows. Their experience with scalable systems helps them anticipate what could break and replace it.
Build a Soft Landing: Marin kept a Toptal profile after leaving Amazon so he could take side projects if money got tight. He says that safety net gave him peace of mind while doing startups.

q: What is OmniSearch and what can it search?
a: OmniSearch, co-founded by Marin Smiljanic, lets site owners and creators make their content searchable, including audio, video, PDFs, Word documents and presentations. Marin explained that "you're able to type something into a search bar and jump exactly to the points in the audio or video files" [02:32].

q: What inspired Marin Smiljanic to build OmniSearch?
a: During his Amazon years, Marin regularly had to go through dense technical training material and often needed to refer back to it, with no particularly good way to find things. "And I would spend hours just, you know, going through the materials" [05:04], he said.

q: How was the first OmniSearch MVP built?
a: Marin described a form where you pasted links to videos stored on S3, which were then transcribed and made queryable, and he thinks it was probably hosted on Heroku or something similar. In his words, it "performed speech to text, and then basically had an API that you could query to get the results" [04:02].

q: Why did OmniSearch focus on online education first?
a: The product started out very general, almost for everyone, and the team decided it needed a market it could double down on. "At a certain point, we figured, okay, we need a sort of a beachhead segment" [07:18], Marin said, and course creators and others in online education proved excited to try it.

q: What mistake taught OmniSearch how to prioritize features?
a: Marin said the team dove into building feature requests for a prospect and lost time when the sale fell through: "And then actually the deal ended up not converting in the end" [16:44]. The lesson was to prioritize features with broad appeal and be more comfortable saying no.

s6-bonus-hacking-the-brainwave-building-closed-loop-sleep-hardware-and-raising-20m-with-aaron-bromberg-of-stimscience

Science Before Product: StimScience spent three-plus years running sleep studies in Berkeley. Aaron says a 15-minute personalized stim session at bedtime halved time to fall asleep and improved the night's sleep more than any sleeping pill.

The Bar of Soap Prototype: A 3D-printed case, one single-sided circuit board and Amazon headbands made 150 test units. They were too uncomfortable for most people to wear overnight, so pilot participants also got Fitbits as a second data source.
Design It Like Sleepwear: Aaron challenged the team to work backwards from sleepwear, not forward from the prototype. Silk and padding surround the electronics, which the engineers shrank by 75%.

Heads Are Highly Variable: The team underestimated how hard it would be to keep sensors and electrodes touching skin across different foreheads. Smaller electronics and flexible circuits helped the design adapt.

Hard Part First: A lesson from a former Amazon manager led Aaron to tackle science and invention risk before branding, pricing or industrial design. He sees the firmware, software and personalization algorithms as the most valuable piece.

q: What is Somnee and how does it work?
a: Somnee is StimScience's at-home headband that uses an EEG sensor to detect your brain's drowsiness pattern, then stimulates at that pattern with a gentle electrical current. Aaron Bromberg explained that it is personalized because it is "detecting your unique pattern and playing it back in a way that optimally promotes sleep" [06:31].

q: What did StimScience's sleep studies find about brain stimulation?
a: After three-plus years of studies, Aaron Bromberg says the team found that a 15-minute personalized session at bedtime improved the whole night's sleep by more than any sleeping pill. On falling asleep, he said, "not only can we cut the time that it takes to fall asleep in half" [04:26].

q: What did the first Somnee prototype look like?
a: It was a 3D-printed plastic enclosure holding a single circuit board, attached with magnets to headbands found on Amazon. Aaron Bromberg recalled that "It looked sort of like a bar of soap on your forehead" [08:33], but it let the team put 150 units in volunteers' hands to validate at-home use.

q: How is Somnee different from a sleep tracker?
a: Somnee does track sleep, but Aaron Bromberg says the team chose not to focus on being the best tracker because customers are already well served there. He described it as different and better "because it's a sleep fixer, not a sleep tracker" [24:19].

q: What mistake did StimScience make while designing its wearable hardware?
a: Aaron Bromberg says the team underestimated how challenging it would be to fit a wearable to many head sizes while keeping good skin contact. He said they underestimated the importance "of human factors, specifically physical factors" [20:16], and went back to the drawing board with smaller electronics and flexible circuits.

s6-e14-the-real-time-ledger-how-banked-scaled-global-account-to-account-infrastructure-with-joe-pettersson

Dogfooding Through a Small MVP: Banked first shipped an iOS app that let small businesses take bank payments, using it to test its own APIs and checkout. The backend was Rails with Postgres and Redis, deployed on Heroku.
Just-in-Time Scaling: Payments leave no room for outages, but Banked avoided overbuilding. Automated load testing simulates traffic against sales forecasts so the team can stay ahead of growth.

Evolving Without a Big Rewrite: To meet the expectations of customers like Bank of America, Banked incrementally broke services out of its Rails monolith, moved from Heroku to GCP, and adopted bring-your-own-keys and HSMs.

One Abstraction for Every Market: A single internal payments abstraction lets product teams code against one interface across geographies, limiting the market-specific code paths that slow global expansion.

Weighing Effort Against Impact: Banked spent significant time on edge cases in an early rewards partner's legacy interface. In hindsight, Pettersson says a more minimal version could have proved the concept first.

q: What is Banked and how do its account-to-account payments work?
a: Banked is building a payment network that moves money directly between accounts instead of over card rails, using systems such as RTP in the US, Faster Payments in the UK and SEPA in Europe. As CTO Joe Pettersson explains, "we enable people to make payments directly out of their accounts" [04:38].

q: What tech stack did Banked use to build its MVP?
a: Joe Pettersson says Banked built an iOS app that consumed backend APIs written in Rails, with Postgres and Redis, and deployed on Heroku to ship quickly. In his words, "We had this Rails app that had a bunch of functionality in it" [09:36].

q: How did Banked approach scalability as a payments startup?
a: Pettersson says Banked could not rely on fixing things when they broke, yet did not want to build for scale its customers did not yet need. He explains that "our goal has always been just-in-time optimization" [17:49], supported by early investment in automated load testing.

q: How does Banked handle payment differences between countries?
a: Pettersson says payment fields, metadata and implementation details vary enormously by market, which can pile up technical debt. Early on, the payments team decided that "there will be a single internal abstraction" [22:04], so other product teams can code against one interface.

q: What advice does Banked CTO Joe Pettersson give technical founders?
a: Pettersson advises building an organization whose culture and structure can adapt, supported by open and transparent communication because change can be frightening. As he puts it, "Really the only thing that you can optimize for as a leader is change." [31:58]

c9b1a44f-ff7e-40dd-a8ba-b79007c30fcd
s6-bonus-unifying-broken-architecture-building-the-insurtech-api-data-layer-and-raising-30m-with-dan-langevin-of-vericred

Middleware Between Carriers and InsurTechs: Vericred gives InsurTech companies a single format and a modern API, while connecting to insurance carriers by whatever means they need, often flat files and batch processes.

Breadth Over Depth MVP: The first version took about three to four months and used easily accessible public data to demo plan shopping by doctor acceptance, leaving many edge cases uncovered on purpose.

A Contract Protects the Architecture: One set of code standardizes carrier formats, with a contract to the systems that process the data. This helped Vericred scale without too much maintenance load and clarified team responsibilities.

Don't Optimize for 1,000x: Langevin says optimizing for 100 or 1,000 times current volume rarely makes sense. Leave enough buffer to find the real stress points in production, then optimize as needed.

Market the Technology Earlier: Looking back, Langevin would invest sooner in product marketing and sales enablement, having learned that how you talk about technology is about as important as how well it works.

q: What does Vericred do?
a: Dan Langevin explains that "Vericred is an API middleware company in the insurtech space" [02:22]. It connects health and employee benefit insurance carriers with InsurTech companies that want to work with that data over an API.

q: How did Vericred get started?
a: Langevin and co-founder Mike first set out to build a credentialing platform for doctors, beginning with data on the insurance they accept. While selling to InsurTechs, Langevin says, "we just recognized this need, broader need for data transparency and fluidity in the space" [04:12].

q: How was the Vericred MVP built?
a: Vericred is a Ruby on Rails shop, and Langevin built much of the initial code base alongside engineers from Pivotal Labs. He recalls that "we spent about four months building" [04:53] the first version, a demo site that used public data to show insurance plan shopping.

q: How does Vericred handle different data formats from insurance carriers?
a: Langevin says one set of code handles standardization into a common format, with a contract between it and the rest of the system that processes the data. He notes that "keeping that contract really helped us to scale things out without creating too much" [12:20] maintenance load.

q: What does Vericred look for when hiring engineers?
a: Langevin says, "the biggest things that we look for are curiosity and accountability" [09:19]. He wants people who are curious about the domain and customers, and who are pragmatic and committed to shipping code that solves business problems.

s6-bonus-the-api-first-playbook-from-twilio-coo-to-building-a-42m-fintech-engine-and-exiting-to-fis-with-roy-ng-of-bond

One API Over Many Providers: Bond built an abstraction layer over underlying infrastructure providers, giving customers one set of universal APIs. Roy says a newcomer can open a bank account and issue a card in the sandbox in 20 minutes.

Validate Before Building Deep: Bond took mock-up screens and funds flows to Money 2020 for three days of meetings with banks and tech companies. A basic MVP then took about nine months to a year, partly because it depended on bank and tech partners.

Built to Outgrow Gen 1: Roy saw customers of early platforms eventually bypass them to build in-house. Bond aimed to support brands from inception to scale, focused on more mature companies, and said no to some earlier-stage ones.
Embedded Pay for Barbers: With Squire, Bond created a card that receives a barber's net pay and tip right after a haircut instead of every two weeks. Squire also earns interchange on card spend.

Vet Vendors Beyond Their Name: Bond chose a large, recognizable vendor for a capability it should have built. After issues that affected customers, it built a direct integration with bank partners and now digs deeper before choosing to buy.

q: What is Bond's embedded finance platform?
a: Bond, co-founded by CEO Roy Ng, offers APIs for bank accounts, debit and credit cards, and money movement such as ACH, wires and bill pay. Ng describes it as "enabling software developers and product builders to leverage a set of APIs on our platform" [02:41].

q: What problem was Bond created to solve?
a: Roy Ng and his college friend Yan Wu saw that developers, including those at SoFi, were spending most of their time on financial infrastructure instead of the applications that engage consumers. As Ng put it, "Everybody's kind of rebuilding the plumbing every time around." [04:49]

q: How long did it take to build Bond's MVP?
a: Roy Ng estimates about three months to get an initial prototype to Money 2020, then about nine months to a year to get the basic MVP out. He contrasted this with the alternative, saying that for a "tech company building directly with bank, it would take you a year" [07:51], or two.

q: How does the Squire Card pay barbers instantly?
a: Bond worked with Squire, which makes software for barbershops, on a card for barbers who typically waited two weeks to be paid. Roy Ng explained that after a haircut, "the net pay plus the tip goes directly to that barber's card that's already in their pocket" [11:59].

q: What did Bond learn about build versus buy?
a: Roy Ng said Bond picked a large vendor to get to market early, found the product wasn't as mature as expected, and replaced that capability with a direct bank integration. His lesson was "don't just kind of look at that vendor from how big they are, you know, what their valuation is." [25:48]

s6-e13-disrupting-supply-chain-logistics-building-an-api-first-tms-and-raising-50m-with-alexander-luksidadi-of-rose-rocket

Nice-to-Have Software Stalls: Freightnext aggregated carrier prices for shippers, sometimes by keying in pricing matrices by hand. Shippers saw it as nice to have, not a system of record, and the business failed.

Integrate Accounting, Don't Rebuild It: Rose Rocket's MVP began with order management and a customer portal. The team skipped building accounting and instead integrated with tools like Xero and QuickBooks.

Choosing SMB Over Enterprise: A decision-making framework called Placemat helped the team pick its focus. They chose SMB, partly because enterprise demanded heavy customization and custom workflows, and partly for the opportunity and vision.

Network Before Marketplace: Rose Rocket customers get real-time direct integration with each other. The plan is to become the system of record and build that network before taking on a load-matching marketplace.

Beware the Distributed Monolith: Luksidadi admits that adopting microservices too early, before the problems were understood, produced a distributed monolith. The team has planned out how to slowly fix it.

q: What is Rose Rocket?
a: Alexander Luksidadi, co-founder and CTO, describes it this way: "Rose Rocket is just a operating system for trucking companies" [02:35]. It also serves freight brokers, 3PLs and others that move freight, and it is built for collaboration between them.

q: Why doesn't Rose Rocket want to be Uber for Freight?
a: Luksidadi believes many companies taking that approach "out there they're just trying to like skip doing the hard part" [14:01]. He wants to first modernize a lagging industry, become the system of record and build a network, and only then consider a marketplace.

q: What did the founders learn from Freightnext before starting Rose Rocket?
a: Freightnext built software that let shippers pull prices from many logistics providers, but it struggled to scale and eventually failed. Luksidadi explained, "We figured out that shippers actually think that this type of software is just nice to have software" [06:28].

q: Why didn't Rose Rocket build accounting into its TMS?
a: Luksidadi said the team was mindful of being early and unable to build everything a traditional TMS includes. They passed on accounting "because there are the best in class accounting software out there, Xero, QuickBooks" [10:30], and built integrations instead.

q: What technical mistake did Rose Rocket make with microservices?
a: Luksidadi says he tried to be fancy with microservices early on, despite being advised against it. In his words, "you don't know your problems yet and I ended up building a distributed monolith" [22:19].

s6-bonus-debugging-live-in-production-building-dynamic-logging-and-exiting-to-dynatrace-with-liran-haimovitch-of-rookout

Observability Without Redeploying: Rookout is a live debugger for any environment, including production. It adds logs, metrics, spans and full state snapshots to a running application without rebuilding or redeploying it.

Protocol Choices Linger: gRPC's native extensions caused packaging headaches in Python and Node SDKs, forcing a costly migration and customer upgrades. Rewriting about 70% of the Python code into Go and some Node, one component at a time, was far easier.
REST to GraphQL: A Python backend built heavily on REST APIs hit concurrency trouble even at very small scale. Moving to GraphQL cut requests by roughly 10 to 100 times per client, service and user.

Hire People Who Take Things Apart: With few clear candidates for SDKs that change running code, Rookout hired cybersecurity and embedded engineers. It valued talent, initiative and the ability to learn over knowing everything upfront.

Pay for Value, Not Increments: Frequent raises still left a fast-growing DevOps engineer far below outside offers. Liran kept him, but the relationship changed, and he now focuses on what people should be making, not what they make today.

q: What is Rookout and what does it do?
a: Rookout, co-founded by CTO Liran Haimovitch, is a dynamic observability platform that collects data from running applications without a new release. Haimovitch describes it as "a kind of debugger that you can use in any environment not just on your laptop" [02:20].

q: How was the Rookout MVP built?
a: Liran Haimovitch and his co-founder built it in his living room, writing a Python SDK and backend with a React web interface. "We spent somewhere between two and three months building that MVP." [04:43]

q: Why can gRPC be a problem when building an SDK?
a: Haimovitch says gRPC relied on native extensions for runtimes such as Python and Node, which complicates an SDK that must run on arbitrary operating systems and packaging setups. In his words, "you'll often find that those native extensions are a headache" [07:58], and Rookout later had to migrate its SDKs.

q: How should startups prioritize customer feature requests?
a: Liran Haimovitch weighs willingness to pay, impact on deals and how often the same complaint comes up, while keeping the product vision in mind. He advises that "It's important when talking to customers to separate the problems" [12:00] from the solutions they propose.

q: What is Rookout's live logging feature?
a: Haimovitch explains that live logging lets engineers decide in real time which logs they want, including targeting a specific customer, environment or account. He asks, "why don't you get debug level logs for that customers without turning the entire system into debug?" [27:12]

s6-bonus-leaving-lyft-to-build-a-1b-fintech-engine-real-estate-syndication-architecture-with-perry-zheng-of-cash-flow-portal

Moonlighting as a Funding Strategy: Perry kept his Lyft engineering manager job for a year and a half, working 80 to 100 hours a week and using his pay to fund outsourced engineers. He had spent over $400K with little to show at that point.

Build for the Biggest Pain: Perry first built post-closing document tools that users wouldn't pay for. Adding an equity raising tool, built over about three months, addressed their biggest pain point, and things started taking off.

Roadmap Without A/B Tests: Perry weighs how often customers raise a complaint, whether it's legitimate and whether it's foundational. He skips analytics and A/B testing, and favors finishing something over perfect prioritization.

Selective Shortcuts Protect Scale: Quick hacks were fine if they didn't make scaling or reverting harder. A two-month data model redo early on meant no migrations or backfills when customers poured in.
Referrals Snowballed the Team: A standout first engineer from Upwork was followed by 20 interviews that went poorly. Most of the team then came through referrals stemming from a few strong people.

q: What is Cash Flow Portal?
a: Perry Zheng describes it as a marketplace where investors can find real estate syndicators and invest in their projects. In his words, "Cashflow Portal is the angel list for real estate investing." [02:14]

q: What problem led Perry Zheng to start Cash Flow Portal?
a: While raising $4.3 million from 70 investors for a 172-unit apartment complex, Perry handled signatures, spreadsheets and wire emails by hand. He recalled, "So that means I need to prepare 70 DocuSigns, send it to the investors, they sign it," [02:40] before extracting each investment amount himself.

q: Why didn't Perry Zheng code the Cash Flow Portal MVP himself?
a: Perry decided his salary was his biggest asset, so he stayed at Lyft and hired engineers while managing their specs and reviewing code. He reasoned that "even if I'm a superhuman coder, I will not be as good as five engineers." [06:19]

q: What was an early product mistake at Cash Flow Portal?
a: Perry built post-closing tools before the equity raising tool, and says he should have reversed the order. He learned that "the biggest pain point they have is the period in which they are raising money." [08:17]

q: How did Cash Flow Portal approach scalability?
a: Perry's team weighed extra development work against quick solutions, avoiding hacks that would force a big migration later. He said that "when the customers start growing and coming in like crazy, we did not have to do a single migration." [15:16]

s6-e12-the-pivot-that-made-app-store-history-how-the-youversion-bible-app-built-a-global-mobile-phenomenon-with-bobby-gruenewald

Failure Led to Mobile: YouVersion began in 2007 as a website for linking media to Bible passages. It didn't work, which led the team to build a Bible app that was among the first 200 in the App Store in 2008.

Licensing Came Before Code: Modern Bible translations are owned by publishers, and Bobby was asking them to license text for a free tool. Most meetings went nowhere, but one yes got the project started.

A Last-Minute Analytics Bet: A day before submitting to Apple, the team added an analytics library. It revealed 83,000 installs in the first three days and helped spur a push into new languages while competition was thin.

Volunteers as a Scaling Engine: As a donation-funded nonprofit, YouVersion lacked startup-style capital, so it tapped passionate users. About 2,000 volunteers help with work such as tech support and translation, led through tiers of volunteer leaders.

Cut Bad Architecture Sooner: The team kept pushing a graph database for social features despite visible problems. It failed at scale and had to be scrapped and rewritten, costing momentum, growth and morale.

q: How did the YouVersion Bible App get started?
a: Bobby Gruenewald got the idea in 2006 in an airport TSA line, when he was struggling to read the Bible consistently despite being a pastor. He recalls asking, "I wonder if there's a way to use technology to help me read the Bible" [02:56], and he registered youversion.com before boarding his flight.

q: What was the biggest early obstacle to building a Bible app?
a: Licensing was the first hurdle, because modern English translations are owned by various for-profit and nonprofit groups. Gruenewald explained, "the first obstacle that we encountered had nothing to do with technology" [06:08]. Without rights to the text, the idea could not be executed at all.

q: How successful was the Bible App when the App Store launched?
a: Using a third-party analytics library added at the last minute, Gruenewald's team watched installs in real time. From Thursday night to Sunday morning, he says, "we saw 83,000 people install the app" [14:51]. The team then shifted its early roadmap toward adding languages and fixing bugs.

q: How does YouVersion scale with volunteers?
a: Gruenewald says capital constraints pushed the nonprofit to recruit passionate users, who help provide tech support and human translation. He described having two or three "full-time staff members to 2 000 volunteers which means we actually have a tiered structure of" [27:51] leadership, where volunteer leaders lead other volunteers.

q: What advice does Bobby Gruenewald give young entrepreneurs?
a: Gruenewald warns that success can pull founders in many seemingly good directions that take them off center. His advice is "to really make sure they know who they are and they know" [41:26] why they do what they do.

s6-bonus-productizing-the-agency-building-automated-media-engines-scaling-growth-with-brandy-ryan-of-kitcaster-by-moburst
Validate Before Building: Ryan starts any project with a hundred phone calls. For Kitcaster, he and Brandy fleshed out the offer and ran a pilot; he called four of his clients and three bought it.

Productizing a Service: Wary of agency scope creep, the founders packaged booking as a monthly service with set deliverables. They tracked outreach like a sales pipeline, moving on from Trello when it didn't work.

Clarity Over Brand Dilution: Kitcaster stays focused on booking entrepreneurs on podcasts. Recurring requests, such as content repurposing, white-label booking and a self-serve guest list, are being spun into separate brands.
Meet Users Where They Are: Rather than pulling people to another dashboard, Ryan wants software built into tools they already use, like SMS, Gmail and Zoom, so it will actually be sticky.
Screen for Client Fit: Ryan admits his sales instinct led him to sign clients despite red flags, which hurt the team. Kitcaster has worked on ways to identify poor fits and politely part ways.

q: What is Kitcaster?
a: Kitcaster is a podcast booking agency founded by Brandy Whalen and Ryan Estes that connects startup founders with podcast hosts. Ryan explained that staying focused has built strong industry relationships, saying "We know that we can be the best in the world at booking." [09:39]

q: How did Kitcaster validate its podcast booking agency idea?
a: Brandy and Ryan fleshed out the offer, put together a pilot program and tested demand before launching. Ryan reported the early result: "I called four of my clients and three of them bought it." [04:14]

q: What tools did Kitcaster use to build its first version?
a: The team began with Trello, then leaned toward tools that work in a sales capacity, since podcast agents pitch conversations much like salespeople. Brandy recalled, "we started out using Trello. We realized quickly that wasn't going to work" [08:43].

q: What is the Podcast Guest List?
a: It is a platform where potential guests can be represented and hosts can browse and connect with them directly, without Kitcaster's involvement. Brandy said it serves people who want to be on podcasts "but maybe can't afford our services" [09:48], and at the time of the interview it was still in beta.

q: What advice do Kitcaster's founders have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Ryan's advice is short: "Sell it before you build it." [34:50] Brandy recommends building a strong support team whose skills differ from your own, especially in areas where you are deficient.

mentorcam-march-josh-campbell
A Brand Is a Promise: Campbell says a brand is far more than a logo or packaging. It's every touchpoint, your reputation and your promise to the consumer, and price, service and value need to match.

Offer a Familiar Alternative: His playbook takes a product that works and meets an existing need, then adds great packaging, experience and story. That's far easier than creating a category for a problem people don't know they have.
Prototype the Old-School Way: Don't burn time and money perfecting physical packaging. Print a label, tape it on, put it on a shelf and watch how people interact with it.

Package for the Context: Human Improvement's packaging was designed to jump off a shelf in the protein aisle, so it left out some copy. On Amazon, without that context, you do need to say it's protein.

Retail and E-Commerce Trade-Offs: Retail adds middlemen, slower payment and chargebacks, but reaches ready buyers and can hit 6,000 doors overnight. E-commerce pays faster, but customer acquisition can crush EBITDA margins.

q: How do you start building a brand?
a: Josh Campbell says to start by figuring out who your audience is and what you're trying to build, rather than with a logo or packaging. As he put it, "The brand is everything, every touchpoint that exists and really the reputation of what you're creating." [02:39]

q: How do you build a brand around a stigmatized or unconventional product?
a: Campbell, who has worked with categories such as essential oils, cannabis and insect protein, starts with a product that works and solves an existing need, then builds the packaging, experience and story around it. His framing to the consumer is, "hey, this is an alternative solution to something you already know is a big issue." [04:47]

q: How should you test packaging for a new physical product?
a: Campbell advises making your own rough prototypes instead of spending time and money trying to get them perfect. His advice is to "just print off it tape it on and see what people think like make your own prototypes" [08:48].

q: How is packaging for retail shelves different from packaging for Amazon?
a: Campbell explains that what looks good on a shelf doesn't always translate online. With Human Improvement, "we designed it to jump off a shelf" [11:01] and left out copy the protein aisle already implied, but on Amazon you do need to say it's protein.

q: What is the story behind So Gay Rosé?
a: Campbell says he launched it with a good friend as a joke meant to spark candid conversation, asking, "what better catalyst for conversation than a really strong rosé?" [13:26] He expected it to be direct-to-consumer, but shoppers wanted to grab it quickly in stores or through GoPuff, so they moved to the three-tier alcohol distribution model.

s6-e11-why-tech-training-fails-engineers-building-live-micro-coaching-engines-with-hywel-carver-of-skillerwhale

Assess First, Then Teach: Skiller Whale assesses each team, breaks curriculum into one-hour modules, and offers only the topics people need. Trainers lead developers to coding exercises and help debug their understanding.

Paper Strips Before Platform: Hywel first ran sessions by sliding cut-up printouts across a table to learners. A feature-complete platform came about a year after the first paying customers, and ideas were coded only once the team was about 95% certain.

Keep Developers in Their Tools: Rather than force experienced engineers into a web IDE, the team built a script that works with any editor and pushes code changes to the backend so trainers can see them.

A Forgotten Session Proved Remote: When a team forgot a free taster session and some had gone home, Hywel ran it over Google Meet. They felt it was just as good as in person, which led to video conferencing being built into the platform.

Scaling Means Scaling Humans: Hywel believes skills need trial, error and feedback, so training stays human-led. Borrowing from his university's grad-student model, Skiller Whale recruits trainers who are passionate about a language and use it every day.

q: What does Skiller Whale do?
a: Skiller Whale, co-founded by CEO Hywel Carver, delivers live, hands-on training based on an assessment of what each development team already knows. Hywel says the focus is on new capability rather than just delivering training: "we work with teams of software developers to change what they're capable of." [04:40]

q: How did Skiller Whale build its first MVP?
a: Hywel Carver started without a software platform, printing session material and cutting it into strips by topic. He explained that "I would sit around a table with the people we were training" [07:14], handing out strips as each person progressed and checking their work over their shoulder.

q: Do developers have to use a web IDE for Skiller Whale training?
a: No. Hywel Carver said experienced developers already have editors they like, so the team built a script that shares their code changes with the trainer. As he put it, "we wanted them to be able to work on stuff in the training session in their normal environment" [13:00].

q: Why can't engineers learn new skills just by watching videos or reading?
a: Hywel Carver distinguishes knowledge, which can be gained passively, from skills and wisdom, which require practice and judgment. In his words, "I think to gain a skill you need to have trial and error with feedback." [21:23]

q: What advice does Hywel Carver give founders who have just built a product?
a: Hywel advises setting the product aside and talking to at least 10 potential customers to understand their problem, then returning to see whether the product solves it. He also warns against seeking validation from the wrong people: "if I'm not your customer, my feedback is useless to you." [32:02]

s6-bonus-when-systems-crash-engineering-facebook-scale-incident-management-exiting-to-pagerduty-with-john-egan

Born From a Missed Tool: After leaving Facebook, Egan's team asked former colleagues which tools they missed. The one that kept coming up was an internal incident tool anyone in the company could use to see what was on fire.

Chat Over Form Fields: Kintaba's MVP paired a dashboard with a collaboration space instead of structured data entry. The team wanted a low barrier to filing, so problems get caught at SEV3 or SEV2 before the whole site goes down.
Charge From Day One: Everyone agrees that putting out fires should be easier, so Egan's real test was whether customers would pay anything at all. The MVP had to be valuable immediately.

Shipping Slower, Breaking Less: Early rapid releases spiked Kintaba's own SEV1s. The team added better unit tests, staging environments and fallbacks, and found a sweet spot of shipping about once a week.

Vision Filters Customer Requests: Egan maps each customer request against the long-term goal of company-wide use. A request for another input field gets translated into an answer that meets the need without making the product scarier.

q: What is Kintaba and what does it do?
a: Kintaba is an incident management and response platform that tracks current and past incidents and keeps the response process consistent, including roles, conversations and postmortems. John Egan explained, "What Kintaba really is, is it's a dashboard for all of your major fires" [05:58].

q: Where does the name Kintaba come from?
a: John Egan says the name derives from Kintsugi, a Japanese art form in which broken pottery is repaired with gold and becomes more valuable. It reflects "this idea that you're actually stronger for your scars" [05:39], with each major incident an opportunity to become more resilient.

q: Why should companies encourage people to file more incidents?
a: John Egan argues that long, intimidating processes and form fields make people reluctant to report problems. A lower barrier means more incidents get filed, and as he put it, "you'll catch them sooner because your barrier is lower" [12:12].

q: What mistake did Kintaba make early on?
a: John Egan says the team brought a move-fast habit that got features out quickly but made the product fragile for early customers. He noted that the chances of breaking other parts of the product "due to rapid shipping were significantly higher than I" [27:00] would have liked.

q: Is incident management only for engineering and SRE teams?
a: No. John Egan sees it as relevant to sales, marketing, PR, legal, the C-suite and engineering, and cites customers using it for an office power outage. In his words, "incident management isn't actually a technical practice" [31:22].

s6-bonus-sovereign-privacy-how-thrivacy-tokenized-identity-verification-without-data-leakage-with-dr-gordon-jones

Two Problems, One Wallet: Student Erica Barnett wanted to protect student identities, while Dr. Gordon Jones was frustrated by slow background checks. They merged the ideas into Thrivacy, treating degrees, work history and licenses as parts of identity.

The Individual Is the Customer: Jones found identity management focused on the enterprise. Even with B2B revenue models, Thrivacy treats the individual as its ultimate customer and aims to avoid building a honeypot of accounts for hackers.

Back End Before Polish: With limited money, the team set aside its full Figma user experience to build core functionality first. A basic interface supports pilots, whose feedback will shape the back end and, over time, the experience.

Degrees as Verifiable Credentials: The first pilot, with the University of South Carolina, will turn college degrees into verifiable credentials in a free Thrivacy wallet, so employers need not hire a third party to confirm graduation.

Recruit Engineering Earlier: After early development stumbles, including a contractor Jones says ran off with their money, he would have pursued an engineer sooner and widened the search beyond South Carolina earlier.

q: What is Thrivacy and what problem does it solve?
a: Thrivacy is a digital identity wallet that Dr. Gordon Jones and his co-founders are building to protect personal data and verify credentials. Jones explained, "we wanted to help people protect their data, privacy," [05:44] so they have freedom to act in both the digital and physical worlds.

q: How did the idea for the Thrivacy digital wallet come about?
a: It combined student Erica Barnett's idea for securing student identity with Dr. Gordon Jones's own experience of a third-party background check when he was onboarded as an adjunct professor. Of that process, Jones said, "I just realized how stupid it is." [04:15]

q: How does Thrivacy use blockchain and verifiable credentials?
a: Dr. Gordon Jones describes a platform that verifies information from credential issuers, leveraging the open source Hyperledger blockchain. For the University of South Carolina pilot, he said, "we're going to be converting those college degrees into these verifiable credentials." [07:48]

q: Can blockchain-based identity scale to hundreds of millions of people?
a: Dr. Gordon Jones set goals of a million members in three years and 500 million in ten, and says Thrivacy will need to stay on the cutting edge or develop its own IP. He cautioned that "the blockchain as it's structured today would not be able to handle a 500 million member ecosystem." [20:06]

q: What advice does Dr. Gordon Jones give young entrepreneurs?
a: Jones advises founders to hold on to their conviction while expecting the solution to change as they learn from customers and the market. He urged them to hold to their "vision and your conviction, but be open minded to the journey that it takes to get there." [37:34]

mentorcam-march-edvard-engeseath

From Doctor to Nurx: Edvard Engeseath handled friends' birth control consultations by phone in Norway. Research on over-the-counter access and U.S. unintended pregnancies led him to tackle the problem.
Angels Versus VCs: Edvard puts typical VC return expectations at 25-35% and angels' at about 20-25%. Angels often do less diligence, partly because much of the data doesn't exist yet.

Founders Come First: Edvard weighs whether the idea excites him and whether he has relevant expertise, but people matter most. He has backed impressive founders without fully understanding their product.

Check Sizes and Risk: Some platforms allow a couple thousand dollars, but checks Edvard has seen usually run from $10,000 to $50,000. Most companies are expected to fail, with a rare winner making up for the rest.

Getting Into Deals: Network, explore AngelList and Product Hunt, or contact founders directly. SPVs, or syndicates, let newcomers join another investor's allocation in exchange for a share of the upside.

q: Why did Edvard Engeseath co-found Nurx?
a: Edvard, a physician, kept helping women get birth control through phone consultations in Norway and began researching access. He found that "birth control is over the counter in more than 100 countries worldwide" [02:30], and saw unintended pregnancies in the United States as a problem to tackle.

q: What is angel investing?
a: Edvard describes it as early-stage startup investing, typically the first money a company gets, at a point when VC or bank capital isn't really an option. In his words, "It's very high risk, but hence also the rewards can be quite good." [03:35]

q: How is angel investing different from venture capital?
a: According to Edvard, VCs typically expect higher returns, take larger chunks of a company and do more rigorous diligence. He also noted that "angels are often family and friends. It doesn't have to be, but it can be." [04:52]

q: How do angel investors decide which startups to back?
a: Edvard looks at whether the company makes sense, whether he can get excited about it and, ideally, whether he has expertise in the area. The top factor when investing this early, he said, "is the people behind it. That is everything." [06:52]

q: How can I get started as an angel investor?
a: Edvard suggests AngelList for people outside tech, along with reading up on your areas of interest and reaching out to founders directly. If you don't know how to do diligence, he advises, "Try to network your way to someone who does this and become part of their syndicate." [11:42]

s6-e10-killing-the-clipboard-digitizing-high-stakes-franchise-operations-with-tommy-yionoulis-of-opsanalitica

Lost Sale, Market Validation: A daily-checklist tool posted on LinkedIn drew a call from Which Wich. They passed on a $60,000 build for a roughly $5,000 alternative, but the interest told Tommy people might want the product.

Sweat Equity Built the Platform: Tommy and co-founder Eric fronted the money, while two others earned equity by building and maintaining the software. Developer Chad worked full time for a year without pay and now heads development.

Borrowed Backend, Then a Rebuild: A Decisions workflow backend supplied user, location, task and reporting features quickly, but the product felt disjointed. The team later spent seven months building its own backend, and Tommy wishes they had done so sooner.
Deals Drove the Roadmap: Lost deals and demo objections dictated what got built, leaving modules 30% to 80% done but good enough to sell. In 2020, the bootstrapped team shifted toward finishing them.

Stop Naming Customers' Problems: For about five years, messaging told prospects what their problems were. An enterprise client reframed the value: OpsAnalitica helped them identify problems they didn't know they had.

q: What does OpsAnalitica do?
a: OpsAnalitica is an operations management and analytics platform for multi-location businesses, working primarily with restaurants. As Tommy Yionoulis explained, "we focus on helping our clients manage and measure their daily" [02:32] team member operations.

q: How did Tommy Yionoulis come up with the idea for OpsAnalitica?
a: Tommy first built an online audit tool at Quiznos, and in 2013 had an employee build a version for daily checklists. Which Wich saw it on LinkedIn and called but did not buy, which Tommy described as his "market validation. And so I was like, okay, maybe people want this." [10:06]

q: What technology does OpsAnalitica use to scale?
a: Tommy Yionoulis said the platform runs its own code as a web app on a Windows environment with SQL, which he considers highly scalable and portable. In his words, "there's nothing more tried and true in this world than a Windows server and a SQL database." [29:42]

q: What was OpsAnalitica's biggest marketing mistake?
a: Tommy said the early "operations data" messaging fell flat, and the company then spent years telling prospects that issues like paper, lazy employees or food safety were their problem. As he put it, "So for five years, we told everybody what their problem was." [35:36]

q: What advice does Tommy Yionoulis have for bootstrapped founders?
a: Tommy advises sticking with it if you can afford to and you are still improving the product, adding sales and delivering value to customers. He warned that "everything takes longer than you think it's going to take." [47:26]

s6-bonus-garbage-in-garbage-out-how-claravine-restructured-enterprise-data-management-with-verl-allen
Fix Data Quality Upfront: Rather than cleaning data after the fact through ETL, Claravine helps large enterprises set data standards upfront, then manage and enforce them across the organization.
Rebuild While Keeping Customers: With the product falling over, Verl's team shored up the old system while building a new platform, reusing less scale-prone pieces with plans to rewrite them later.

Share the Hiring Pipeline: To land early engineers as a non-engineer, Verl swapped candidates with friends at a much larger local company and let people self-select. This yielded two talented hires, one now chief architect.
Date Your Tech Debt: Future-proofing everything is costly, so the team makes tough trade-offs in quarterly planning, estimating when debt must be repaid, such as 18 months out.
Meet the Enterprise Bar: A large athletic shoe maker warned it would rip out its only startup vendor if things went wrong. Verl reports 96% revenue retention last year with a team of about 40.

q: What does Claravine do for enterprise data integrity?
a: Claravine helps large brands set data standards upfront and enforce them across the enterprise, typically selling into marketing organizations. Verl Allen contrasts this with cleaning data after the fact, saying "we take a different approach, which is very proactive rather than reactive to data quality" [03:07].

q: How did Claravine rebuild a product that was breaking?
a: Verl Allen's team hired its own engineers instead of relying on outsourced ones, then worked on the old and new products in parallel. As Verl described it, "we had to shore up the existing system that was falling over" [08:34] while also developing a new platform.

q: How can a non-technical CEO hire the first engineers?
