a: Verl Allen, whose background is in finance, worked with friends leading engineering at a much larger local company, and they passed candidates back and forth. His thinking was, "I want to find good people and let them self-select where they want to end up" [06:42].

q: How does Claravine decide when to take on tech debt?
a: The team weighs the cost of future-proofing against when a fix will need to be revisited, and makes those calls in quarterly product planning, sometimes after long debate. Verl says, "we're very clear on what the trade-offs are and why we're making them each time" [21:46].

q: How do customers shape Claravine's product roadmap?
a: Large customers pull Claravine into other parts of their organizations, revealing problems the team did not know about. Verl notes that "our customers are kind of pulling us into opportunities that we never even really kind of anticipated" [13:41].

whats-your-problem-with-jacob-goldstein

Logistics Was the Real Problem: Seeing expired medicine stacked outside a Tanzanian warehouse showed Keenan Wyrobek that supply wasn't the main issue. Getting it to doctors was, and on-demand drones could leapfrog the obstacles.

Health Systems Welcomed Change: Wyrobek feared national health systems would reject disruption. Instead, Rwanda's health minister gave the team two weeks to make the health and economic case, and Rwanda became Zipline's first customer.

Building Drones From Scratch: The best quote was $200,000 per drone, with a 200-flight warranty only if it wasn't flown in rain. Those economics failed, and customers needed delivery in any weather, so Zipline built its own.

Powered by Smartphone Technology: Zipline's drones use many of the same kinds of components as phones, including GPS, cell modems, sensors and similar processors, which Wyrobek praised as power efficient and capable.

Automated Delivery and Recovery: Drones with roughly 10-foot wingspans fly themselves, drop cake-box-sized packages by paper parachute, and are caught on return when motorized poles snap a line into the plane's tail hook.

q: How did Keenan Wyrobek come up with the idea for Zipline?
a: Wyrobek's wife, an epidemiologist, pointed him toward health campaigns that were getting stuck on logistics, and he researched the problem in Central America and Africa. After seeing expired medicine outside a Tanzanian warehouse, he recalled that "it clicked of like, okay, supply is actually not the big problem." [05:16]

q: Why did Zipline build its own drones instead of buying them?
a: Wyrobek went to drone companies first, but the offers made the economics unworkable and could not meet the need to deliver in rain. He said the best "quote I got for a drone was $200,000 per drone with a 200 flight warranty" [07:10].

q: How does a Zipline drone delivery work?
a: A doctor or nurse orders by app, phone or WhatsApp, and the team packs the item into a drone that is sent off from a launcher. Wyrobek explained that "It's flying automatically all the way out to the delivery site." [10:43] There it drops the package with a paper parachute.

q: How do Zipline drones land?
a: They don't land in the way a small plane would; instead, they fly between two motorized poles with a thin string between them. At the last fraction of a second, Wyrobek said, "the motors on those poles will snap those poles up" [12:43], flinging the line into the plane's tail hook.

q: What smartphone technology do Zipline's drones use?
a: Wyrobek said the drones carry GPS, cell modems and sensors like those in phones, along with very similar processor technology. Of that technology, he said, "They're so power efficient and they're so capable." [08:34]

mentorcam-march-benjamin-balazs

Retention Or Love Defines MVPs: Benjamin calls an MVP solid when it has retention or great feedback, not big numbers. If 10 people love your product, he believes you know you can go on to 100, then 1,000.

Be Your Own Real Customer: Benjamin likes building products he would use himself, in real action rather than in theory. His first startup, a photography website platform, grew from wanting a great site of his own.

Rebuilding Mentorcam's Backend: Six months into the MVP, the team replaced its Ruby backend with Firebase. Securing it wasn't easy, but it took about four to six weeks, and Benjamin calls it the best decision.

Clean Code Has A Cost: Benjamin's obsession with a super clean codebase meant shipping much later than he could have. He accepts that trade-off so he can keep extending the code without one day hitting the iceberg.
Plan For Scale Early: Benjamin thinks about scalability from day zero, though he notes his products haven't served millions of users. He favors modern, serverless tools and maintaining less code.

q: What makes a solid MVP for a startup?
a: Benjamin Balazs, co-founder and CTO of Mentorcam, looks for retention or strong feedback rather than large numbers. He considers something a solid "MVP when you either have retention or great feedback." [02:39]

q: Why did Mentorcam switch its backend from Ruby to Firebase?
a: Six months into building the MVP, Benjamin found the existing setup clunky and a bad user experience, so the team changed the backend completely. As he put it, "I realized that we have a technical debt that cannot be pushed down the line." [05:37]

q: How can you tell if your product has technical debt?
a: Benjamin says it shows up both in the customer experience and in how hard the code is to maintain and extend. His developer test is a feature that "should take a day and then you spend four days on it, now you have technical debt." [06:48]

q: When should a startup think about scalability?
a: Benjamin personally thinks about it from day zero, while acknowledging his experience is limited because his products haven't been used by millions. He recommends investing in modern tools when you can switch without re-engineering the whole stack, because "The less code you maintain, the better it is." [08:56]

q: How do you find product-market fit?
a: Benjamin admits he hasn't found a recipe, but ties product-market fit to retention and building something people want. He says luck sometimes plays a part, but ultimately "it comes down to iterating fast." [09:44]

s6-e9-bootstrapping-the-knowledge-economy-scaling-learnworlds-to-a-32m-growth-engine-with-panos-siozos
Two Years Before Real Users: LearnWorlds skipped the MVP and built a full platform in stealth for about two years. Real users then found parts too complex, so the team had to trim features.

Failing Locally Opened the US: Amid Greece's financial crisis, local businesses and trainers weren't buying, and some learners offered to mail a 10 euro note. That pushed the team toward the more mature US online course market.

Selling Mattered as Much as Teaching: The team paused much of its e-learning roadmap to build missing e-commerce features, including tools for sales, invoices and admin. Customers effectively became co-designers.

First Jobs, Devoted Team: Unable to pay competitive salaries while youth unemployment was around 50%, LearnWorlds hired inexperienced graduates. They grew with the product, and senior professionals joined around 2018 and 2019.

Manual Trials Before Automation: Early free trials were built by hand, with the CTO cloning databases and changing DNS records. The team lived with that until automation became a priority, cutting access time to seconds.

q: What is LearnWorlds?
a: Co-founder and CEO Panos Siozos describes it this way: "LearnWorlds is an online platform for creating and selling online courses." [02:20] Creators can build courses with video, text, assignments, assessments and certificates, and Siozos compares it to a Shopify for online courses.

q: Did LearnWorlds start with an MVP?
a: No, the team built a full platform because Panos Siozos and his co-founders felt learning was too deep an experience to test with a small product. Looking back on that first version, he said, "It was probably a maximum valuable product at that moment." [11:23]

q: Why did LearnWorlds focus on the US market instead of Greece?
a: The team struggled to win Greek customers during the financial crisis, and local online payments were still primitive. Siozos calls this probably one of the best "things that happened to us because we failed locally. So we couldn't find any local customers." [12:21]

q: How did LearnWorlds handle free trials in its early days?
a: Each trial was created by hand after someone filled in a form, and Siozos then emailed the login details. He recalled that "my co-founder and CTO, Fanis, had to go in, clone a few databases by hand, change a few DNS" [21:26] records.

q: What would Panos Siozos do differently if he started LearnWorlds again?
a: Siozos said he wouldn't want to change the journey overall, but he would have looked to the US sooner, put more into e-commerce, sales and marketing, and possibly pursued funding harder. As he put it, "we were great scientists and developers." [32:53] but they could not yet sell the product very effectively.

s6-bonus-the-156m-devsecops-blueprint-from-open-source-checkov-to-acquisition-with-barak-schoster-of-bridgecrew

Fix Cloud Issues in Code: Rather than only scanning live cloud environments and opening Jira tickets, Bridgecrew scans code such as Terraform and suggests fixes in pull requests, automating part of the code review teammates were doing by hand.
Checkov's Fast Open-Source Start: Released in November 2019 with 50 rules and only Terraform support, Checkov hit 60,000 downloads in its first month and 300K after two months.

Deployment Speed Before Scale: The team chose not to design for scale at first. It invested in serverless, monitoring and a CI/CD pipeline that shipped to production 9 to 11 times a day, turning release decisions into pure prioritization.

Repetition Beats Logo Size: Paying customers came first, along with repeated asks across sales, customers and open-source users. A common cloud-native stack mattered more than chasing Fortune 100 requirements.

Be Transparent With Contributors: Barak says they could have done better early on at easing contributions and explaining what would be open source or paid. A public roadmap might have grown an even bigger community.

q: What does Bridgecrew do?
a: Bridgecrew scans infrastructure as code, GitHub workflows and open-source packages for misconfigurations, then suggests code fixes. Barak Schoster explained that "It helps to secure any code that a DevOps or SRE platform engineering team would write, would produce." [02:31]

q: How was the Bridgecrew MVP built?
a: It began as manual work: Barak Schoster's team got access to customers' code and, as he put it, "we started manually reviewing their pull requests." [06:13] Repetitive patterns first became PDF reports and later a GitHub application that commented with suggested code fixes.

q: How popular was Checkov when it launched?
a: Checkov, Bridgecrew's open-source project, was released in November 2019 and took off quickly. Barak Schoster said that in the first month "we got 60,000 downloads. And after two months, we had 300K downloads." [05:34]

q: What scaling bottleneck did Bridgecrew hit with AWS Lambda?
a: Barak Schoster said compute was easy to scale through Lambda configuration, but the next constraint was "which is not compute, it's your database." [15:18] The team built its own RDS proxy to maintain database connections and later migrated to the RDS Proxy product from AWS.

q: How much customer research did Bridgecrew do before writing code?
a: Barak Schoster said that "before we wrote the first lines of code of BridgeCrew, we interviewed 120" [30:15] people, including SREs, security practitioners and DevOps engineers. He suggests that new founders could stop at 30 to get validation.

mentorcam-march-max-samuel
Early Stage Bets on Founders: Max says early-stage VC leans less on long-run growth, traction and financial metrics, and more on big, bold ideas and conviction that the founders can execute on them.

Team Comes First: Max looks for founders with personal experience or unique expertise in the problem. With co-founders, he likes a long-standing relationship and complementary strengths, such as a technical and a business lead.
The Secret Others Miss: A lens Max learned working with Peter Thiel is whether founders know a secret about the world that others don't, and are building a business around it.

Market and Moat Matter: He favors transformational or market-creating ideas over incremental ones, with barriers such as hard-to-replicate technology or unique team expertise, strengthened by network effects as users grow.

Break In by Doing: You don't need a traditional path into VC. Max suggests lending your services to incubators, writing a blog or investment theses, and sending that portfolio of work to venture firms.

q: How is early-stage venture capital different from other VC?
a: Max Samuel says early-stage analysis depends less on growth trajectory, traction and financial metrics, and more on big ideas and the people behind them. As he put it, "we are backing founders and their ideas" [03:24].

q: How do venture capital firms evaluate startups?
a: Max looks at three broad areas: the team, the market and defensibility. Drawing on his time with Peter Thiel, he asks whether founders "have some secret to the world that others don't know?" [05:13].

q: What should a startup pitch deck include?
a: Max advises distilling the key considerations into just a few slides, showing why this team is uniquely suited to the problem and what its vision is for changing it. Because investors see many presentations, founders need to "convey powerful information in a very dense format" [07:36].

q: How do you start a career in venture capital?
a: Max says business school, finance and entrepreneurship are common routes, but they aren't required. He explained, "a good way to break in to the industry is to just get involved" [09:47], for example by helping incubators or publishing your own analysis.

q: What would Max Samuel do differently if he started his VC career again?
a: Max would get more hands-on operating experience, since his legal work at Wilson Sonsini put him close to many startups but only in passing. He said, "it would have been fun to have a bit more operational experience" [11:33].

s6-e8-killing-the-ssh-key-building-identity-native-cloud-access-and-a-1b-unicorn-with-ev-kontsevoy-of-teleport
Certificates Only, Even for Google: With almost no revenue, Teleport turned down a Google team that wanted public-private key support, choosing to stay 100% certificate-based.

Open Source as Recruiting Tool: Teleport reached GitHub to attract engineers who wanted open source work. Stars, bug reports and feature requests followed, then paying Enterprise customers via a note in the docs and README.

Simplicity as Scalability: Teleport was designed as a single binary that can run across thousands of locations. Ev argues a system needing a giant tech stack underneath isn't truly scalable, even if it handles lots of traffic.

Two Products Split Focus: Gravity and Teleport were both selling and growing, so the team kept both too long. Ev believes going all-in on Teleport sooner could have made the company two to three times bigger.
Machines Need Secure Access Too: Ev calls API keys just passwords and wants them replaced. He sees Teleport becoming a secure, trusted message bus for both humans and machines.

q: What is Teleport and what can it access?
a: Ev Kontsevoy describes it this way: "Teleport, it's the easiest way to access securely all of your computing infrastructure." [02:28] It is a remote access solution covering SSH servers, Kubernetes clusters, databases such as MongoDB, MySQL and Postgres, and Windows desktops over RDP.

q: How was the first version of Teleport built?
a: Teleport began as an internal tool for securely reaching portable Kubernetes deployments, even on other networks. Kontsevoy says the MVP was coded "by our CTO, Sasha, in literally a weekend" [08:36], and it was based entirely on certificates.

q: Why doesn't Teleport support SSH public-private keys?
a: Kontsevoy says the team wanted to move away from shared credentials, secrets and passwords, which they believed would not scale. When a Google team asked for key support, the answer was "we will never do that because it's really important for us to remain 100% certificate-based." [13:58]

q: Why did Teleport become open source?
a: At first, Kontsevoy's team didn't think Teleport could be a product, since it was a component of another one. He says they chose to open source it "and put it on GitHub strictly for recruiting purposes." [11:37]

q: What was the biggest business mistake Teleport made?
a: Kontsevoy points to a lack of focus, with the company running both Gravity, a Kubernetes deployment system, and Teleport for too long. Had they committed to Teleport earlier, he says, "we probably could have been two three times bigger by now" [25:18].

s6-bonus-beyond-standard-logging-building-full-stack-workflow-telemetry-and-analytics-with-prabhjot-singh-of-pyze

Validate With Open-Ended Questions: Pyze ran about 25 validation interviews before writing MVP specs, but Singh feels the questions reaffirmed what the team already believed. Far fewer developers used the product to make decisions than they had hoped.

Pivoting From Apps to Processes: Pyze began as a freemium mobile analytics product and reached tens of thousands of users, not the millions it needed. Moving to enterprise shifted its focus from applications to the business processes they enable.

Manual Work Can Power MVPs: Instead of a real-time AI pipeline, the early product ran queries every one to six hours and the results were manually pushed to customer accounts. People and tooling can cover what the product can't yet do.

Costing Every Workflow: Pyze combines process timing with employee, pay and CRM data to find bottlenecks and anomalies. Knowing how long a task takes and what it costs lets companies compare the cost of different workflows.

Scale Just Ahead of Demand: Pyze made early cloud-native choices, including Kubernetes, but Singh advises against designing for load two or three versions out. Serve current and near-term customers, then stay ahead of expected load.

q: What does Pyze do?
a: Pyze analyzes key business processes, such as selling insurance policies or processing claims, to show where bottlenecks are and how work can be done better, down to the task level. As Prabhjot Singh put it, Pyze "automated this process of understanding how work gets done within an organization" [03:36].

q: Why did Pyze pivot from B2C to enterprise?
a: Prabhjot Singh says the freemium product for mobile app developers needed millions of users to scale, but it reached only tens of thousands and didn't seem likely to get there. The team also realized that for the average mobile developer, "our capabilities were kind of overkill" [06:20].

q: How did Pyze build its MVP?
a: Singh describes starting with wireframes and feedback, and favors lean iteration. Early automated insights relied on scheduled queries and manual delivery, which he calls an example that "the product doesn't necessarily have to fully deliver on the promise" [12:18].

q: What data does Pyze use to analyze business processes?
a: Singh says Pyze brings in process data, such as time spent at each step, along with employee, pay and customer CRM data. In his words, "what we do is hook up the different data sources that are available to fully understand that process" [32:07].

q: What mistake did Pyze make during customer validation?
a: Prabhjot Singh says the initial focus on app developers cost the company several months of development and commercialization. Looking back at the validation interviews, he feels the questions were "there to reaffirm what we thought we knew" [23:45] instead of being more open-ended.

mentorcam-march-rune-hauge

Target a List, Get Introductions: For its $1.5 million pre-seed, raised before applying to Y Combinator, MentorCam identified about 100 relevant angels and VCs, then worked out who could introduce them to each one.

Fit Means Stage and Chemistry: Look for investors who back your stage and industry (Rune's team used Crunchbase Pro), then check rapport. Investors tend to stay on your cap table until a liquidity event.
Create Urgency in Cohorts: Open by saying you're not really fundraising, talk to 10 or more investors, then circle back with news of interest. Too much pressure or hardball gets sniffed out.
Stop at the MVP: MentorCam began raising with a very simple marketplace of about 10 mentors. Extra bells and whistles add cost and delay launch, while a little traction shows a founder can hustle.
Be Transparent With Y Combinator: Rune applied multiple times before getting in. He credits clarity and traction, and advises honesty, no vanity metrics, and recommendations from YC founders.

q: What is MentorCam?
a: MentorCam, co-founded by Rune Hauge, connects people with experts in areas such as startups, tech and business. Rune describes it as a "marketplace for people to get access to high profile experts that are typically not that" [01:08] easy to reach otherwise.

q: What is a startup fundraising strategy?
a: Rune Hauge says it starts with preparation: building a target list of investors and finding people who can introduce you to them. In his words, "a fundraising strategy means knowing what investors to target, when to target them and how to target them." [02:09]

q: How do you create investor FOMO when raising a round?
a: Rune suggests speaking with a cohort of 10 or more investors, then circling back to say there is a lot of interest and the round could fill quickly. He advises, "what is really key is to try to talk to a lot of investors at once." [05:01] He also cautions that investors can tell when the urgency doesn't feel genuine.

q: Do you need an MVP and traction before pitching VCs?
a: Rune believes both are very important unless you are a famous founder or have already had an exit. An MVP shows you can build, and he recommends getting a little traction "because that also shows that you have the ability to hustle more than anything else" [06:58].

q: How can founders improve their Y Combinator application?
a: Rune Hauge, who applied multiple times before getting in, recommends being very clear about what you're building, showing some traction and seeking recommendations from YC founders. He also stresses honesty: "Even if some things don't look extremely great, just be very, very transparent." [08:33]

ce2c1af1-62d0-4c45-a5a1-7126ef3fcc9d
s6-e7-how-doppler-built-the-universal-secrets-management-platform-with-brian-vallelunga

Built for Developers First: Brian saw that secrets tools were made for security teams, then forced on developers who avoided them. Doppler targets developers while still meeting security and compliance needs.
Buying Secure Storage Early: With secrets still in plain text, Doppler chose Very Good Security, at far more than its rent, so the team could focus on the management and automation layers.
Learning From Lost Customers: Objections shaped the roadmap most. Doppler dropped SDKs for a CLI, rebuilt it in Go with no dependencies, and added integrations so it wasn't in the hot path.

Interviews Built Around Real Work: Engineering candidates get two conversational phone screens, then an onsite with a roughly four-hour project like real Doppler work, a defense of their choices and an ask-us-anything session.

Growth Isn't Product Marketing: Brian hired a head of growth and built a growth team, then realized about eight months in that no one was telling product stories. The team was rebuilt with both functions.

q: What is Doppler and what does it do?
a: Doppler is a universal secrets platform for storing and managing things like API keys and database URLs across projects, infrastructure and developers. Brian Vallelunga explains that "we're kind of like GitHub for secrets" [02:23].

q: Why did Brian Vallelunga start Doppler?
a: While struggling to launch a crypto machine learning marketplace, Brian kept running into problems with environment variables and secrets, and other developers told him they had the same trouble. He found existing tools were built for security people, and says "the big insight that I had was like, let's just make this for developers" [05:44].

q: How did Doppler secure customer secrets in its early days?
a: Brian admits secrets were at first stored in plain text, and the team then chose Very Good Security (VGS) to store them securely. Doing storage properly themselves was more than simple encryption, and Brian said it "would take a lot of focus away from building the core thing" [08:15].

q: Why did Doppler build its CLI in Go instead of using SDKs?
a: SDKs didn't work because secrets must be available before the rest of an application's code runs, and Brian's first CLI in JavaScript forced customers to include a JavaScript runtime. The team rebuilt it in "Go as a custom executable that didn't have any dependencies" [11:47].

q: How does Doppler avoid being a single point of failure for its customers?
a: Customers told the team they didn't want to go down if Doppler did, so it built integrations that push secrets to places like Heroku, Vercel, AWS and GCP. Brian describes a hub-and-spoke model where "Doppler is your central source of truth for all your secrets" [12:12].

s6-bonus-building-a-video-automation-platform-for-14-million-users-with-raghav-r-s-of-animaker

Full Product Before Small Bets: Animaker didn't start with an MVP, since video needs music, sound effects, editing and graphics. New products launch full scale after heavy research, then improve through small, MVP-style bets.

Letting Trends Go: Raghav names the biggest trade-off as not chasing every new idea in a chaotic creative market. The team focuses on a few bets, assuming most trends will die, and says that restraint made the company what it is.

Four Roadmap Pillars: Animaker's roadmap draws on founder and team intuition, customer feedback via success and support teams, lessons from complaints about competitors, and the pace of industry innovation.

Hire for Obsession: Raghav looks for people obsessive about their work, which he considers stronger than passion. If the first 10-20 hires have that trait, they define the culture and set the standard.
Delay Hurts More: Looking back, Raghav says delaying decisions hurt more than making wrong ones. Given another run, he would act faster on whatever data and thinking he had at the time.

q: What is Animaker and why was it built?
a: Animaker helps non-professionals create professional-quality videos, animations, designs and graphics, with uses ranging from learning content and marketing to social media posts. Raghav R S says it grew out of "absolute frustration out of professional tools. I mean last month we crossed more than 14 million" [02:29] users.

q: What inspired the idea behind Animaker?
a: Raghav was influenced by PowerPoint, where he felt you could sit down and create almost anything. He wanted to bring that approach to animation and video, asking "Why can't we create a PowerPoint version of animation tools and video tools?" [03:16].

q: Did Animaker start with an MVP?
a: No, Raghav says the team set out to build a complete product first because video creation requires so many tools, and switched to MVP thinking for features once in the market. He explained, "whenever we launch a new product or anything big, we'll go full scale." [04:23].

q: How did Animaker handle scaling challenges?
a: Raghav describes the first two years of growth as very messy, with quick fixes such as scaling up the company's RDS, while longer-term work meant finding bottlenecks and patterns. As he put it, "over the years, we got matured identifying those bottlenecks before it got messy." [10:51].

q: What advice does Raghav R S give young entrepreneurs?
a: Raghav suggests hearing plenty of advice but not acting on it until you believe it will work, because each journey is different. He added that "learning how to learn and whom to learn is super important than actually learning." [17:36].

s6-e6-the-synthetic-frontier-how-gretelai-weaponized-generative-ai-to-protect-privacy-with-john-myers

Privacy as Engineering: Gretel's idea is to let engineers make safe versions of data where it's created, before it lands in databases or warehouses and gets replicated. Anything shared with teams or partners is then already clean.

An MVP With One Goal: Instead of a hosted service, Gretel built Docker-based REST APIs driven by Python Jupyter notebooks and took them on a roadshow. The goal was initial funding, and a public beta followed eight months after securing it.

Real-Time Demos Hid a Gap: Beta one returned instant results on small JSON blobs, but struggled when users arrived with five-gigabyte files. Beta two added an API that pushes large data sets to workers for asynchronous processing.

Progressive Disclosure of Complexity: Modeled on the easy starts of tools like Stripe and GitHub, Gretel's roadmap lets developers sign in, try a few API calls, then follow tutorials to operationalize.

Build Billing Hooks Early: Preparing for general availability with consumption pricing, John wishes the team had built usage tracking and business model mechanics in sooner, rather than retrofitting them into the code base.

q: What is Gretel and who is it for?
a: John Myers, Gretel's co-founder and CTO, describes it as a toolkit for quickly creating safe versions of data so teams can be more productive. In his words, "Gretel is a privacy toolkit that allows developers, engineers, and scientists" [02:33].

q: What problem led John Myers to start Gretel?
a: While building a threat analysis product on customer network data, John found that anonymizing it was probably more work than building the product itself. He needed something developer friendly, explaining, "I needed to put something in the path of this data pipeline that we were building" [04:25].

q: How was the Gretel MVP built?
a: The team built locally deployable tools in Docker containers with REST APIs, plus Python Jupyter notebooks that called them. John said the aim was to take complex work "such as detecting PII or creating synthetic data and actually just put it behind a friendly API call" [06:57].

q: What mistake did Gretel make with its first beta?
a: The first beta was built around real-time results on small pieces of data, which demoed well but didn't scale to large files. John said the mistake was that "we knew what problem we were trying to solve, but we didn't really know how people wanted" [20:06] to consume the product.

q: What advice does John Myers give early-stage founders about roadmaps?
a: John advises staying the course and not letting a handful of customers drive the roadmap with bespoke requests just to get revenue sooner. He told founders to hold steady, saying "no one knows their product better than you do" [30:21].

s6-bonus-merging-hardware-with-code-restructuring-subsea-cables-and-global-networks-with-jim-fagan-of-gcx-global-cloud-exchange

Turnaround Starts With the Customer: GCX refocused on customers, restructured quickly and prioritized its "big rocks." Fagan says it went from cash negative to a $95 million trailing-12-month cash EBITDA.

Follow the Data Centers: GCX first extends infrastructure toward regions where hyperscalers are building data centers, then fills in the "capillaries" to markets where they want a presence without making big investments.

Build for Scale Early: Fagan says GCX has to be built to scale from day one despite added cost and complexity. The three-to-four-year end state stays in view while priorities have pivoted along the way.

Owning the Wrong Bet: GCX put heavy resources into IP products expecting quick wins that weren't there. The team was transparent and slowed the effort, though Fagan says it probably cost growth in other products.

Make Subsea Networks Cloud-Like: Networking is still very manual and point-to-point, Fagan says. GCX aims to tie its software layer to subsea infrastructure so large content players can shift workloads to the markets where they need them.

q: What is Global Cloud Exchange (GCX) trying to build?
a: Jim Fagan explains that GCX began as Flag, a builder of early large subsea cable systems, and later added global enterprise managed network services. The question now is "how do we actually take that and combine infrastructure with software" [03:48].

q: How did Jim Fagan and his team turn GCX around?
a: Fagan says they refocused on customers, restructured quickly, made hard trade-offs and aligned the company on a common vision. He reports that "for the trailing 12 months, we actually were able to turn a $95 million cash EBITDA." [06:29]

q: How does GCX decide where to expand its subsea and network infrastructure?
a: Fagan says the decision comes down to market trends and where customers want to be, including large streaming, gaming and digital companies. He described the approach this way: "follow the data centers. So we look to kind of follow into region" [11:02], tracking where hyperscalers are going.

q: What mistake did GCX's new leadership team make during the turnaround?
a: According to Fagan, the team invested early in IP products for near-term growth, but the expected quick wins weren't there. Admitting it openly was a credibility worry, yet he believes it helped establish a culture where "it's okay to make mistakes." [20:45]

q: What is the future of subsea networking according to GCX?
a: Fagan wants to expand GCX's global footprint and make subsea network infrastructure behave more like on-demand cloud services, while acknowledging the physical limits of laying fiber. His goal is to "make it, again, make it very cloud-like." [22:15] He also sees GCX playing a critical role in edge and 5G for hard-to-reach markets.

s6-e5-cracking-government-compliance-how-aceable-productized-state-mandated-learning-with-blake-garrett
Make It Required Learning: A dad-focused trivia app made about $5 a day. An investor urged Blake to apply mobile and game mechanics to things people have to learn, which led him to driver's ed.
The Cost of iOS Only: Launching on iPhone kept the focus on mobile, but with no web version, Google AdWords couldn't work profitably. Web followed about seven months later.
New Markets Over New Features: Aceable weighted its roadmap roughly 80/20 toward opening new markets, later maybe 70/30, since legacy competitors had invested little in product differentiation.

Start at the Career's Beginning: Texas real estate continuing education bombed, which Blake tied to agents already knowing other brands. Pre-licensing, a $400 product launched in February 2018, gained traction.

Rethinking the Multiplayer Experience: Aceable removed its separate parent experience in driver's ed to cut code complexity. Blake now thinks that was likely wrong, since involving others can make online courses less lonely.

q: What is Aceable and what kind of courses does it offer?
a: Aceable, founded by Blake Garrett, makes online and mobile-first courses for compliance-related education, starting with driver's ed and then real estate. Describing the driver's ed product, Garrett said, "We took the boring classroom experience and turned it into" [02:40] a mobile app with an engaging story, social mechanics and light game mechanics.

q: How did Blake Garrett come up with the idea for Aceable?
a: After a series of gamified content ideas, Garrett pitched an investor who called his idea awful, then suggested applying it to things people are required to learn. Garrett recalls the logic: "But if they had to buy it, you'd sell a lot, lot, lot, lot more of it." [08:23]

q: Why did Aceable launch on iOS first?
a: Blake Garrett saw a mobile app as the way to stand apart from competitors with web offerings, and felt hybrid development platforms of the time weren't responsive enough. He said the "true way to differentiate was through a mobile learning experience that could be consumed on" [14:37] the go.

q: Why did Aceable's first real estate course fail?
a: Aceable started with Texas continuing education because it was much cheaper to build, but could not get meaningful traction. Garrett says a board member, Charles, reframed the setback by asking, "What if continuing education in Texas is just a false negative?" [25:15], and the company pushed ahead with pre-licensing.

q: Did Aceable build its product to scale from day one?
a: Not primarily, because Blake Garrett says the company was built for survival and erred on the side of growth and traction amid recurring crises. His philosophy was, "I just want to be able to have the conversation if we didn't do this in a scalable way" [20:49] while the team was still employed by the company.

0f782359-aeff-4eb9-bb16-12ddb27ccbf4
s6-bonus-fueling-the-ai-engine-optimizing-unstructured-data-pipelines-for-vector-databases-with-michel-tricot-of-airbyte

Open Source for the Long Tail: Airbyte argues closed-source tools can't cover the endless list of data silos. Because every connector eventually breaks, a shared repository lets many companies use one connector and split the maintenance.

MVP in Three Months: After many iterations, the team settled on an open-source product in July 2020, gave itself three months, and released around late September or early October. It wasn't very stable, but it drew valuable feedback.

Shortcuts That Got Repaid: Airbyte started on Singer, then quickly replaced it with its own protocol because Singer wasn't reliable or maintained. Its homegrown scheduler took longer to swap for a proper scheduling solution.

Single Node Before Scale: To minimize time to value, the first version ran on a single Docker node rather than a cluster. The team built primitives so connectors could stay the same as the platform later moved to Kubernetes.

Cutting a Selling Product: An early marketing-focused product had inbound interest and buyers, but poor team fit, and COVID froze marketing teams. The team made a clean cut, and the many customer calls had taught them what Airbyte should be.

q: What does Airbyte do?
a: Airbyte moves data from SaaS applications, databases, files and spreadsheets into a central warehouse, so companies can get a full view across them. Michel Tricot explained, "what we allow you to do is just get this data" [02:34] from all those silos, with warehouses the main focus for now.

q: Why did Airbyte choose open source for data integration?
a: Michel Tricot says companies keep adding new data silos, and connectors break because they pull from systems you don't control. In his words, "It is not possible for a closed source solution" [06:00] to address that long tail, while open source lets users build connectors and share the maintenance.

q: What trade-offs did Airbyte make when building its MVP?
a: The team first relied on the open-source project Singer so it could focus on the platform, then quickly replaced it with its own protocol. It also skipped tools like Airflow and Prefect, and as Michel Tricot put it, "we built our own scheduler, which is not a good idea" [09:08], though it got them started quickly.

q: How did Airbyte approach scalability?
a: Michel Tricot said scalability was not the initial focus, because requiring a cluster would have made adoption too complex. He explained, "what we focus on is just single node deployment on Docker" [14:39], and the team later worked to make Kubernetes stable around mid-2021.

q: What mistake did the Airbyte team make early on?
a: Before settling on Airbyte's current direction, the team built a product for marketing teams, then stopped it after COVID froze those teams. Michel Tricot reflected, "the mistake was just going too quickly into a field" [19:26] that didn't make the most of the team's strengths, though they learned a lot from it.

s6-bonus-ending-the-api-debugging-nightmare-building-real-time-observability-networks-with-vedran-cindric-of-treblle
Born From Agency Pain: Maintaining up to about 50 apps and APIs across time zones, Vedran's agency built a logging tool to see what developers had done overnight. That tool became Treblle.

Scaling Nearly Killed It: The team dropped the project over fears of scaling cost and slowing customers' APIs. Vedran got the idea for a fix while working on something else with AWS videos playing in the background.

A Deliberately Narrow MVP: The first version had real-time API logging, error tracking and auto-generated documentation. Analytics and quality scoring came later, shaped by feedback from developers and clients.

Simplicity Powers Scale: Treblle relies on serverless technology and heavily on S3. Vedran says monthly timing aside, volume grew from about 200,000 API calls in July to about 4 million, with logs processed within 400 milliseconds.

Examples Over Documentation: Vedran's end goal is to remove the need for traditional API docs, moving toward example-based documentation that shows real tested responses and can notify developers when they change.

q: What is Treblle and what does it do?
a: Treblle is an SDK you add to your API code that provides real-time monitoring, logging, error tracking, auto-updated documentation, analytics and a quality score. As co-founder and CEO Vedran Cindrić put it, "it's a service that helps developers build and ship APIs faster" [02:32].

q: Why was Treblle built?
a: Vedran Cindrić's agency was supporting developers in other time zones who often couldn't tell why an API call wasn't working. He traced much of the confusion to the fact that "nobody actually understood nor saw how that was working or what they were doing" [04:16].

q: How does Treblle avoid slowing down the APIs it monitors?
a: Vedran says two guiding principles were handling the same load as the customer's API and never slowing it down. He explains that the open variable today is log processing time rather than API performance: "It's just a matter of when we will process the logs." [19:11]

q: What features were in Treblle's first MVP?
a: Vedran Cindrić says the MVP centered on real-time API logging, error tracking and automatically generated documentation, without analytics, quality scoring or test running. He described the approach this way: "the idea is let's just get the data into our system and then we'll figure it out" [09:21].

q: What would Vedran Cindrić do differently if he started Treblle again?
a: Vedran would focus more on getting the core architecture right before going to production, because re-architecting with live traffic is stressful and painful. Even if it meant shipping fewer features, he said, "I would rather have the core working perfectly than anything else." [29:55]

s6-e4-scaling-from-seed-to-enterprise-engineering-hyper-growth-pipelines-with-mike-boufford-former-cto-of-greenhouse

Productizing a Known Practice: Greenhouse turned structured interviewing, long studied in academia, into software companies could roll out. Mike says organic growth, helped by VC talent partners, carried it to 200 customers without much marketing or sales.

Dropping Tests to Survive: With refactoring tests eating 30 to 40% of their time, the team treated the product as a prototype and stopped writing them, with agreement to restore coverage later. It now has roughly 70,000 to 80,000 automated tests.

Sharding by Customer Organization: After outgrowing the biggest databases available, Greenhouse moved from Heroku to AWS and scaled horizontally. Each organization only needs its own data, making it a natural shard key.
Why Engineers Stayed: Mike says no one left by choice in the first five years, as engineering grew to about 60. He ties departures to fairness, respect, growth and feeling unable to change things.

Data Models Are Hard to Undo: Mike would model prospects and candidates more polymorphically, not as two overlapping types. Once enough poorly encapsulated code knew about a model, it became really hard to change.

q: What is structured interviewing, and how does Greenhouse use it?
a: Mike Boufford explains that it starts with defining what a job requires, then asking questions or running assessments that test for those things. He describes it as "as simple as figuring out what it is that's most important for somebody to actually succeed in the" [04:20] job, and Greenhouse built it into its applicant tracking system.

q: How long did it take to build the first version of Greenhouse?
a: Mike, the first developer, says the initial version was rough, with gaps such as custom fields that could be created but not deleted. As he put it, "the very first version of Greenhouse took about 10 months to build, did not work" [08:04] particularly well.

q: Why did Greenhouse stop writing tests in its early days?
a: The product was changing so often that refactoring tests was slowing new feature work, and the company needed customer validation before its runway ran out. Mike said "the biggest time saver was that we decided to start writing code cowboy style and stop writing tests." [13:27] He planned from the start to restore coverage once customers arrived, and the team later did.

q: How did Greenhouse scale its database as it grew?
a: Mike says the team moved from Heroku to AWS and adopted horizontal scaling, putting different clusters of customers on different databases. He saw the customer organization as "the perfect shard key. They don't need to know about other organizations' data." [21:15] The approach also provided isolation and allowed upgrades to roll through without taking everyone down.

q: What caused the Greenhouse outage that looked like a hack?
a: A pair of headphones left on the return key in an internal admin search box, which had no rate limiting, flooded the site with requests and caused about half an hour of downtime. Mike's lesson was to "rate limit people, even if you think no one can take you down that way." [28:10]

s6-bonus-unlocking-the-content-black-box-how-casted-monetized-b2b-rich-media-with-lindsay-tjepkema

Unlocking the Content Black Box: Casted helps mid-market and enterprise B2B marketers publish audio and video, break it into smaller pieces, share it across channels and with sales, and measure whether it drives revenue.

Interviews Shaped the MVP: In her first one to two months, Lindsay talked with roughly 75 to 100+ marketers. The most common thread became the MVP: a podcast hosting platform built specifically for B2B marketing teams.
Small Bets Over Big Features: Casted time-boxed small features, weighing what Zachary believed would sell against what Adam's small team could feasibly build without too much tech debt.

Culture Chose the Co-Founders: At their first in-person meeting, Lindsay, Adam and Zachary spent five to ten minutes on the product opportunity and vision, then an hour on the workplace and culture they wanted to build.

Podcasting Label Versus Bigger Vision: Leading with B2B podcasting put Casted on the map, but the vision was always audio and video. Lindsay says perhaps that broader messaging could have started sooner.

q: What is Casted and who is it for?
a: Casted is a software platform for B2B marketing teams, specifically mid-market to enterprise companies in any industry. As co-founder and CEO Lindsay Tjepkema explained, "what we exist to do is to help those teams harness the power of audio content like this" [02:19], along with video content.

q: What problem led Lindsay Tjepkema to start Casted?
a: As a longtime B2B marketer, Lindsay struggled to get full use out of the audio and video her teams created, and found no platform that did what she needed. She described content disappearing into "this little silo, this little black box of a podcast" [03:38].

q: How did Casted decide what to build for its MVP?
a: Lindsay interviewed marketers about their challenges and ideal product, and Chief Product Officer Adam categorized the feedback to find what came up most. Lindsay said "that common thread is what became our MVP" [07:49], which was a podcast platform made for B2B marketing teams.

q: What is amplified marketing?
a: It is Casted's approach in which a conversation is captured and published, then repurposed across channels to extend its reach and revenue impact. Lindsay said, "The future is amplified marketing, which is this category that we launched early in November" [20:32].

q: What advice does Lindsay Tjepkema give first-time founders?
a: Lindsay warns that it is tempting to become whoever investors, customers or recruits want you to be. Her motto is "boldly be yourself. It sounds really cheesy." [25:32], and she urges founders to stay true to their vision because that is ultimately why people will get behind them.

s6-bonus-engineering-speech-processing-tuning-proprietary-natural-language-engines-for-high-noise-edge-environments-with-rob-carpenter-of-valyant

Build Over Rent: Valyant spent six to nine months trying to make Dialogflow work, then abandoned it. It built its own speech-to-text, NLU and natural language generator because off-the-shelf options weren't commercially viable.

Humans Backstopped the MVP: In the October 2018 live test, a teammate used call-center-style software to fix the AI's mistakes on the fly. This kept the product viable enough for the restaurant to keep it and for real data to keep flowing.

Real Conversations Are Messy: Customers change items, modify earlier ones and trail off mid-sentence. Valyant had to carry context and merge fragments like "Can I have" with what follows, while aiming for a 1 to 1.5 second round trip.

Integration Slows Scaling: POS settings differ store by store, so a fix for one location can break others. Valyant also contends with headset systems up to 20 years old and unreliable car presence sensors.

Price to the Real Job: Charging $9.50 an hour, like a full-time employee, failed because most order takers also handle payments, bags and drinks. Good Times ended the partnership, and Valyant moved toward a monthly SaaS fee.

q: What does Valyant AI do?
a: Valyant, founded by Rob Carpenter, uses conversational AI to take drive-thru orders, combining its own software with hardware that connects to the restaurant's headset system. As Carpenter put it, "Valyant automates drive-thru order taking at quick serve restaurants" [02:16].

q: Why did Valyant build its own natural language processing instead of using Dialogflow?
a: Carpenter said the team spent six to nine months on Dialogflow before concluding it was far from what a commercially viable product required. They realized that to get the company off the ground, "we were going to have to build our own NLP system" [10:47].

q: What did the first version of Valyant's drive-thru hardware look like?
a: Carpenter said it was a plastic container holding a Raspberry Pi and the rest of the computer, with holes drilled in the side for wires. In his words, "our senior electrical engineer literally borrowed a piece of Tupperware from his wife" [07:06].

q: Why is speech recognition so hard in a drive-thru?
a: Carpenter explained that speech-to-text that works in a quiet lab faces a very different environment in a live drive-thru lane, where even birds have confused the audio. "good luck replicating that when you've got leaf blowers, you've got car horns," [14:59] he said.

q: What business model mistake did Valyant make?
a: Carpenter said Valyant planned to charge for the AI like a full-time employee, at $9.50 an hour, but most restaurants could not eliminate a whole position by automating order taking. By around 2020, the team found that "the market really couldn't bear that price point" [29:37].

s6-e3-streaming-the-paycheck-building-real-time-earned-wage-access-with-matt-pierce-of-immediate

Flat Fee Over Percentage: Immediate first considered charging a percentage, such as 5% of each withdrawal, but that started to look like a loan. It chose a flat rate viewed more as a convenience fee, much like an ATM fee.

Time Data Beats Assumptions: Estimating wages from past paychecks risked Immediate being regulated as a lender. Time tracking integrations instead show what each employee has actually earned since the last payday, with data pulled as shifts end.

Scrappy First Integration: The first customer's payroll system had no public API. Matt signed up for that payroll service himself, as a one-person company paying $7.25 an hour, so the team could access it and build the integration.

Staffing Ahead of Sales: Immediate usually overstaffs customer success so sales don't outrun onboarding and support. Matt warns that long launch queues would hurt user experience, stunt growth and frustrate salespeople.

Roadmap Shaped by Users: After shipping an enhancement that nobody really used, the team improved how it gathers input, including year-end surveys on planned features. Users get a say, but Immediate keeps the final call.

q: What is Immediate and how does earned wage access work?
a: Immediate is a financial wellness company that connects to employers' time tracking and payroll systems to calculate what employees have earned since their last payday. Matt Pierce explains that users can "access their own earned but unpaid wages before the next payday for a nominal transaction fee" [06:41].

q: Why does Immediate charge a flat fee instead of a percentage?
a: Matt Pierce says the team initially considered taking a percentage of each withdrawal but changed course for regulatory reasons. In his words, "when you put percentage in there, it starts to look and feel a little more like a loan" [13:54].

q: Why does Immediate integrate with time tracking systems and not just payroll?
a: Pierce says relying on payroll history would have meant assuming what people were currently earning, which is risky in a highly regulated space. To make sure "we're not viewed or regulated as a lender, then we've got to go build these time tracking" [15:03] integrations.

q: How was the first version of Immediate Pay built?
a: Matt Pierce, who doesn't code, brought in Jason Guzdala, now his CTO, after months of legal and regulatory work that Pierce says "essentially gave us a roadmap of how we should build the MVP" [08:18]. The product was designed in Flutter, first released on iOS, and went from first line of code in April 2019 to a first customer that September.

q: What would Matt Pierce do differently if he started Immediate again?
a: Pierce says he probably would have started with a web app instead of an iOS app, since there are fewer hoops to get a first version out. He also would have handed off sales sooner, admitting "I held onto the reins pretty tightly for a long time" [43:40].

s6-bonus-solving-the-data-blindspot-how-hustle-fund-backed-pyrl-cryptographs-commerce-with-adam-newman

Research Before the MVP: Nearly two years of legwork, including six national consumer surveys and informal talks with retail executives, pointed to privacy as the MVP's focus. Once the scope and key team members were set, building it took about six months.

Win-Win Over Legal Pressure: Newman says beating corporations over the head with privacy laws only goes so far. Pyrl aims to give consumers control of their data while privacy-complying companies gain trust and measurable financial benefit.

On-Prem Option for Enterprises: Enterprises can run a Pyrl server on their own premises or private cloud, behind their existing firewall with full admin rights. That lets CIOs and CISOs pilot without having to trust a startup with their internal controls.

Azure Over AWS: Newman's last business went all in on AWS, but Pyrl chose Azure after retail executives voiced concern about reliance on Amazon, a competitor. The team architected for scale without building it all on day one.

Consumer-First Go-to-Market Pivot: Pyrl first planned to start with a consortium of enterprise pilot partners, which proved an uphill battle. The team corrected course and aimed the MVP at everyday users with privacy concerns, building a community of early adopters.

q: What is Pyrl?
a: Pyrl is a company founded by Adam Newman that gives consumers privacy for, and access to, data about what they buy. Newman describes it this way: "Pyrl is the world's first purchase privacy platform." [02:34]

q: What inspired Adam Newman to start Pyrl?
a: Newman lost his father to cancer, which led him to think about product-based causes of disease and the link between purchase data and health. Of that loss, he said, "for me in an unexpected way that was the spark behind Pyrl" [05:26].

q: How does Pyrl's sign-up process work?
a: Users create an account, set their privacy preferences and list where they spend money, either manually or by linking a credit card. As Newman explained, "you appoint us as your data privacy agent, and then you just tell the platform where you spend money." [25:27]

q: Why did Pyrl build on Azure instead of AWS?
a: Retailers are a major set of partners for Pyrl, and Amazon competes with them. Newman said retail executives told the team that "they're not particularly thrilled with a platform like ours being reliant on AWS." [20:08]

q: What early mistake did Pyrl make in going to market?
a: The team first approached the market through a corporate lens, planning to gather large enterprise pilot partners before focusing on consumers. Newman said this was flawed in several ways, "Because we lost track of the roots." [24:12]

s6-bonus-the-duolingo-for-data-literacy-building-ai-assessment-engines-with-matt-cowell-of-quanthub

Two Lines of Business: QuantHub assesses data skills for hiring roles like data scientists and engineers, and upskills whole organizations, including sales, marketing, HR and operations, in data literacy.

Least Product That Delivers Value: An in-browser code editor, video interviewing and online proctoring waited. Early coding skills were assessed with multiple-choice questions while Cowell's team listened for what customers truly needed.

From 30 Testers to 3,600: A large customer's campus recruiting sent about 3,600 assessments after only about 30 people had ever been tested. Prior performance testing helped QuantHub get through a Sunday-night rush.
Costly Conference Bet: QuantHub spent about $100,000 on conferences in its first 12 months and, in Cowell's view, not enough on SEO to build the inbound funnel faster.

Microlearning Over Long Courses: Cowell argues long-form training is quickly forgotten. QuantHub leans on learning science, with a little learning every day, much like Duolingo and other language platforms.

q: How did QuantHub get started?
a: QuantHub spun out of an AI consultancy that had been using assessments to improve its own hiring, and Matt Cowell came on to run it as a separate company. As Cowell put it, the consultancy had a proof of concept "that was the beginnings of our assessment platform" [03:49].

q: What is the "Duolingo for data literacy" approach to learning data skills?
a: Matt Cowell describes QuantHub as a microlearning platform where people learn a little every day instead of attending long training sessions they soon forget. "we're much more like the language learning platforms, like the Duolingos of the world" [21:57], he said.

q: Who needs data literacy training?
a: Cowell says data skills are no longer optional and are not just for data or technical professionals. QuantHub's upskilling work focuses on "helping salespeople, marketing, HR, operations be more effective at using data" [02:59].

q: How did QuantHub decide what to leave out of its MVP?
a: Matt Cowell says there was no magical process, just listening to customers and asking questions to separate what they asked for from what they needed. The guiding question was "what's the least product that we can give them" [08:43] that still delivers on the value proposition.

q: Did QuantHub's assessment platform scale from day one?
a: No, Cowell says it was not built to scale efficiently at the start, and a large customer's campus recruiting soon put it under heavy load. He recalled that "we had tested like 30 people ever at that point" [14:36], though performance testing and fixes beforehand helped the team get through it.

s6-e2-scaling-a-2b-neobank-moving-money-at-the-edge-with-current-co-founder-trevor-marshall

Owning the Core Banking Engine: Rather than relying on a processor for ledgering, account types and transaction types, Current built its own engine, seeing the balance system of record as the key bridge to other financial back ends.

Teen Banking as the Wedge: After a Ripple proof of concept and chat app payments, Current launched teen banking, which took about two years. It offered a market gap, value without a full network and lessons in multi-user design.

Resharding a Live Ledger: An unsharded MongoDB ledger faced the limits of vertical scaling. The team added an API layer, replicated every document to a sharded cluster, then cut over reads, because downtime for balances and history was unacceptable.

Outcomes Drive the Roadmap: Current's North Star is improving members' financial outcomes. That led to smoother onboarding for parents, allowances and paid chores, then an individual account with incoming ACH and paychecks two days early.

Tighten Feedback Loops Early: Marshall wishes log aggregation, metrics and alerting had come sooner. Current tracked product funnels early, but only added PagerDuty in 2020, after building automated measurement.

q: What is Current and who is it for?
a: Current is a financial technology platform offering a checking account, and Trevor Marshall says it has mostly served people poorly treated by the existing financial system. He explains that people living with low balances pay hundreds "of dollars in fees a year just to have the same service" [04:49] that wealthier customers get for free.

q: Why did Current build its own core banking engine?
a: Trevor Marshall says the team wanted to eventually bridge people into new financial networks, and realized the ledger was the key to doing that. As he put it, the technology layer is "functionally the system of record for the account balances, is the critical integration point" [07:59].

q: What was Current's MVP and how was it built?
a: Marshall considers the teen banking product, built on Current's core banking platform, to be the MVP, and it took about two years with many changes of direction. He admits the rush to prove the idea before money ran out "created an insane spaghetti of bad decisions and quick actions" [12:18], and the team did a fairly large refactor in 2018.

q: How did Current scale its ledger without downtime?
a: Trevor Marshall's team moved from a vertically scaled MongoDB cluster to a sharded one by putting an API layer in front of the database, replicating every document and then swapping reads over. He says the hard part of such a change is often not the underlying problem: "It's the operations around making that transition, which are extremely nuanced" [24:07].

q: What would Trevor Marshall do differently if he started Current again?
a: Marshall says he would think about scale much earlier and build observability and alerting from the start rather than a few years in. Speaking about improving a running system, he said "you can't improve it if you can't measure it" [27:36].

s6-bonus-the-pop-culture-video-engine-bootstrapping-scaling-classhook-to-acquisition-with-alexander-deeb

Engagement Gap Drove the Idea: Alexander Deeb's team found research showing student engagement falls from about 74% in fifth grade to 32% in 11th, and bet that popular TV shows and movies could make learning feel relevant.

A Bare-Bones Rails MVP: The first version was a Ruby on Rails listing of video clips with short descriptions. Teacher conversations then added details like grade levels and how many teachers had used each clip.

Crowdsourcing Kept the Scope Broad: Hoping teachers would submit clips, ClassHook opened to all K-12 subjects. Submissions still arrive, but teachers mainly come for content, and Deeb would now start with a niche like elementary science.

Validate Before Building Social Features: An early Twitter-like Activity Feed saw little use and had no usage metrics. Deeb calls it a waste of time, launched without understanding what teacher pain it would solve.
Hiring Self-Starters With Empathy: With a small team, Deeb looks for autonomous self-learners who understand users' pain, and in some cases starts them on part-time contracts to reduce hiring risk.

q: What is ClassHook and how do teachers use it?
a: ClassHook lets teachers find educational scenes from TV shows and movies, then use them with live discussions, embedded questions and a vocabulary finder. Alexander Deeb says it "helps K-12 teachers and students create more fun learning experiences" [02:23].

q: How was the first version of ClassHook built?
a: Deeb built the MVP as a Ruby on Rails application that listed video clips with perhaps a description of each. In his words, "I coded it up and it was pretty much just like a listing of clips." [06:26]

q: How did ClassHook decide what features to build?
a: Deeb says the team had no good sense of a roadmap early on and let teacher conversations guide it, digging into why each request mattered. Contrasting this with his previous education startup, Deeb described "talking to users all the time, obsessively in the beginning" [09:34].

q: What would Alexander Deeb do differently if he started ClassHook again?
a: He would prioritize and manage his time better, and begin with a narrower audience so that audience had a deeper library of clips. As Deeb put it, "The other thing would be catering the product to a more specific niche." [18:11]

q: What is the future vision for ClassHook?
a: Deeb sees the company moving toward technology that automatically finds learning moments in media, with more data scientists and a product catering to media and entertainment companies. He said, "We will be transitioning more to a machine learning company" [15:36].

s6-bonus-from-plaid-to-a-1b-unicorn-killing-the-password-with-reed-mcginley-stempel-of-stytch

Start Narrow with Magic Links: Stytch's MVP was one passwordless method, email magic links, offered as an API only. Customers owned the UI while the team focused on a backend that could scale if an early customer took off.

Roadmap Breadth and Depth: Stytch weighs how much a product expands the pool of developers who could use it and how hard it would be to build in-house. WebAuthn scored on value because it is difficult to integrate securely and its spec is confusing.

Engineers with Product Instincts: Approaching 30 people, Stytch still had no PMs. Engineers are expected to think like both developer and end user, and final-round interviews included an hour-long product hypothetical.

Source Before It Hurts: Reed admits recruiting sometimes lagged as customers and product surface grew. His reminder to himself is to source for a role tonight, even if the pain of not filling it is six or eight weeks away.

Wait Longer on SDKs: In hindsight, Reed might have stayed API-only for a couple more quarters, until there were five or six products, before shipping a front-end SDK. It took a couple quarters to work out how the SDK should function.

q: What is Stytch and what does it do?
a: Stytch provides APIs and SDKs that let developers add passwordless authentication, such as biometrics, email magic links, SMS login and OAuth, to apps and websites. Co-founder and CEO Reed McGinley-Stempel said, "I sometimes describe us as the stripe for authentication." [03:10]

q: Why does Stytch want to get rid of passwords?
a: Reed McGinley-Stempel and his co-founder, who both worked on adaptive authentication at Plaid, were frustrated by the security risks of passwords and the low conversion they caused at sign-up and login. A core problem Reed described is that "users reuse passwords relentlessly across many different sites." [04:19]

q: How did Stytch build its MVP?
a: Reed McGinley-Stempel explained that the team narrowed its focus, saying "we decided to start just with one basic passwordless authentication method, which was email magic links." [05:45] Tools included AWS, Kubernetes and Argo CD, with most API code written in Go.

q: Did Stytch build for scale from the beginning?
a: Yes, particularly for the core authentication APIs and SDKs, while the marketing website and dashboard front end were less pressing. Reed McGinley-Stempel said that for critical infrastructure, "we probably spent a lot more time thinking about how does this scale at the beginning than your average startup needs to." [15:39]

q: What does Stytch look for when hiring?
a: Reed McGinley-Stempel said technical hires need strong product instincts, thinking about both the developer integrating the product and the end user. Across everyone, he said the two main "traits we just look for in everyone is are they kind and are they ambitious?" [14:28]

s6-e1-scaling-to-1-trillion-messages-building-the-real-time-fabric-of-the-internet-with-stephen-blum-of-pubnub

Performance From the Kernel Up: PubNub is written in C from the edge to the PubSub bus. Going directly to Linux kernel APIs, rather than importing a library, was key to its low latency, efficiency and control of the network stack.

Auto-Scaling Came Later: Scaling was manual and predictive for years. Starting in 2020, PubNub moved to containers, CI/CD and Kubernetes auto-scaling, which absorbed a surge of millions of users during a BTS online audience experience.

When Retries Become a DDoS: After a vendor's DNS mistake, an SDK retry policy on 120 million AT＆T phones flooded PubNub. The team siphoned those clients to an endpoint returning success, which reset them to one retry per second.

Spend 90% on Promotion: Blum says founders should put 90% of their time into promotion. He wishes PubNub had invested more in it and dreams of a dedicated media studio showing what the product can do.

Hire for Drive: Blum values inspiration and motivation over credentials or years of experience. He sets key objectives and outcomes, then leaves the team open to define goals and create solutions that move business metrics.

q: What is PubNub and what is it used for?
a: Stephen Blum describes PubNub as powering virtual spaces where multiple parties interact, such as food delivery updates, multiplayer games, chat and collaboration. In his words, PubNub empowers "that connection in that virtual space. So you can facilitate the multi-party environment." [03:21]

q: How did PubNub get started?
a: Stephen Blum and his team set out to build an app with a button that ordered a taxi. While building it, "it turned out that we need something like PubNub." [04:32] They opened up the API, and game developers became one of the first big groups of paying users.

q: How does PubNub achieve low-latency messaging at scale?
a: Stephen Blum credits a tech stack written in C and a design that runs globally across every data center. He said that "a key part of what made PubNub possible was actually just directly going to the kernel" [11:18] to use the capabilities Linux already offered.

q: How did PubNub handle a DDoS caused by its own SDK retry policy?
a: Stephen Blum explained that after a DNS issue was fixed, AT＆T phones stuck in a retry loop overwhelmed the network. The team isolated that IP block, and "we had a separate endpoint that would return successful statuses to all those phones." [23:10] Healthy traffic was then migrated back to the main network.

q: What advice does Stephen Blum give early-stage founders?
a: Blum warns that launching a product is only the beginning and that instant unicorns are rare. He urges founders to build promotion into the business plan: "I would always go back to say, spend 90% of your time on promotion." [29:35]

s5-bonus-the-science-of-scaling-engineering-repeatable-b2b-growth-experiments-with-techstars-alum-shelby-stephens

Fractional Specialists Over Early Hires: Startup challenges keep changing, so Stephens hires fractional experts for the problem at hand. They are usually more experienced than a team could afford full time.

Off-the-Shelf Alpha: Growth Match's alpha runs on Sharetribe's entry-level plan, about $150 a month, augmented with Airtable. The team accepts tight limits to ship core features fast and gather feedback.
Discovery Before Building: The founders ran about 60 customer interviews in two months across both sides of the marketplace. Knowing both customers firsthand helped them recruit participants faster.
Sales Exposed Demand-Side Gaps: Supply acquisition worked quickly, but demand took longer because the problem wasn't nailed. Several sales cycles showed the team how its value proposition was off.

Brand Too Close to Competitor: Rushing to market, the team built a brand and a landing page too similar to a competitor's. After hearing from that company, they quickly changed some elements and began designing a new aesthetic.

q: What is Growth Match?
a: Growth Match, co-founded by CEO Shelby Stephens, connects startups with vetted fractional specialists, and both sides are screened before joining. Stephens explains, "It's a marketplace that matches startups with specialists." [08:29]

q: Why should an early-stage startup hire fractional specialists?
a: Shelby Stephens argues that a specialized early hire may not be experienced in the next challenge the startup faces. A fractional expert can help solve the current problem faster, and as Stephens puts it, "you can usually hire someone significantly more experienced and better fractionally" [08:16].

q: How was the Growth Match MVP built?
a: Stephens and co-founder Zach chose a no-code route instead of custom development, using Airtable to augment the product. Stephens said they found an off-the-shelf marketplace "builder called Sharetribe that we have used to set up the alpha." [13:04]

q: What happened to Jolly during COVID?
a: Jolly was a market network with roughly 40,000 to 45,000 users, mostly freelance-type workers in events, when the pandemic hit. Shelby Stephens said, "Our entire beachhead market, the event space, just completely imploded." [02:58] The team later turned it into a tool for independent workers to sell services online.

q: What would Shelby Stephens do differently when starting Growth Match?
a: Stephens would put more work into understanding the startup side of the marketplace, where acquisition took longer to become effective. Stephens said, "I would have spent a bit more time in customer discovery on validating the problem" [38:41].

s5-e30-from-heroku-to-muse-rethinking-personal-computing-local-first-software-with-adam-wiggins

Prototype Broadly, Then Port: After prototypes across tablet platforms, the first version of Muse was built for Chrome OS. The tablet platform disappointed, so partner Yulia ported it to iPad in about two weeks, and that became the MVP.

Speed Over Platform Conventions: Muse aims to keep up with the iPad's 120 fps screen. Cards drag instantly, with no press-and-hold delay, which meant skipping Apple's default APIs and accepting that some users would find it confusing.

Explain the Weird Stuff: Adam estimates the team spent as much time on explanatory materials, including a video handbook and the Metamuse podcast. Some odd lab ideas were cut or made more standard so the app stayed comprehensible.

Partners Instead of Founders: Muse was five people after two and a half years, all called partners, with big ownership stakes and many hats. Adam favors this high talent density over management overhead, though growth may strain it.

Old Data Still Matters: An ink migration skipped one early beta format, and some of the most loyal customers lost ink on archived boards. The data was still on disk in SQLite, so a recovery build could restore it as images.

q: What is Muse and what is it used for?
a: Muse is a tool for thought that, at the time of the interview, ran only on the iPad. Adam Wiggins described it this way: "You use it for deep thinking with this kind of spatial canvas where you put images and ink and PDFs" [26:25].

q: How was the Muse MVP built?
a: The idea came out of research at the Ink and Switch lab, and the first version was built for Chrome OS with web technology. Adam Wiggins said Yulia then ported that over to iPad: "prototype to the iPad in about two weeks. And that sort of became our MVP." [06:51]

q: Why doesn't Muse use Apple's default drag behavior?
a: Adam Wiggins explained that the team wanted cards to move the instant a finger touches them, in line with its focus on performance. As he put it, "We can't use any of the default Apple APIs because they all depend on some delay" [09:25].

q: What is local-first syncing in Muse?
a: At the time of the interview, Adam Wiggins said the team was working on syncing technology that is device-centric and not dependent on the cloud. He described "storing all the data locally, but you can still sync it between all your devices." [27:05]

q: What advice does Adam Wiggins give young entrepreneurs?
a: Adam Wiggins warns against status games and comparing yourself to peers, whether over funding valuations or revenue growth graphs. Instead, he says to focus on what you're making, asking whether "you're making and are you proud of it? And do you think it will help people in their lives?" [36:35]

s5-bonus-from-pop-charts-to-the-app-store-coding-the-linkedin-for-golfers-with-lydia-davies-founder-of-teemates
Location-Based Tee Times: Teemates lets golfers post a tee time, see players in their area and invite them. It also has a golf-only social newsfeed and a marketplace for selling or trading equipment.

Social Feed Drives Engagement: Tee time linking was the core feature, but Lydia added a golf-only newsfeed to draw in people who might be hesitant to meet strangers. The marketplace came near the end and had been used less than she expected.

Launching Too Soon: Already well behind schedule, the team launched after testing only among themselves and friends. Bugs followed, and iOS update approvals taking up to three days left users waiting for fixes.
Feedback Shapes the Sprints: About 50 friends reviewed the app early on. Lydia also adds each user as a friend, welcomes them and asks for feedback, which the team compiles and ranks into sprints.

Startup, Not Just App: Lydia says she set out to create an app and only then built the startup around it. In hindsight, she would organize better and shape the company's big picture while building the product.

q: What is the Teemates golf app and how does it work?
a: Teemates is a location-based app that connects golfers, with tee time invites, a social newsfeed and an equipment marketplace. Lydia Davies described setting up a tee time and inviting players: "It will show me everyone in my area. So I can then invite them and they get a notification" [02:32].

q: Why did Lydia Davies create Teemates?
a: Lydia built it with her husband in mind, and also because she couldn't find enough women in her area to play with. In her words, "I created it because of my husband traveling and playing alone." [03:20].

q: How was the first version of Teemates built?
a: Lydia created the framework in XD, then brought on a development team that started building around August or September 2020 and launched in June. Simplicity was a priority for Lydia, who said they wanted "to make sure that the flow was simple because that's one thing people get bored so easily" [05:04].

q: What mistake did Teemates make at launch?
