a: Lydia said the app needed a few more weeks to a month of testing with a wider audience before release. As she put it, "we definitely launched the app too soon without doing enough beta testing." [15:28].

q: What is Lydia Davies' advice for new startup founders?
a: Lydia advises slowing down, setting five and ten year plans, and understanding why you're making the product and why it will work. She also stresses persistence and flexibility, saying "being versatile and fluid as well is really important for any startup business." [21:53].

s5-e29-coding-the-designers-brain-reengineering-fashion-with-ai-alongside-nick-clayton-of-savitude
A Blank Page Revealed the Gap: Savitude's shape-based recommendation page sometimes came up empty. Nick Clayton hunted for a bug, then found there was nothing to recommend for some body shapes.

Custom Vision Beat Off-the-Shelf: Telling a V-neckline from a deep V needed domain-specific work. Early TensorFlow prototypes scored slightly higher than IBM Watson, so Savitude built its own pipeline.

From Spotting Gaps to Filling Them: Savitude first analyzed retailers' collections manually with its visual recognition engine to find assortment holes. Demand for fixes drove a pivot to analytics and generative design suggestions.
Scale Where Costs Live: Clayton prefers building scalably from the start, but accepts shortcuts for deadlines and conference demos. Optimization effort goes to cost drivers such as image recognition.

Pivot Sooner: Clayton says Savitude stayed in recommendations much too long. Its shape-based approach was unique but struggled to get attention in a crowded field, and he admits being overly attached to it.

q: What problem does Savitude solve in fashion?
a: Savitude addresses body shape: Nick Clayton says designers and retailers typically design with only one or two shapes in mind, leaving many people struggling to find clothes that fit. He noted that "The hourglass body shape is not even a quarter of the population in the United States." [02:51]

q: Why did Savitude move from a recommendation engine to design tools?
a: For some body shapes, the recommendation page could show up blank, and Clayton initially suspected a software fault. He recalled that he "Couldn't find any bug and eventually figured out that the recommendations were working." [03:59] That, along with other thinking by the team, led them to apply the technology upstream in the design process.

q: Why did Savitude build its own visual recognition pipeline?
a: Clayton's team tested existing systems, primarily IBM Watson, but needed much finer distinctions than general object classification. As he put it, "we were looking to classify a V-neckline versus a deep V-neckline versus a round neckline," [06:46]. Preliminary TensorFlow prototypes also achieved slightly higher accuracy.

q: What would Nick Clayton do differently if he started Savitude again?
a: Clayton would leave the recommendation space much earlier, since it was crowded and hard to get attention in despite Savitude's unique shape-based approach. He admitted, "Part of that was my fault in being overly attached to what we had built." [23:47]

q: What advice does Nick Clayton give new entrepreneurs about technology?
a: Clayton advises understanding the problem and its root causes before settling on a solution or becoming enamored with the technology. He summed it up by saying, "So I think looking for simple solutions to real problems" [26:28] is the best advice he has. He gave the example of someone seeking machine learning who only needed some creative use of hashes.

s5-bonus-the-evolution-of-apis-building-the-ai-gateway-of-the-future-with-marco-palladino-cto-of-kong

Pivot to the Hidden Asset: After five years and 300,000 developers, the Mashape API marketplace's business model wasn't working well. In 2015 the founders open sourced the gateway underneath it as Kong, which drew a thousand GitHub stars on day one.

Sort Technical Debt Early: Kong split debt into feature debt, prioritized by how many users asked, and architectural debt, which Palladino worked hardest to prevent because it is very hard to reverse later.

Draw the Open-Core Line: Palladino treats deciding what is open source and what is commercial as being as important as software architecture. Set that expectation with the community early, because breaking it breaks trust.
Hire Sales Before You're Ready: Palladino wishes Kong had hired its first salesperson sooner. Customer conversations show that some things founders think are important don't really matter to buyers.

Scaling People Beats Product Difficulty: Building an organization past 100 people proved much tougher than building the first product. Palladino now understands why some founders sell before reaching that stage.

q: How did Kong get started?
a: Kong came out of a pivot from Mashape, an API marketplace that Marco Palladino and co-founder Augusto Marietti ran for five years. Palladino said that in 2015 "we decided to take our underlying technology, the one that was powering this marketplace" [03:24] and open source it.

q: What does Kong's API gateway do?
a: Palladino describes it as infrastructure that adds security, logging, observability, traffic control and governance on top of the APIs developers build. In his words, "Building the API is half of the job." [11:30] The other half is having the right infrastructure to run it.

q: How should an open source company decide what to charge for?
a: Palladino advises setting expectations early that some features, support or services will be commercial and not part of the open source project. He considers this decision as important as software architecture because "it is the architecture of the business itself" [14:15].

q: How did Kong handle technical debt in the early days?
a: Palladino said the team categorized debt as either architectural or feature-related, with feature debt prioritized by user demand. Architectural debt worried him most because "the thing about architecture is that it's very hard to change" [09:40] later on.

q: When should a startup hire its first salesperson?
a: Palladino believes Kong waited too long because the team wanted to be ready first. His view now is that "you really want to hire the first one when you're not ready" [25:50], so you can iterate early on what potential users care about.

s5-e28-putting-money-on-autopilot-building-self-driving-banking-tech-with-oona-rokyta-of-lance

Forward-Looking Freelancer Finance: Oona Rokyta and her co-founders found accountants and software mostly looked backwards. Lance aims to help variable-income workers plan cash flow, taxes, savings and business expenses ahead.

Automation Beat the Dashboard: Users found a synced dashboard useful, but kept asking for something that would set up allocations for them. Lance put recommendations and automation of where funds go at the center of the product.

Rebuilding From the Ground Up: Lance scrapped its first version and a half, including a tax-swiping experiment. Moving from a Plaid-integrated dashboard to banking required a rebuild, though much of the visual design carried over.

Partners Chosen to Scale: Lance built its banking platform with Unit and integrated Abound to validate tax calculations. Rokyta talks with both CEOs regularly and expects any integration to scale from thousands of users to millions.

An Early Fraud Lesson: A fraudster arrived on day one of the public launch and passed the fraud score. Lance shut the account after an unemployment check in someone else's name came in, and has been more conservative about who it admits.

q: What is Lance and who is it for?
a: Lance is a platform that gives freelancers, consultants and flexible workers a financial framework for their business finances. Co-founder and CEO Oona Rokyta explained, "We really just help organize all of your business finances." [02:41]

q: What problem led Oona Rokyta to start Lance?
a: Rokyta and her co-founders struggled to get ahead of their finances on variable freelance incomes, even with accountants and invoicing software. Describing those tools, Rokyta said, "It was just looking at our bank statements or looking at what we'd already spent," [03:28].

q: How did Lance's first product evolve into a banking platform?
a: An early experiment had people swipe expenses into tax-deductible categories, followed by a dashboard that synced financial accounts in one place. Rokyta said that "Going from a Plaid integrated dashboard to a fully functioning banking platform and allocation system, we really had to rebuild from the ground up." [07:46]

q: What did Lance learn about fraud when it launched?
a: Rokyta expected some fraud at public launch, and it came immediately: "There was a fraudster that came in the very first day" [19:07]. The team shut down the account after seeing an unemployment check in a different name, which jump-started its learning about fraud and identity theft in fintech.

q: What advice does Oona Rokyta have for new founders?
a: Rokyta advises holding on to the original reason for the company and the people it serves while opinions pull in different directions, and growing as quickly as you can with the insights you have. In Rokyta's words, "the best advice I can give is stay true to why you came up with this idea" [27:35].

ee60a0d2-c19c-43ba-a66e-70699e33aceb
s5-bonus-stopping-account-takeovers-fighting-the-ai-driven-fraud-wave-with-ari-jacoby-of-deduce

Borrowing From Ad Tech: Ari Jacoby saw that data was freely shared in ad tech and marketing tech but not in cyber risk and fraud. Having built two large identity graphs before, he saw a chance to build one to fight fraud.

Scores Need Explanations: Deduce's first product, Risk Index, returned only a score. Companies were excited about the data but wanted explainability, so the team added metadata, real signals and substantially more data.

Speed Without Overbuilding: Deduce has to return data in under 150 milliseconds, which carries a cost. The team planned for horizontal scaling in the cloud rather than paying early for far more capacity than it needed.

Test Use Cases Fast: To avoid building in a vacuum, the team asked many questions, took sample product to customers and prospects for a thumbs up or down, and quickly returned with alternatives. It still iterates in two-week sprints.

Network Effect and Easy Setup: Jacoby says Deduce's identity network spans over 150,000 sites and services with over 1.2 billion daily transactions, and that customers can get value from its API in an hour or two.

q: What does Deduce do?
a: Deduce, founded by CEO Ari Jacoby, works to stop fraud against businesses and their consumers using a real-time identity network. As Jacoby put it, "Deduce is focused on preventing account takeover and new registration fraud for businesses" [02:25].

q: How does Deduce's identity network work?
a: Jacoby says the network comprises over 150,000 sites and services and sees over 1.2 billion transactions every day, and he expects it to get smarter as more customers join. In his words, "So we've got a true network effect" [15:37].

q: How fast does a fraud detection API like Deduce's need to be?
a: Jacoby says speed is critical in the industry, and that building clumsily at first gets very expensive. He explained, "We've got to be able to return data in under 150 milliseconds." [05:58].

q: What mistake did Deduce make with its first product?
a: Its first product, Risk Index, offered a score without explaining it, while the market wanted explainability. Jacoby owned the decision, saying "it was my brilliant idea to only have scoring available in our earliest product without explainability." [14:03].

q: How long does it take to implement Deduce?
a: Jacoby contrasts Deduce with vendors in the category whose implementations have often been long and painful. He said the team focuses on "making sure that we are drop dead simple to implement" [16:46], and that customers can extract value from the API in an hour or two.

s5-bonus-scaling-to-1-trillion-requests-how-ipinfo-built-a-global-api-with-ben-dowling

An Evening to First Version: Curious why a website placed him in Texas while he was in Seattle, Ben Dowling registered a domain and built an IP-on-a-map page in a couple of hours. Over the following weeks it evolved into an API.

API Before Dashboard: Early on there were no logins or user database. Stripe handled payments, and Dowling answered usage and card-update requests by email, for probably a year or more, while focusing on reliability, latency and data fields.

Own the Data Quality: IPinfo began as a thin layer over existing data sets. Repeated reports of wrong locations pushed it to produce better data itself and add context such as VPN detection and carrier information.
Fail Open on Rate Limits: Rate limiting was asynchronous and designed to fail open. If it went down, some users might exceed their limits, but paying customers would keep working.

Simplicity Over Global Redundancy: Multiple providers, then many AWS regions, added cost and complexity and slowed feature launches. After asking customers, IPinfo moved to a single Google Cloud region and found it seemed a non-issue.

q: What is IPinfo and why was it created?
a: IPinfo provides IP address context data, including geolocation, mobile carrier and VPN or proxy detection. Ben Dowling started it to avoid maintaining geolocation files and update jobs across several side projects, with a simple API where you "pass an IP address in and we'll give you the geolocation data back" [03:34].

q: How long did it take to build the first version of IPinfo?
a: The initial website, which showed your IP address on a Google Maps widget, took Dowling a couple of hours. As he recalled, "The very first version I built in an evening." [05:49] The API followed over the next few weeks.

q: Why did IPinfo start building its own IP geolocation data?
a: Users kept reporting wrong locations, and at first the company told them to report errors to the upstream data source. As the feedback continued, Dowling's team asked, "okay, well, can we produce better data ourselves?" [04:49]

q: How does IPinfo handle rate limiting if its infrastructure fails?
a: Dowling designed rate limiting to be asynchronous and to fail open, so an outage there does not block paying customers. In his view, "it's much better to give away a few extra requests" [18:18] than to upset them.

q: What was a major mistake IPinfo made with its free API?
a: IPinfo gave free users no way to sign up for a couple of years, leaving it unable to tell them about new products or approaching rate limits. Dowling said one of the main mistakes "was not capturing email addresses of free" [21:54] users early on.

compiler-what-is-the-recipe-for-burnout

A Four-Part Burnout Recipe: The episode names four ingredients: a seemingly unending workload, no healthy boundaries, guilt or a sense of never doing enough, and criticism that makes the other three stand out more.

Guilt Keeps Maintainers Going: Nolan Lawson recalls a team using PouchDB for Ebola contact tracing hitting a bug he knew about but hadn't fixed, leaving him wondering whether he had impeded their efforts.

Toxicity Is Rare but Heavy: Researchers estimated that less than 1% of GitHub issue conversations contain toxicity, with entitlement a common theme. Even a rare hostile comment can affect someone for days or longer.

Recovery Meant Letting Go: Lawson handed off repos and publish rights, and marked projects he no longer cared about as unmaintained. Some carried on with their communities, while one-person projects essentially died.

Scope Small to Stay Healthy: Lawson now favors small, well-defined projects, states in the README what each is not meant to do, takes breaks of weeks or more, and no longer feels obliged to rescue every user.

q: What causes burnout for open source maintainers?
a: The episode points to endless work, weak boundaries, guilt and criticism. Maintainer Nolan Lawson described the workload as "having a line of 100 people standing outside your door" [07:33], each one bringing a problem.

q: Why do maintainers keep working even when they are burning out?
a: For Nolan Lawson, a sense of obligation to people struggling with bugs was a major driver. He said "the guilt was a huge part of it" [09:15], as users told him about problems such as permanently lost data.

q: How common is toxicity in GitHub issues?
a: Researchers trained a classifier on labeled comments and applied it to years of GitHub issues. By their estimates, "less than 1% of conversations of issues contain instances of toxicity" [14:15], and Naveen Rahman reported that the overall rate decreased significantly over the period studied.

q: How did Nolan Lawson recover from open source burnout?
a: Lawson stopped looking at the project's issues and pull requests and gave others control of its repos and publishing rights. As Lawson put it, "I passed over maintainership to other people" [15:54], and he also marked some of his smaller projects as unmaintained.

q: How can developers avoid burning out on side projects?
a: Nolan Lawson keeps his projects small and limited in scope and takes long breaks when he needs them. He explained, "I'm mostly not doing open source every single weekend, every single weeknight." [18:52]

s5-e27-fixing-the-edge-dropping-traffic-by-95-with-max-stoiber-of-graphcdn-stellate

Born From Spectrum's Outages: As Spectrum's CTO, Max saw the service crash once or twice daily for months. Most posts were identical for every user, and he believes an API cache could have cut traffic tenfold.

Fast Invalidation Is Essential: Edits to cached API data must show up almost immediately, everywhere. Co-founder Tim spent three months of nights and weekends researching providers and landed on Fastly.

Rules Beat Per-Type Config: Configuring cache settings type by type got unwieldy on huge GraphQL schemas. The team spent a week or two re-architecting around reusable rules that group types by business use case.

Speed Over Developer Experience: GraphCDN runs on Fastly's Compute@Edge despite what Max calls rough edges and a poor developer experience, because its speed matters to customers such as e-commerce companies.
Invest in People Early: GraphCDN hired Sue Odeo, who had scaled startups past 100 employees, to run its people function early on. Max still says they waited too long to hire and would start sooner.

q: What problem led to the creation of GraphCDN?
a: Max Stoiber ran into scaling trouble as CTO of Spectrum, where most posts were the same for every user but requests still went to the database. As Max put it, "We should just be putting a cache in front of our GraphQL API" [09:12].

q: Why is cache invalidation so important for GraphQL edge caching?
a: Max explains that API data is often very dynamic, so an edited news article can't sit stale in a cache for 10 or 15 minutes. He said "you need to be able to invalidate the cache really, really, really quickly" [11:51], which is even harder across worldwide edge locations.

q: How did GraphCDN's cache configuration change after the private beta?
a: The first system had users attach cache control settings to individual types in a large JSON or YAML file. Max said "we very quickly realized that that gets unwieldy incredibly quickly" [15:03], so the team moved to rules that apply when a query contains certain types or fields.

q: Why is GraphCDN built on Fastly's Compute@Edge?
a: Max says Fastly handles enormous traffic and was by far the fastest edge provider the team tested, even though its developer experience was rough at the time of the interview. In his words, "It is so fast that we're happy to incur that developer experience hit" [26:27].

q: What advice does Max Stoiber give young entrepreneurs about building something people want?
a: Max recommends reading The Mom Test and asking potential customers what problems they have before pitching anything. His summary is that "you don't talk about your solution, you talk about their problems" [37:02].

s5-bonus-stop-guessing-getting-to-the-aha-moment-in-product-validation-with-darshan-mehta-of-iresearch
Talk First, Then Survey: Darshan argues surveys alone don't get at why people buy. Starting with focus groups or one-on-one interviews produces better survey questions and answer choices.

Chat Lets Everyone Answer: In iResearch's online focus groups of about 10 to 15 people, everyone can respond without interrupting. Quieter thinkers get heard, and transcripts are much longer than a few fast talkers would produce.

Hire Thinkers, Doers, and Hungry: While bootstrapping, Darshan outsourced to teams in the US, Europe and Asia. He screened them in conversation for those three traits, plus the critical thinking to see more than one way to solve a problem.

Easy, Affordable, Time-Saving, Plus Emotion: Darshan designed his product to be easy, affordable and time-saving. He believes evoking an emotion on top of that can multiply a product's chance of success.

Insights Are More Than Facts: Darshan defines an insight as facts, observations, and social and tech trends combined into an "aha." Gathering them is ongoing, and out-innovating yourself helps control your obsolescence.

q: What is iResearch and how much does an online focus group cost?
a: iResearch is a SaaS platform Darshan Mehta built to run focus groups on demand, from anywhere and in any language. On price, he said "each session is no more than the cost of a nice lunch for two people" [03:05].

q: Why use chat-based focus groups instead of face-to-face ones?
a: Darshan found that participants can all respond at once, then read and build on each other's answers, and that writing makes them a bit more thoughtful. He explained, "When you pose a question in a chat, everyone can answer without interrupting each other." [06:15]

q: Are surveys enough to understand why customers buy?
a: Darshan says no: people favor surveys because they are familiar and cost less, but most respondents skip open-ended questions. In his words, "in reality, the surveys never get at the why" [03:57], so he recommends having conversations first and using both methods.

q: What does Darshan Mehta look for when hiring development teams?
a: Darshan has a conversation with candidates to see whether they can think through a problem, even without the exact solution up front. He said, "those three things are one, are they thinkers? Are they doers? And are they hungry?" [13:14]

q: What is Darshan Mehta's advice on product validation and product-market fit?
a: Darshan advises gathering insights and testing early, before spending heavily on development, production and marketing, so you can pivot sooner. He said the market will speak to you either way, and "Your choice ultimately is do you want to listen sooner or later?" [31:06]

s5-bonus-no-more-hotfixes-debugging-live-production-applications-without-redeploying-with-ilan-peleg-of-lightrun

Shift Left Observability: Lightrun lets developers add logs, metrics and traces to live applications at runtime from their IDE, instead of predefining everything before shipping and analyzing it later.

A One-Command CLI MVP: The first version was a command line tool that did one thing, add a new log to a running application. The goal was to learn how developers reacted to the capability and what to build next.

Security Controls Before Polish: Early on, Lightrun had a thorough management UI for permissions, privacy and access visibility, even without a really nice developer interface. Inserted instrumentation was verified as read-only.

On-Premise From the Start: Alongside SaaS, Lightrun offered a lightweight on-premise deployment that kept data inside the customer's organization, which helped it get into large, heavily regulated enterprises early.

Hire Leaders and Market Earlier: Peleg wishes he had hired VP-level managers sooner to support rapid growth. Starting over, he would begin marketing and go-to-market work before writing a single line of code.

q: What is shift left observability?
a: Ilan Peleg uses the term for putting observability in developers' hands, rather than relying on tools that mainly target operators and require data to be predefined before release. With Lightrun, as Peleg described it, developers can "add new logs, metrics, traces to live applications" [05:20] while those applications are still running.

q: What did Lightrun's first MVP look like?
a: Peleg said the first version skipped the native IDE plugin and the full set of observability pillars. In his words, "our MVP was a CLI actually, a command line interface" [07:33], and its only command added a new log to a running application.

q: How does Lightrun address security concerns about developers accessing production?
a: Peleg said a management server lets operators enforce security and privacy controls and see who is accessing which service and environment, under which permissions. Lightrun also focused on "verifying at the same time that all the insertions are read-only and we do not change anything in the original flow" [11:00].

q: Can Lightrun be deployed on-premise?
a: Yes, Peleg said Lightrun supported both a SaaS product and an on-premise option from its early days because of data privacy and compliance needs. He described the latter as "a very lightweight on-premise deployment" [22:15] that keeps the data flow managed within the organization.

q: How did Lightrun avoid building only for its first few customers?
a: Peleg said the team learned from design partners but also tested its hypotheses with the wider developer community, even before it had paying customers. He warned that "when you lack customers, you can be very biased and it's dangerous" [16:19].

s5-e26-rehearsing-surgery-how-armor-bionics-built-the-3d-gps-for-complex-operations-with-bruno-demuro

Scrappy Six-Month MVP: Bruno combined GitHub and open-source code with his own integration work, with no UI, and test-printed on a crude self-assembled 3D printer. It took about six months to turn 2D scan images into 3D.

Quality Over Speed: Early on, the team traded rendering and print time for better models, accepting that finer layer heights could stretch a 24-hour print to 48. Top quality became the company's guiding star.

A Service, Not Hardware: Rather than have hospitals own printers and software, Armor Bionics works as a service. Images are dragged and dropped, the doctor states what's needed, and the team builds a 3D model for approval and optional printing.

Designers Over Doctors for Modeling: The team found it far easier to teach industrial designers anatomy than to teach doctors image segmentation. A flexible, on-call workforce scales with demand and helped the company survive COVID's surgery halt.

Global Reach From Uruguay: Bruno estimates about 3 million images processed and over 250 surgeries assisted in more than 25 countries. A Shapeways partnership hands off production so the team can focus on design and 3D modeling.

q: What does Armor Bionics do?
a: Armor Bionics turns CT and MRI scan images into full-color, patient-specific 3D models that help surgeons plan operations. Bruno Demuro explained, "we transform those 2D images into 3D patient-specific" [02:34] models that replicate the patient's anatomy.

q: What inspired Bruno Demuro to start Armor Bionics?
a: Bruno's mother had a penny-sized tumor in her meninges removed through an opening the size of a grapefruit. The surgery went well, but he could not accept that this was necessary: "there had to be a way for a doctor before surgery to pinpoint the exact location" [05:47].

q: How does Armor Bionics fit into a surgeon's workflow?
a: Images are uploaded to the platform, the doctor requests what should be converted to 3D, and Armor Bionics processes it and returns a model for approval. Bruno said, "we should just be another tool in his toolbox that he can take out when he needs us" [17:37].

q: What product mistake did Armor Bionics make?
a: Bruno said the team spent a couple of months so caught up in designing the product that it lost sight of the customer, though it corrected course in time. He called it a big no-no to "focus on the product and take your eye" [26:19] off the customer.

q: What would Bruno Demuro do differently when starting a healthcare startup?
a: Bruno would seek funding earlier instead of bootstrapping for so long, because habits formed while scraping by don't work when scaling. In healthcare, he noted, you will need "eventually funding for regulations to get certifications to start" [32:28], as well as money for marketing.

s5-bonus-solving-the-data-firehose-problem-hybrid-sqlnosql-architectures-with-kyle-bernhardy-of-harperdb

Born From a Data Firehose: Analyzing World Cup tweets at 250,000 per second kept crashing a relational database. Adding DynamoDB and a custom ETL tool worked around it, but the complexity and cost inspired HarperDB.

Time-Box What You Defer: The MVP shipped without a SQL layer or data distribution so the team could build core operations first. Both were committed to a later phase and required before an official release.

Unique Storage Hit a Wall: HarperDB's homegrown file-system data store had significant scaling issues after about two years. Moving to LMDB, an open source key value store, left data size limited mainly by disk.

Trust, but Verify: A rushed partnership to rebuild the data store cost money and three months of two engineers' work. The founders owned the decision and learned the store had to run embedded within HarperDB.

A Customer Need Accelerated Roadmap: Custom functions were envisioned from the start, but a proof of concept for a potential customer pulled them forward. They let users run their own JavaScript endpoints alongside the data.

q: What is HarperDB?
a: Kyle Bernhardy describes HarperDB as a globally distributed, single data model NoSQL database with SQL semantics. He explained that "things are stored similar to a document store, but you can execute SQL against that." [02:43]

q: What problem led to the creation of HarperDB?
a: While processing massive volumes of tweets at a sports and entertainment data company, Bernhardy's team had to bolt DynamoDB and a custom ETL pipeline onto a relational database. As Bernhardy put it, "our database infrastructure got super complicated" [05:45], and it was costing what he estimated as $10,000 to $20,000 a month.

q: How was the HarperDB MVP built?
a: The team built it in Node.js, drawing on their experience and open source libraries from NPM, starting in March 2017 and releasing an MVP that September or October. Bernhardy said that "Putting SQL to the side so that we can focus on sort of the core" [10:27] operations was very freeing.

q: What did HarperDB learn about evaluating technology partners?
a: A partnership to rebuild the underlying data store failed because the two products were not a good fit, which Bernhardy attributes to too little due diligence by his own team. His approach to a promising product now is, "I'm going to run it through its paces and make sure it does what I need it to do." [31:33]

q: How does HarperDB approach edge computing?
a: Bernhardy said centralized cloud setups can introduce latency and choke points, so HarperDB aims to bring data and logic closer to users. He explained that many use cases they address now are "about decentralizing your data and scaling it" [33:44] across the globe.

s5-bonus-building-a-passwordless-authentication-revolution-with-cherish-santoshi-of-sawo-labs
Passwordless Auth as an SDK: SAWO lets developers add OTP-less, password-less logins to web and mobile apps, with the aim of cutting bounce and churn and improving user onboarding.

Trading Java for Django: SAWO built its MVP in Java for familiarity and easier hiring, then moved to Django after raising funding. The switch brought scalability, but also technical debt that slowed high-priority work.
Bottom-Up Beats Enterprise Sales: Long enterprise sales cycles pushed SAWO to sell directly to developers, product managers and founders, since check writers usually want developer buy-in first.

Compatibility Before Extra Features: SAWO prioritized working across stacks and platforms, including iOS, Android, web, Flutter, WooCommerce, Shopify and Bubble, ahead of add-ons like dashboard customizations.
Built for Massive Concurrency: Cherish says SAWO can handle 1 million simultaneous auths per second, with cases like a hugely popular streaming platform's audience all logging in at once in mind.

q: What is SAWO Labs and what does its product do?
a: SAWO is a developer-facing tool for creating OTP-less, password-less login flows. Cherish Santoshi explains that "SAWO is an auth SDK that helps developers and businesses to enable passwordless logins on their web and mobile apps." [02:15]

q: Why did SAWO move from Java to Django?
a: Cherish Santoshi says the team started with Java because it was a comfortable stack and talent was easier to source. After raising funding they switched, accepting technical debt, because "django seems far more scalable to the use cases that we serve" [05:43].

q: Why did SAWO focus on developers instead of enterprise sales?
a: Cherish Santoshi says enterprise deals took far longer to close than deals with smaller startups and product-centric communities. He also notes that although a CTO or founder may write the check, "The person who has the influence of using the tool will always be a developer." [07:01]

q: How many authentications can SAWO handle?
a: Cherish Santoshi says the team has always built to scale because auth is part of the larger problem of identity management. As of the interview, he says "SAWO can take 1 million auths any given second" [16:04].

q: What does SAWO look for when hiring?
a: Cherish Santoshi looks for ownership, integrity and intelligence, and says the hiring bar has usually been very high. In his words, "the things that i look forward to whenever i hire are ownership" [12:58], meaning seeing a job from end to end.

s5-e25-when-production-burns-bobby-ross-of-fire-hydrant-on-automating-incident-response-and-eliminating-downtime

Runbooks Replaced a Static Process: FireHydrant first ran the same Slack, Jira and status page steps for every incident, which didn't fit larger companies. The team spent two and a half months building Runbooks so customers could define their own process.
Design for the Split Early: FireHydrant started on a single database but put an account ID on every record and restricted every query by it, leaving a path to split the data later.

Abstractions as Compounding Interest: Domain-driven design, a shared data access layer and Google Pub/Sub felt over-designed early on. Later, the team built a missing, production-ready feature in a week.

Founders Must Leave the Editor: Ross says continuing to write features as CEO was a mistake. The opportunity cost was time he could have spent hiring or on marketing, which he now wishes he had focused on from day one.

Pay for Great Recruiters: With three engineer co-founders who had never recruited, FireHydrant paid outside recruiters to hire across engineering, sales and marketing. Ross says he would run that play again, and the company now has an internal recruiting team.

q: What is FireHydrant and what problem does it solve?
a: FireHydrant began as an incident management tool and now focuses on reliability, including service ownership, service catalogs, status pages and retrospectives. Bobby Ross argues that reliability is not just for engineers: "We truly believe that it's a business metric because people view" [03:05] it as belonging to the whole business.

q: How did FireHydrant get started?
a: Bobby Ross was recording a video series to help bootcamp graduates learn production software, using FireHydrant as the real-world example. A friend told him that "what you're building, FireHydrant, is way more valuable than the web series" [05:16], and development sped up once he stopped recording.

q: What are FireHydrant Runbooks and why were they built?
a: Runbooks let customers set up their own incident process, such as creating a Slack channel based on severity. Ross said the team started from the question, "how do we make our product flexible for anyone to create their own process?" [12:28]

q: How was FireHydrant built to scale?
a: The Ruby on Rails application moved quickly from Heroku to Kubernetes, uses Google Pub/Sub for event-based functionality and has a unified data access layer on top of Active Record. Bobby Ross credited the team's early design work, saying of good abstractions, "it's compounding interest. That's what it is." [23:44]

q: What would Bobby Ross do differently about raising venture capital?
a: Ross said he would wait to raise until the product had more traction, because venture money brings an expectation of an exit. He would start on the side "and try to get just a couple paying customers, even if it's 10 bucks a month" [39:24] to get validation first.

s5-bonus-from-co-creating-typescript-to-rewriting-cloud-infrastructure-with-luke-hoban-of-pulumi

Follow the Market Pull: Pulumi first focused on helping application developers use the cloud, but found the strongest demand in infrastructure as code, from teams scaling from tens of cloud resources to thousands or tens of thousands.

Start Thin, Then Rebuild: The MVP supported only AWS and one language. Pulumi later rebuilt pieces on existing foundations, such as the Node.js runtime and open source resource providers, so it could expand to more clouds and languages.

Design for Cheap Expansion: For clouds, languages and CI/CD integrations, the team aimed for a fixed upfront cost and a low cost for each addition, so it could respond quickly when customers needed something new.

Pricing Shaped Product Usage: Pulumi moved from stack-based to per-user to consumption-based pricing. Stacks confused newcomers, while per-user pricing held back customers who wanted their whole team to use and see the infrastructure.

Revisiting an Expedient Bet: Building on open source Terraform providers gave Pulumi broad cloud support early on. It has since invested in native providers for AWS, Azure, GCP and Kubernetes to solve more customer problems.

q: What is Pulumi?
a: Luke Hoban, Pulumi's CTO, describes it as a modern infrastructure as code tool that lets engineers use familiar programming languages, IDEs and debuggers to manage cloud infrastructure. The idea is to bring software engineering practices to it, or as Luke put it, "treat it like code, version control it and manage" [03:01].

q: How did Pulumi's focus change after the company started?
a: Pulumi began with more of a focus on application developers who wanted to take advantage of the cloud. Luke said the team then saw that the greatest "demand the most pull from kind of the existing market was actually more around" [05:00] infrastructure as code.

q: How was the Pulumi MVP built?
a: The team built its own runtimes for existing programming languages and its own AWS libraries, initially supporting just one cloud and one language. To scale out, Luke said, "we kind of went back and rebuilt those things on a foundation that would allow us to" [07:09] support any cloud, language or architecture.

q: Why did Pulumi build its product around open source?
a: Luke said customers would be building on Pulumi and betting on it deeply, so the company put effectively all of the value of what it builds into the open source project. In his words, the team knew it would be "important for it to be built around an open source foundation because folks were going" [16:34] to build on top of it.

q: Why did Pulumi switch to consumption-based pricing?
a: Luke explained that per-user pricing discouraged organizations from giving everyone on their teams access, including people who only touched infrastructure occasionally. As he put it, "we realized that sort of the pricing model is actually holding back" [19:33] how Pulumi and its customers wanted the product to be used.

s5-e24-engineering-a-fintech-powerhouse-thejo-kote-on-scaling-and-exiting-airbase

Mockups Before Code: Thejo spent about six months talking to CFOs, controllers and accounting managers, then showed high-fidelity mockups and pre-sold Airbase to about a dozen finance leaders on handshake agreements.

Software Over Plastic: Airbase launched with corporate card spend management, but avoided competing on cash back and rewards. It focused on pre-approval workflows, virtual card controls and automated accounting.

De-Risk With Milestones: In the first 18 months, Thejo self-funded and set out to prove the target segment, the buyer, real usage, acceptance by non-finance employees and how much Airbase could charge.

Distributed Talent Strategy: After building Automatic around a San Francisco office, Thejo made Airbase fully distributed, with most of the team across India and engineers in places like Chile and Romania, without lowering the hiring bar.

Earn the Next 10x: Thejo advises building to cover at least the next 12 to 18 months with a path to scale, avoiding both over-engineering and heavy tech debt. Bigger architectural changes come once growth earns them.

q: What is Airbase and what problem does it solve?
a: Airbase is a spend management platform that Thejo Kote founded to replace the separate systems companies use for corporate cards, bill payments and expense reimbursements. He described the goal as "to bring all those elements together into a single platform right so every single non-payroll dollar" [05:54].

q: How did Airbase validate its idea before building the product?
a: Thejo researched the problem with dozens of finance and accounting people, sketched a solution and worked with a designer on high-fidelity mockups before writing code. In his words, "I essentially pre-sold the product to about a dozen CFOs and controllers." [09:25]

q: How does Airbase decide what to build next?
a: Thejo said customers largely drive the roadmap, and the team prioritizes the most popular requests against the capacity it has each quarter. As he put it, "planning process 95% of it is almost exclusively just coming straight from" [00:24] what customers are saying.

q: Why did Thejo Kote build Airbase as a distributed team?
a: At his previous company, Automatic, Thejo found hiring in San Francisco highly competitive and expensive, so he opened Airbase to talent elsewhere, including many engineers in India. Thejo said of the remote model, "it's now a competitive advantage for us, right? In that we can literally put, you know," [25:18] far more engineering and product capacity behind the problem.

q: What founder mistake did Thejo Kote learn from at Automatic?
a: Thejo said he did not control the company's destiny: it was unprofitable and depended on venture funding, and it later had to do layoffs to extend runway. He recalled that he "desperately needed the money every single round of funding that we raised" [33:38].

s5-bonus-fixing-the-broken-pipeline-shinji-kim-on-automating-data-lineage-and-governance-at-select-star

Design Mock Before Code: Shinji Kim tested a high-fidelity design mock with potential users and recruited 10 beta customers before raising a seed round. A very basic V0 then took roughly two to three months.

Fundamentals First, Then Follow Usage: Select Star started with table and column documentation, ownership, similar tables and lineage. Bare-bones lineage grew well beyond the original mock because customers kept asking for it and using it.

Architecture Mapped From Day One: The data model connected tables, queries, data sources, users and activity so it could support planned features. The app began as a monolith, with microservices left as a later option and infrastructure scaling still in progress.

Opendoor as Stress Test: Early customer Opendoor, running close to a million SQL queries a day, tested the system end to end. The team had to rework how large lineage graphs were displayed and improve front-end and back-end speed.

Hiring for Async Independence: The fully remote team skips full-day interview loops in favor of an initial interview, a take-home assignment and references. Kim looks for people who can execute independently and communicate asynchronously.

q: What is Select Star and what problem does it solve?
a: Founder and CEO Shinji Kim describes it this way: "Select Star is an automated data discovery tool that helps everyone to find and understand" [02:22] their own data. It addresses the difficulty of getting the right context once a company has piled up many data sets across its warehouses and BI tools.

q: How did Shinji Kim validate the idea for Select Star?
a: Data discovery was one of three data ideas Kim had, and it came up repeatedly in conversations with data platform managers. Kim explained that "what I actually initially did was creating a design mock" [05:09], then gathered feedback from potential users and recruited beta customers before building the product.

q: Where does Select Star get its metadata and data lineage information?
a: Kim said most data warehouses have an information schema or system table listing databases, schemas, tables and columns, and Select Star also parses SQL queries to build relationships. Kim noted that "Snowflake has a query history view that has the log of all the queries" [19:05], while Postgres and Redshift need logging set up or enabled.

q: How did Select Star handle scaling to large amounts of metadata?
a: Kim pointed to early customer Opendoor, saying "they have a lot of metadata and a lot of SQL queries like they run close to a million" [17:25] every day. The team iterated on how to display large amounts of data interactively and improved performance, and Kim called scaling an ongoing effort.

q: How does Select Star hire for its remote engineering team?
a: Shinji Kim's process uses an initial interview, a take-home assignment and then reference checks instead of a full day of interviews. Kim said the company is a "fully remote team and we want each person to be independent and can execute and also communicate" [13:05] asynchronously.

s5-bonus-ditching-the-saas-tax-rebuilding-hubspot-level-marketing-automation-on-open-source-with-adrian-tobey-of-groundhogg

Self-Hosted Instead of SaaS: Groundhogg runs natively on WordPress, so businesses keep control of their data and choose where it is hosted. Agencies can also export content to a JSON file and import it into another site running the plugin.

A Two-Month MVP: Version 1.0 shipped with no beta, using jQuery, AJAX and PHP. It had delay-based funnels, a block email editor and a basic CRM, with a linear automation builder instead of a drag-and-drop flowchart.

The Costly React Rewrite: A 3.0 rebuild planned for three months was still unreleasable after eight, with well over $100,000 invested. Adrian laid off the React team and returned to familiar tools to get about 95% of the same result.

Doubling Prices to Grow: After WordPress plugin founders told him Groundhogg wasn't expensive enough, Adrian doubled prices and moved more features into premium and higher tiers. He says that the next month, "we doubled."

Borrow Audiences to Build Yours: Adrian targeted digital agencies and pitched podcasts serving them, with about 10% replying. His advice is to pick an ideal customer, because marketing to everyone is like marketing to no one.

q: What is Groundhogg and how is it different from HubSpot or ActiveCampaign?
a: Adrian Tobey describes it this way: "Groundhogg is a CRM and marketing automation platform specifically for businesses that use WordPress." [02:45] Unlike the SaaS tools he compares it with, it is self-hosted on your WordPress site, so you control your data and choose where it lives.

q: How was the Groundhogg MVP built?
a: Adrian built it in about two months with jQuery, AJAX and PHP, covering marketing automation, a block-based email editor and CRM basics. He said "it was very much a just get it done focus for the MVP." [07:01]

q: Why did Groundhogg abandon its React rewrite?
a: Adrian expected version 3.0 to take three months, but after eight it was still not releasable and development costs were unsustainable for the bootstrapped company. As he put it, "We invested well over $100,000 at this point into this project with this React team." [26:20]

q: How did Adrian Tobey change Groundhogg's pricing to increase sales?
a: At an event, successful WordPress plugin business owners told Adrian his product was not expensive enough. He recalled, "I literally doubled the price across the board for everything." [45:38] He also moved features into premium and higher-priced plans, and says that the next month they doubled.

q: Can a WordPress-based CRM and email platform scale?
a: Adrian says scalability was a priority from day one, with load testing and improvements to the event queue and AWS SES integration. He noted, "We have customers with lists of well over 500,000 people" [28:21], and said they send 500,000 emails per day without any issue.

s5-bonus-solving-the-scattered-data-nightmare-how-file-finder-indexes-the-modern-cloud-stack-with-brandon-white

Search the Way People Remember: Brandon White argues most people can't recall enough for Boolean search, but they do remember people, places, time, topics and groups. File Finder is built to find files through those cues.
An MVP Built to Test: White sketched the flow, used Balsamiq, and paid friends in Argentina to build a simple SQL-search version. He then interviewed users from a group of roughly 75 to 100 people.

Security Audit as a Gate: Google requires a third-party security audit for products touching Gmail or Drive. White put the cost at $15,000 to $25,000, repeated yearly, and the team was still weighing how to fund it.

A Ground-Up Rebuild: The first version sat on one cheap server, had hard-coded pieces and got hacked before any data was in it. The team rebuilt the original PHP code to handle heavy attachment processing and pass the audit.

Set Time Commitments Explicitly: White asks part-time teammates for 20 hours a week, so nobody assumes five hours while others expect far more. He also wants to know how their partners view the commitment.

q: What is File Finder and what problem does it solve?
a: Brandon White, co-founder and president, describes it this way: "File Finder is effectively a search engine that helps you find files you know you have" [02:23]. The idea came from watching his wife, who manages a family office, struggle to locate documents, mostly in email, while switching accountants.

q: How is File Finder's approach different from Boolean keyword search?
a: White says people often can't remember enough about a file to build a Boolean query. His starting point was that "what you do remember is people, places, time," [07:55] as well as topics and groups, so File Finder lets you search by what you can recall, such as a location or a company.

q: Did File Finder's first version scale?
a: No, White says it ran on a single cheap server without Docker or Kubernetes, and it was hacked, though no data had been loaded yet. The team had to "rebuild the code from literally the ground up" [27:30].

q: How does File Finder handle processing very large inboxes?
a: White says making users wait days would lose them, so the aim is to give an immediate piece of information, such as email and attachment counts, to get them engaged. In his words, "what we've had to really figure out is how to batch process this" [29:35], while keeping the cost per user economical.

q: How does the File Finder team decide what to build next?
a: White credits co-founder Sergey with reining in scope creep and insisting that each step be validated before moving on, down to individual features. As White explains, "we literally have graphed and said, here's our core premise." [18:13]

s5-e23-from-engineering-siri-to-designing-the-ultimate-dev-flow-state-with-ulf-schwekendiek-of-centeredapp

A One-Month MVP: Ulf went from quitting his job to an MVP and pre-seed money in a month. The prototype, built with TypeScript, React and Electron, was a to-do list with a play button, a Pomodoro countdown and purchased music.

Overbuilding Before Product-Market Fit: An offline-first design with local SQLite syncing to a custom GraphQL backend quickly became unmaintainable. By version three, none of it remained, and Centered now runs on serverless Firebase to iterate faster.

Accountability Drove Retention: Version one had retention and growth problems. Version two's coached video "flow halls" lifted retention but lost the surrounding work tools, so version three combined task management with optional quiet co-working.

Investor Ideas Can Derail Roadmaps: Ulf dropped planned work to build features investors suggested during fundraising, often to prove the team's speed. The investors who ultimately backed Centered never asked for that.

Narrow the Target User: Aiming at all knowledge workers made the persona hard to pin down. Centered chose to build first for product engineering teams, which changed how the team thought about the product and its roadmap.

q: What is Centered and how does it help you reach a flow state?
a: Centered is a desktop app where you list your tasks, estimate how long each takes, and work on one at a time with flow music and a digital guide that nudges you when you get distracted. Ulf Schwekendiek said of the music, "That is music specifically designed to help you concentrate for longer." [03:43]

q: How was the Centered MVP built and how long did it take?
a: Ulf built the first prototype with TypeScript, React and Electron, plus a little C and Swift as glue, drawing on his experience building desktop apps with web technologies. Of the month it took to get from quitting his job to pre-seed funding, Ulf said, "It really was just a month of me, like, coding and designing something." [10:40]

q: What technical mistake did Centered make with its first architecture?
a: Ulf built an offline-first framework around a local SQLite database that synced with a custom GraphQL backend on Heroku, expecting it to scale while the company searched for product-market fit. Ulf said it "was a complete wrong decision to say, okay, we need to have all of this in place at first" [13:09].

q: How did Centered improve user retention?
a: Ulf's team rebuilt the app around accountability, with video flow sessions led by a coach, then merged that idea with task management in version three. Ulf said that with the second version, "we learned from that version that retention was a lot higher" [17:08].

q: What advice does Ulf Schwekendiek have on choosing a target customer?
a: Ulf said that targeting anyone who works on a computer was the wrong decision, and Centered chose to focus first on product engineering teams. As Ulf described the shift, "we'll start with a very narrow segment that we understand really well and build it for" [30:24] that persona.

s5-bonus-the-evolution-of-the-modern-web-guillermo-rauch-on-the-architecture-behind-nextjs-and-vercel

Zero Config From Day One: Next.js grew from Rauch's frustration setting up webpack for a simple React signup page. The MVP contract was no configuration, plus one command each to develop, build and run.

Stable Boundaries, Evolving Internals: Vercel fixed its contract early: git push or one command returns a URL. The team has kept changing the infrastructure underneath based on what frameworks and customers need.

Contrarian Bet on Server Rendering: While much of the JavaScript world was excited about single-page apps, Next.js focused on server rendering. It fit e-commerce and SEO-minded companies and supported fast initial loads.

Strong Core Over Features: Early on, the team prioritized reliable, reproducible deployments, predictable performance and customer SLAs. That meant saying no to enticing features and sometimes pointing users to user-land solutions.

Open Source as Growth Engine: Rauch calls open source the best tool for finding product-market fit, and Next.js reached production remarkably fast. Most initial hires also came from the open source ecosystem.

q: What is Vercel and what does develop, preview, ship mean?
a: Guillermo Rauch describes it simply: "Vercel is a developer platform for front-end teams." [02:31] Teams develop with a modern front-end framework, preview each code push on a shareable live URL, and ship to a global edge network, with analytics informing the next round.

q: Why doesn't Next.js include its own database or ORM?
a: Rauch deliberately made Next.js a front-end layer, unlike predecessors such as Meteor, as the industry was moving toward APIs. He decided it would not have "its own database, its own ORM, its own opinionation about how you would get your data." [06:50]

q: Why did Next.js focus on server rendering instead of single-page applications?
a: Rauch believed it was extremely hard, if not impossible, to get great initial load performance for complex apps without server rendering or pre-rendering. Looking at Google Search and Facebook, he noted that "The common pattern was they both use server rendering at scale." [17:49] He also felt single-page apps did not scale well across teams.

q: What mistake or lesson did Vercel learn about backwards compatibility?
a: Rauch said, "I would say that we learned really quickly how valuable backwards compatibility can be." [21:35] He believes that since Next 0.1 and Now V2, neither the framework nor the platform has had a single meaningful breaking change, which pays off for production users.

q: What does Guillermo Rauch see as the future of front-end development?
a: Rauch is particularly excited about edge computing and React Server Components. He described edge computing as "our ability to not just put the static parts of a website next to your customer, but to personalize and dynamicize" [23:13], making things like personalization and A/B tests fast and broadly accessible.

s5-bonus-solving-the-chicken-and-egg-dilemma-how-voicescom-scaled-to-200m-in-marketplace-sales-with-david-ciccarelli
Charge Early for Membership: Voices skipped freemium and sold voice talent a $49 annual membership. A long-form email with a PayPal link brought in $5,000 in sales over the first weekend.

A Domain That Tripled Traffic: At 10,000 users, InteractiveVoices.com became Voices.com in a deal of about $30,000, paid in quarterly installments. Organic Google traffic tripled virtually over a weekend.
Escrow Solved Buyer Ghosting: Some buyers vanished after receiving audio files, and talent held Voices responsible. Voices now captures payment up front and acts as the trusted intermediary.
Build for 10x Today: David buys and builds systems 10x bigger than needed. Moving audio files to Amazon S3 early replaced a $2,000-a-month Rackspace cost comparison with $2.13 a month.

Anticipate Who Feels Threatened: Despite customer interviews beforehand, acquiring a competitor sparked backlash from people worried about their livelihoods. Voices now weighs how releases might be perceived.

q: What is Voices.com and who uses it?
a: Voices is an online marketplace for hiring voice talent for work such as radio commercials, podcast spots and explainer videos. David Ciccarelli explained, "We connect voice buying clients, think of people at advertising agencies, video production companies, with that voice talent." [02:36]

q: What did the first version of Voices look like?
a: David Ciccarelli designed a static site himself with library books and Dreamweaver, with no database or login system. It grew out of his recording studio's page, which he described as "a brochure-style website I initially used to advertise the recording studio I operated" [09:12].

q: How did Voices first make money?
a: David Ciccarelli and his co-founder Stephanie sold voice talent a $49 annual membership that promised marketing and access to job opportunities. Of the first email offer, David said "we did five thousand dollars of sales so we knew like oh wow we're definitely on to something" [19:53].

q: How does Voices make sure voice talent get paid?
a: Voices built an escrow service after some buyers received finished audio and then disappeared without paying. David Ciccarelli said, "if you find somebody you want to work with, we capture the payment up front by credit card." [24:20] If the talent becomes unavailable, Voices can help the client hire someone else or issue a refund.

q: What mistake did Voices make when acquiring a competitor?
a: David Ciccarelli said they underestimated the customer response, even after interviewing the competitor's customers without disclosing the deal. When he went back to see them, he found "they were concerned for their livelihoods" [39:48], though he still believes the acquisition was strategically right.

s5-e22-measuring-developer-love-how-orbit-built-an-analytics-engine-for-open-source-with-josh-dzielak

Simplifying an Over-Architected MVP: Orbit first paired a Rails backend with a Next.js frontend, but changing APIs and the frontend together slowed iteration. After about three months, the team returned to a Rails monolith.

Use Cases Before Polish: Early design tweaks drew compliments but not clear answers about what customers would use. Orbit chose rougher pages, Tailwind CSS and Rails partials so it could iterate on use cases faster.

Broad and Deep Feedback: Orbit paired five to 10 design partners, who got two to three hours a week, with a wider group of about 100 people. This kept the roadmap from being boxed in by partners or driven only by loose suggestions.

When Materialized Views Stop Scaling: Postgres materialized views for member "love" scores worked at far lower volume, then became the database's top I/O consumer. The team is moving to tables and now asks about 10x or 100x scale.

Structure That Raised Velocity: Orbit moved from a flat engineering group to teams with an engineering organizer, a tech lead, a product manager and five to six engineers. Josh says velocity went up with the added structure.

q: What is Orbit and what does it do for community builders?
a: Orbit, which Josh Dzielak calls mission control for your community, connects tools like Slack, Discord, GitHub and Twitter. Josh says the goal is to "give those community builders a universal sense of their community" [02:54], including who their members are and whether the community is growing or shrinking.

q: How is the Orbit model different from a sales funnel?
a: Josh Dzielak describes the funnel as a model for marketing and sales, while the Orbit model is built for community, with some members at the center and others nearer the edges. As he put it, "In the orbit model you care about all of your community members" [04:03].

q: What tech stack was Orbit built with?
a: The first MVP used a Rails backend with a Next.js frontend, and Josh Dzielak says the team "eventually went back to just a Rails monolith." [06:19] At the time of the interview, Orbit ran on Heroku with Postgres and used Tailwind CSS on the front end.

q: Why did Postgres materialized views become a scaling problem for Orbit?
a: Orbit used materialized views, recalculated on a rolling basis, to score each community member's engagement, known as love. Josh Dzielak, who says the idea was his, found a few months later that "the number one consumer of io on our database is the generation of these materialized views" [22:41], so the team began re-architecting to use tables.

q: What would Josh Dzielak do differently if he started Orbit again?
a: Josh would be more "use case focused and probably try to prioritize product design and product" [28:54] management thinking earlier. With engineers driving the roadmap, Orbit built a number of features that did not turn out to be the right ones.

s5-bonus-fixing-broken-tech-teams-matt-dixon-on-optimizing-engineering-culture-and-performance
Coach the Whole Team: After tough projects Front Range Systems saw as successful but clients didn't, Matt Dixon set out to coach everyone together, including management, developers, designers and QA.

A Deliberately Bare-Bones MVP: The Code Program's website is just two HTML pages with CSS and images, with no content management system or forum. Dixon held back the urge to build things customers didn't need.

Core Curriculum Plus Customization: The six-month program started with just 12 slide decks, two per month. Everything else is tailored to each customer, such as one client's request to teach developers to give better presentations.

Don't Hire Another You: Dixon hires for the team's gaps and strengths, involves more people in interviews, and uses trial runs when unsure. He also asks candidates how weird they are on a scale of one to ten.
Scale to Client Needs: Dixon no longer aims for a $100 million company. He plans shared core sessions to limit headcount, adds coaches for customized work, and wants to stop being the bottleneck.

q: What is the Code Program?
a: The Code Program is Matt Dixon's customized coaching program for teams, currently focused on the tech industry and run as a separate business from his software consultancy, Front Range Systems. Dixon sees a gap in the market, noting that "there aren't a lot of team coaches" [03:44].

q: How did Matt Dixon come up with the idea for team coaching?
a: The idea came after a few difficult projects in a row, where Dixon's team thought they had succeeded but the client didn't. He couldn't see "how that project could have been more successful other than embracing the whole team" [02:43], including the client.

q: How did Matt Dixon build the MVP of the Code Program?
a: Dixon worked with a designer, a marketing person and a scrum master to develop a core curriculum, and kept the extras to a minimum. He said the website "is literally two HTML pages and some CSS and images" [06:34].

q: What does Matt Dixon look for when hiring for his team?
a: Dixon looks at the team's strengths and gaps, and wants people who are confident and comfortable in their own skin. As he put it, "when I hire anyone, I don't need another me" [09:34].

q: What mistake did Matt Dixon make as a junior developer?
a: While trying to delete a duplicate record in production, Dixon said, "I forgot the where clause. So I deleted all the" [14:09] people in the database. The latest backup was a month old, and the team responded by improving its backup strategy.

s5-bonus-stop-building-dashboards-how-to-ship-customer-facing-analytics-without-the-engineering-overhead-with-oleg-friedman-of-verb-data

Validate Before Writing Code: Verb Data logged about 150 conversations, then iterated on a clickable InVision prototype with those people. It was about six months before the team wrote a single line of code.

Ingestion Came First: For the MVP, supporting common data sources mattered more than having the perfect chart, since users who couldn't get data in would never reach later steps. Other sources were added on customer request.

In-House Builds Are Competition: Verb views internally built dashboards as one of its biggest competitors. Its pitch is the same value without the engineering work, so much of the roadmap focuses on making developers' lives easier.

Thread the Scaling Needle: Oleg warns against both over-architecting and ignoring scale. Design for the customers you realistically expect, assume vendors may change, and avoid a full rewrite if a customer requires a different cloud host.

The Flat File Surprise: Verb expected engineering teams to connect databases and didn't anticipate how often people would use Excel and CSV files. The experience had to be completely redesigned, though it was mostly UI work.

q: What is Verb Data?
a: Oleg Friedman, CTO of Verb Data, describes it this way: "Verb Data is an integrated, embedded solution for dashboards and any data visualization" [02:45]. It helps SaaS teams connect to data sources, ingest, model and transform data, and build visualizations for their end customers, embedded with a couple of lines of code.

q: How did Verb Data validate its idea before building the product?
a: Oleg says the team started with conversations, before even sketching the product: "We had about 150 conversations that we've logged and recorded before we ever" [06:18]. They then built a clickable InVision prototype and kept returning to those same people for feedback.

q: How did Verb Data decide what to build first in its MVP?
a: Oleg's team looked for the first roadblock a user would hit, which was data ingestion. As he explained, "if they could never get their data into our system to begin with," [10:54] they would never reach the later steps, so broad coverage of common data sources took priority over specialized charts.

q: Does Verb Data replace BI tools or data warehouses like Snowflake and Redshift?
a: Oleg says Verb can integrate with warehouses and ingest data from them or from a core application database. He noted that "in a lot of our customer implementations we sit side by side with their BI strategy." [19:05] Verb focuses on the data experience for the end users of a company's existing customers.

q: How should a startup think about architecting for scale?
a: Oleg calls over-architecture one of the biggest sins a startup can commit, but adds that "not designing or architecting for scale is also one of the biggest sins." [17:01] His advice is to plan for the size of customer you realistically expect to sell to, so that growth doesn't force you to rewrite large amounts of code.

s5-bonus-preventing-the-ai-meltdown-re-engineering-data-centers-for-100kw-gpu-racks-with-phill-lawson-shanks-of-aligned

Heat Is the Real Constraint: Phill says bringing more power into a data center is manageable, but removing the heat is the critical part. Fixed, room-ringing cooling units can leave customers unable to upgrade to newer hardware.

Delta Cube Adds Flexible Cooling: One four-foot Delta Cube removes 146 kilowatts of heat, and units stack three high. Customers can mix low- and high-density cabinets or ramp to 50 kilowatts in every cabinet.

Air Volume Beats Velocity: Aligned manages air pressure differentials so more air moves more slowly over the hot surface. It constantly monitors fans, air, water temperatures and energy to tune performance.

In-Wall Units Protect Customer Space: Moving from heavy overhead units to wall-based ones reduced the structural burden and lets Aligned maintain cooling from outside the room, which suits customers with security or compliance needs.

Pre-Buying Beat Supply Shortages: With hyperscalers buying up manufacturing cycles, Aligned pre-purchased 50 megawatts of capacity from suppliers. Inventory let it keep deploying when COVID closed factories making a key PDU component.

q: What is Aligned's Delta Cube cooling technology?
a: The Delta Cube is Aligned's cooling unit, which Phill Lawson-Shanks says can be stacked and deployed to match each customer's needs. As he described it, "It's a four-foot cube. And just one of those will remove 146 kilowatts of heat." [08:17]

q: Why is cooling such a big challenge for high-density data centers?
a: Phill Lawson-Shanks explains that getting more energy into a building is not insurmountable, but servers, storage and network devices keep drawing more power and producing more heat. In his words, "But removing the heat generated by those devices," [06:34] is the critical part.

q: Can data centers be cooled without using water?
a: Phill Lawson-Shanks says Aligned can be entirely waterless and already is in several of its centers, while its older sites use far less water, if any. He added that "all our future data centers will be totally waterless." [11:03]

q: How did Aligned handle data center supply chain shortages?
a: Hyperscalers were buying up manufacturers' production cycles for key equipment such as generators and UPSs, so Aligned planned ahead. Phill Lawson-Shanks said, "So we went out and pre-purchased 50 megawatts of capacity" [21:07], and having inventory later helped it keep deploying during COVID factory closures.

q: What advice does Phill Lawson-Shanks give early-stage founders?
a: Phill Lawson-Shanks urges founders to stay open to pivoting, since markets change and a product may end up serving an unexpected purpose. About a founder's product vision, he said "what I would say is hold that with a light touch" [33:05], while also encouraging them not to give up on their dreams.

s5-e21-from-microsoft-technical-fellow-to-startup-zero-to-one-with-laura-butler-of-uplift

Carfax for Condos: Uplift wants buyers to get trustworthy HOA information before making an offer. Today, budgets and minutes often arrive only after an offer, leaving a short contingency window to read hundreds or thousands of pages.

Pivots Led to Resale Reviews: A preventative maintenance plan stalled as COVID hit, and board consulting proved hard to scale. A real estate agent's comment about buy-side pain led to reviewing HOA documents for buyers, delivered as a PDF report.

Three Pillars Structure the Report: Uplift sorts HOA operations into finance, governance and maintenance. About 20 reviews shaped a standard format, and a roughly 25-page report with a glossary distills the hundreds of pages buyers receive.

OCR Is the Biggest Hurdle: Many HOA documents are scanned images, some blurry, sideways or huge, including one around 20 gigabytes. Even a pet rule can require reconciling old resolutions and later amendments.

$10,000 and a Real Test: The founders set out to put in $10,000 total and prove that strangers would pay. Revenue had just passed $10,000, mostly from the prior six months, and they had not yet hired.

q: What is Uplift Group?
a: Uplift Group, co-founded by CTO Laura Butler, aims to bring transparency to homeowners associations for condo and townhome buyers. As Butler put it, "So what Uplift Group is, well, we're building the Carfax of condos" [02:46].

q: Why can buying a condo with an HOA be risky?
a: Laura Butler explains that buyers take on obligations and restrictions, yet HOA details are hard to get before making an offer. The first place she almost bought, she learned, "was just about to have a really big special assessment because they need to replace the windows" [06:19].

q: What was Uplift's MVP for HOA resale reviews?
a: It was a report reviewing the HOA material a buyer receives, with added help answering questions and meeting with customers. Butler said, "So our MVP is really output as a PDF" [11:53], and noted that having a human available gives buyers peace of mind.

q: What is the hardest technical problem in analyzing HOA documents?
a: Laura Butler had hoped to automate the analysis and save human time for judgment, but many documents are unsearchable scans. She found that "optical character recognition is actually like our single biggest" [21:59] problem.

q: What advice does Laura Butler give new entrepreneurs?
a: Butler advises founders to dig into why the problem matters to them and to others, and who needs it solved, without getting tied to one implementation. In her words, "the why is more important than the how or the what" [46:02].

s5-bonus-engineering-an-infinite-runway-anthony-castrio-on-bootstrapping-indie-worldwide

Shrink the Room: Anthony Castrio found people usually feel better about events where they get to talk, and more than eight in a room leaves some silent. He used Zoom breakout rooms and aims for groups as small as one-on-ones.

A Half-Hour MVP: Indie Worldwide began as an RSVP page and a Zoom link, set up in about half an hour, plus another half hour for a graphic. For about a year, Anthony's goal was to make one improvement each month.

Members Signaled Willingness to Pay: Founders Club began as a free weekly one-on-one matching service. After a few people said they'd pay, Anthony began charging, and it has since grown to roughly 70 or 80 paid users.
Challenges Drove Growth: The 100 in 100 challenge, to get 100 new paying users in 100 days, brought in sponsors. Anthony calls challenges the community's biggest marketing win by far.
Pick a Sustainable Pace: Burnout led to a few months of downtime and a near relaunch. Anthony now builds up slowly, and recently pushed back a finale event and the next challenge after getting sick.

q: What is Indie Worldwide?
a: Indie Worldwide is a community, mostly on Slack, that Anthony Castrio founded for indie founders, who are often solo, technical and not raising money. Anthony describes its members as "people trying to bootstrap their startups" [02:37]. It runs live events twice a month, along with a podcast, YouTube videos and challenges.

q: Why did Anthony Castrio start Indie Worldwide?
a: Anthony was freelancing as a digital nomad and starting in-person indie hacker meetups in new cities. He explained, "every time I moved I'd lose my friend group that I'd made over the last few months" [04:19]. He took the meetup virtual, beginning with a monthly Zoom call.

q: How do you keep people engaged at online community events?
a: Anthony's approach is to give everyone a chance to talk by using breakout rooms and one-on-ones. As he put it, the goal is often "how do I shrink the group size as much as possible" [06:43]. He said people came out of the smaller groups with a positive attitude.

q: How does Indie Worldwide make money?
a: Anthony said about 90% of what the community does is free, with revenue coming from the paid Founders Club and from sponsors. At the time of the interview he had not quit freelancing, but said the last couple of months had "been ramen profitable, paying my fairly low bills here in Mexico" [10:46].

q: What mistake did Anthony Castrio make while building his community?
a: Anthony said he may have tried to do too much at once, burned out, and had to almost relaunch the community after a few months of downtime. His fix, he said, was that "the solution was just pick a pace that I can sustain" [15:48] and increase it slowly over time.

s5-bonus-slashing-the-cloud-bill-in-half-automated-kubernetes-optimization-with-leon-kuperman-of-castai

Automate, Don't Just Recommend: CAST AI focuses narrowly on Kubernetes, where the rules are clearly defined, and automatically rebalances workloads for cost and performance within guidance set by the customer.
Work Backwards to the MVP: The team began with a high-level vision of the user journey instead of code, then extracted the smallest valuable piece: an autoscaler that took costs into account.

Pivot From Multi-Cloud: CAST AI first built its own multi-cloud Kubernetes, but found most customers weren't ready. It pivoted to optimizing inside the services they already used, starting with Amazon EKS.
Show Savings in Seconds: A one-line script installs a read-only agent that reports cluster waste and how CAST AI would configure it differently. Kuperman called this hook the eureka moment.

Engineers Own Production: With no QA or DevOps team, engineers test, deploy and take on-call rotations. New hires ship code on day one, and every production change must be reversible within 30 minutes.

q: What does CAST AI do to reduce cloud costs?
a: CAST AI optimizes customers' Kubernetes environments for cost and performance by rebalancing and reorchestrating workloads. Leon Kuperman said nobody wants to act on recommendations manually, so "everything that we do has to be a fully automated or autonomous approach" [03:26].

q: Why does CAST AI focus on Kubernetes?
a: Leon Kuperman expects the vast majority of organizations to move to some version of Kubernetes over time. Its clearly defined rules also let CAST AI act on changes instead of only suggesting them, because as he explained, "Everything is defined in the K8s world" [04:37].
