q: Why did CAST AI pivot away from multi-cloud Kubernetes?
a: Kuperman said customers liked the cost management and resource reallocation features, but many weren't ready for multi-cloud high availability or to trust a startup with their control plane. The team decided that "we're going to meet customers where they run Kubernetes" [21:20], beginning with Amazon EKS.

q: How does CAST AI show value to new users quickly?
a: A one-line script creates a read-only agent that reports the waste in a Kubernetes cluster within a few seconds. Kuperman advises anyone building a SaaS tool that "you've got to have that early engagement" [22:44] that gives prospects a sense of value very early.

q: How does CAST AI release to production so often without taking on too much risk?
a: Kuperman argues that small, frequent changes are less risky than large batches because their likely impact is smaller and rollback is easy. The team's rule is that it must be able "to roll back any change within 30 minutes" [32:41].

s5-e20-building-an-ai-inside-sales-agent-that-passes-the-human-test-with-nate-joens-of-structurely

Validate Before Building: Nate, not a software engineer, stitched together chatbot builder Maya and messaging tool Smooch, then demoed the rudimentary MVP to realtors and at two major real estate conferences to gather feedback.

Build General, Market Specifically: Structurely built its product around real estate terminology, then had to generalize every part of it. Nate estimates a general framework from day one would have saved at least six months of debt work.

PaaS Changed Distribution: Integration partners asked to white label and resell the product, leading to an API that is purely the conversational AI engine. Selling into CRMs and lead gen tools also helps lock competitors out.

Don't Hack the First Deal: The first PaaS customer got a hacked-together API without enough discovery or scoping, and Structurely is still paying for it. Nate now urges deliberate discovery and trying to get customers to pay upfront.

Integration-First Market Expansion: Rather than chasing each industry's niche CRMs, Structurely is targeting big platforms like HubSpot and Salesforce that cut across markets, while Zapier connects it with many CRMs and lead gen tools.

q: What does Structurely do?
a: Structurely is a conversational AI company that texts and emails leads, then holds two-way conversations to qualify them, set appointments or move them to longer-term nurture. As Nate Joens put it, "We follow up, qualify, and nurture leads of all sorts, basically." [02:21]

q: How was the first Structurely MVP built?
a: Nate Joens built the first version himself with chatbot builders, including Maya, plus Smooch for Twilio and live chat integration. His goal was to answer, "can I prove this idea with an MVP and validate that someone finds it useful" [05:49] without spending a bunch of resources.

q: How is Structurely different from a typical chatbot?
a: Nate Joens contrasts it with button-based bots that get confused when someone says the wrong thing. He said "the big differentiation between us and just like a typical chatbot is just having a human-like conversation." [19:03] A script customization builder also lets customers tweak what the AI says.

q: What is Structurely's platform as a service (PaaS) offering?
a: It is an API that lets technology partners send in a lead and its message, and get back a response plus extracted data inside their own product. Nate Joens described it as essentially "our conversational AI engine as a service, nothing else." [12:06]

q: What would Nate Joens do differently if he started Structurely again?
a: He would avoid tying the product and its positioning so tightly to specific industries, which now leads some prospects to think it isn't for them. Nate Joens recalled advice from a local dev shop that when "you're building a product, build generally and market specifically." [09:23]

s5-bonus-scaling-to-100m-arr-the-product-evolution-of-callrail-with-ryan-johnson

Concept Car Roadmapping: Founders feared a published roadmap would be set in stone, so Ryan pitched an aspirational "concept car" that wouldn't be built exactly to spec. The team time-boxed 30 days to explore it, then chipped the list down to an MVP.
Phased Path to Paid: The first alpha took about a quarter, followed by a month or two of feedback, then a beta and a paid MVP. All in, it was roughly six to nine months.

Protect UX, Cut Features: CallRail's DNA is user experience, so the team didn't cut refinement. It trimmed to what customers needed to succeed, making many cuts to form building because the data mattered most.

Three Sources Shape the Roadmap: Ryan estimated 30-50% came from product and engineering, 25% from direct customer feedback and 20-25% from go-to-market teams. A 12-month view narrows to quarterly commitments.

Platform Growth Exposes Seams: Moving from a single product to a platform meant rethinking things like buried settings. Growing from 100 to 300 people also showed where old ways of working no longer held together.

q: How does CallRail's call tracking work?
a: Ryan Johnson explained that CallRail provides unique phone numbers, for example on a billboard or dynamically swapped on a website, that route to the business's own phone. As he put it, "because we have that unique phone number that you called and I called, they can attribute, oh, Noah came from Google." [04:47]

q: Why was CallRail started?
a: Ryan said co-founder Andy ran a directory listing for European automotive shops and couldn't tell whether the listings were producing leads. The existing products were clunky and built for enterprise, and Ryan recounted Andy's goal: "I need to make something affordable for small, medium businesses and the agencies that support them." [05:34]

q: What is the concept car approach to product roadmaps?
a: Ryan used the automotive concept car to help leaders explore an ambitious vision without feeling committed to building all of it. He recalled that "it resonated with them. And I said, I want to build a concept car." [09:38]

q: How did CallRail decide what to cut from its form tracking MVP?
a: Ryan said the team defined what success looked like and kept the features customers needed to get there, without sacrificing user experience. It made many cuts to form building, where countless templates and customizations already existed elsewhere, and Ryan said, "We weren't gonna win that game, nor were we trying to" [16:47].

q: What would Ryan Johnson do differently at CallRail?
a: Ryan said CallRail's bootstrapped, profitability-minded roots made it conservative about spending, even after raising money. Adam recalls someone advising him, "You should just spin this out, make it its own product and connect it to everything" [07:09].

q: What did the GetEmails MVP look like?
a: Adam Robinson says it began as a tab on the Robly website with text, a video and a Google form, and the pixel was sent to interested testers by email. He admits it was "so crude and nasty in the form that we got our first round of beta testers on it" [11:15]. The goal was to get people using it as quickly as possible.

q: What would Adam Robinson do differently on SaaS pricing?
a: Adam Robinson would move to higher-priced SaaS sooner rather than pitching a discount to customers poached from other vendors. In his experience it is easier to "sell a thousand, $2,000 a month guy than a $15 a month guy" [24:56], and he notes that higher-priced SaaS compounds.

s5-bonus-eliminating-the-security-deposit-scaling-a-1b-proptech-disruptor-with-paraag-sarva-of-rhino

Insurance Instead of Cash: Rhino's flagship policy replaces the cash security deposit, often a month's rent or more. On a $2,000 rental, a renter can pay as little as $8 to $12 a month instead of $2,000 up front.

Critical Path Before Fundraising: The founders bootstrapped for about a year, identifying insurance partners and first customers. After raising capital, they built the product front to back in about 90 days, with first transactions in August 2017.
Digital Front, Manual Back: Rhino prioritized a fully digital renter flow that sells a policy in under a minute. Much of the back-end process was handled by a robust manual effort.

Renters Drive the Market: Emotional emails from early renters showed Sarva it was a mistake to see Rhino mainly as a services business for real estate. The company reoriented around renters' experience and value.

Scaling Through COVID Uncertainty: Rhino expected a crushing summer 2020 leasing season, then hesitated to invest as the pandemic hit. Volume still multiplied before the company was set up for scale, and the team muscled through.

q: How does Rhino replace a security deposit?
a: Rhino offers renters a security deposit insurance policy in place of a cash deposit at move-in. Paraag Sarva explained that they "replaced that $2,000 deposit with a security deposit insurance policy that costs as little as $8, $10, or maybe $12" [03:22] per month.

q: How long did it take to build Rhino's MVP?
a: After about a year of groundwork, the team had a 90-day dash from roughly May to late August 2017, with CTO Brian Woods as the only full-time engineer, managing offshore freelancers. Paraag Sarva said that was when "we built an entire product experience from front to back" [08:55].

q: What trade-offs did Rhino make in its early product?
a: Rhino focused on a nearly instant, fully digital experience for renters and left parts of the back end to be iterated on later. For work further back in the process, Paraag Sarva said, "we built a pretty robust manual effort to address" [12:04] it.

q: What mistake did Rhino's founders make early on?
a: Renters' stories about what the cash savings meant to them changed how Paraag Sarva saw the company. He said, "we had made a mistake in thinking about the business and as really like a services business for the real estate market" [28:06].

q: What is the renter's choice law?
a: Paraag Sarva described it as a law passed in Cincinnati and Atlanta that gives renters alternatives to a lump-sum cash deposit, such as paying in installments or buying insurance. In his words, "it's called the renter's choice law, which gives renters options at move-in" [26:00].

s5-e15-fighting-a-400b-food-waste-problem-with-ai-matt-schwartz-of-afresh

Built for Fresh, Not Barcodes: Matt says most, if not all, food industry technology was built for packaged goods. Afresh started with store-level produce ordering, deciding how much each store should get every day to cut waste and maximize grocer profit.

A Google Sheet MVP: Without permission for a full integration, Afresh put AI order recommendations in a Google Sheet that store managers keyed into their system. It showed the team how critical that last human step is.

Enterprise Reliability From Day One: Grocers handed Afresh the keys to produce ordering, so a bad order was not an option. Matt says the team deployed every customer on time, with no outages that affected orders.

Scale Changes in Kind: At almost 250 stores and about $1.5 billion of produce ordered yearly, Afresh was aiming for 3,000-plus stores that year, which required rethinking parts of its infrastructure and data platform.

Commercial Hires Came Late: Afresh invested heavily in technical talent first. Matt wishes they had brought on sales and marketing leaders sooner, saying the delay cost them the chance to grow even faster.

q: What problem is Afresh trying to solve in fresh food?
a: Matt Schwartz says fresh, perishable food was underserved by technology, leading to inefficiencies that cause food waste and lost profit. In his words, most of the industry's technology "was built for stuff that comes in a package" [02:33].

q: What does Afresh do?
a: Afresh's first product is a store-level ordering tool that helps grocers order the right amount of produce for every store each day. Matt describes the larger goal as "building the brain of the fresh food industry" [03:07], powering critical decisions from the farm to the consumer.

q: How did Afresh build its first MVP?
a: The team found a grocer willing to let them work with its data and processes, then built a lean AI model in a matter of weeks. Matt explained, "we actually created a Google Sheet in which these recommendations would show up" [07:46], and store managers entered the orders into their own system.

q: How much food waste has Afresh prevented?
a: Matt says the team compared customers' waste year over year at chain-wide scale and applied ReFED's methodology to estimate environmental impact. He reported that "we prevented almost 5 million pounds of food waste" [00:13], and added that the company had since far exceeded those numbers.

q: What advice does Matt Schwartz give early-stage founders?
a: Matt urges founders to confirm they have, or are building toward, product-market fit before pouring time into a product nobody wants. He believes that whatever you are building, "there are super lean approaches to making an MVP and validating your hypotheses" [29:36].

96df38e3-25b0-4ab9-a3ff-4dfe92b97d3c
s5-bonus-the-two-suitcase-minimalist-who-built-a-global-storage-empire-with-cody-candee-of-bounce

Prototype in a Couple Hours: Bounce began as a website offering bag pickup by phone, plus some AdWords. A call came within 30 minutes, and about a dozen customers showed people would hand their bags to strangers from the internet.

Dropping Delivery Altogether: Testing local depots revealed that people were willing to drop off and pick up in the same location. That allowed a lower price, removed logistics entirely, and led to an MVP that went from first code to production in about a month.

Replacing Manual Work With Code: Cody once called the store and customer around every booking. Switching from an hourly timer to per-day pricing and adding common FAQs to customer emails let transactions run without him.

Small Business Sales Differ: Cody says an early mistake was missing how unlike enterprise sales it is. Adding stores takes a high-volume machine of processes, calls, emails and reps with targets, which affects who you hire.

Build Distribution Into Product: Cody started out focused on building the best product and finding users afterward. He would now tie user acquisition in from the start, noting that channels like SEO influence product decisions in many ways.

q: What is Bounce and how does it work?
a: Bounce, founded by Cody Candee, offers luggage storage and package acceptance inside local businesses, which earn extra revenue and foot traffic. Cody explained, "bounce is a network of local businesses all around the world mainly in big cities" [02:25].

q: How did Cody Candee validate the idea for Bounce?
a: Cody built a prototype in a couple of hours, bought some AdWords and fulfilled early pickups using city bikes. He recalled, "We made a website that said, we'll come and pick up your bags and just call this phone number." [06:08]

q: Why did Bounce move from luggage delivery to in-store storage?
a: Picking up and delivering bags was time intensive, and Cody didn't think the economics of hiring a delivery network would work. After testing local depots showed people would drop off and pick up at the same spot, he realized "we don't have to deal with logistics and delivery at all" [09:33].

q: How did the pandemic affect Bounce?
a: Cody said Bounce lost all of its revenue when travel stopped, and experiments were deferred because there wasn't enough traffic to test them. Speaking in June 2021, he said "we have recovered fully from the pandemic and are growing faster than we've ever grown before" [21:59].

q: What advice does Cody Candee have for early-stage founders?
a: Cody warns against waiting for perfection and a long list of features before launching, and says customer insight is underrated. In his words, "you just have to get your product in front of customers as fast as possible." [26:15]

s5-bonus-fixing-broken-developer-workflows-how-a-hack-day-built-shortcut-formerly-clubhouse-with-andrew-childs

Hack Day Origin Story: After a move from Pivotal Tracker to Jira frustrated the team, Andrew Childs built a Trello-like, multi-project Kanban board on Pivotal's API. The engineering team moved back to Pivotal to use it.

Speed as Secret Weapon: Shortcut's MVP loaded almost all data up front and kept it in memory, knowing it wouldn't scale. It made the product extremely fast, but years later the team still grapples with that choice for large customers.

The Cost of Custom Frameworks: Childs wrote a lightweight custom framework for stability and control. As the team grew, engineers needed findable answers and transferable skills, and Shortcut has been moving to React.

Duplication Over Premature Abstraction: Shortcut tolerated duplicated code to keep bugs isolated and let pages evolve independently. The trade-off was inconsistent design and UI from page to page, which the team is now addressing.
Make Backlog Ratios Explicit: Childs advocates separate backlogs for features, debt and bugs, with a defined ratio of effort among them. He admits this is still aspirational at Shortcut.

q: How did Shortcut get started?
a: Andrew Childs's team at his previous company had moved from Pivotal Tracker to Jira and struggled with it, so he used a hackathon to build an alternative. As Childs put it, "I took it upon myself to build effectively like a Trello-y UI on top of the Pivotal Tracker" [05:42]. He and Kurt later saw an opportunity to build their own API, left the company and started Shortcut.

q: How did Shortcut make its product so fast?
a: The original product loaded almost all of a customer's data up front and held it in memory, so everything after the initial page load felt basically instant. Childs said, "I think that the speed of it was like kind of our secret weapon and still is." [09:51] The approach has been harder to manage as customers have grown to hundreds of thousands of stories.

q: Why did Shortcut move from a custom front-end framework to React?
a: Childs built a custom, lightweight framework so the team could focus on user experience and optimize deeply, but it became a drawback as more engineers joined. He explained that "nobody wants to work on a one of a kind kind of framework" [12:15]. Engineers also need to be able to find solutions to problems, and Shortcut has been moving to React.

q: Why did Shortcut allow duplicated code?
a: Childs saw duplication as easy to fix later, while shared components can cause regression bugs and make engineers afraid to change code. In his words, "when you deduplicate code, you're creating a hard problem." [21:13] The downside was inconsistency in design and UI across pages, which the team is working to improve.

q: What advice does Andrew Childs have for founders building a new product?
a: Childs advises caring more about the user experience than your own developer experience or using the newest technology. "Nobody uses a product because of the tech stack" [29:10], he said. He recommends solving somebody's problem really well, even if there is only one user to start.

s5-e14-taking-on-calendly-how-derrick-reimer-built-savvycal-to-win-an-indescribably-crowded-market

Scheduling Without the Anxiety: Reimer saw that scheduling links can wreck a maker's calendar and feel like pushing work onto others. SavvyCal aims to protect time and make booking feel collaborative.

Tight MVP, Built to Last: Work began around March 2020, with first customers in June or July. Reimer focused on a calendar-like interface and Google Calendar, while building a foundation he wouldn't have to throw away.

Practical Over Pure Technology: An Elm front end slowed his previous product, Level. For SavvyCal he chose Elixir, React and Tailwind, server-rendering simple pages and using React where heavy interactivity was needed.

Learn Before the Big Launch: Reimer invited waitlist users gradually, adding more when learning slowed. He opened signups in early September and waited until January for Product Hunt, which delivered a solid base of MRR.

Nimbleness Against Incumbents: Reimer argues larger players struggle to change products that hundreds of thousands rely on. A startup can serve a niche's neglected concerns and should aim for a five to 10x improvement.

q: What problem does SavvyCal solve with scheduling links?
a: SavvyCal is a scheduling tool that lets you send a link showing when you're available, then puts an invite on everyone's calendar. Derrick Reimer wanted to ease the worry of exposing his calendar, saying "I always had a ton of anxiety when I was going to use a scheduling tool" [04:27]. He also wanted booking to feel more collaborative for the recipient.

q: Why did Derrick Reimer build SavvyCal in Elixir?
a: Reimer sees Elixir as keeping the good parts of Ruby while adding a functional paradigm built on Erlang. In his words, "it's just inherently more performant and built for like parallelism and high scale" [07:55]. At the time of the interview, he said SavvyCal still ran on a single Heroku dyno.

q: How does SavvyCal plan to compete with Calendly?
a: Reimer believes established companies become harder to steer and innovate as they grow, which gives a nimble newcomer an opening. Reimer's view is that a startup should "give a five to 10 X improvement over what the incumbents are doing" [20:30]. His focus is on offering power-user features in an interface that is hopefully even friendlier than simpler tools.

q: How did SavvyCal get its early users and growth?
a: Reimer built a launch list through a landing page and Twitter, invited people gradually, and later launched on Product Hunt. Each scheduling link also carries SavvyCal branding, and as Reimer put it, "So sort of has this viral loop component built in" [14:22].

q: What did Derrick Reimer learn from his failed Slack competitor, Level?
a: Reimer had customer conversations and even took pre-sales, then spent many months building the first version. When it was ready, he said, "I could really not, not convince anyone to actually adopt it on their team" [33:16]. He learned how hard it is to get unbiased feedback from supportive people, and recommends the book The Mom Test.

s5-bonus-from-art-to-a-salesforce-acquisition-the-troops-story-with-greg-ratner

No-Code Concierge MVP: Sales reps texted CRM updates to a Twilio number managed in Front, and Troops staff logged into Salesforce to enter them. It couldn't scale securely, but it shipped in days and tested demand.

Nothing Is Precious: Creating a new category meant shipping rough experiments, gathering feedback fast and scrapping what failed. People who were very precious about their creations didn't do well at Troops.
A Slow, Selective Early Team: Hiring six people took almost a year, with hundreds of phone screens by Ratner. He wanted strong, entrepreneurial engineers and says he'd do it again 10 times out of 10.

The Costly Big Bet: A collaborative deal product took an engineering team over 10 months to ship, plus months of polish, and won only a handful of customers. Ratner owned the flop and recommitted to starting small.

Scale When It Matters: Troops didn't build for scalability up front, since whole product lines got scrapped. As the product matured, buying bigger Amazon instances often bought time to fix efficiency properly.

q: What does Troops.ai do?
a: Greg Ratner explains that Troops connects to systems such as Salesforce, HubSpot and Zendesk, detects data changes and suggests next steps in Slack or Microsoft Teams. In his words, "we're able to notify the person who needs to know" [04:16].

q: How did Troops build its first MVP?
a: Ratner says the first version required no code, connecting a Twilio number to Front while Troops staff made Salesforce updates behind the scenes. "we just had sales reps at the time text this number whenever they needed to make a CRM update" [06:48], he recalls.

q: How did Troops hire its early engineering team?
a: Ratner says the founders refused to compromise on talent, looking for people who were technically strong, entrepreneurial and willing to throw out work that failed. The process was slow and painful: "it took almost a year to hire six people" [15:12].

q: What was a major product mistake Troops made?
a: Ratner points to a large bet on a collaborative product for working on opportunities and deals, which drifted from the company's MVP approach and ultimately flopped. He says "it took an entire engineering team offline for over 10 months to bring this product to market" [24:59].

q: Did Troops build for scalability from day one?
a: No. Greg Ratner says early investment in scale would have delayed time to market, especially since entire product lines were sometimes scrapped, so "we definitely did not build in scalability out of the gates" [17:27].

s5-e13-building-a-1b-saas-unicorn-from-a-boring-niche-with-andrew-butt-of-enable

Problem Found Firsthand: Andrew Butt and co-founder Dennis Short saw the problem inside Short's UK distribution business, where trading agreements and incentives were core to management and held much of the margin.

From Custom Builds to SaaS: Enable first built custom software for one company at a time on Microsoft SQL Server and .NET. The SaaS MVP came later, a core engine shaped closely with one big US customer and one big UK customer.

Scale Exposed Performance Limits: Some huge customers were a great feature fit, but loading hundreds of millions of transaction lines caused performance problems. Enable had to refactor and rebuild key parts of the system as volume grew.

A Niche With Network Effects: Enable focused on distributors and retailers of physical goods, including construction products. Distributors then wanted suppliers on the platform, and those manufacturers asked to use it themselves.

Say No More Often: Butt says being pulled by individual customers' requests cost time during the several years it took to reach product-market fit. Being more ruthless would have meant turning away revenue but getting there faster.

q: What does Enable do?
a: Andrew Butt describes Enable as a software platform where distributors, retailers and manufacturers create trading agreements and incentives tied to buying and selling. In his words, it is meant "to facilitate kind of trade through the supply chain, getting products" [02:24] from manufacturers to end customers.

q: How did Andrew Butt come up with the idea for Enable?
a: Butt met his co-founder, Dennis Short, through flying school while Short was growing a UK distribution company where trading agreements and incentives were central. Butt said, "we kind of discovered this problem firsthand within his distribution business" [03:20] and then realized how big the need was across the industry.

q: What was Enable's MVP?
a: Early on, the team built custom software company by company and learned what customers required. Butt does not count that as the MVP, saying "the MVP was the genuine SaaS product that we built later" [04:33], a core engine that a couple of companies were using.

q: How did Enable grow from distributors to manufacturers?
a: Enable initially stayed focused on distributors and retailers receiving agreements and incentives from manufacturers. Butt explained that "we found there was a network effect because those distributors were wanting to bring their manufacturers," [07:16] and suppliers onto the platform, and those suppliers then asked to use it themselves.

q: What would Andrew Butt do differently if he started Enable again?
a: Butt would focus more, raise venture capital sooner and relocate to the US sooner. On focus, he said Enable could have reached product-market fit "faster if we'd been more ruthless and it would have been more difficult to fund and more painful" [12:22].

s5-bonus-from-police-officer-to-tech-founder-how-spidr-tech-revolutionized-public-safety-communication-with-rahul-sidhu

Start With One Simple Message: Facing the prospect of running out of money, the team narrowed its product to an automated email or text with basic information for people who had a police report filed. SPIDR Tech grew from there to over 60 agencies in the U.S. and Canada.

Free Pilots Lowered the Risk: Grover Beach and Tucson started unpaid, helping win over a slow, risk-averse market. The first paying customer came about six months after the first free deployment, and Rahul says they never had to give the product away again.

Roadmap From Value Overlap: The team looked for where community members' wants overlapped with departments' time and money savings, such as updating 911 callers so they feel less need to call back and tie up lines.

Balance Tech Debt and Scale: Early on, the team built enough features to get customers in the door, then chipped away at scalability. A move from Flynn to Kubernetes took a lot of time, but Rahul says it was the only way they could really scale.

Evolve as a CEO: Rahul admits he micromanaged and didn't trust his team enough as the company grew. It took members of his leadership team sitting him down to change, and he doubts the company would have gotten as far otherwise.

q: What does SPIDR Tech do?
a: SPIDR Tech provides automated customer service communications for public safety agencies, including texts, emails and surveys for people who interact with police. Rahul Sidhu says its main focus is to "help law enforcement agencies improve the services that they provide" [02:30], which ultimately improves public perception.

q: What was SPIDR Tech's first MVP?
a: After realizing the original product probably wouldn't reach market before the money ran out, Rahul and his team chose something much simpler for people who had a police report filed. He described it as "just an automated email or text that goes out to people." [06:09]

q: Why did SPIDR Tech give its product away to early police departments?
a: Rahul explains that government is slow to change and risk averse, so removing the financial risk gave agencies a reason to try a startup. "For us, it wasn't about making immediate cash." [08:24] The goal was to prove the value and then use that success to accelerate real sales.

q: What leadership mistake did Rahul Sidhu make as CEO of SPIDR Tech?
a: Rahul says he didn't evolve fast enough as the company grew and was slow to delegate. In his words, "I didn't trust my team enough. I was still micromanaging more than I really should" [22:09], until members of his leadership team told him how they felt.

q: How should GovTech founders find their first customers?
a: Rahul advises calling as many potential customers as possible to learn which ones will help build the product, instead of spending time on late adopters. He recommends seeking "chief executives that are hungry for innovation and are risk takers" [29:31], like the early partners SPIDR Tech found in Grover Beach and Tucson.

s5-e12-building-tech-for-what-matters-most-with-chris-wexler-of-krunam

Proving Data Access First: Because CSAM is illegal to hold, the MVP had to prove data access and reliable identification. The team worked on site in a Faraday cage at the UK Home Office, with nothing connected to the internet.

Do One Thing Extremely Well: Rather than build a full suite, the team focused on identifying and classifying CSAM, using APIs to plug into existing investigative and content moderation systems and partnering for front ends.

Predators Shaped the Roadmap: The image classifier came first, then video as abuse material shifted that way. Live streaming followed when COVID travel limits pushed offenders toward live-streamed abuse.

Built for Weak Hardware: The original use case was a Windows 95 machine on a detective's desk in Scotland. The product also had to scale to a billion images a day, and ships through Docker for easy integration.

Sell the Solution, Not Tech: Pitching AI teams, who are rewarded for building, proved a hard way in. Traction came from approaching trust and safety, PR and board members about the problem and its risks.

q: What does Krunam do?
a: Krunam is a public benefit corporation whose technology identifies and classifies child sexual abuse material (CSAM) using computer vision and deep learning. Chris Wexler explains why the term "child porn" is avoided: "pornography implies consent, and children just can't consent" [02:39].

q: How is Krunam's CSAM detection different from earlier technology?
a: Wexler says earlier technology could identify perhaps only 5 to 10 percent of what is out there, while Krunam focuses on finding novel images too. Of those earlier tools, he said, "They could only identify what had been found in the past" [05:18].

q: How was the first version of the technology built?
a: It began around 2015 as pro bono work for the UK government by the team behind Vigil AI, now part of the Krunam joint venture. Wexler recalled that "the MVP was dragging their equipment into a Faraday cage at the UK home office" [08:53] to work on the database.

q: How does Krunam handle both old police computers and enterprise scale?
a: The product had to run on very weak law enforcement hardware, yet also handle up to a billion images a day without disrupting workflows. Wexler said that "we had to build it so it worked efficiently" [24:02], and Docker lets customers plug it into their systems quickly.

q: What sales mistake did Krunam make early on?
a: The company first approached AI teams, whose incentives favor building tools over buying them, before finding other ways in through trust and safety, PR and boards. As Wexler put it, "instead of selling the solution, we were selling the technology" [27:02].

s5-bonus-productizing-an-engineering-nightmare-turning-integration-debt-into-an-api-powerhouse-with-brendan-wood-of-passiv

Automate Your Own Tedium: Passiv began as a 50-line Python script Brendan Wood wrote over a weekend to rebalance his own ETF portfolio. It cut an hour or two of monthly work to about 15 seconds, and friends wanted it too.

Manual Entry Fell Flat: An early public version had no accounts or broker link and saw little use over about six months. That pushed the team to build user accounts and brokerage integrations that pull portfolio data automatically.

Permission Was the Hard Part: One-click trades weren't mainly a technical challenge. Getting the broker, users and Canadian regulators comfortable with how trade orders would work took about six months.

Rewrite Sooner, Not Later: Data models built around one broker forced a full backend rewrite to support Alpaca, the second broker. It took about a year, and Wood argues waiting would have meant re-implementing even more.

Hire for Learning Rate: Wood's main hiring test is how quickly someone can pick up new skills from zero, because startup roles change fast. Interviews and code tests are designed around that, not existing expertise.

q: What is Passiv and how did it get started?
a: Passiv is software that helps self-directed investors manage and rebalance investments in their own brokerage accounts, which Brendan Wood likens to a do-it-yourself robo-advisor. It grew from a personal script, which he described as "a 50-line Python script that I wrote for myself over a weekend, just out of frustration" [05:10].

q: Why didn't the first public version of Passiv catch on?
a: It had no user accounts or broker connection, so people had to type in their portfolios themselves, and hardly anyone used it. Brendan Wood said it left him asking, "is it really that much better than a spreadsheet if you still have to manually type in your assets?" [08:24].

q: What was the hardest part of building one-click trades?
a: According to Brendan Wood, the code was not the main obstacle, since the team also had to satisfy brokers and securities regulators. He explained that "The hard part was getting permission from the broker to have a trade integration on thousands" [10:33] of customer accounts.

q: Why did Passiv rewrite its app from top to bottom?
a: The original app was never designed for more than one broker, so adding Alpaca meant rebuilding the backend to be flexible enough for essentially any broker. Brendan Wood noted that "all of our data models are built around this one broker's data model" [16:47].

q: Why is the Passiv team exploring a developer API for trading?
a: The team had to build its own brokerage integrations with trading, and now wants to let other fintech companies use that technology to help their users place trades. Brendan Wood said "there's no off-the-shelf thing you can buy that gives trading integrations to brokers" [28:46].

s5-e11-breaking-the-integration-bottleneck-engineering-seamless-workflow-automation-with-alexander-alimovs-of-automationsio

Automation for Non-Technical Teams: Automations.io lets business users visually map processes linking third-party apps, employees and AI without code or APIs, much as Wix and Squarespace opened up website building.

Cut What Isn't Core: The MVP took six to nine months, which Alimovs now thinks was too long. He dropped extra CRM contact management features because they distracted from getting to market, and they still haven't been built.

Batteries-Included for Velocity: As a solo founder, Alimovs favors tools that work out of the box over assembling his own stack, so he can focus on the product instead of picking routers or testing frameworks.
Serverless Does the Heavy Lifting: A Dockerized Node.js API on Kubernetes acts as the control plane for defining automations, while AWS Lambda, SQS and similar services handle execution at scale.

Sell Sooner, Code Less: Alimovs says his growth focus should have started about six months earlier. He now spends 99% of his time on growth and customers, coding only in response to their requests and feedback.

q: What is Automations.io?
a: Automations.io is a platform founded by Alexander Alimovs that helps companies automate repetitive work through visual, process-map style automations. Alimovs compares it to website builders, taking "the same mindset where we want to allow non-technical people to automate the business processes" [04:24].

q: How is Automations.io built to scale?
a: Alimovs describes a single page application, a Dockerized Node.js API on a Kubernetes cluster, and AWS serverless services that run the automations. As he explained, "if you run your automation a million times a day, there'll be a million Lambdas running" [15:35].

q: How can non-technical users add AI to a business process without code?
a: Alimovs gave the example of a French company that wanted to detect the language of inbound emails and reply with the matching template, using a visual if statement. He said users don't need to know "what is an API or machine learning they just get this canvas and then suddenly they can visually" [21:08] plug AI into their process.

q: How do you decide which features to cut from an MVP?
a: Alimovs advises identifying the core of your product, building it, and involving customers or potential customers as soon as possible. He cut additional CRM contact management features after realizing "it wasn't core to the product and it was distracting from getting the product to the market" [07:44].

q: How can early-stage founders get customer feedback and first customers?
a: Alimovs searched LinkedIn for relevant experts and asked for their thoughts on what he was building, and some of those people later became customers. He said, "People love when they're approached for advice and they love to share their knowledge." [23:35]

s5-bonus-goodbye-waiting-for-builds-engineering-instant-preview-environments-with-colin-chartier-of-webappio-formerly-layer-ci

Hibernation Powered the MVP: The first tech demo abused hibernation to copy an already set-up environment, so each developer's change could be evaluated without rerunning setup. A push to GitHub created the environment automatically.

Ship Requests the Same Day: With a two-week roadmap horizon, Colin would build, test and ship an early paying customer's request the day it was asked, then get feedback while it was still top of mind.

Fundamentals Beat Keyword Resumes: Colin found hiring for experience gave only marginal benefits after six months. The team tested developers on core computer science, such as graphs, operating systems and syscalls, rather than screening for Go and React.

Spending Innovation Tokens Carefully: The team spent its innovation tokens on Go, chosen for being boring with few language features, and Kubernetes. Running Kubernetes on developer laptops keeps local development close to production.

Sell to the Developer's Pain: Months went into pitching staging servers for product people and designers, but developers treated it as a chore. What mattered most was how developers interact with other developers during code review.

q: What does LayerCI (now Webapp.io) do?
a: It helps software developers review changes proposed by other developers, so they can try the product and check that nothing has broken. Colin Chartier explained that "LayerCI essentially gives developers an environment that has everything set up with this new change." [02:56]

q: How was the first version of LayerCI built?
a: Colin Chartier describes the MVP as more of a tech demo, run on free servers and offered to friends in open source. It relied on copying hibernated machines, or as he put it, "abusing the hibernation feature to create multiple copies of everything." [05:37]

q: Why did LayerCI run Kubernetes on developer laptops?
a: Colin Chartier said it makes local and production environments so similar that code working locally is almost guaranteed to work in production. He acknowledged the choice is a little unusual for a startup, "but it really bakes scalability into the development experience." [14:43]

q: What did Colin Chartier look for when hiring developers?
a: He looked for strong fundamentals, past experience and base skills more than matching technology keywords. Drawing on his time as a CTO, Colin said that after "six months, hiring for experience only gave you very marginal benefits." [11:56]

q: What advice does Colin Chartier give B2B startup founders?
a: Colin Chartier recommends landing paying customers early, even through many rejections, and then iterating quickly with them. He said the "advice I tell everyone that asks is get customers as soon as possible" [25:06].

s5-e10-from-the-dorm-room-to-deep-learning-scaling-ai-product-architecture-with-slater-victoroff-of-indico

Accessibility Over Novelty: Indico's first MVP offered ML models such as sentiment analysis as simple API calls for developers. The market didn't want that product, and Indico's focus now is making complex ML usable by non-technical users, primarily on documents.

Write the Readme First: Indico uses readme-driven development, inspired by Python's requests library. Defining the interface first often exposes the real bottlenecks, so engineers don't spend effort being clever where it may not matter.

Documents Are a Hard Abstraction: A document is image and text data, and each use case can call for a different format. Slater says each improvement to that abstraction is like a major product revision, with three shots at it in seven years.

Keep Product Surface Area Small: An advisor's analogy says the best products are like spheres, with minimum surface area and maximum volume. Every shipped feature must be maintained, and that growing "wake" can kill a company.

Trust Your Gut Over Pedigree: Slater says trusting credentials over his own judgment nearly ended Indico, costing months, maybe years, on consumer-style ideas. He removed some advisors, and later moved from CEO to CTO when Tom came in as CEO.

q: What does Indico do?
a: Indico is an intelligent process automation company that applies complex machine learning primarily to documents, which combine image and text data. Slater Victoroff describes the goal as the "idea of how do we take that technology and make it accessible specifically to non-technical users." [02:57]

q: What is readme-driven development and how does Indico use it?
a: It is a design approach where you write the readme, and so define the interface, before working out how to implement it. Slater Victoroff explains, "You start by writing your readme. You say, okay, what's the interface that I want to use to control" [08:48] whatever you are building.

q: How should founders think about product scalability for an AI product?
a: Slater Victoroff says the product and delivery model must scale from day one, rather than relying on custom features for every customer. He rejects the idea that solving many specific problems will reveal a generic solution, saying it "doesn't work like that you have to build the general solution first right and then test your" [21:21] solution on specific cases.

q: What was the biggest mistake Indico made in its early years?
a: Slater Victoroff says he took advice from people who didn't understand what Indico was building, which led the team to chase consumer-style app ideas. He calls it probably one of the things that brought Indico closest to not existing, explaining that he trusted "people's credentials over my own gut feeling and over my own expertise in the space." [23:47]

q: What does Indico look for when hiring engineers?
a: Slater Victoroff watches for people who overcomplicate problems and values candidates who are open about not being experts and willing to be trained. On favoring simplicity, he said, "when there is the simple solution, identifying that and going for that, that's a huge, huge, huge advantage." [16:17]

s5-bonus-killing-tool-sprawl-how-jody-shapiro-built-productiv-to-solve-the-enterprise-saas-nightmare
SaaS Sprawl Lacked Data: CIOs struggled to say what they spent, who bought which app and why. Some were gathering answers through surveys and spreadsheets as purchasing spread into business units.
Value Over Minimal: Shapiro's team treats the V in MVP as "valuable," aiming to understand the problem, reach a useful solution quickly and maximize what he calls learning ROI.

Enterprise Design Partners Early: Productiv built with design partners resembling its target enterprise customers, whose security, scale and complexity needs differ sharply from a 200-person company's.
Intentional Early Hiring: The founders defined culture and values before hiring. About five months in, a recruiting funnel of over a thousand people had yielded roughly eight hires.
Design for Future Scale: Drawing on experience at Google, Amazon, Microsoft and eBay, the founders avoided hacks that wouldn't scale. The system now streams in billions of data points in real time.

q: What problem does Productiv solve for enterprise IT teams?
a: Productiv takes a data-driven approach to managing a company's SaaS portfolio, an area where Jody Shapiro found CIOs struggling with spend, ownership and overlapping tools. Describing their questions, he said "It's hard to understand what do we have in the portfolio?" [05:51].

q: How did Jody Shapiro come up with the idea for Productiv?
a: Shapiro left Google to start a company without knowing which one, then talked to CIOs, CFOs and CTOs to find a big, widespread problem. He saw that IT needed the kind of data marketers already had, recalling that "I was coming from the Google Analytics world" [07:15].

q: How did Productiv build its MVP?
a: Shapiro's team focused on understanding the problem first and leaned heavily on design partners who represented future enterprise customers. As Shapiro put it, "the goal is, how do I get to a valuable solution as quickly as I can" [09:20].

q: How did Productiv approach scalability?
a: Shapiro said the founders designed from the start for growth of 100x or 1000x, while continuing to re-architect parts of the system as needed. Explaining the load, he said "We're literally bringing in billions and billions of data points in real time" [24:48].

q: What advice does Jody Shapiro give early-stage entrepreneurs?
a: Shapiro encourages founders to balance conviction with a reality check by evaluating the market, the solution and the team as an investor would. He suggests asking, "if somebody else was doing it, would you invest in it?" [37:31].

s5-bonus-the-future-of-the-sdlc-eliminating-technical-debt-with-no-code-architecture-with-ken-gavranovic-of-unqork

Building Blocks Over Custom Code: Unqork lets enterprises drag and drop enterprise-grade components to solve a business problem, with the aim of a repeatable solution free of the maintenance and debt that come with writing code.

Define Success Before Building: Gavranovic asks teams to state the customer's business problem and how success will be objectively measured. If they can't articulate both, it's usually not worth starting.

Look Past the Requested Feature: A customer may ask for one specific integration when the real need is flexible integration. Probing for the business problem shapes the roadmap, alongside a product vision that's vetted with customers.

Single-Tenant by Design: Unqork gives each customer its own database and instances, so data isn't commingled. The platform was designed from day one for highly regulated industries that need security and reliability.

Observability Is More Than Tools: Scaling starts with defining a great customer experience through SLIs and SLOs. What matters is how you instrument systems and set error budgets per team, service or experience.

q: What is Unqork and how does it help eliminate technical debt?
a: Ken Gavranovic, Unqork's head of engineering, describes it as a no-code platform where enterprises drag and drop enterprise-grade building blocks to create applications. The reasoning starts with the cost of custom code, because as he puts it, "the second you write code, you've got maintenance." [02:57]

q: How much faster can enterprises build applications with Unqork?
a: Gavranovic says Unqork sees customers "going three to six times faster" [06:21] from a delivery perspective, measured from idea to production. He adds that some deploy in months what might otherwise have taken years.

q: How does Unqork keep customer data secure in regulated industries?
a: Unqork uses single-tenant SaaS, so each customer has its own database and instances, which Gavranovic says are highly available by design. He explains that this approach "allows you to make sure that your customer's data, again, these are highly secure systems, is not commingled" [14:29] with anyone else's.

q: Will no-code replace traditional software development?
a: Not entirely, according to Gavranovic, who says, "it's not that all software is going to be built with no code" [19:45]. He expects a large set of enterprise software to be built that way and to make development accessible to more people with a developer mindset, though he doesn't believe in the citizen developer concept.

q: How should product teams balance customer feedback with their product vision?
a: Gavranovic advises digging into the business problem behind each request while still keeping a vision for where the product is going. In his words, "you listen to the customers, but you don't do exactly what they say." [11:03]

s5-e9-the-science-of-changing-minds-valerie-coffmans-journey-architecting-swayables-analytics-engine

Prove the Core Question First: A $5,000 pilot testing seven or eight clips ran on Mechanical Turk, a one-off Jupyter notebook and flat files. To the team's surprise, it detected statistically significant shifts in opinion.

Focus on the Money Page: During Y Combinator in early 2018, Swayable hacked together survey setup and logins, using Auth0 for authentication, and put its energy into data collection, analysis and the results dashboard.

Internal Tooling Became the Debt: Survey designs were reviewed with clients in a Google Doc template, then translated into the system, early on as JSON files. Coffman says deferring internal tooling and self-service was the biggest trade-off.

Benchmarks Give Results Meaning: Customers could see an ad moved people 7.8 points but not whether that was good. After thousands of tests, Swayable added benchmarks that rank results against similar tests.
Complexity Scaled Inside Each Test: More content, metrics and segments multiplied calculations and output. Results eventually hit MongoDB's 16 MB document limit, forcing a schema revision.

q: What is Swayable and how does it measure whether an ad is persuasive?
a: Swayable is a data science platform that measures the persuasive impact of advertisements, and Valerie Coffman is its CTO and co-founder. She explained, "We use randomized control trial survey experiments to rigorously measure how an advertisement" [02:28] changes someone's opinions on its topic.

q: How did Swayable validate its idea with a first prototype?
a: An agency building ads about climate change paid for a pilot, and Coffman analyzed the Mechanical Turk survey data in a one-off Jupyter notebook. Of that first client, she said "they paid us $5,000 to test seven or eight different" [04:07] clips.

q: What did Swayable prioritize when building its MVP?
a: The team hacked together survey creation and logins so it could focus on data collection, analysis and the front end, especially the results page. Coffman said, "The money page, the real thing that's most important where the customers are getting all of their value is the dashboard" [06:34].

q: How does Swayable help customers tell whether their ad test results are good?
a: Coffman said customers could see baseline scores and how far an ad moved people, but didn't know what the numbers meant. After building up thousands of tests, Swayable could offer what are "called benchmarks, which basically show how you rank compared to similar tests." [12:51]

q: What scaling problem did Swayable run into with MongoDB?
a: As tests added more content, metrics and segments, the volume of aggregate results grew well beyond what the team had foreseen. Coffman noted that storing results as before "doesn't work in Mongo if your results are larger than 16 megabytes." [18:13] The team hit that document size limit and revised the schema.

s5-bonus-stop-building-features-nobody-wants-mastering-jobs-to-be-done-with-jay-haynes-of-thrv
Define Markets by the Job: Customers hire a product to get a job done, such as creating a mood with music. Records, CDs and streaming all serve that same job, giving product teams a stable target.

Minimum Valuable, Not Viable: Haynes swaps minimum viable product for minimum valuable product. Working software isn't enough; it has to satisfy unmet needs well enough that people will pay or switch.

Let Customer Effort Set Priorities: THRV builds its roadmap on quantitative customer effort scores. Where customers struggle most is where to focus, replacing heated debate and the highest paid person's opinion.

Teach the Method Inside Tool: Separating the course from the app was a mistake THRV has been working to fix. The goal is for teams, even those new to Jobs to be Done, to learn while using the software.
Hire Process and Metric Thinkers: For its Jobs to be Done product team, THRV looks for process-oriented, metric-driven people, since a job is essentially a set of customer needs that can be measured.

q: What is the Jobs-to-be-Done framework?
a: Jay Haynes describes it as the idea that customers aren't really buying your product but using it to accomplish a goal. In his words, "What they're doing is hiring it to get a job done" [02:53]. THRV builds its enterprise product management software around this method.

q: What is a minimum valuable product, and how is it different from an MVP?
a: Haynes argues that "viable" is the wrong standard, because a product can work and still give no one a reason to pay or switch. As he puts it, "It doesn't matter that your product is viable, but is it valuable?" [00:28]. THRV's first minimum valuable product was a way to see insights into customers, markets and competitors.

q: Why did the Microsoft Zune fail, according to Jobs-to-be-Done?
a: Haynes says the Zune worked but didn't satisfy any unmet needs in the customer's job, while Microsoft defined its market around the iPod. Pandora launched around the same time and grew quickly, and Haynes said, "there were clearly unmet needs in the market that Pandora was satisfying" [05:34].

q: How do you prioritize a product roadmap using Jobs-to-be-Done?
a: Haynes recommends gathering quantitative data on where the market is underserved, including customer effort scores, which he says research shows predict success better than satisfaction or Net Promoter Scores. He explains that "when people struggle to get a job done, that's when they're willing to pay for something new" [15:12].

q: What advice does Jay Haynes give early-stage entrepreneurs?
a: Haynes says the biggest mistake he sees is founders talking about their widget instead of why it matters to the customer. His advice: "be able to explain the customer value of your product" [29:13]. That means explaining the customer, their struggle and how you help them overcome it.

s5-e8-eliminating-the-deploy-sweat-building-world-class-cicd-with-marko-anastasov-of-semaphore

Speed Through Bare Metal: Semaphore went against the cloud computing trend and ran users' workflows on bare metal hardware. Marko calls this the primary reason it has been the fastest product in its space.
A Deliberately Narrow MVP: Rather than support every language and workflow, the team covered only Ruby on Rails web apps. The goal was that it should just work, with setup in about five clicks.
Duct Tape Behind the Scenes: Early users saw only a spinner, not job output, while the team manually watched almost every workflow and restarted servers to keep the unstable backend running.

Protect Product Wholeness: A large company's partnership led Semaphore to build a big, poorly integrated feature for a marketplace that flopped. Some plans stalled for maybe six months, teaching a lesson in focus.

Rebuilding to Escape Dead Ends: In late 2018, Semaphore changed course and built a new product, Semaphore 2.0, because the original design couldn't run many applications and workflows and customers could outgrow it.

q: Why was Semaphore created?
a: Marko Anastasov and his team at the web development consultancy Rendered Text needed a fast, simple way to test and integrate code, and the state of the art meant running Jenkins on your own server. Marko recalled that "it took me three days to set up one project" [04:28].

q: How did Semaphore make its CI/CD platform so fast?
a: The team made speed an early priority so developers would get feedback as soon as possible. Instead of following the cloud computing trend, Marko said they chose to "actually run our users workflows on bare metal hardware" [06:41].

q: What did the Semaphore MVP include?
a: The MVP was built mainly with Ruby on Rails, relied on GitHub's API for code change notifications, and supported only Ruby on Rails web applications. Marko said that to set up continuous testing, "it should take you like maybe five clicks" [08:35].

q: What mistake did Semaphore make with a large company partnership?
a: The team pulled people off other projects to build a large feature for a big company's new marketplace, which flopped when that company changed priorities. Marko took from it that "it's a lesson of focus and kind of staying on your track" [21:46].

q: Why did Semaphore build Semaphore 2.0?
a: The original product, now called Semaphore Classic, was not capable of running many types of applications and workflows, and the team wanted to grow with its customers. Marko said the aim was a fast, simple tool and "something that no organization can really outgrow" [23:06].

s5-bonus-the-death-of-the-resume-building-science-backed-hiring-tech-with-josh-millet-of-criteria

Resumes Send Weak Signals: Millet says experience and education do correlate with performance, but not nearly as strongly as cognitive ability and conscientiousness, which Criteria's assessments focus on.
Usability as the Edge: Facing old-line assessment publishers that weren't tech companies, Criteria bet on software that SMBs could adopt with minimal training, while trying not to dilute the science.

A Lean Nine-Month MVP: The platform took about nine months to build, with a four-person team and one engineer, Wayne, now CTO. It launched with just a few assessments, within six months of a 2008 hiring freeze.
Price With Evidence: Despite being data-driven, Criteria didn't examine pricing rigorously and chronically underpriced its product. Millet now advocates having one person whose only job is pricing.

Segment Before Moving Upmarket: Enterprise is now about half the business, but Millet wishes they had segmented customers earlier instead of relying on intuition and anecdotal feedback from bigger accounts.

q: What is Criteria and what does it do?
a: Criteria is a talent decision platform that offers software, assessments and structured interviewing tools to help companies make better hiring decisions and remove bias. Josh Millet, its CEO and co-founder, said "we help them do their hiring, do their talent acquisition in a more science-based, more evidence-based way" [02:36].

q: What predicts job performance better than a resume?
a: Josh Millet says experience and education are helpful but weaker signals than traits Criteria's assessments measure, citing decades of organizational psychology research. In his words, "cognitive ability is one of the best predictors and conscientiousness is a really good predictor" [11:44].

q: How was Criteria's first product built?
a: The original platform took about nine months and launched as a pretty minimal product with just a few assessments. Millet recalled, "There were four of us in the beginning and only one engineer, a guy named Wayne" [04:49], who has since served as CTO.

q: What pricing mistake did Criteria make?
a: Millet says the company didn't study pricing in as evidence-based a way as it should have, despite being very data driven. As he put it, "we kind of chronically underpriced our product for a long time" [17:05].

q: What advice does Josh Millet have for founders as their company scales?
a: Millet says CEOs will need to hand off different areas over time, but should stay actively involved in product, even with a strong Chief Product Officer in place. His view is that "product should be the last thing you let go of" [23:52].

s5-e7-fixing-the-broken-developer-onboarding-process-with-kristen-buchanan-founder-of-edify

Fake the Bot First: Before writing code, Edify prototyped in Figma and Botsociety, then had Jamie pose as a bot in a customer's Slack for two weeks. The test showed that engineers will interact with a bot and can enjoy it if it's well designed.

Cut Deep to Ship: Product lead Jamie erased about 85% of Kristen's feature list to fit a self-imposed three-month deadline. The half-code, half-flow MVP took about three and a half months and reached beta customers in August 2020.

Build the Core, Buy Around: Edify chose to build its defensible core and buy integrations. Low-code FlowXO got a first version out, but the team later outgrew it and needed to bring core functionality in-house.

Kill Onboarding Friction: The MVP asked engineering managers to complete a roughly 70-question SurveyMonkey survey to generate a plan. It took far longer than expected, so replacing it with a web UI was the first post-launch change.

Vet New Platforms Hard: Moving to NLX, a newer tool, without enough research contributed to Edify missing the public launch timeline it had shared with investors and beta customers, planned for right after Q1.

q: What is Edify and what does its Eddie bot do?
a: Edify is an AI platform for engineering teams, and its first product, Eddie, is a bot that deploys team-specific technical onboarding plans to new hires. Kristen Buchanan explained that Eddie supports each hire "for their first 30 days, giving them tasks, activities," [02:57] along with people to meet and daily check-ins.

q: How did Edify test its onboarding bot before building it?
a: Kristen Buchanan's team first shared a no-code Botsociety prototype with customers, then ran a two-week experiment inside an early customer's Slack. As Kristen described it, "we actually pretended to have Jamie be a bot" [09:03], which gave them real data on whether new hires would respond.

q: How did Edify decide what to build versus buy for its MVP?
a: Kristen Buchanan separated the defensible part of the product from the integrations and the way it functions outside that core. Referencing Twilio founder Jeff Lawson's book, she said "we chose to build the core functionality of our" [12:49] product and buy the rest.

q: What did Edify change after getting feedback on its MVP?
a: The first fix was ingest, the process that collects information from an engineering manager so Eddie can build an onboarding plan. Kristen Buchanan said "we had them complete basically a 70 question SurveyMonkey survey" [15:12], which proved full of friction and was eventually replaced with a web UI.

q: What would Kristen Buchanan do differently if she started Edify again?
a: Kristen would have moved faster instead of spending about a month and a half to two months worrying over which contractors to work with. She wishes they had simply hired "a couple of code school grads and started working, to be honest." [33:46] Her reasoning is that shipping sooner means learning from customers sooner.

s5-bonus-building-a-modern-tech-beacon-scaling-architecture-and-engineering-leadership-with-angel-munoz

Gaming as the Blueprint: Munoz applied game-design thinking to video calls, focusing on aspect ratio, color saturation, sound and resolution. The goal is to make you feel you're in the same room as the other person.

Adapt to Every Device: The team spent seven to eight months trying to give everyone an equal experience, while phones overheated and computers rebooted. Beacon now adjusts bit rate, resolution and other settings to each device.
From 70% Failures to Under 5%: During a year of beta testing, 70% of calls failed in the first seven months. An early test with 10 people on robust gaming PCs crashed seven of the machines.

Forking Beyond Standard WebRTC: Beacon began on WebRTC, the open-source video standard, but couldn't scale the quality the team wanted. They forked it to build a more vivid experience, with up to 4K resolution.

Hiring Through Community: Munoz says the team has never had to hunt for hires. People came through chance online encounters, including its G-Tribe network, and the company measures results rather than hours.

q: What is Beacon and how is it different from other video conferencing platforms?
a: Beacon is a browser-based audio-visual communication platform that Angel Munoz describes as heavily informed by video games, with an emphasis on quality, simplicity and speed. Describing its purpose, Munoz said "You want to teleport the person, your mind into the person's reality." [03:51]

q: How does Beacon deliver high-quality video on different devices?
a: Beacon detects the device it is running on and adapts the experience, so users with powerful hardware such as gaming PCs get a richer result. Munoz explained, "So the compromise that we had to make came down to bit rates." [13:48] Resolution and a list of smaller settings are adjusted too.

q: What was the biggest technical challenge in building Beacon?
a: Reliability was a major struggle during the year-long beta, when 70% of calls failed over the first seven months. Referring to cutting that failure rate, Angel Munoz said, "To get that down to less than 5% was the main job." [15:41]

q: How does Beacon handle call encryption?
a: Munoz says Beacon uses insertable streams, a technology developed by Google, which allows a server to sit in the middle of a call without decrypting it. As he put it, the call passes through a "server between the call and it stays encrypted on the server." [06:50]

q: How much does Beacon cost?
a: At the time of the interview, Munoz said the free Beacon X offered unlimited time, with Beacon Plus ($4.95 a month, up to 25 people) and Beacon Max ($14.95 a month, up to 100) as paid tiers, Plus due in a few months. Of the free version, he said "you only can have up to six people on a call. That's the only limitation." [25:51]

s5-e6-streaming-video-from-the-edge-how-raven-built-a-real-time-telematics-platform-with-braden-stenning

Near-Zero Operator Effort: Raven moved to a tablet with a very lightweight UX where operators make quick taps. Guided by lean manufacturing, the team gave up some full context because typing into a screen is rarely value-added work.

Scale the Product First: Raven planned from the start to serve both single-process operators and executives overseeing 100 plants. Technical scalability was left as an option in the architecture and added when monitoring showed limits.

Rethinking the Stack: The team moved much of its data pipeline from Python to Elixir. Stenning also says they drifted into more microservices than necessary, leaving a small team with thin coverage, and have been simplifying.

Blame the System: When mistakes happen, such as deploying the wrong software or deleting a node, the team solves the problem without judgment. A failure causes inquiry then looks at the system, not the individual.
Beyond the Factory Floor: Stenning cites customers going from single-digit effectiveness to the high 70s in under 18 months. A variation of Raven is also now installed in a hospital operating room.

q: What does Raven do for manufacturers?
a: Raven helps manufacturers and the people who work there use their time more productively by showing where losses happen and how to avoid them. Braden Stenning says it helps them understand what happened and "get a record, the truth of what it was" [02:39].

q: How did Raven design its user experience for shop floor operators?
a: After engagement and UX problems with the initial product, Raven moved to a tablet attached to the process with a very lightweight interface. Stenning explained, "we really wanted to have almost no effort on the operator's part, which meant just quick" [10:30] taps, even though that did not necessarily capture full context.

q: Did Raven build its platform to scale from day one?
a: Stenning says product scale was considered from the beginning, while technical scale was not always implemented right away. The team chose extensible, flexible architecture, and as he put it, "we would try to leave ourselves the options" [17:29].

q: Why did Raven move its data pipeline to Elixir?
a: The shift came over the last couple of years, with performance issues and developer joy among the considerations Stenning raised. He noted that Python remains important, saying "It's still a big part of our back end, but we've moved a lot of our data pipeline to Elixir" [27:24].

q: How does Raven's team handle mistakes and outages?
a: Stenning says the team focuses on solving the problem without judgment, then runs a failure causes inquiry to go through what happened and make the system more robust. The guiding idea is "we're part of a system here and it's not the individuals, it is the system" [21:31].

s5-bonus-from-software-engineer-to-ceo-how-silk-sonder-built-a-high-retention-wellness-app-with-meha-agrawal

A Two-Week Paid Test: Meha gave herself two weeks to prototype a guided journal and see if someone would pay a dollar or more, or she would scrap it. The first version used a local printer found on Yelp, a friend's design help and user feedback.

Facebook Group as Product Test: A Facebook group tested whether analog journal users would engage digitally. They used it to share and support one another, which informed the mobile app and shaped the decision to become a VC-backed business.

Cut to the Core Behavior: To move members off Facebook, the app focused on posting, comments and replies and left other social features for later. It still had to look polished, because a janky app could hurt the established brand.

Android Couldn't Wait: Launching iOS first left Android members feeling hurt and forced the team to downplay the release. Waitlist signals had been there, so they accelerated Android and kept the Facebook group running while they built it.

Roadmaps Beyond Analytics: Meha pairs product-market fit surveys, interviews, polls and usage data, then stack ranks features by effort and impact. Each feature must solve a user problem and tie to a business goal such as growth or retention.

q: What is Silk and Sonder?
a: Meha Agrawal explains that "Silk and Sonder is a self-care membership for modern women" [02:44]. Members get a monthly guided planner and journal, a mobile app with the Sonder Club social network, and access to Sonder Circles guided journaling sessions and audio content.

q: How did Meha Agrawal come up with the idea for Silk and Sonder?
a: While working as a software engineer at Stitch Fix, Meha felt anxious, stressed and underfulfilled, and began adding structure to an empty journal. She described "thinking about what I was grateful for, writing it down, thinking about what was making" [05:51] her anxious, and noticed a shift in her emotional health.

q: How was the first Silk and Sonder MVP built?
a: Meha chose pages, got design help from a friend, had the journal printed, gathered user feedback and iterated before putting it on a website. She initially found it "easier to code on Ruby on Rails integrate with Stripe with the Stripe subscription offering" [08:31] than to navigate ready-made tools, though Shopify later proved the right choice.

q: How do you move a community from a Facebook group to your own app?
a: Meha's team looked for the minimum features that would preserve members' familiar behavior, plus something extra to make the app more enjoyable. On the most important activity, Meha said "it was just about posting and responding to posts" [12:46], along with comments and replies.

q: How does Silk and Sonder use product-market fit surveys to plan its roadmap?
a: Meha uses an approach she credits to Superhuman, identifying the best customers as those who would be very disappointed if Silk and Sonder were discontinued. To find gaps to fill with new features, Meha said, "we look at those that are in the somewhat disappointed camp" [17:15].

s5-e5-engineering-high-concurrency-marketplaces-handling-automated-rights-and-music-licensing-with-kirt-debique

Discovery Was the Front Door: SyncFloor spent about a year and a half on deep technology for Natural Language Music Search, which turns creative descriptions into real-time results and explains why each came back so users can iterate.

Build a Platform First: Treating the first product as a platform later let the team build SyncFloor.com, songsforpodcasters.com and embeddable sync stores for label and publisher partners in a reasonably straightforward way.

Seed Supply With a Tool: To tackle the marketplace chicken-and-egg problem, the first target was helping people mine their own catalogs, which could bring their content into the ecosystem before demand arrived.

The One-Stop Reset: Accepting any part of a partner's catalog hurt discovery, access and licensing. With the index nearing 40,000 tracks, the team reset it and curated only one-stop music, where rights sit with a single entity.

Scale in Repeatable Units: A stateless architecture lets SyncFloor treat a pod of data and execution as a set of cloud boxes it can replicate for more capacity, while keeping the actual setup simple for its current stage.

q: What is SyncFloor?
a: SyncFloor is a platform and marketplace for licensing commercial independent music for film, TV, ads, podcasts, games and more. Kirt Debique, its co-founder, CEO and CTO, describes it as "a platform for connecting all sorts of people, websites, services, applications" [02:36] into that music corpus.

q: What problem does SyncFloor solve in sync licensing?
a: Kirt Debique saw that independents struggled to find opportunities, while people seeking music faced a manual process of emails, calls and collating results. In his words, "It's really difficult to figure out" [07:17] who is looking for what.

q: How does SyncFloor's Natural Language Music Search work?
a: It interprets a natural creative description, converts it into a taxonomy for search and returns real-time results with an explanation of why they matched. Kirt Debique said that before productizing it, "We spent a good year and a half, you know, on the order of that, working on the sort of deep technology." [09:50]

q: Why did SyncFloor switch to only one-stop music?
a: Music rights span both the composition and the recording, so licensing a track can require approvals from several parties, and including any part of a catalog caused structural problems for users. Kirt Debique recalled the change to one-stop content: "We were closing in, I think, 40,000 tracks in our index." [21:36]

q: How can a new marketplace handle the chicken-and-egg problem?
a: Kirt Debique says startups often begin with supply by offering software that is useful as a tool before there is demand, though he would prefer to attract demand first if he could find a way. On the supply-first approach, he said "you try to figure out ways to get people on the supply side to want to use your thing" [12:26].

s5-bonus-billions-of-connected-devices-how-mapped-built-an-enterprise-iot-data-fabric-with-shaun-cooley
Integration Was the Bottleneck: Cooley saw customers spend a year on an IoT pilot, then redo the integration from scratch at the next factory or refinery. Mapped set out to automate that work.

Hardest Problem First: Mapped began with an edge gateway that uses passive monitoring and active device interrogation to discover what's on a network, then worked up the stack instead of starting with an application.

Connectors Got Shortchanged: The team over-focused on the data pipeline and its security, underinvesting in connectors for cloud-first sensor vendors. It can now add a new connector in a couple of days.
Rebuilding the Graph Core: After many months on an RDF graph database, the team saw it couldn't reach their target scale. They redid queries, permissioning, access control and sharding.
Start Smaller, Ship Sooner: Cooley would begin with one or two connectors and get to market in a month or two. He believes building big first cost a year or more of customer feedback.

q: What is Mapped and what does it do?
a: Mapped is a data infrastructure platform that sits between the raw device network and business applications in commercial and industrial environments. Founder and CEO Shaun Cooley says, "We bring together all the people, places, and things" [02:29].

q: How does Mapped discover devices inside a building or factory?
a: Cooley built an edge gateway that watches network traffic for protocols such as S7, OPC, Modbus and BACnet, and also probes devices directly. He describes "interrogating each individual device on the network to see if it speaks the" [08:21] protocols the system is looking for.

q: Why is it so hard to scale an industrial IoT pilot to other sites?
a: Cooley found that systems installed by different integrators, with different vendors and naming, had no commonality from one site to the next. Integration and data extraction work from a pilot therefore had to be repeated, and as Cooley put it, "It had to be done from scratch because that factory across the street or the refinery" [05:51] shared nothing with the first one.

q: Why did Mapped move away from an RDF graph database?
