q: What advice does Adam Wathan give to founders and developers building something new?
a: Adam advises sharing your work long before it is finished, since teaching others how you solve problems is a powerful form of marketing. He sums it up like this: "distill it down into like one thing, it's basically like work in public" [37:06].

s3-e8-designing-for-product-led-growth-the-tech-and-ux-behind-userlist-with-jane-portman

Polish Before Beta: Userlist, built on Rails, took a year or more to reach beta and began actively onboarding after about a year and a half, because a faulty automated email could damage customers' reputations.

Simplicity Means Saying No: Userlist offered one basic but polished email template and limited customization, despite requests for visual builders and rich content. The team focused on helping users send nice-looking email at the right time.

Shaping Replaces the Roadmap: Borrowing from Basecamp's Shape Up, the team keeps two or three important features being shaped on a board and picks the next one after finishing current work. Feature ideas are documented in Notion.

Email Delivery Takes Negotiation: Userlist chose SparkPost to deliver email, then spent time negotiating sending limits and rates to fit its customer base. Portman flags this as something to consider if you build an email service provider.

Funding for Braver Bets: TinySeed funding gave the team salary runway while staying bootstrapped in spirit. Userlist had also just launched a $9 plan, its equivalent of a free plan, and was already seeing better traction.

q: What is Userlist and who is it for?
a: Userlist is a tool for behavior-triggered email and in-app messages, focused on users and what happens after they sign up. Jane Portman said the idea was to "build a relatively simple, relatively affordable tool for small to medium-sized SaaS companies" [03:12].

q: Why did Userlist take so long to launch its MVP?
a: Jane Portman explained that the automation engine was complex, and the team also wanted compliance paperwork, templates and help docs in place. The stakes were high "because our customers' reputations on the line, if they send something wrong, that's going to hurt" [05:29].

q: How does Userlist use the Shape Up method?
a: Portman said the team borrowed parts of Basecamp's method rather than all of it, mainly the practice of defining a feature's design, time budget and limits up front. In her words, "The idea is that features before being built, they need to be shaped." [11:02]

q: What is challenging about building an email automation platform?
a: Jane Portman pointed to choosing a delivery provider, which led Userlist to SparkPost, and then arranging limits suited to a company of its size. "Like sending limits are a big thing." [15:24]

q: What advice does Jane Portman give new SaaS founders?
a: Portman passes on advice from Alex Yumashev of Jitbit: "the wisdom of that advice is to start products in existing product categories that" [23:55] have a good market. She also advises founders to be consistent, keep shipping in line with their values and settle in for a long journey.

s3-bonus-eliminating-the-aws-surprise-bill-how-cloudforecast-fixes-cloud-waste-with-tony-chan

Reports Instead of Dashboards: CloudForecast chose not to replicate competitors' fancy dashboards, focusing on proactive daily, weekly and monthly AWS cost reports sent to engineers by email and Slack.

A Scrappy Six-Month MVP: Built on nights and weekends, the MVP took about six months, including validation. It used Rails, Mailgun and AWS, and Chan, a non-developer, built the first front end with Bootstrap.

Ask About Their Day-to-Day: Showing people finished features created false positivity. The team now asks how they handle cost monitoring, and hearing the same story three or four times signals what to build.

Distribution Was a Costly Mistake: The team spent time on a channel that wasn't driving leads, traffic or conversions. Chan wishes they had learned SEO and persona-fit channels sooner, and they now question and iterate faster.

Audience Before Product: Francois and Chan quit their jobs at the end of 2018 and went a year without salary, then spent 2019 building an audience. Chan wonders about building it first, but doesn't regret going full time.

q: What does CloudForecast do?
a: CloudForecast is a B2B SaaS product that sends AWS cost reports to engineers by email and Slack and alerts them to anomalies and significant increases. Tony Chan says it helps companies monitor costs and "eliminate wasted AWS costs through just easy-to-understand daily reports for engineers" [02:45].

q: How can startups avoid a surprise AWS bill?
a: Tony Chan's approach is proactive reporting that flags cost anomalies and significant increases before the end-of-month invoice arrives. Chan says the goal is to be quick and simple, "alerting them of any significant increases so they can catch it right away" [03:20].

q: Why doesn't CloudForecast focus on dashboards like its competitors?
a: Tony Chan says the pain point is saving engineering time, and engineers often don't want another tool. The team's biggest trade-off was "not building those fancy dashboards, not building those beautiful UI and whatnot" [09:48], in favor of email and Slack reporting.

q: How was the CloudForecast MVP built?
a: It took about six months of nights and weekends, using Rails, Mailgun and AWS services such as Lambda and EC2, with feedback from the founders' network. Tony Chan recalls that "our first version was just very, very hacky" [07:38].

q: How does CloudForecast decide what to build next?
a: Tony Chan says the roadmap is driven by customer conversations about day-to-day problems, plus a yearly product survey. Chan explains that "if we hear the same story three or four times over" [14:45], that points to the product or feature the team should be working on.

s3-e7-disrupting-higher-ed-the-tech-stack-and-growth-playbook-of-unibuddy-with-kimeshan-naidoo

Selling Before Building: Unibuddy began pitching universities with a PowerPoint design months before the product existed. Their feedback shaped the spec, and the three-part MVP then took about two to three months to build.

Speed-First MVP Stack: The team chose a Python GraphQL monolith, React, MongoDB and Heroku to move fast. Naidoo says that, knowing today's traffic and reliability demands, they would probably make some of those choices differently.

Microservices for Team Independence: The monolith worked for 5 to 10 engineers, but at around 20 it caused deployment bottlenecks and unclear code ownership. That pushed Unibuddy to start extracting services its product squads can own.

Lockdown Exposed Technical Debt: Traffic rose 1,000% in lockdown, revealing gaps in infrastructure, testing and reliability. The team shifted its focus from speed and innovation toward quality, reliability and customers.
Budget for Infrastructure Early: Naidoo advises starting with at least a 1:5 ratio of infrastructure to product engineers. Unibuddy was at 1:10 and was moving to grow its infrastructure capacity.

q: What is Unibuddy and how does it work?
a: Unibuddy lets prospective students chat online with current students at a university to help them decide where and what to study. Co-founder and CTO Kimeshan Naidoo described the first version as "a platform that is embedded on a college's or university's website" [03:27].

q: What tech stack was used to build the Unibuddy MVP?
a: The MVP used a React front end, a Python GraphQL backend and MongoDB, with the backend on Heroku and the client apps on AWS CloudFront and S3. Naidoo recalled, "It was a single monolithic API. At that point, it was just me and one engineer." [04:48]

q: Why did Unibuddy move from a monolith to microservices?
a: As the engineering team reached 15 to 20 people, a shared repository and deployment pipeline left engineers waiting on each other. Naidoo said the first trigger was "to help the team become more effective and help them become more independent" [13:21].

q: How did lockdown affect Unibuddy's infrastructure?
a: Naidoo said that after focusing on speed for about two and a half years, the team had neglected infrastructure and technical debt. In lockdown, "our traffic increased by a thousand percent. And all of a sudden we realized we didn't have" [16:40] the infrastructure, testing or reliability measures to handle it.

q: Which service should a startup separate from its monolith first?
a: Naidoo cautions against starting with microservices because a new startup doesn't yet know where its service boundaries are. Some are clear early, though, and he said, "the first thing I would decouple is an authentication service." [21:07]

s3-e6-from-immigrant-to-iconic-cto-how-elias-torres-co-founded-drift-built-a-1b-saas-unicorn-and-disrupted-b2b-tech

Earn a Place on Websites: Drift's MVP took about three months and was ugly by Elias's account. It aimed to put enough chat on B2B websites to talk with buyers, not support, testing a need people didn't believe in.

Reuse Platforms, Choose Familiar Tools: The team outsourced as much as it could and built on Java, React, Amazon and containers. Elias picked Java because he already knew it and could move fast, keeping engineers focused on the core problem.

Validate With Money: Drift spent about three quarters proving, in turn, that people would install it, use it to message buyers, and pay for it. Elias prefers early revenue to chasing a million users first.

Don't Prematurely Optimize for Scale: Drift adopted microservices and Terraform early but used integer, not long, database IDs. Elias fixed that after passing four billion objects rather than freezing to architect for scale up front.

Be Patient With Big Hires: Elias says early pressure to put butts in seats led to hiring mistakes that cost time, resources and equity. He now advises raising the bar continually and fixing a bad hire early before it turns the culture toxic.

q: What does Drift do?
a: Drift helps B2B marketing and sales teams meet buyers in real time, through channels such as chat and messaging, at whatever hour the buyer shows up. Elias Torres explained, "we're here to help increase the business effectiveness of go-to-market teams" [04:05].

q: What was Drift's MVP and how long did it take to build?
a: Elias Torres says the first version took about three months and was ugly, with just enough chat to get started. The goal, step one of the Drift master plan, was "to get on B2B websites to chat with buyers, not to chat with support" [04:43].

q: What tech stack was Drift built on?
a: Torres says the backend was Java, the front end used React, and everything ran on Amazon with containers. His advice for the early days is to "Outsource as much as you can," [05:15] so the team can focus on the core problem.

q: How did Drift validate product-market fit?
a: Over about nine months, the team worked on getting people to install Drift, then to message with buyers, and then to pay for it. Torres said, "I'm a big believer that you have to validate it with money and value" [09:25].

q: What would Elias Torres do differently if he started Drift again?
a: Torres would be more disciplined and patient in hiring, having felt pressure early on to grow and fill seats. The line he now repeats to himself "is to say, don't be in a hurry to make a mistake." [23:09]

s3-bonus-the-co-coiner-of-agi-peter-voss-on-building-cognitive-ai-with-long-term-memory-at-aigo

Back to Thinking Machines: Voss argues most AI is narrow, with the intelligence coming from programmers. In 2001, he and two others coined "artificial general intelligence" to signal a return to machines that learn and reason.

Infrastructure Crowded Out Intelligence: At SmartAction, building its own data centers for a SaaS call center product consumed energy and resources. After about five years, Voss exited to start Aigo and get back to raising the system's IQ.

Hiring AI Psychologists: Two-thirds of Aigo's staff are non-programmers, including "AI psychologists" with linguistics and cognitive psychology backgrounds. Voss sees long experience in narrow AI as almost a negative.
Memory and Interactive Learning: Aigo focuses on remembering what users said, even a year earlier, understanding language deeply and learning during conversation, all with sub-second responses.

Deploying in the Customer's Cloud: Instead of SaaS, Aigo gives large companies an image of the "brain" to run behind their firewall. This eases security, redundancy and scaling work, though it only suits firms with their own infrastructure and support teams.

q: Who coined the term artificial general intelligence (AGI)?
a: Peter Voss says he got together with two other people in 2001 to coin it, signaling a return to building thinking machines. In his words, "we coined the term artificial general intelligence, AGI" [05:03]. He describes Aigo's current product as proto-AGI rather than full AGI.

q: How is Aigo different from chatbots like Siri and Alexa?
a: Voss says Aigo is built around memory, deeper language understanding and the ability to learn interactively. He criticized Siri, Alexa and "all of the commercial chatbots from the big companies. They have no memory." [12:01] He also said they rely on pattern matching rather than deep parsing.

q: What is an AI psychologist at Aigo?
a: It is a term Peter Voss invented for staff whose backgrounds are in linguistics and cognitive psychology rather than programming. As he put it, "I call them AI psychologists that understand the brain of the AI" [10:40]. He says two-thirds of Aigo's staff are non-programmers.

q: Is Aigo offered as SaaS or deployed on-premise?
a: Aigo is not offered as SaaS; it is deployed within the customer's own cloud, and Aigo helps with integration. Voss explained that "we actually deploy it behind our customers firewall" [19:01]. He says large companies prefer this because of the potential security holes in SaaS services.

q: What was Peter Voss's biggest mistake as an AI founder?
a: At SmartAction, his first commercial AI company, Voss says his biggest mistake was "not finding the right partners, key staff in the company and compromising on that" [22:54]. The core management team was never strong enough, which left much on his shoulders and made scaling hard.

s3-e5-from-early-app-store-pioneer-to-a-mobile-ai-acquisition-the-nami-ml-story-with-dan-burcaw

Timing the Subscription Ask: Nami ML's original thesis was to score a user's propensity to purchase and prompt an upgrade only when they seemed likely to buy, instead of hitting them with "buy now" messages at every launch.

Privacy Through On-Device ML: The first prototype had to prove a cloud-trained model could run on a phone fast enough to act in the moment without draining the battery. Dan's team did it in about four weeks using open source tools and Apple's Core ML.

Machine Learning Isn't a Product: Proving the technology took weeks, but building a product around it took far longer: about six months to get really positive early feedback, then probably another six to reach something the team was comfortable with.

Three-Queue Roadmap: Each week the team balances work from a vision backlog, a customer feedback backlog and a code quality backlog, so that no single one crowds out long-term goals, customer needs or technical health.

Show It Sooner: Dan says the team talked to many people but was late to actually show the product, partly from wanting perfection. Wider exposure brought new ideas and even new words for describing what the company does.

q: What is Nami ML and what does it do?
a: Nami ML, co-founded by CEO Dan Burcaw and Joe Pizzillo, handles the technical work of in-app subscriptions so developers and brands can focus on pricing and positioning. As Dan describes it, "it's a way to sell subscriptions inside of app experiences" [05:47], whether on Apple, Google Play or other platforms.

q: Why did Dan Burcaw start Nami ML?
a: Dan was bothered by heavy reliance on marketing messages and data selling, and began looking at other ways for apps to make money. App Annie data stood out to him: "fewer than 3,000 apps on the App Store were making more than a million dollars a year" [04:46] from direct consumer revenue.

q: How does Nami ML use machine learning while protecting user privacy?
a: Dan says a core tenet was running the algorithm on the device rather than building massive user profiles in the cloud. The first prototype had to answer, "can we train a model in the cloud, push it down to an app inside of a smartphone" [08:11], and have it run fast enough to affect the experience.

q: How does Nami ML decide what to build next?
a: Dan's team meets weekly to balance vision items, customer-driven requests and code quality work. He describes the process as "pulling items from the vision queue, the customer queue, and the quality queue" [13:48], shifting the mix as urgent items are cleared.

q: What advice does Dan Burcaw give first-time founders?
a: Dan says perseverance matters, but founders also need to make exercise, mental health and time to decompress part of their routine. He admits "it took me three startups to figure out how to operate" [34:54] day to day without putting himself last.

f4cead35-e00f-4b07-9da7-d1cee93c4aa6
s3-e4-building-stripe-for-investing-scaling-alpacas-trading-apis-globally-with-yoshi-yokokawa

Pivot From Models to APIs: Alpaca began by building deep neural net prediction models for trading firms and hedge funds. The struggle to integrate with broker-dealers that had no open API documents led the team to build a stock trading API instead.

A License Before an MVP: To offer stock trading by API, Alpaca had to become a fully licensed broker-dealer, which took about a year, and connect to the market and clearing houses. The backend had to be complete, while mobile apps and polished web interfaces were left out.

Go and Free Hosting Credits: The team built the backend in Go and picked hosting where it had free credits. Heavy spending on backend and compliance forced thrift elsewhere, and the hosting choice later caused painful moments.

Interviews Drove the Roadmap: Yoshi ran about five or six user interviews a day after launch. Users wanted more than buying and selling stocks, so Alpaca quickly added features such as short selling and margin lending.

Volatility Forced a Mindset Shift: Pandemic-era market swings caused spikes in Alpaca's system, requiring quick fixes and upgrades. Over a few weeks, the focus changed from growth alone to making sure operations were stable.

q: What is Alpaca and why did it pivot to a stock trading API?
a: Alpaca offers a U.S. stock trading API and aims to become API infrastructure for financial assets in general. It started with prediction models for financial firms, but Yoshi Yokokawa said, "the pain point actually is at this interface with developers to handle financial assets" [03:27].

q: Why did Alpaca's MVP require a broker-dealer license?
a: Yoshi explained that to build a stock trading API, "we actually had to be a registered, fully licensed broker dealer" [04:00]. The license took about a year, and the team also had to connect to the market and clearing houses before the product could work.

q: What programming language did Alpaca use to build its backend?
a: Performance was a priority, and the team approached the problem from a technology perspective rather than a financial firm's. Yoshi said, "we chose Go as the code for us to build our backend" [05:59].

q: How did Alpaca gather user feedback and decide what to build?
a: The team found potential users through Craigslist, Reddit, Stack Overflow and API product forums, then used Intercom after launch to start conversations and book meetings. Yoshi recalled, "I was doing probably five, six user interviews a day after launching the product" [08:00].

q: How did pandemic market volatility affect Alpaca's platform?
a: Yoshi said the volatility caused spikes in the system, and the team had to move extremely quickly to fix and upgrade it for the increased volume. Stability became a priority, and as he put it, "we actually really changed the mindset over the course of a few weeks" [12:39].

s3-bonus-from-mit-physics-to-deep-tech-founder-the-invention-story-of-looking-glass-factory-with-shawn-frayne

Two Non-Negotiables for the MVP: The Looking Glass had to be genuinely three-dimensional and able to move. That ruled out Pepper's Ghost reflections like the Tupac performance and static laser holography.

Sell the Prototypes: When a prototype excites the team enough, they typically build a few dozen to a hundred and try to sell them, learning about resolution needs, eye strain and whether people need to reach into the light field.

Kickstarter as Proof: A 2018 Kickstarter approached $1 million and put the first-generation display in the hands of thousands of developers, showing that something widely thought impossible was not snake oil.

Hire on What They've Made: Shawn hired a Unity SDK lead after playing his games. A lead mechanical engineer stood out by turning Edison's phonograph sketch into a workable SolidWorks model in a test of about half an hour.

Buy Time for Big Swings: Shawn might have started three years later, when the enabling technology had arrived. He keeps burn rate particularly low to buy time for more experiments until the timing converges.

q: How is a Looking Glass holographic display different from AR and VR headsets?
a: Shawn Frayne contrasts Looking Glass with HoloLens and Oculus, explaining that "our systems don't require you to put something on your head." [06:00] He likens it to gathering around a campfire or radio, where a group can see the same three-dimensional field of light together.

q: Why are commercially viable holographic displays possible now?
a: Shawn points to faster computers, dense high-refresh screens driven by gamers, tablets and phones, and plenty of 3D content stuck on 2D screens. He describes a moment "where computers are fast enough to actually run and calculate full holographic light fields on the fly" [04:40].

q: How did Looking Glass Factory fund and validate its first holographic display?
a: The team sold early laser-cut dev kits to developers, which gave them more confidence in pricing, and then ran a Kickstarter in 2018. Shawn said it "approached a million dollars, and it got thousands of developers to have this first" [14:12] generation holographic display.

q: What is the Looking Glass used for?
a: Developers can build and deploy holographic apps with tools such as Unity, Unreal and Three.js. Shawn also described a partnership with Schrodinger in molecular modeling, where users can view their designs "holographically, which is vital for molecular modelers and others in that industry." [17:02]

q: How does Shawn Frayne hire for Looking Glass Factory?
a: Shawn cares about demonstrated work and passion far more than resumes or colleges. As he put it, "The only things I remember about when we were, when we hire someone is what they've done." [19:54]

s3-e3-building-nature-based-tech-how-wild-ventures-merged-art-code-and-got-featured-by-apple-with-mark-hendriks

No Servers to Run: Wild Ventures delivers Wild Journey's roughly two gigabytes of content through Apple's on-demand resources, avoiding backend upkeep and a potentially large cloud bill when subscription conversion is below 1%.

Cordova Got Them Started: The first two apps, built with Cordova, were featured by Apple and earned meaningful revenue. Background audio, lock screen controls, plugin lag and small interaction delays eventually pushed Mark to Swift.

A Bigger First Version: Mark and his wife spent about a year on Wild Journey's version one, reasoning that an app asking $50 a year needed far more than three landscapes and a design that could expand for years.

Two-Week Release Rhythm: Wild Journey ships every two weeks, with specific plans about six weeks out. Usually one big technical update lands each month and the other release is content only, which helps the founders stay balanced.

Test Every New iOS Release: After a good summer of iOS 13 testing, Mark skipped testing 13.1. An audio problem crashed the meditation apps, bringing one-star reviews and angry emails before a quick fix led most reviewers to raise their ratings.

q: How did Wild Ventures get started?
a: Mark Hendriks, a designer, saw his wife's nature landscape illustrations and thought of using them in an animated weather app, which became Wild Weather. As he recalled, "that would be really cool to use for a wild, in this case, Wild Weather, like a weather application" [02:43].

q: How does Wild Journey deliver its content without a backend?
a: The app uses Apple's on-demand resources, where assets are tagged, uploaded to Apple's servers with each release and retrieved by tag. Hendriks said, "We made sure to use all the infrastructure provided by Apple, so we don't have any service" [08:12].

q: Why did Wild Ventures move from Cordova to Swift?
a: Hendriks found that Cordova depended on available plugins, felt slightly slow and struggled with the app's background audio and timers. On the audio side, he said it "was really hard to do in Cordova. I could not figure out how to keep the app active" [10:41].

q: How does Wild Ventures plan its product roadmap?
a: Hendriks and his wife plan about six weeks ahead in detail, fill two-week release slots with new content and smaller work, and draw on conversations with customers. He explained, "With Wild Journey, we do an update every two weeks." [14:03]

q: What was Mark Hendriks' biggest mistake building his apps?
a: He did not test iOS 13.1 after testing of iOS 13 had gone well over the summer, and an audio problem caused crashes. As Hendriks described it, "it turned out all the meditation apps broke at the same time" [20:01].

s3-e2-the-spotify-acquisition-how-chartable-built-the-ultimate-podcast-analytics-engine-with-dave-zohrob

Speed Before Reliability: Early Chartable accepted broken pages and buttons that led nowhere to get feedback faster. With many customers now relying on it, the team has to balance speed with reliability.

Borrowing From the App Store: Dave Zohrob saw podcasting's once-a-day download numbers and underdeveloped infrastructure as parallel to early iPhone apps, and pitched Chartable as something like App Annie for podcasts.

Prefix-Powered Analytics: Chartable's prefix sits in a podcast's RSS feed and gets pinged before each download. At the time of the interview it tracked about 750 million downloads a month, over 100 million requests a day.

Microservices Only Where Useful: Data ingestion sources are split into microservices because their uptime and deployment needs differ, while the customer-facing product remains a large Rails monolith.
Own Your Outages: When the prefix went down and the backup plan failed, thousands of podcasts couldn't be downloaded. The team owned up, then built and tested a new backup plan.

q: What is Chartable and who is it for?
a: Chartable is a podcast analytics and attribution service that helps creators, publishers and networks understand and grow their shows. Co-founder and CEO Dave Zohrob also described the advertiser side: "we help advertisers figure out if the ads they're buying on podcasts are actually working." [02:26]

q: How was the Chartable MVP built?
a: Zohrob and his co-founder used technology they already knew, including Rails, wrote a spec, and had a prototype in front of podcasters within weeks. Zohrob said "it was really about building something that people want, not about building something that I thought was cool." [06:01]

q: How does Chartable's analytics prefix track podcast downloads?
a: According to Dave Zohrob, the prefix sits in a podcast's RSS feed, and when an episode is downloaded, "our server gets a ping first." [14:28] Chartable uses that to count downloads and help podcasters measure their marketing spend.

q: How did Chartable respond when its service went down?
a: Zohrob said the service in front of downloads had gone down completely twice, and the last time a cloud provider failed and so did the backup plan. The team then built and tested a new backup, and Zohrob explained, "we just really tried to be as transparent as possible with our customers" [17:33].

q: What does Chartable look for when hiring engineers?
a: Dave Zohrob values raw talent, self-motivation and the ability to learn over a great resume. As he put it, "I'm much more concerned with somebody's ability to learn and to want to do better" [11:42].

s3-bonus-disrupting-logistics-how-outrider-built-an-autonomous-yard-management-empire-with-andrew-smith

Three-Part Minimum Viable Product: Outrider found that automating a truck alone wasn't enough. Its MVP combined cloud-based dispatch software, an autonomous yard truck that connects to and disconnects from trailers, and minimal site infrastructure.

Narrow the Problem First: The team began on a narrowly defined section of one customer's yard, with simple moves, very slow speeds and minimal perception requirements. Smith says to pick a tractable problem where you can be exponentially better.

Spend Your Time on Team: Smith says he spent 10% of his time on team at his first company and aimed for 90% at Outrider. Within about 60 days of meeting a veteran robotics group, 12 autonomous vehicle engineers had joined.

Constraints Drive Scalable Design: Smith has engineers first design with cost ignored, then rework the idea under a limit such as less than $10,000. Outrider also considered from day one how customers could easily scale the system across a yard.

Traction Can Strain Teams: Smith admits that early momentum led to saying yes to too many projects and customer requests. People who had been delivering perfectly became overburdened, and his lesson is to grow fast but keep your eye on the ball.

q: What does Outrider do?
a: Outrider, founded by Andrew Smith, automates distribution yard operations, where yard trucks shuffle semi-trailers between parking spots and dock doors. Smith describes it as a company whose "sole focus has been the automation of distribution yard operations" [02:14], using an electric, zero-emission autonomous system to improve efficiency, safety and sustainability.

q: What was included in Outrider's MVP?
a: Andrew Smith says the MVP had three pieces: management software for dispatching, an autonomous vehicle that can hitch and unhitch trailers, and minimal site infrastructure. As he put it, "you couldn't just automate a truck and throw it in a yard" [06:24].

q: How does Outrider's autonomous yard system work?
a: On-site dispatchers use cloud-based management software to tell vehicles to move trailers. The trucks make real-time driving decisions themselves, and Smith explains that on the vehicles "we have sensor and compute hardware so that that vehicle can be" [07:51] responsive to its environment.

q: How did Andrew Smith build Outrider's early engineering team?
a: Smith searched in California, Texas and Colorado before being introduced to people who had founded the robotics company PercepTek, which Lockheed Martin acquired. He says that "within about 60 days, we had 12 of the best autonomous vehicle engineers in the world" [14:24] join Outrider.

q: What advice does Andrew Smith give to new founders?
a: Smith advises founders to work on something they are truly passionate about, which he frames as "rocking chair goals," because passion sustains persistence and grit. He warns that "It's going to take way longer than you think to bring your idea into fruition." [26:57]

s3-e1-building-the-imdb-of-podcasts-solving-audio-discovery-with-cole-raven-of-podchaser

Born From A Reddit Post: A Reddit post asked whether an IMDb-like tool for podcasts existed. The community said no, and developers in Melbourne offered to help build it, aiming to fix poor episode-level discovery.

Invite Keys Sparked Early Growth: Each person who registered for exclusive access got three more keys to share. Over 6,000 people redeemed keys and signed up in the first week, even though the early product was very basic.

Creators As The Growth Engine: Podchaser built creator tools like page claiming early, betting podcasters would bring their listeners. Surveys, with 40-50% response rates, helped prioritize features such as lists.

Hiring For A Founder Mentality: Staying capital efficient, Podchaser used 30-day trials, and probably 20 people didn't make it through, for a team of about eight full-timers. Cole says even 60 days is sometimes too long to act.

API Over A Mobile App: Despite heavy demand for an app, building one would take several hires and shorten runway. Podchaser chose to power other apps with credits, ratings and reviews through its API.

q: What is Podchaser and why is it called the IMDb of podcasts?
a: Podchaser is a podcast discovery platform with ratings, reviews, lists and creator credits. Cole Raven said the original idea started from the fact that "episode-level discovery for podcasts is terrible" [02:17], while tools like IMDb made it easy to judge TV episodes.

q: How was the first version of Podchaser built?
a: The team bootstrapped it on evenings and weekends, with community input from Reddit and Slack. Cole Raven said "it was built on React and PHP and Laravel" [05:31], along with Elasticsearch.

q: How did Podchaser decide which features to build?
a: Cole Raven spoke with hundreds of podcasters, and the team made a large list of potential features and surveyed the community to prioritize them. Cole said the team has always prioritized "just getting something, anything out to the public and getting feedback on it" [07:44].

q: Why doesn't Podchaser have a mobile app?
a: Cole Raven explained that an app would take several hires and significantly reduce the company's runway, though he didn't rule one out for the future. Instead, the focus is on supporting other apps, and as Cole put it, "It's really going to be all about the API." [23:09]

q: What advice does Cole Raven give early-stage entrepreneurs?
a: Cole Raven advises expecting longer timelines and raising far more money than seems necessary, lessons tied partly to running out of cash at a first company. In Cole's words, "Things will always take longer than you expect and raise three times as much money" [30:18].

s2-e20-data-driven-supply-chain-logistics-e-grocery-solutions-with-daniel-gebler-of-picnic

Prove Demand Before Building: Picnic's MVP built only the shopping app and ran everything else on pen and paper or Google Sheets. After an unbranded stealth launch and then PR, demand far outran its few cars, so it created a waiting list.

An App Shaped by Habits: With money for one platform, Picnic chose native iOS and Android. The app mirrors the fridge sticky note, letting shoppers add items as they run low, and past purchases became one of its most used features.

Build What's Mission Critical: Picnic built route planning itself because nothing on the market fit its milkman-style delivery model. It began with off-the-shelf warehouse management, then later insourced that stack to pursue robotic fulfillment.

Self-Learning Delivery Operations: Factors such as a customer's floor, distance from the street and day or night delivery feed stop-time estimates. New operational data improves delivery accuracy day by day without software changes.
Quality Is Not Negotiable: Picnic tracks technical debt and test coverage weekly and won't let quality regress. In talks with business teams, only scope or timeline can flex.

q: How did Picnic build its first MVP for online grocery delivery?
a: Daniel Gebler says Picnic built the consumer shopping app first and handled the rest manually to test whether customers wanted the service. As he put it, "Everything else was a very simple pen and paper or a Google Sheet solution" [03:12].

q: Why did Picnic choose a native mobile app instead of a web shop?
a: Daniel Gebler explains that the team saw web declining and app traffic increasing, and it rejected a hybrid approach in favor of native iOS and Android. Budget forced a choice: "So we had only money for one platform." [05:58]

q: How does Picnic decide whether to build or buy its supply chain software?
a: Daniel Gebler says the team weighs which systems are mission critical and which can come from a third party. Route planning was built in-house because, in his words, "our last mile model, is a unique milkman-based distribution model" [09:31].

q: How does Picnic use data to improve delivery times?
a: Daniel Gebler describes refining each delivery time using observations from previous days' deliveries, accounting for how long each customer stop takes. He said of the improvement, "There's no software change, it's pure feedback" [16:31].

q: What did Picnic learn about managing deadlines and quality in software projects?
a: Daniel Gebler says the team learned to separate hard deadlines from soft ones, since launching in a new country or city comes with fixed commitments. He is firm that "quality is something you can never debate about" [25:20], leaving scope or timeline as the variables to adjust.

s2-e19-saas-payment-integrations-and-hubspot-fintech-extensions-with-denis-lunev-of-depositfix

Charging for a Bare MVP: The first version had no UI, and customers had to write JavaScript to set up a payment form. When clients paid $50 a month for it anyway, Denis saw that it might have big potential.

Plugins Before Core Features: Rather than adding everything to the main product, the team built a plugin system with tweaks for individual clients' payment pages. This let them move quickly and deliver exactly what clients needed.
Dig Beneath Feature Requests: A request for HubSpot deals integration turned out to be about seeing two numbers every week. Emailing those numbers would save the client a lot of time.

Scale on Clear Signals: Slow, unstable payment processing and some downtime appeared about four months in. The team then split the system into modules and used Amazon SQS messaging, which held up for about two years without scale problems.

Communicate Business Logic: A rewrite handed to a skilled TypeScript freelancer was technically good but missed on business logic. Denis learned to explain the problem, the audience, the approach and how features work with other systems.

q: What is DepositFix and how does it work with HubSpot?
a: DepositFix is a payment integration that runs on top of HubSpot, with an embeddable checkout widget and a backend that syncs data. Denis Lunev describes the second piece as "a backend integration that syncs data between payment gateways and HubSpot" [03:51].

q: What tech stack is DepositFix built on?
a: DepositFix uses Java and Spring Boot on the backend, Postgres for the database, AngularJS for client dashboards, and runs on AWS. Denis Lunev chose it from experience and calls it "a pretty unusual stack for a startup." [05:03].

q: How does DepositFix prioritize its product roadmap?
a: The team uses the RICE framework, scoring feature requests on reach, impact, confidence and effort, then sorting by the totals. Denis Lunev explained that "RICE stands for reach, impact, confidence, and effort." [08:40].

q: When did DepositFix start optimizing for scale?
a: Scalability was deliberately not a priority until the product had traction, and performance problems showed up about four months into the MVP. Denis Lunev said, "we decided to focus on business problems instead of premature optimization." [14:06].

q: What advice does Denis Lunev have for new founders?
a: Denis Lunev advises talking to potential clients before building, so you understand the problem and what they actually need. His words were "Talk to clients first before even thinking about the product" [21:57].

s2-e18-serial-side-projects-indie-product-launching-with-mubashar-mubs-iqbal-of-pod-hunt
A Two-Week MVP: Mubs started Podhunt on a two-and-a-half-hour train ride and had a working MVP in about two weeks. The core was simple: sign up, submit an episode, upvote and see the list.

Twitter as the Identity Layer: Podhunt uses Twitter OAuth so hosts and guests can be tagged by handle under one consistent identity. Mubs expects to need another login option someday, given Twitter's shifting stance on API use.

Seeding a Two-Sided Community: Early on, Mubs submitted two or three episodes a day to keep the site active. About 10 weeks in, he typically submitted only on weekends, with weekdays seeing around eight episodes.

Scale When It Matters: Mubs avoids over-optimizing. When his WillRobotsTakeMyJob.com site drew four million page views in its first week, moving from a $5 to a $20 DigitalOcean Droplet kept it running smoothly.
Hiring for Passion and Range: A future teammate would need a love of podcasts, expertise in one area and an appreciation for the rest, from design and development to SEO, sales and marketing.

q: What is Podhunt and how does it help with podcast discovery?
a: Podhunt is a site where people submit and upvote individual podcast episodes, so listeners can find new ones beyond the usual leaderboards. Mubashar Iqbal said you may see a big name each day, "but chances are it's somebody that you've never heard of" [28:46].

q: What tech stack is Podhunt built with?
a: Mubashar built Podhunt with Laravel and some Vue, and hosts it on DigitalOcean Droplets. As he described it, "Laravel PHP is using some Vue as well in the front end" [03:58].

q: Why does Podhunt use Twitter to log in?
a: Mubashar wanted users to be able to tag episode hosts and guests by their Twitter handles, without having to link separate email and Twitter accounts. Using Twitter for sign-in may not have been the only way, he noted, "but I think it just made it more cohesive" [06:26].

q: How did Mubashar Iqbal handle a sudden traffic spike on a side project?
a: His site WillRobotsTakeMyJob.com got four million page views in its first week, and he responded by upgrading its server. Mubashar said he went "from a five dollar to a twenty dollar Droplet instead, and, uh, and that was all that it took" [22:25].

q: What advice does Mubashar Iqbal give for launching a first side project or startup?
a: Mubashar advises aiming big but starting small: launch with the fewest features you can, then let users tell you what they actually want. In his words, "especially when you're starting, just make as little as you can" [32:48].

s2-e17-enterprise-mqtt-brokers-and-large-scale-iot-messaging-with-dominik-obermaier-of-hivemq

Built for IoT Scale: Dominik saw that train connectivity projects relied on technology designed for the human internet, like HTTP. HiveMQ pivoted in 2014 around a commercial, cloud-ready broker based on the MQTT protocol.

Simplicity Before Scalability: The three-month MVP had no graphical interface and handled only tens of thousands of connections. The team prioritized ease of use and high availability for operators to test whether demand existed.

Rewriting the Core: Third-party clustering capped HiveMQ at about 50,000 to 100,000 devices, so the team rewrote the core. At larger scale, it found cloud providers' networks became the limiting factor.

Testing at Massive Scale: An in-house simulator can mimic tens of millions of devices on real infrastructure. Quality test suites run basically all the time because small code errors can cause catastrophic problems for customers.

CTO Out of the Code: Dominik jumped back into coding during a time-pressed major rewrite. His rusty skills and working outside the Kanban process hurt quality and nearly delayed the product, until the team stepped up to ship without him.

q: How are MQTT brokers different from traditional message queues?
a: Dominik Obermaier explains that classic queues offer features like transactions and suit inter-service communication, while MQTT brokers are built for huge numbers of IoT devices, with some trade-offs. In his words, "these MQTT brokers, are fundamentally different from classic message queues people have used since the 1980s" [04:40].

q: How many devices can HiveMQ connect?
a: Dominik says HiveMQ customers send hundreds of thousands or millions of messages per second, and the team aims to eventually reach 100 million devices. As he put it, "our customers use our product to connect more than 10 million devices" [05:41].

q: How did HiveMQ solve its early scalability limits?
a: The team found that third-party clustering technology held the software back, so it changed the foundation and invested in distributed systems research, including work with universities. Dominik said they "basically rewrote the core of our software and we did a lot of research" [21:27].

q: Can HiveMQ run on-premise and in the cloud?
a: Yes, HiveMQ started as on-premise software that customers also ran on public clouds, and it now offers a managed service as well. Dominik said that with it, "our customers don't need to install anything on their own infrastructure, but we run it" [13:33].

q: What advice does HiveMQ's CTO give startup founders about product-market fit?
a: Dominik Obermaier advises building an embarrassing MVP, selling early, iterating on customer feedback and bootstrapping if you can. He says the best way to validate "that product market fit is actual customers paying you money for it" [35:15].

s2-e16-developer-workflow-devsecops-chatops-and-platform-scaling-with-kyle-campbell-of-ctoai
Services Before Platform: CTO.ai bootstrapped by selling DevOps as a service, learning customer pain points and profitably testing ideas until a pattern emerged around the Ops platform.
Permission to Throw Code Away: Kyle's team kept early builds thin and probably discarded four to five versions, getting stronger each time while avoiding crippling technical debt.

Opinion First, Then Data: Kyle set an early roadmap in milestones from 0.1 to 1.0, watching for the point where user input outweighs his intuition. ICE scoring (impact, confidence, effort) helps rank work.
Hire for the Stage: Be clear about which business stage you're hiring for and leave headroom to grow, such as hiring a director rather than a VP. Train the team to uphold the hiring standard.

Owning a Painful Downsizing: After ramping up quickly without anticipating COVID, CTO.ai went from 60 people to 21. Kyle called it his mistake, shared full transparency and focused on supporting those leaving.

q: How did CTO.ai get started before building its platform?
a: Kyle Campbell chose to bootstrap and focus on professional services rather than raise money immediately off his prior success. He explained, "We provided DevOps as a service." [03:30], which let the team learn developer experience pain points and test ideas with customers.

q: Why does CTO.ai bring developer tools and DevOps into Slack?
a: Kyle believes the shift to remote work makes it more important for development teams to collaborate and see how they're working. In his words, "there is a strong need to bring developer tools and developer experiences to the place where communication collaboration happen" [33:45], meaning Slack.

q: How does Kyle Campbell prioritize features on a product roadmap?
a: He starts with an opinionated founder roadmap, then lets user data take over once it becomes more validating than his own view. To rank work, he described it this way: "the idea of an ICE score is impact plus confidence divided by effort." [13:36] With a larger user base, reach is added to make a RICE score.

q: When should an early-stage startup worry about scalability?
a: Kyle's view is to wait for a clear tipping point of product-market fit, giving the example of 30% month-over-month growth with less than 10% churn. Before that, he said, "you don't have to worry about scalability and you shouldn't worry about scalability." [24:44] CTO.ai did invest in it fairly early, once the team thought it knew what to build, partly because DevOps is its focus.

q: What is Kyle Campbell's advice on hiring at an early-stage startup?
a: Kyle recommends defining the attributes you want, hiring with plenty of headroom to grow and teaching the team to look for those same qualities. He stressed that "when you're hiring people, you're clear with them about what stage of the" [19:53] business you are hiring them for.

s2-e15-from-roller-derby-to-tech-founder-building-a-trusted-babysitter-marketplace-with-desi-mcadam-of-nanno

Founders as Subject Experts: Desi McAdam and her co-founder Liz built the MVP in Ruby on Rails around how they and their friends would book childcare. It took about six months, and caregiver onboarding was built earlier than needed.

Manual Work Behind Bookings: The team focused on getting a sitter to a parent's home fast and handled things like cancellations by hand. Those missing back-end features are now what's holding back scale.

Dropping the 48-Hour Limit: Nanno first allowed only last-minute bookings, then learned within a month or two that the restriction was artificial. Opening up advance booking meant adding reminder messages.
Avoiding Golden Apples: Inspired by the book Radical Focus, the founders are trying to resist distracting opportunities, using quarterly OKRs to focus on the core product and scaling.

Doubling Exposed Weak Spots: Revenue doubled in August, revealing trouble spots. One surprise was that carriers may limit high-volume texting on long codes, while a short code is about $3,000 a month.

q: What is Nanno and what problem does it solve?
a: Nanno is a platform co-founded by Desi McAdam that connects parents with vetted sitters when and where they need them. Describing the mission, McAdam said, "We want to make it so that parents are able to do the things they want" [07:16] and need to do without feeling guilty.

q: How was the Nanno MVP built?
a: Desi McAdam, a web developer, built the MVP around how she, her co-founder and their friends would use it, and it took roughly six months. On the technology choice, McAdam said, "So I just built it in Ruby and Rails to start off with." [02:56]

q: How does Nanno decide what to build next?
a: McAdam said the founders have struggled with shiny objects, and the book Radical Focus is helping them identify distractions. To stay on track, McAdam explained, "we've decided to use OKRs and we are doing quarterly" [10:02] goals.

q: What scaling challenges has Nanno run into?
a: McAdam pointed to missing features that leave a person handling tasks the system should manage, saying, "That's actually our impediment for scalability right now." [14:10] Doubling revenue in August also exposed other trouble spots, including limits around high-volume text messaging.

q: What advice does Desi McAdam give new founders?
a: McAdam advises listening to others while also trusting your own understanding of what you are building and are passionate about. The advice is to be "willing to take criticism but also don't lose faith in yourself" [20:37].

s2-e14-the-marketplace-to-enable-saas-business-productization-with-rob-moore-of-floom
Craftsmanship Over a Rushed MVP: Rob spent roughly 300 to 400 hours on Floom's MVP, doing customer development separately so he could build quality code he'd want to return to on weekends.
Shortcuts Without Corners: Rather than learn AWS step functions, Rob ran a Lambda function for 10 seconds to check on order fulfillment. It cost more, but worked and could be replaced later.

Fewer Decisions, Serverless Stack: Floom pairs Vue.js with AWS Lambda, AppSync and Cognito. Rob chose Vue partly to limit future decisions, and says the verdict is still out on AppSync given its documentation.
Same-Day Product Launch: Inspired by an Instagram post, Rob built a tool that turns a tweet into a typing video, deployed it to AWS Lambda, listed it on Floom and got orders that day.

Signup Friction Hurts Conversion: Skipping social login left users confirming email with a code, and analytics showed many reaching the signup page without signing up. Rob hopes adding Google or Facebook will help.

q: What is Floom and who is it for?
a: Floom is a marketplace where developers list products they've built and start selling them. Rob Moore says its focus is developer tooling: "So my main goals with the product roadmap are providing developer tools to make it easier" [12:10] for developers to get their tools on the market.

q: What tech stack is Floom built on?
a: Rob Moore uses Vue.js on the front end, deployed with Netlify, and a serverless back end with AWS Lambda, AppSync and Cognito, plus Stripe for processing. Describing AppSync, he said "it's basically a GraphQL wrapper over DynamoDB" [04:00].

q: How long did it take to build Floom's MVP?
a: Rob Moore estimates the MVP took around 300 to 400 hours, and he launched it in July 2019. He took longer than a typical MVP because, in his words, "I wanted to actually build something that I was proud of." [05:35]

q: How do you take technical shortcuts in an MVP without creating problems later?
a: Rob Moore works out the best long-term solution, then builds a less complete version that can be improved later. Of his temporary Lambda workaround for order fulfillment, he said "it was something that didn't pin me in the corner." [09:22]

q: Where does Floom find developers to list products?
a: Rob Moore looks to Product Hunt and Indie Hackers, particularly the latter, and at the time of the interview was working individually with developers who wanted to list. He describes Indie Hackers members as people who on weekends "are building things that provide real value." [21:43]

s2-bonus-personalized-audio-of-your-grandmas-childhood-stories-with-andrew-overton-of-saga

No-Code MVP in Two Weeks: Saga first ran on Google Docs, YouTube, Calendly and a call-recording app, with VidHub for listening. Turning a call into audio and a transcript took about 24 hours and didn't scale, but it validated the business.

Manual Before Automated: With no full-time engineer, the three-month Django and React build cut scope aggressively. Some tasks early users likely assumed were automated, like notifications, were handled by co-founder Amelia Lin's mom.

Scaling When It Mattered: Saga began with everything on one tiny Linode server. Ahead of public release, it moved to AWS, using ECS and RDS. This took longer to set up than an option like Heroku, but left room to scale.

Splitting the Codebase Backfired: Keeping a legacy version while building a new one meant syncing commits and a tricky data model. After advisor Kier explained why it wouldn't work, Overton listened and reversed his decision.

Raising More Than Planned: Saga initially targeted about $500,000, but investors urged a higher amount, and the seed round was significantly oversubscribed. Accepting more, despite added dilution, left the company comfortable when COVID-19 tightened funding.

q: What is Saga and how does it record family stories?
a: Saga helps people record their loved ones' life stories on audio, sending a new question each week and sharing answers privately with family channels. Answers can be recorded by phone, app or website, and Andrew Overton explained, "you can call in with any telephone to record your answer" [03:03].

q: How did Saga build its first MVP without code?
a: Amelia Lin recorded phone calls, uploaded them to YouTube for automatic captions, then sent people their audio and transcript. Overton said that "within two weeks of starting on it, we had a product that was built with Google" [05:08] Docs, YouTube, Calendly and a call recording app.

q: How can an early-stage startup decide what to automate?
a: Overton said Saga was very pragmatic about what to automate and what to do by hand, because automating everything can take more time when resources are limited. He revealed that some things "early users probably thought were automated, but funnily enough, were actually Amelia's mom behind the scenes" [09:09].

q: Why did Saga choose AWS over Heroku?
a: Overton wanted Saga prepared to scale before its general public release, and AWS could grow with the company, with ECS for the application and RDS for a backed-up database. He acknowledged the trade-off: "it definitely took us longer than if we were going to just kind of use an out-of-the-box" [17:56] solution.

q: How did Saga speed up its product iteration?
a: Andrew Overton said that building features and then testing them with families already on the platform was too slow. The team moved to testing slides of their ideas through tools like UserTesting and UserBob "because our pace of iteration was just too slow before" [27:34].

s2-e13-from-pixar-intern-to-healthtech-founder-solving-the-medical-credentialing-nightmare-with-adrienne-bolger-of-blochealth
Three MVP Must-Haves: BlocHealth's MVP needed blockchain-based primary source verification, a common application to replace repetitive credentialing forms, and a way to move data both in and out.

Expertise Over Framework Preference: Angular beat React because the chosen blockchain contractors couldn't staff a React front end. Their blockchain skill mattered more, and the front end could be switched later if needed.

Bulk Workflows Became Crucial: After the first live customer, bulk uploads, downloads, queries and access control went from nice-to-have to top priority, since onboarding another customer depended on bulk import.

Roadmap Follows Business Model: The team starts with revenue goals, pares them to what can be built, adds non-negotiable table stakes like security, backups and audit logging, then prioritizes by the next problem they'll hit.

Buy More, Build Less: Looking back, Adrienne would survey the full range of commercial and commercial open source services up front, because early database and front end choices ruled out many later options.

q: What problem in healthcare credentialing is BlocHealth trying to solve?
a: Adrienne Bolger describes credentialing as full of duplication, data silos and lengthy forms that ask for the same information. Each hospital or insurer, she said, "has a 50-page application that's just slightly different from the next company down the road" [02:47].

q: How does BlocHealth use blockchain for credentialing?
a: BlocHealth uses technology from the Ethereum blockchain to address distrust over where files came from, known as primary source verification. To handle scaling limits, Adrienne explained that with tree data structures, "you hash part of something onto the blockchain and then you can prove things that branched" [19:50] off of it haven't changed.

q: Why did BlocHealth choose Angular over React?
a: Adrienne said the choice wasn't technical: the blockchain contractors the company had already vetted couldn't also staff a React front end, but they had Angular experts. As she put it, "ultimately we decided that their blockchain expertise was more important" [05:52].

q: What did BlocHealth learn from onboarding its first customer?
a: The team did much of the initial data entry themselves and found that bulk data workflows, which had been considered nice-to-have, were essential. Adrienne recalled, "we literally will not be able to onboard another customer if we don't have bulk import features" [10:54].

q: Should an early-stage startup build or buy software?
a: Adrienne Bolger says that if she started over, she would buy more software and spend more time evaluating available services, while noting that integrating them is often difficult. In her view, "it's almost always cheaper to buy the thing you're looking for" [28:00].

s2-e12-hacking-the-charts-jack-rhysider-on-the-art-of-technical-storytelling-darknet-diaries

Invent a Category, Then Lead: Jack defined his own niche, true crime meets cybercrime, and set out to be first and best in it. Darknet Diaries tells researched hacking stories from beginning to end, often years after the events.

Scope for One Person: The first episode used a cheap USB mic, free software and a script Jack thinks he wrote in Google Docs. Knowing he couldn't match 20-person shows, he benchmarked against one- and two-person podcasts and capped time per episode.

Prove It Before Promoting: Jack asked listeners where they tuned out and tweaked the show. Binge listeners asking for more, about four to six episodes in, showed he had something. He released weekly at first to build practice and a back catalog.

Guerrilla Marketing Took Work: Jack used his blog, queued months of social posts with about two in ten self-promotional, and handed out stickers at conferences. He hit 10,000-follower goals in about a year and began making money about six months after launch.

Three Revenue Streams: At the time of the interview, Jack cited about 200,000 downloads per episode, with income from two ads per episode, $10,000 a month on Patreon and t-shirts. Combined, it beat his engineering pay.

q: Why did Jack Rhysider create Darknet Diaries?
a: Jack Rhysider wanted complete hacking stories instead of breaking news followed by months of small updates, and the podcast world wasn't offering that. As he put it, "I want the full story from the beginning to the end all laid out" [04:20].

q: What equipment did Jack Rhysider use to start Darknet Diaries?
a: Jack started with a Blue Snowball USB mic that had been sitting in a drawer, plus free software, and he thinks he wrote the first story in Google Docs. He welcomed the constraint, saying "if I have just like a cheap USB mic and a computer, that's my limits" [07:40].

q: How did Darknet Diaries grow its audience?
a: Jack promoted the show to his Twitter followers and blog readers, posted heavily on social media, spoke at a conference and used guerrilla marketing inspired by Seth Godin. He also went to conferences "and just handing out, I mean, literally 3000, 5,000 stickers in a weekend." [21:59]

q: How does Darknet Diaries make money?
a: Jack described three income streams: sponsor ads, Patreon support and a shop selling t-shirts based on episode artwork. He said the "streams of income here and combined is definitely more than what I was making as an engineer" [33:46].

q: How did Jack Rhysider handle a disputed story on Darknet Diaries?
a: After people told Jack that a guest had fabricated his claims, he added an "addendum at the end of the episode saying there's some controversy here." [30:23] He was still weighing the evidence at the time of the interview, and expected he would have to remove the episode once there was enough information.

543798da-dd97-4548-b64a-f17aade6dedd
s2-e11-the-y-combinator-blueprint-how-sift-built-an-ai-fraud-prevention-empire-with-jason-tan-of-sift

Outsiders Spotted the Gap: Jason Tan didn't know what a chargeback was when friends cited fraud as a pain point. He found legacy rules-based systems reactive and hard to maintain, while big tech companies used machine learning.
A Slow, Simple MVP: The MVP took about 18 to 20 months. Customers sent user events such as logins, account creations and transactions through an API, and Sift returned a risk score.
Early Stack, Later Regrets: Rails and MongoDB made it easy to start and iterate, but Mongo didn't fit where Sift was headed. The company switched to HBase and later to Bigtable on Google Cloud.
Beyond the Risk Score: Sift matured along three lines: more accurate models, a console that helps human review teams decide faster, and workflows that let customers automate actions based on risk.
Culture Built Bottom-Up: At 40 people, Tan handed down values that weren't well received. He restarted, met every team member in groups of four or five, and arrived at five core values.

q: What problem does Sift solve?
a: Sift assesses whether user behavior looks trustworthy or suspicious, helping businesses fight fraud without relying on reactive rules-based systems. Jason Tan saw a chance to "democratize access to that kind of technology, large scale, real time machine learning" [05:08] for companies that can't afford armies of expensive engineers.

q: How was Sift's MVP built?
a: Jason Tan said it took about 18 to 20 months, partly because the founders lacked fraud expertise, with Ruby on Rails for the console and MongoDB as the database. Functionally, it took in customer event data and returned a risk score, and as Tan put it, "the MVP was very simply just input and output through an API." [09:49]

q: Why does accuracy matter so much in fraud detection?
a: Jason Tan called accuracy the most important area of improvement, pursued through more model features, different algorithms and more data. In his words, "if we aren't accurate at assessing risk, our core value proposition is moot." [13:47]

q: What is Jason Tan's vision for trust and safety online?
a: Tan wants to help everyone trust the internet and to remove friction that today often feels like airport security. He argues that "most of us should deserve a TSA Pre experience" [07:15], with extra security added only when someone isn't trustworthy.

q: What would Jason Tan do differently if he started Sift again?
a: Tan said he would have sought support for the emotional baggage he was carrying, including seeing a therapist. He also said, "I would have gotten an executive coach starting on day one." [32:08]

2afbbc6e-928f-427c-9dc0-14ffbcba8b46
s2-e10-from-professional-clarinetist-to-tech-founder-rebuilding-critical-infrastructure-with-steven-naimark-ofziptility

Between GIS and Spreadsheets: Ziptility serves mostly rural and mid to small water utilities, sitting between powerful GIS software and the Excel spreadsheets, paper and notepads many operators rely on.

Mapping Built for Flexibility: The team moved from Leaflet to Mapbox in a big overhaul, drawn by its iOS and Android SDKs and web vector maps. They also tried React Native but chose to build natively.

A Stable Feature List: A list of 10 to 20 basic features didn't change from when it was made until the fundraise. The team kept testing the vision with customers and skipped work that wasn't at the heart of the problem.
Scale When It's Needed: With usage still modest, Steven watches areas like messaging to confirm they could scale horizontally, but tries not to add scaling work before it's needed.

Containers Saved the Day: Steven accidentally deleted a server that clients relied on, with deletion protection off. Because the setup used basic container practices, an image let the team restore it in about five to ten minutes.

q: What is Ziptility and who is it for?
a: Ziptility is a platform for water utilities, focused primarily on rural and mid to small size operations. Steven Naimark places it between "the powerhouse software out there for GIS work and the Excel spreadsheet" [04:54].

q: Why did Ziptility switch from Leaflet to Mapbox?
a: Steven Naimark said Leaflet was a great library, but the team wanted options for the future and people use Ziptility on both phones and the web. A key draw was that "Mapbox had the SDK for iOS and Android" [07:21], along with web vector maps.

q: How did Ziptility decide which features to build?
a: The team worked from an early list of basic features and kept checking its vision with customers and prospects. Steven explained that if something didn't feel like it was "at the heart of what we were trying to solve, we just didn't do it" [09:08].

q: How did Ziptility recover from accidentally deleting a server?
a: Steven Naimark deleted the wrong server while clearing out one the team was done with, and then spun up a replacement from an image in about five to ten minutes. He recalled, "I'm grateful that we set everything up using basic container" [21:54] practices.

q: What advice does Steven Naimark give early-stage startup founders?
a: Steven says founders who want a successful business need to learn about business and finance, and should try selling their idea early. His advice is to "keep building it, go sell it. If you validate it, go try to sell it immediately" [28:20].

s2-e9-from-ar-gaming-to-webar-saas-the-code-architecture-behind-seek-with-thane-brimhall-of-seek
From Treasure Hunts to SaaS: Seek began with paid hunts for real cash, moved to AR and an app, then found its business in web-based AR that companies add to their own sites for product visualization.
Trading Control for Access: Going web-based meant giving up some control to Google and Apple's AR APIs. Seek decided that removing the app download and lowering the barrier to entry was worth it.
One Model, Many Formats: Early on, platform-specific 3D files were generated and synced to the server by hand. Now one input model is automatically turned into maybe five to seven optimized versions.

Hire the Self-Taught Problem Solvers: Seek's top hiring signal is building something cool in your free time, not degrees or frameworks. One new hire made a Linux battery indicator styled as Zelda hearts.

The Tagging System Lesson: Thane chose a simple list of strings over a robust database table for model tags. About two weeks after launch, another client needed the fuller system, and it had to be rebuilt.

q: How does Seek add augmented reality to an e-commerce website?
a: Seek lets shoppers place a product, such as a couch, into their camera feed from a website without installing an app. According to Thane Brimhall, "it's three lines of code using our SDK to install an augmented reality" [03:25] experience onto any website.

q: Why did Seek move from a mobile AR app to WebAR?
a: Thane explained that finding, downloading and logging into an app was too much effort for an experience lasting only 15 or 20 seconds. As he put it, "eventually we said, look, nobody wants the app." [05:12]

q: How does Seek convert 3D models for iOS, Android and web?
a: Each platform, and even different iOS versions, can need different formats or features, so Seek built an automated pipeline from a single 3D model. Thane said "we automatically generate maybe five, six, seven that are platform specific," [11:55] each optimized to give users the best experience.

q: How does Seek scale its WebAR platform?
a: Thane said many of Seek's network requests are read-only, so the team can lean heavily on caching and CDNs. The harder part is the CPU-intensive 3D conversion pipeline, and the system is designed to be cloud agnostic, as he noted: "we actually have servers on Azure and AWS," [16:04].

q: What would Thane Brimhall do differently if he started Seek again?
a: Thane would have focused the earlier technology on B2B SaaS revenue instead of a consumer platform that created a two-sided market problem. Of the current model, he said "we only have to sell to companies and that is exponentially easier." [24:08]

s2-e8-transitioning-healthcare-to-the-home-how-dina-built-an-ai-care-stack-with-erin-karam-of-dina-formerly-prepared-health

Connecting the Care Continuum: Prepared Health links hospitals, health plans, skilled nursing, home health and other providers with real-time chat, safe transition tools and case management for at-risk chronic patients.

Lean MVP, Real Trade-Offs: The MVP still lives in the product. Keeping burn low meant a very small team, and Erin would reconsider starting with a junior engineer rather than a stronger senior partner.

Watching Users in Real Time: A Slack feed called Pulse shows user activity, while Stackdriver monitoring and Sentry help the team spot problems, sometimes before they grow, and harden the MVP for enterprise healthcare.

Regulation Shapes the Roadmap: Long-range and 12-month visions must flex for customers and legislation. With a new discharge planning rule, Erin said the tool already covered nine of 10 gaps, leaving a two-week sprint for the last.

Stop Shouldering It Alone: Erin carried infrastructure, security and data science to shield product engineers. Hiring specialists helped, and sharing ownership with the wider team left everyone more connected.

q: What does Prepared Health do?
a: Erin Karam describes Prepared Health as a platform connecting providers across the care continuum, from hospitals to home-based care, to help people stay healthy and at home. Karam said the aim is to be the "fabric between these providers and provide the right insights, the right information to the" [03:48] right person at the right time.

q: What tech stack does Prepared Health use to scale?
a: Karam said, "we have a backend that's built on Google Cloud, Google App Engine" [15:44], which scales automatically with load behind a REST API. She also described a Cosmos store on Azure that scales horizontally by shard, Kinesis for data ingestion and an event-driven architecture for asynchronous work.

q: How does a small healthcare tech company build its product roadmap?
a: Karam explained that "we have our three to five year vision. We know where we're headed." [13:15] That sits alongside a 12-month view, and the team adjusts for customer needs, integration problems and changing legislation.

q: What mistake did Erin Karam make as a technical leader?
a: Karam tried to keep product engineers in a bubble by managing infrastructure, security and data science herself. She eventually realized, "I wasn't actually doing anybody any favors." [19:32] She hired help and later pushed ownership of these areas back into the wider team.

q: What would Erin Karam do differently with startup hiring?
a: Karam said that "having the right people is the most important decision." [22:45] She looks for people who are bought into the mission, curious and willing to coach peers, and believes making the tough call quickly on a poor fit would have saved heartache.

s2-e7-scaling-fintech-financial-data-infrastructure-with-ryan-graciano-of-credit-karma

Boring Stack, Clear Scaling Path: In 2007, Graciano chose LAMP for its proven scaling playbook and because PHP recreates context on every request. It served Credit Karma well for roughly eight or nine years.

Premature Scaling Wasted Effort: The team put work into scaling social features like comments and voting, expecting them to go viral. Totally different things ended up needing to scale, though early investment in security was deliberate.

Surviving the 2008 Crisis: With revenue tied to members getting better loan deals, a banking collapse broke the model. Credit Karma got through 2008 to 2010 with advertising, cell phone sales and white-label products.

A Four-Year Services Migration: The team prototyped services, scaled up within the platform group, had every app team build at least one, then set out to kill the monolith. A homogeneous stack made security controls easier to build in.

Debug Process Like a Product: Service deployment first took about 60 days. The platform team tightened feedback loops and automated manual steps, reaching a two-to-three-day timeline before rolling it out to everyone else.

q: How does Credit Karma make money, and how did the 2008 crisis affect it?
a: Ryan Graciano explained that Credit Karma earns a finder's fee on loans, saying they essentially "make money when the customer saves money" [11:04]. When banks stopped lending in 2008, the company turned to advertising, cell phone sales and white-label products to survive.

q: What tech stack did Credit Karma use to build its first product?
a: Graciano went with LAMP because it was tried and true, with a well-understood path to scaling. He also wanted as little state as possible, noting that "PHP recreates the context in every request." [06:48]

q: Why did Credit Karma standardize its technology when moving to services?
a: Graciano said the team chose to be extremely homogeneous and very specific about which technologies could be used at each layer. His reasoning was that "security is number one and a homogeneous environment is a very good way" [21:03] to build controls across the stack, with gains in maintainability, reliability and tooling.

q: How did Ryan Graciano hire Credit Karma's first engineers?
a: Graciano searched resumes on Craigslist and reached out to people about specific experience or side projects that stood out to him. It took real effort and could not last forever, but as he put it, "handpicking while a lot of work, the hit rate was amazing." [17:30]

q: What advice does Ryan Graciano give early-stage founders about scaling?
a: Graciano advises staying focused on the member or business problem and avoiding premature replatforming to solve issues years away. He warned, "You're much more likely to be killed" [36:51] because your business didn't work than because of one too many outages.

s2-e6-from-the-navy-to-fintech-founder-building-a-peer-lending-app-with-dennis-cail-of-zirtue

Keep the MVP Narrow: Zirtue started coding in April 2018, soft launched that October and hard launched in February 2019. Cail avoided over-engineering by sticking to the core: lending between friends and family with automated repayment.

Build Once, Deploy Twice: Cail's JavaScript background made React Native a natural choice, paired with Node.js, MongoDB and AWS. One codebase served both app stores and got the product to market faster.
Let Users Shape Pricing: Zirtue began with a 5% service fee, then surveyed users. Almost 80% preferred a subscription, so it switched: lending stays free and borrowers pay $5 a month.

Lending Creates Network Effects: Every loan needs another person, and the average user invites two new users. Cail said this keeps customer acquisition costs very low compared with other fintech companies.

Partnerships Direct Funds to Bills: Through an AT＆T partnership, users can borrow to pay wireless or cable bills directly. Lenders know where the money goes, and the company has a better chance of getting paid.

q: What is Zirtue and what problem does it solve?
a: Zirtue is a fintech app for loans between friends and family, with automated ACH repayment. Dennis Cail came up with it after having limited success getting back money he lent to relatives, and recalls, "there has to be a way to help make people more accountable" [01:59].

q: What tech stack was used to build the Zirtue app?
a: Zirtue was built with React Native, a Node.js backend, MongoDB and AWS servers. Dennis Cail explained, "my background is in JavaScript, so React Native was a natural path to launch the app with" [03:03].

q: How does Zirtue move money between lenders and borrowers?
a: Zirtue has partnered with Dwolla for ACH payments since day one, and Dennis Cail said he thinks they had a working sandbox prototype within a few weeks. Describing the decision, Cail said, "we went through this sort of build versus buy exercise" [15:03].

q: How does Zirtue make money, and is it free for lenders?
a: Zirtue moved from a 5% service fee to a subscription after surveying its users, and borrowers now pay a $5 monthly fee. According to Dennis Cail, "it's still 100% free for lenders, friends and family who loan money" [07:27].

q: How has Zirtue grown its user base?
a: At the time of the interview, Dennis Cail said Zirtue had been growing 60% month over month, helped by invitations built into the lending process. As Cail put it, "the average user on our platform invites two new users to the platform" [13:45].

f1df1ebd-5db1-4b1f-bc5b-f33437671c6d
s2-e5-the-future-of-crypto-rewards-how-lolli-makes-earning-bitcoin-effortless-with-matt-senter-co-founder-cto-of-lolli

Bitcoin Rewards as Onboarding: Lolli uses a traditional cashback model but pays in Bitcoin, so people can start earning it without buying on an exchange. Senter said about 40% of users got their first Bitcoin or satoshis through Lolli.
Hosted Services Speed the Build: Senter built on Google Cloud, using hosted services such as its managed Redis. Original prototypes, without design, took roughly two weeks to a month.
