Security Drove the Kubernetes Move: App Engine was too rigid for the network partitioning Senter wanted, so he learned Kubernetes. He now says he doesn't know how he could live without it.
Custodial-Only Was a Mistake: Lolli launched without a way to move funds to a personal wallet. Bitcoin enthusiasts pushed back, and the team rolled out withdrawals as fast as it could.

Build Internal Tools Early: Senter wishes he had built dashboards, support tools and richer shopping history sooner. Without them, engineers spend time pulling reports from the database to answer business questions.

q: What is Lolli and how does it work?
a: Lolli is a Bitcoin rewards platform that follows a cashback model, with rewards paid in Bitcoin into a custodial wallet. As co-founder and CTO Matt Senter explained, "You shop online, you get Bitcoin back on your purchases." [01:57]

q: How was the Lolli MVP built?
a: Matt Senter built it on Google Cloud, applying lessons from his previous company, Cosmic Cart. He said "One of the lessons was just using as many available hosted services as I could find." [05:50]

q: Why did Lolli use Kubernetes instead of Google App Engine?
a: Senter first tried App Engine for fast deployment, but it could not handle the way he wanted to secure and partition the network. He recalled that "since it couldn't support the use case that I had, I had to learn Kubernetes" [07:09].

q: What mistake did Lolli make at launch?
a: Matt Senter and co-founder Alex Adelman planned a fully custodial wallet, not expecting that users would want to move their Bitcoin elsewhere. Senter admitted "there was just no feature there for people to move their funds off of" [20:07] the platform, and the team quickly added it.

q: What advice does Matt Senter have for new startup founders?
a: Senter advises finding a business partner who can take on a large share of the work, and not worrying about equity dilution. Speaking about complementary co-founders, he said "I think finding somebody like that is really, really important" [28:21].

s2-e4-scaling-high-volume-customer-engagement-push-notification-apis-george-deglin-onesignal

Born from a Game Studio: After pivoting from a virtual identity network to mobile games, George Deglin's team struggled to re-engage players. Poor notification tools and best practices gave them the vision for OneSignal.

Ship an Embarrassing MVP: Low on money, Deglin and one engineer listed 12 must-do items, bought a $49 template and cobbled together open-source tools. They accepted technical debt to get user feedback quickly.

Rebuilding Delivery in Rust: A forked, single-threaded Ruby library was hitting its limit around 5 or 6 million notifications a day. OneSignal re-architected in Rust and now sends over 5 billion daily.

Stick with Familiar Tools: The early product was very much a monolith, and the team avoided new technology that added overhead. They still resist adopting tools for hype when something already in use does the job.

Don't Compromise on Values: Deglin has always regretted hiring people who disagreed with the company's vision or values, even when badly wanting to fill a role. Early hires also needed to be gritty generalists with quick impact.

q: How did the idea for OneSignal come about?
a: George Deglin's team was running a mobile game studio and found notifications surprisingly hard to use effectively for bringing players back. He described the challenge as "how to get users to re-engage with our games after initially playing them" [03:39].

q: How was the OneSignal MVP built?
a: Deglin and one engineer had to build SDKs, a dashboard, an API, a login system and analytics, using shortcuts such as a $49 template and open-source solutions. George recalled deciding, "we've got to do these 12 things in order to have something" [06:49] that was usable.

q: How did OneSignal scale its push notification delivery system?
a: The original system was a fork of an open-source Ruby library that ran on one thread and, according to George, clearly wasn't scaling after the first year. Of the fix, he said, "we actually re-architected it using Rust" [12:49], and that backend now sends over 5 billion notifications a day.

q: What did George Deglin look for in OneSignal's early hires?
a: George wanted generalists who could work on several things at once, shared the company's values and vision, and could make an impact very quickly. He listed traits such as "being very hardworking, being gritty, and able to be comfortable with change" [15:42].

q: What would George Deglin do differently in OneSignal's early days?
a: George said he spent a lot of time keeping servers running, building and answering support tickets, when hiring people to take over would have helped the company move faster. In hindsight, "Perhaps I'd have been more willing to let there be a little bit of downtime" [26:55].

s2-e3-democratizing-the-startup-process-how-startupscom-built-a-ecosystem-for-founders-with-wil-schroter-founder-ceo-startupscom

Question the Hype Cycle: Fundable launched amid a rush of equity crowdfunding platforms, but Wil saw many companies unready to raise and little change in investor numbers. About a year in, he told his team it wasn't a good bet.

Acquiring to Move Faster: To build a virtual incubator without waiting to create every tool, bootstrapped Startups.com bought six venture-funded companies in about 18 to 24 months, after what Wil puts at north of 200 to 300 meetings.

One Master Stack: Acquired products ran on different, often aging tech. The team is building shared components like user profiles and search, mainly around React, then migrating what's needed and sunsetting the old stacks.

The Original Team Is a Bet: Wil argues early hires are chosen with the least possible data, so turnover can be necessary. He says confusing loyalty with outcomes blinded him to poor performance and cost him close friends.

Plan Only to Friday: Wil says project, dev and marketing planning at the 200-person company never extends past Friday. Short horizons leave no room to push work out, so build the smallest thing you can now.

q: What is Startups.com and how does it help founders?
a: Wil Schroter describes Startups.com as a virtual incubator that offers education and tools from idea validation through customer acquisition and funding. Its roadmap follows the places founders get stuck, or as Wil put it, "let's be there whenever Noah has a problem" [17:10], using the host as his example founder.

q: Why did Fundable's equity crowdfunding bet lead to a broader platform?
a: Wil saw a flood of companies that weren't ready to raise capital, while investor supply stayed largely flat. In his words, "there was no demonstrable change in the number of investors" [09:13], and founders also needed help with planning, customer acquisition, education and mentors.

q: How did Startups.com build its platform so quickly?
a: Building every tool in-house would have taken too long, so Wil moved his family to San Francisco and met nonstop with companies he might buy. He said that "we ended up acquiring six companies" [13:34], all of them venture-funded, even though Startups.com was bootstrapped.

q: What does Wil Schroter advise founders about early hires and team turnover?
a: Wil says founders won't pick all the right people at the start and shouldn't treat the original team as permanent. As he explained, "The original bet was the bet you made with the least possible data." [25:11]

q: How does Startups.com plan its work?
a: Wil says all project, development and marketing planning stops at Friday, which keeps teams focused on small, near-term deliverables and makes delays harder to hide. As Wil put it, "you can't fake Friday" [36:07] when the work is due that week.

s2-e2-fixing-bad-remote-audio-how-squadcast-revolutionized-podcast-tech-with-zach-moreno-co-founder-cto-of-squadcast
Validating at Podcast Movement: Knowing zero podcasters, the team built an MVP in under six months and took a booth. Within minutes, an attendee said they had come looking for exactly this solution.

Rebuilding Right After Launch: SquadCast launched V1 in January 2019 on Polymer, then immediately started over with Ionic, Angular and TypeScript, partly to get past data-flow friction and move toward mobile.

Progressive Upload for Fault Tolerance: After 10 or 11 attempts, SquadCast records locally and uploads in the background, with a lower-quality cloud backup. Zach says no audio has been lost in two years.

Rolling Back a Broken Release: A deploy made before a Philadelphia conference mangled some users' audio. Zach resisted reverting, then rolled it back; a properly tested progressive upload followed in what he thinks was under two months.

Narrowing an All-in-One Vision: The original plan spanned recording, editing, hosting, listening and ads. Advisor Harry Duran urged them to drop the rest and be the best in the world at remote recording.

q: Why did Zach Moreno build SquadCast?
a: Zach and his team wanted to make a sci-fi audio drama with remote voice actors, but tools like Skype and Zoom delivered poor audio quality. In Zach's words, "It's like these things weren't made to record audio." [02:18]

q: How does SquadCast prevent lost audio in remote recordings?
a: Zach explained that each person is recorded locally, with the audio "uploading it progressively in the background" [32:10] so it is already in the cloud if someone disconnects. A lower-quality backup of the whole conversation is also recorded over the cloud as a second layer of redundancy.

q: Why did SquadCast use microservices from the start?
a: Zach admits it seemed like overkill at first, but the team wanted separation of concerns between things like payments and audio and video. As he put it, "we wanted the ability to scale them independently of one another," [12:55] even though they did not need that scale yet.

q: What advice shaped SquadCast's product focus?
a: Zach credits founding advisor Harry Duran with steering the team away from building an all-in-one podcasting app. Zach recalled the advice as "Be the best in the world at that remote recording and the rest of it, you can just plug in with" [48:22] integrations, or possibly build it later.

q: What is Zach Moreno's advice on bootstrapping versus raising venture capital?
a: Zach is not against venture capital, but he believes founders should first see how far they can get without it, since the option to raise remains open. He said, "So I think we should all try to bootstrap." [53:34]

s2-e1-bootstrapping-a-global-creator-community-indie-startup-world-with-courtland-allen-of-indie-hackers
A Checklist Picked the Idea: With about six months of runway left, Allen scored ideas against a list of about 10 criteria, such as buildable in weeks and light on code. Indie Hackers scored highest.

Blog First, Community Later: The MVP was a blog of founder interviews, built in three weeks with EmberJS and Firebase. Its empty forum page collected emails to test demand before Allen spent about eight days building the forum.
Seeding an Empty Forum: Allen made fake accounts and talked to himself to start conversations, and used the newsletter to send people to forum posts. The forum eventually became the home page.

Caching a Dynamic Site: Server-side rendering was expensive under load, so a cron job now saves fresh homepage and forum HTML about every 30 seconds. Users get a fast static file that is only slightly out of date.

Charge as Early as Possible: Allen burned out chasing traffic, then found the numbers barely mattered when he began selling sponsorships. He says he would try to generate revenue first and learn from why buyers say no.

q: What is Indie Hackers?
a: Indie Hackers is a community of mostly developers and creators who want the freedom that comes from making a living online. Courtland Allen described it as "an online and in-person community nowadays where these founders can" [02:19] come together, swap ideas, get feedback and share stories.

q: How long did it take to build the Indie Hackers MVP?
a: Allen built a blog from scratch using EmberJS and Firebase and launched it with his first 10 interviews. He recalled, "I think it took three weeks from the time I came up with the idea" [07:23] to launch, by far the fastest he had ever shipped anything.

q: How did the Indie Hackers forum get started?
a: Allen first put up an empty forum page that asked interested visitors to leave their email address, and many did. He wanted a forum because he needed "to build something that could be bigger than me" [14:26] and would not depend entirely on his own blog posts.

q: What mistake did Courtland Allen make while building Indie Hackers?
a: He took on long coding projects, including a product directory that he over-designed and that gave people little reason to use their product pages until he later added a milestones leaderboard. Allen said it took a while before "I really stuck to my guns and said, I'm never working on anything that's going to take me longer" [32:20] than a few days, or a week at most.

q: What advice does Courtland Allen give founders launching a new product?
a: Allen advises being careful whose advice you take, including his own, and starting very small. He suggests taking your idea and working to "figure out how you can get it done in a week," [43:02] in its most bare-bones version.

s1-e20-sophisticated-online-safety-ai-alerts-for-parents-brandon-hilkert-bark

Alerts With Context, Not Surveillance: Bark surfaces only suspected issues to preserve kids' privacy. When parents couldn't interpret a lone flagged line, the team added the five messages before and after it.

Building Data From Scratch: With no ready cyberbullying dataset, the team scraped YouTube comments, message boards and Reddit, then labeled examples largely with internal employees. The MVP focused on cyberbullying.

Kid Speak Breaks Generic Models: Off-the-shelf classifiers are only a starting point, Brandon says, because kids use acronyms, rarely spell properly and share different adult content than those models target.

Offloading the Fastest-Growing Table: A free schools product reached a million kids in about six weeks, speeding the move of Bark's write-heavy message table from Postgres to DynamoDB. Everything else stayed in Postgres.

Choosing Customers Over iOS Coverage: When Apple's crackdown kept locking parents' iCloud accounts, Bark shut off iOS monitoring and explained why. Customers left, and finding another way took months.

q: What is Bark and how does it help keep kids safe online?
a: Bark is a subscription product for parents that monitors kids' social media, text and email accounts and alerts parents when it finds an issue. Brandon Hilkert says the company began "with the intent to use machine learning to surface issues on kids' social media, text," [03:24] and email accounts.

q: Does Bark let parents read all of their child's messages?
a: No, Brandon explains that parents only get involved when Bark's classifiers believe there is an issue, which preserves the child's privacy. To give a flagged message context, the team decided to show "the five messages before and the five messages after for the parent to see." [17:33]

q: What tech stack was used to build the Bark MVP?
a: Brandon built the web app with Rails, Postgres, Sidekiq and Redis, while the data science side was Python behind a small Flask API. Describing his standard web stack, he said, "For me, it was Rails, the Postgres backend." [10:44]

q: Why aren't off-the-shelf AI models enough to detect cyberbullying among kids?
a: Brandon says generic classifiers can be a starting point, but Bark's use case differs from things like toxic comments on Amazon reviews. One challenge he points to is that "Kids use a ton of acronyms and never spell things properly." [21:34]

q: Why did Bark stop monitoring iOS devices?
a: Bark had been accessing iCloud backups, and after Apple cracked down, parents' accounts were repeatedly locked. Brandon's team did not think that experience was right for customers, despite the business impact, and as he put it, "So we shut monitoring off for iOS" [33:38].

s1-e19-scaling-one-of-the-internets-top-platforms-chris-slowe-reddit

A Minimal First Version: Steve Huffman built the Common Lisp MVP in under a month. It was a list of outbound links with voting and popularity ranking, and comments didn't arrive until about six months later.

Moving From Lisp to Python: The small pool of Lisp developers and the need for a language ecosystem pushed Reddit to rewrite in Python. Chris also valued Python's well-defined coding style when several people write code.

Scaling Without a Playbook: Traffic doubled about every three months in the early days. To keep the front page fast, the team avoided recomputing the ranking on every page view, using a HOT algorithm that has stayed largely unchanged.

Fearless Generalists on Tiny Teams: For its first six years, engineering never exceeded about five people. Reddit relied on generalists who would dive into unfamiliar stacks, stay calm during outages and skip blame and technology religious wars.

Community-Built Features Guide Product: Letting communities style themselves directly with CSS was powerful but obtuse. Users built features such as flair and new ways of voting, which helped shape what Reddit built next.

q: How was the first version of Reddit built?
a: Chris Slowe explains that the original Reddit was written in Common Lisp and was a listing of links with voting and popularity ranking, but no comments. As Chris put it, "Steve single-handedly got together an MVP that took less than a month to build." [04:51]

q: Why did Reddit switch from Lisp to Python?
a: Chris says few people could write Lisp, and the team also had to consider the language ecosystem around the app. Ruby and Python both seemed reasonable, and the team picked Python as a simple, straightforward language where, in Chris's words, "the coding style is very well defined" [08:23].

q: What made scaling Reddit hard in the early days?
a: Chris describes traffic that doubled about every three months, with the team learning things like Postgres configuration while the site was down. Looking back at 2005 and 2006, he said "there just wasn't a lot of common knowledge on how to actually build and scale things." [10:46]

q: What kind of engineers did Reddit hire for its early team?
a: Chris says Reddit hired brilliant generalists who were willing to take a chance and could handle pressure without panicking. He said the good ones are not necessarily smarter than typical engineers, but "They're just willing to dive into basically any problem" [13:05].

q: How does Reddit's CTO Chris Slowe think about tech debt?
a: Chris sees tech debt as a sign that a company has had enough success to move past existential emergencies and improve things for future developers. He considers it "actually a luxury to be able to complain about tech debt." [18:40]

s1-e18-creating-an-on-demand-marketplace-for-healthcare-nomads-bill-eager-nomad-health

A 90-Day MVP: Nomad Health built an ambitious first version in about 90 days using Python with Flask, MongoDB and Heroku. By March 2016, doctors were signing up, building profiles and applying to jobs on the platform.

Speed Over Premature Scale: The small team kept a monolith, used schemaless MongoDB to change the data model easily and accepted technical debt, while still investing in unit tests and continuous integration.

Catching Scale Problems Early: The team alerted on basically all error logs and worked to understand every "rattle or clank" in the application, heading off small troubles before the whole infrastructure fell over.

Design Beyond Two Clinician Types: Adding nurses to a doctor platform, Bill says they should have designed for any clinician doing any type of work. Missing that made later changes to individual work types difficult.

Hiring for Growth and Mission: Early engineering hires were chosen for EQ, collaborative spirit, growth trajectory and connection to the mission, which Bill says helps people fill in gaps on their own.

q: What problem does Nomad Health solve for travel nurses and doctors?
a: Nomad Health is an online marketplace for short-term clinical work, including travel nurse contracts and locum tenens positions for doctors. Bill Eager contrasted it with the existing options, describing brokerages "and all pen and paper, fax machines, really high margins." [03:22]

q: How was the Nomad Health MVP built, and how long did it take?
a: Bill Eager said the feature set was maybe a little ambitious, "but we were able to put it together in about 90 days." [03:59] The team used Python with Flask, MongoDB as the primary data store, and launched on Heroku.

q: Should an early-stage startup build a monolith or services?
a: Bill Eager's team kept a monolithic code base because it was easier for a small team to get their heads around. He acknowledged that a monolith can break for companies later on, "But it's a smart thing to do if you're a small team." [06:16]

q: What mistake did Nomad Health make when expanding from doctors to nurses?
a: Bill Eager said the team adapted the platform for two clinician types without thinking through where that trajectory led. He called it "one of those zero, one, infinity exercises" [19:05], meaning the platform should have been designed to support any type of clinician doing any type of work.

q: What advice does Bill Eager have for founders and early startup employees?
a: Bill Eager encourages people to take on new responsibilities, speak up with questions or ideas, and listen to everybody they can. He also urges them to "be aggressively curious about the business that you're working on." [26:47] Finding a mentor and a network matters too, because building a startup can be lonely.

s1-e17-smart-building-automation-and-property-tech-engineering-blake-miller-homebase

Born From Smart City Work: Homebase grew out of Blake Miller's work on the Kansas City Smart City Initiative, applying its connected infrastructure framework to buildings. It began as an incubation project with local real estate and construction partners.

A Year Of Pilot Learning: The hardware and software MVP went into a roughly 15 to 20-unit community, largely vacant apart from advisors and partners. It took about a year to work out the integrations, devices and a scalable way to deploy them.

Adapting Single-Family Devices: Most smart locks and thermostats were designed for single-family homes, so Homebase worked closely with partners to adapt them for multifamily use, while weighing what to build around waits for partner APIs.

Wi-Fi As Owner Revenue: Building-wide Wi-Fi connects the smart devices and lets owners sell their own bandwidth tiers. Residents can upgrade in the app, with the charge added to the rent bill and paid via Dwolla.

Narrow Wedge, Big Vision: Miller advises finding the narrowest niche that can reach or show meaningful profitability and grow quickly without a long sales cycle. He also admits that building extra functions caused confusion about what Homebase was.

q: What does Homebase do for apartment buildings?
a: Homebase combines hardware and software to give residents a smart living experience while helping owners save money and create new revenue beyond raising rents. Blake Miller explained, "we help apartment owners and managers automate the management of their building" [03:21].

q: What was hard about bringing smart home devices into multifamily housing?
a: Homebase had to work closely with integration partners to make devices work across apartment communities, and building things between a startup and large corporations took a long time. Miller said of thermostats, locks and similar devices that "they were meant for the single family home" [08:32].

q: How does Homebase handle resident move-ins without physical keys?
a: Access control is tied into the Homebase app, so residents can go straight to their unit without seeing a leasing agent and get into the building and apartment with their phone. Miller said, "We've given the ability for people to be able to move in without having to grab a key" [10:49].

q: How do rent payments work in Homebase?
a: Homebase partnered with Dwolla and built payments into the same app residents use for their door, thermostat and maintenance requests. Miller said the partnership lets them "basically for free move the largest check of somebody's wallet every month" [11:15].

q: What is Blake Miller's advice for new startup founders?
a: Miller recommends picking a very focused way into the market that can grow quickly, without losing sight of the larger vision. His starting point is to "Find the narrowest niche that you can" [25:55], one that helps you reach or show meaningful profitability.

s1-e16-building-tech-infrastructure-for-oil-gas-investment-aalok-shah-energyfunders

Lower Barrier to Entry: EnergyFunders cut direct oil and gas investment minimums from at least $250,000 per investor per project to $5,000 for accredited investors, working with trusted operators and vetting each opportunity.

A Costly False Start: Analysis paralysis and too much outside advice led to the wrong outsourced team and tech stack for version two. After almost six months, the team scrapped the build and restarted from scratch.

Security Over Launch Features: The version two rebuild made security a focal point, with testing as features were built and a third-party penetration test. The cost was slower development and functionality cut from launch.

Understand Manual Work First: Version two launched with heavy manual work, especially in admin. Developers worked closely with investor relations and vetting teams before automating KYC, dividend payouts and project documents.

A Platform-Driven Roadmap: After the executives read Platform Revolution, they reprioritized around investor, operator and admin experiences, balancing investor demand with project supply and budgeting for technical debt.

q: What is EnergyFunders and who can invest through it?
a: EnergyFunders is an online platform for direct investments in energy projects, primarily oil and gas, aimed at everyday accredited investors. Aalok Shah, its CTO, said the company lowered the barriers for "these kinds of investments to minimums of $5,000" [02:36].

q: What tech stack does EnergyFunders use?
a: Version one was built with PHP and MySQL, while version two uses Node.js with Express, React.js and cloud hosting on AWS. Shah said the team considered MongoDB, but "we knew that our data is highly relational and so we decided on continuing with MySQL" [08:46].

q: How does EnergyFunders handle investor payments and dividend payouts?
a: EnergyFunders uses Dwolla's API to move investments from investors' bank accounts to the fund account and its mass pay feature to distribute project earnings. Shah explained that the team wanted to do "everything bank to bank so that we can kind of keep the costs down" [19:22].

q: What mistake did EnergyFunders make when rebuilding its platform?
a: Shah said the team went down the wrong development path with the wrong outsourced team and technology stack, losing significant time and money over almost six months. In his words, "our team responded by scrapping that build" [25:21], then restarted with internalized user stories and local development resources.

q: What advice does Aalok Shah have for someone starting out in tech?
a: Shah passes on advice from a mentor: focus on something that really matters to you, whether an industry, cause, technology or challenge. He suggests thinking hard "about what fascinates you, what challenges you in a good way, what motivates you" [31:13] and following that trail.

s1-e15-modernizing-bill-payments-payouts-invoicing-systems-omri-mor-routable
Validate Before Writing Code: Omri Mor and his co-founder had each built B2B payment infrastructure in-house. They spent nine months interviewing about 300 people before deciding to build Routable.

Six Weeks to Moving Money: Routable estimated three to six months for an MVP but shipped a live one six weeks into Y Combinator, using React and Django. It sent about $200,000 in payments during the program, then had to be rewritten.

Integrations Make or Break It: Without an accounting software integration, buyers wouldn't purchase. Routable started with Xero for its API docs, and each integration needs its own MVP because features like webhooks and deep links vary.

Accountants Wanted Spreadsheets: An early mobile-optimized card view backfired with accountants, so Routable moved to tables. For significant features, the team now usually gets feedback from five to 25 customers.

Hire an Integrations Lead Earlier: Much of year one went to endless refactoring around integrations. Mor would have hired someone like Justin, now head of integrations, sooner to help build a repeatable model for adding new ones.

q: What is Routable and what problem does it solve?
a: Routable provides accounts payable and accounts receivable as a service for companies making hundreds or thousands of business payments a month, with no consumer payments. Omri Mor's research found a gap, noting "that at some point most businesses, if they're technical, build their own B2B payments infrastructure" [04:35], while non-technical ones hire a lot of people.

q: How long did it take Routable to build its MVP?
a: Omri Mor and his co-founder Tom first expected it to take three to six months, and their initial two-week attempt during Y Combinator failed. As Mor put it, "But we did ship something, a real working, money-moving MVP six weeks in" [07:14], built with a React front end and a Django back end.

q: Why are accounting software integrations so important for B2B payments?
a: Omri Mor said Routable's first MVP only sent money, which was not enough to take to market. He explained, "So in our industry, if you don't have an integration to an accounting software," [09:09] people won't buy your tools.

q: What product design mistake did Routable make early on?
a: Omri Mor said the team designed its own way of displaying payment information without asking users, and accountants wanted spreadsheets instead. In his words, they "had built it in a card view, optimizing for mobile." [26:12] The team quickly corrected course with tables.

q: What advice does Omri Mor give to new startup founders?
a: Mor's advice is "Quit your job faster. Commit faster." [33:23] He also recommends announcing what you're working on, asking for help, sending supporters a monthly update, and not sacrificing quality of life for the startup.

s1-e14-saas-customer-interaction-and-scaling-online-reputation-dennis-steele-podium

Selling Within Weeks: Dennis Steele and Eric Rea sketched Podium in a notebook, used outsourced engineers to build a Ruby on Rails MVP, and were selling it door to door within weeks. The first version focused on getting businesses more online reviews.

Founders Learned to Code: Working with overseas developers pushed the founders to attend DevMountain while building and selling. Dennis says the base knowledge greatly improved their ability to solve technical problems, such as guiding customers from a text to an online review.

Product Before Sales Hiring: For roughly the first couple of years, Podium kept about two engineers for every salesperson. Dennis warns that hiring tons of salespeople before the product is really built can hurt.

Customer Time Is Required: Executives, product managers and engineers must spend one-on-one time with customers and do research every week. That feedback shapes the roadmap, including the hard calls about what not to build.

Owning a Mobile Miss: When the new team chat product fell short on mobile, Podium reshuffled priorities and put a team of top engineers on it. Dennis recalls they spent about four weeks bringing it up to standard.

q: What is Podium and what does it do?
a: Dennis Steele, Podium's co-founder, explains that "Podium is an interaction management platform for businesses" [03:05]. It helps customers message and text local businesses and keeps that channel of communication open through the customer journey, though it started out focused on getting more online reviews.

q: How did the idea for Podium start?
a: Dennis was helping local businesses with their online reputation, while his co-founder Eric Rea was being asked for help with reviews by his father. As Dennis tells it, "Eric's dad had a tire shop up in Canada" [04:39], and the two saw they could build something to help businesses like it.

q: Why did Podium's founders go through a coding bootcamp?
a: They were relying on overseas developers and found it hard to communicate exactly what the product needed to do, so they attended DevMountain to level up their skills. Dennis says that "once we had that base knowledge, our ability to solve those problems from a technical perspective increased a ton" [13:08].

q: How does Podium decide what to build next?
a: Dennis says the team works closely with customers to find what is most valuable, then keeps validating that value with them. He notes that executives, product managers and engineers are "required to spend one-on-one time with customers and do extensive research every" [09:59] week.

q: What product mistake did Podium make with team chat, and how was it fixed?
a: Dennis says it became clear after launch that Podium had not invested enough in mobile development for its team chat product, admitting "this is not up to par with our standard of product" [21:33]. The company shifted priorities and assembled a team of some of its best engineers, who spent about four weeks improving the mobile app.

s1-e13-the-technical-journey-of-moving-money-via-api-ben-milne-dwolla

From Consumer App to Infrastructure: Dwolla's consumer product grew over four or five years to a million people moving a billion dollars a year. The team then pivoted to white-label infrastructure, which they saw as their true best-in-class strength.

Proof of Concept First: Version one was a hacked-together system that produced files to deliver to financial institutions. The team later moved to AWS and began shifting parts of the old .NET stack to Scala and microservices.

Let Banks Integrate to You: Going all in on direct, bank-by-bank integrations was a painful mistake that took three years to figure out. Dwolla flipped the model with a framework that lets banks integrate into its platform.
Goals That Tie Together: As headcount doubles, Milne says, communication has to be rethought. Dwolla sets quarterly company goals that cascade to individual goals, including his own as CEO.
Make Debate Safe: Dwolla builds honest debate into off-sites, one-on-ones and weekly meetings. Changing your mind carries no judgment, much like a blameless retro.

q: What does Dwolla do?
a: Ben Milne explains that Dwolla connects its clients' software to bank infrastructure so they can move money. The company is not a financial institution and does not hold the funds; as Milne put it, "Our only incentive is to securely transmit the bits and the instructions." [08:24]

q: Why did Dwolla pivot from a consumer product to an API infrastructure company?
a: Dwolla began as a consumer product for moving money through banks without card networks, born from the credit card fees at Milne's first company. Despite its growth, Milne said the team concluded the consumer business was not its strength: "What we were best in class at was infrastructure." [05:26]

q: How was the first version of Dwolla built?
a: Ben Milne says version one used a pre-MVC Microsoft product and generated files to be delivered to financial institutions. He described that initial build as a "hacked together system to just demonstrate a proof of concept." [06:42]

q: What was one of Dwolla's biggest mistakes?
a: Milne points to the decision to sell directly into banks and build integrations with each one, a long and painful process given how hard it is to get banks to move on your timeline. The better model was letting banks integrate into Dwolla's platform, though Milne admits "it took us three years to figure it out." [20:30]

q: How can third parties build on Dwolla without touching the money?
a: At the time of the interview, Milne said Dwolla planned to release a standardized technical implementation at Money20/20, with clients controlling which partners get data or capabilities. He described it as rules of engagement for third parties to build on client applications "without ever touching the money." [22:53]

s1-e12-fintech-platform-for-automated-lending-and-loan-origination-bernard-worthy-loanwell

One Hub for Community Lending: LoanWell combines applications, underwriting, servicing, money movement, e-signature and reporting for community lenders, who Bernard says were using disparate services to do one job.

Serverless From the Start: The team built on Lambdas, microservices, DynamoDB and an API-driven single-page app. Bernard calls serverless their single best early decision because services could be added or removed as the product changed.

A Demo Sparked the Pivot: LoanWell began with peer-to-peer lending. When asked to refer borrowers, a local financial institution asked to license the tech instead, shifting the paying customer from borrower to lender.

Don't Rebuild Payment Rails: The team explored running its own pass-through account but backed away over regulation, KYC and ACH mechanics. It chose Dwolla for its sandbox, documentation and synchronous verification.

Listen More, Build Less: Bernard says building before vetting demand was costly in time and money. Talking to enough customers to find common needs now makes the roadmap far clearer and cuts guesswork.

q: What is LoanWell?
a: Bernard Worthy, co-founder of LoanWell, describes it this way: "LoanWell is a custom loan origination platform for community lenders." [03:36] It serves credit unions, community banks, loan funds, private lenders and brokers, covering the process from the borrower's application through underwriting, servicing and reporting.

q: How did LoanWell find product-market fit?
a: LoanWell started in 2017 as a direct-to-consumer, peer-to-peer lending product, then moved to an enterprise platform after a financial institution asked to license its technology. Bernard explains that in talks with these institutions, "our customer changed from the borrower paying us in some kind" [28:20] of way to the lender paying, while the mission stayed the same.

q: What architecture is LoanWell built on?
a: LoanWell uses a serverless architecture of Lambdas and microservices, with DynamoDB tables and an API that drives a single-page app. Bernard says the best choice "that we made at the outset is the serverless architecture." [11:23]

q: Why did LoanWell choose Dwolla for ACH payments?
a: Bernard says Dwolla's fully featured sandbox, simple setup and good documentation were major factors. The team also wanted "synchronous ACH verification or KYC verification." [21:18] to keep the product consumer-friendly and scalable.

q: Should non-technical founders learn to code?
a: Bernard, a non-technical business graduate, attended a coding bootcamp and calls it the best decision of his career. He believes founders of tech companies need some knowledge of the inner workings, noting, "I'm the best salesperson for us right now because I know how it works." [35:54]

s1-e11-scaling-enterprise-lifelong-learning-platforms-eric-sharp-degreed

Skills Over Stale Degrees: Degreed measures current skills and learning rather than a degree earned decades ago. Its early MVP focused on tracking formal college courses, breaking degrees apart to show what was inside them.

Good Enough Beats Perfect: The team shipped weekly or biweekly using vertical slices of business value. Scaling problems they had discussed early resurfaced about five years later, and Eric still wouldn't do it differently.

From Consumers to Enterprises: Degreed started direct to learners, then saw a learning management market built on training and compliance. It added analytics, admin features and cataloging of company content for enterprises.
Scaling Without Rewrites: A product designed around teams of 20 met businesses with 60,000 to 80,000 employees. The team avoided rewrites, trusting most of the bones and refactoring iteratively.

Culture Built on Principles: Remote from the start, Degreed hired around principles like empathy and flexibility, turned down brilliant engineers over ego, gathered product tech teams quarterly and gave new engineers mentors.

q: What is Degreed and what problem does it solve?
a: Degreed is a SaaS learning platform that helps learners and businesses build and measure skills for the future. Eric Sharp argues that citing an old degree is a poor measure, comparing it to claiming fitness because you ran a marathon long ago: "it's a terrible way to describe your fitness" [03:34].

q: What tech stack was Degreed's MVP built with?
a: Eric Sharp said the back end was C Sharp with ASP.NET MVC, hosted on Azure, with Visual Studio as the IDE. On the front end, in his words, "We early on with the MVP used jQuery," [06:32] and the team later moved to Angular calling REST APIs.

q: How did Degreed structure its product and engineering teams?
a: Inspired by the Spotify engineering approach but simplifying its terminology, Degreed formed teams around strategic initiatives, with a separate people management structure as it grew. Eric Sharp explained, "we're going to have cross-functional product teams that are" [16:50] based around those initiatives.

q: How did Degreed build its culture with a remote team?
a: The company was remote from the beginning and focused on shared principles, hiring around them and gathering product technology teams every quarter. Eric Sharp said, "I believe culture is really just the end result of the principles that you have in a company." [14:05]

q: What advice does Eric Sharp give to startup CTOs?
a: Eric Sharp advises tech leaders to make technology enable the business and to focus on culture early by identifying principles and using them in interviews, one-on-ones and team meetings. On chasing new technology, he warned, "if you don't have any business value justification for it, maybe you should shelve it" [32:20] until later.

s1-e10-building-a-social-professional-network-for-gig-workers-shelby-stephens-jolly

Reputation That Travels: Jolly lets gig workers build a profile and reputation they control, aggregated from various sources, including endorsements, instead of leaving it stuck inside a single marketplace.

Network Before Jobs: Jolly deferred gigs to build core network features first, asking thousands of weekly signups to be patient. Shelby says growth and engagement soared once work opportunities arrived.

From SaaS Tool to Network: The team first built a freelancer management system for businesses. Researching the freelancers on it revealed a much bigger need, and the system became one way to monetize a larger network.

Research Drives the Roadmap: Analytics, surveys, interviews and more form a "river of feedback." An impact matrix sets who reviews what and how often, feeding outcomes, user opportunities and solutions.

Testing a Distributed Team: Candidates take structured tests, then a more sophisticated project. Beyond technical skill, Shelby looks for excitement about the product, proactive communication and diligent work tracking.

q: What is Jolly and who is it for?
a: Jolly, co-founded by CEO Shelby Stephens, is a professional network for project-based and gig workers that helps them build reputation, grow connections and find work. Stephens explained the problem with existing options: "a lot of marketplaces enable freelancers to build a reputation, but it's kind of stuck inside the marketplace" [03:45].

q: Why did Jolly build its social network before adding a gig marketplace?
a: Shelby Stephens said the team believed reputation and connections were valuable on their own, and that job opportunities would amplify that value later. In his words, "we decided to build the network first and then later amplify all that natural network value with economic opportunity" [13:45].

q: How does Jolly plan to make money?
a: Stephens pointed to the company's freelancer management system, which businesses pay for, as an important source of revenue. He said the network can be sustained through "subscription products, not by taking a cut out of the transaction" [19:28], which he sees as a long-term strategic advantage.

q: What tech stack is Jolly built on?
a: Shelby Stephens said that "Jolly is built with Mongo, Express, React, and Node" [08:48], running on Heroku. The team also uses tools such as Segment, Amplitude, Twilio and Mandrill, plus the Dwolla API for domestic payments.

q: What mistake did Shelby Stephens and the Jolly team learn from?
a: The team relied on an outside research consultant for too long before she taught them to do the work themselves. "So not doing our own research from the very beginning was a mistake" [30:53], Stephens said, calling the shift to in-house research a major turning point.

s1-e9-solving-legal-diligence-contract-review-andy-abbott-heretik
Research Before Writing Code: Abbott says Heretik went almost six months without writing product code, studying AI and data science, customers, competitors, entry points and its local network first.

Cloud Gave Way to On-Prem: Heretik began cloud-first, then re-architected its MVP after facing per-firm security audits and clients whose sensitive documents sat on networks with no internet connection.

Building Inside Relativity: Heretik runs within Relativity, already deployed at law firms, so users review contracts without exporting and importing results. It also built its own document viewer for long documents.

Throwing Away the Viewer: A sprint or two from release, the team scrapped its document viewer over robustness and modularity concerns. The rebuild took about three weeks or less and now handles 2,000-page agreements.

Competing Against Regulatory Fines: Heretik is shifting from M and A toward compliance work like GDPR, Brexit and LIBOR. There, a rival can be the fine itself if paying it costs less than reviewing every document.

q: What problem does Heretik solve in contract review and due diligence?
a: Heretik focuses on reviewing corporate contracts at scale, an idea shaped by the diligence burden Andy Abbott faced when his previous company, BookedOut, was acquired. Looking at thousands of lengthy contracts, Abbott thought "There might be a way to look at that information at scale" [08:42] to organize it and extract information more efficiently.

q: Why did Heretik move from a cloud architecture to on-premise software?
a: Law firms required security audits, and some customers worked on networks that could not connect to the internet because the documents were so sensitive. As Abbott explained, "We quickly decided we needed to pivot, we couldn't deploy or create really a cloud offering" [17:46].

q: How does Heretik work with Relativity?
a: Heretik is built on top of Relativity and uses a system of job queues and workers that clients can scale up or down for a case. Abbott said competitors' results have to be imported into Relativity, while with Heretik "you're basically never leaving Relativity" [20:12].

q: What did Heretik learn from rebuilding its document viewer?
a: Abbott's team threw away its first viewer shortly before release because they doubted it could grow with customer needs, then rebuilt it in about two and a half to three weeks. In Abbott's words, "the lesson learned there is it's never too late to throw your code away and start over" [29:38].

q: Who does Heretik compete with on large regulatory compliance reviews?
a: Abbott said one of Heretik's largest competitors is not a company at all: a business may simply pay a penalty if reviewing its documents would cost more. He described it as "competing against the fines that these regulatory laws are incurring on customers" [33:28].

s1-e8-bootstrapping-a-modern-podcast-hosting-platform-jon-buda-transistorfm

Built for One Show First: Jon built the bones of Transistor to host Cards Against Humanity's daily Good News Podcast by January 1, 2018. It had an RSS feed, website and basic analytics, but no billing.

Complementary Co-Founders, 50-50 Split: Jon first turned down Justin Jackson's offer to partner after an earlier podcasting venture ended badly. He reconsidered because his development and design skills complemented Justin's marketing and product strengths.

Shaping Over Endless Backlogs: Inspired by Basecamp's book Shape Up, the two-person team moved from a huge backlog to shaping ideas and betting on six-week cycles. A feature that can't make the deadline gets shelved.

Early Dependencies Can Bite: Transistor used the Caddy web server for automatic SSL certificates before it was fully production ready. When certificates expired, the site, dashboard and RSS feeds went down, leading to SSL monitoring and a closer tie with Caddy's makers.

Support as Secret Weapon: Transistor stands out through responsive, hands-on help, including Justin's hour-long Skype calls with customers. Many new podcasters don't know what an RSS feed is or that they don't upload audio directly to Apple.

q: What is Transistor.fm?
a: Jon Buda, co-founder and lead developer, explains that "Transistor.fm is a podcast hosting and analytics platform." [02:49] It is a subscription service that hosts audio files, generates RSS feeds, helps distribute shows to platforms like Apple Podcasts and Spotify, and offers podcast websites and embeddable players.

q: How did Transistor.fm get started?
a: While Jon Buda was working at Cards Against Humanity, the company needed hosting for the Good News Podcast it planned to fund. Jon offered an alternative to a product he had previously helped build: "I build a new one, and if it's done in time we can use that." [05:37]

q: What tech stack does Jon Buda use to build Transistor?
a: Jon builds with Ruby on Rails and has more recently adopted Vue.js as front-end interactivity needs have grown. He likens his early building process to sketching with code, saying "Ruby on Rails is really good at that." [14:44]

q: What technical mistake did Transistor make early on?
a: Jon says it may have been a mistake to depend so early on Caddy, a web server that automates SSL certificates through Let's Encrypt. When the certificates expired without the team knowing, Jon recalls that "our website didn't work, our dashboard didn't work, all the RSS feeds stopped working" [25:10].

q: How does Transistor.fm set itself apart from other podcast hosts?
a: Jon Buda admits the founders had a hard time defining this, since much of what they do matches other companies. He concluded that "our secret weapon really has been our customer support." [31:22]

s1-e7-reengineering-ridesharing-rebuilding-tech-for-safety-and-scale-jonathan-campos-alto

Safety Changed His Mind: Campos first doubted another ride-hailing company could survive Uber and Lyft. Research and his wife's fear of riding alone convinced him there was room for Alto, with its focus on safety and women passengers.

The MVP Hit Limits Fast: A Node.js monolith on AWS with GraphQL and Prisma faced growth that would outpace it within months. Alto began moving to microservices on Kubernetes, Istio and Knative, with Firebase for real-time data.

Prioritize by Impact and Effort: Alto gathers customer and driver pain points, then plots top items on a two-by-two of customer impact versus effort. High-impact, low-effort work is an easy win, and big features get cut down to an MVP.

Two Juniors per Senior: On a team of about 12, Campos paired two junior developers with each senior on front end and back end. Juniors get mentors, seniors get to teach, and the budget stays manageable.

Don't Rush a Key Hire: Eager to fill an important role, the team cut short its own interview stages and quickly saw a mismatch. After months of trying to recover, they parted ways and Campos explained to the team the steps taken.

q: How is Alto different from Uber and Lyft for riders?
a: Jonathan Campos says Alto owns its cars, so riders can control the radio, volume and lighting directly from their phones without asking the driver. As he put it, "Because we own the car and we can actually put specific technology in the car" [29:44].

q: How does Alto use in-car technology to monitor driver safety?
a: Campos explains that cars have monitors for drivers, including a plainly visible camera, and that harsh braking and distracted driving get an immediate response. "With this, we track every one of our drivers." [29:05], he said, adding that drivers know about the technology and are trained around it.

q: Why did Alto rebuild its MVP technology?
a: Campos found that the monolithic Node.js application, which used GraphQL and Prisma, would not handle the coming growth, and the team later dealt with a memory leak for months. He recalled that the "growth trajectory was going to outgrow the MVP within months" [11:16].

q: How does Alto prioritize its product roadmap?
a: Campos says the team listens to customers and drivers, then maps top items by customer impact and level of effort to decide what to tackle in the next quarter. Large items are often trimmed to an MVP version, because "even getting that 20% of the feature out" [18:06] can improve most of customers' usage.

q: What advice does Jonathan Campos give new developers?
a: Campos urges new developers to build and launch a small project they care about and see it through from beginning to end. "but launch something, really put it out there, really work on it and love it and own it" [34:55], he said, since it teaches how the pieces fit and gives you something to show in interviews.

s1-e6-building-an-api-driven-solution-for-background-checks-jonathan-perichon-checkr

Fake It for the MVP: Checkr's first version had a UI and API that looked automated, but behind the scenes the founders were manually requesting background checks through a different background check company.

Build What Customers Want: The founders built an API first, but early customers didn't want one yet. They added a simple form so an operations lead could enter consumer information and invite people to fill in the rest.

Match the Database to the Data: Using MongoDB as the main data store for every data model was an early mistake. It suited some use cases, but relational ones didn't scale, so parts were quickly migrated to MySQL.

Automation as the Differentiator: Jonathan says most competitors review every criminal record, some with offshore teams that add delays and errors. Checkr uses machine learning to classify charges and return results almost instantly.

Hire for Humility and Grit: Early hiring favored humble people with grit over stars who weren't nice. Checkr then defined core values early and built them into interviews and performance management to scale the culture.

q: What inspired the founding of Checkr?
a: Jonathan Perichon and co-founder Daniel saw the problem at Deliv, an on-demand delivery company running background checks on hundreds of new drivers every week. Jonathan was shocked by the industry's API documentation, describing hundreds of pages as a "page of SOAP API on a Word document" [05:03].

q: How did Checkr build its MVP?
a: The founders built a front end and an API, then handled the checks by hand using another background check company. Jonathan explained that "behind the scene, we were manually requesting background checks using a different" [07:09] provider, while the product looked automated.

q: What tech stack did Checkr use?
a: Checkr mostly used Ruby with Sinatra rather than Rails, and started the front end in Angular before beginning a move to React. On the Sinatra choice, Jonathan said, "we really wanted to decouple the UI from the backend." [10:26]

q: What is the biggest technical challenge in building background check software?
a: Jonathan points to domain complexity, with requirements and workflows that can differ by city, county or type of customer. Although Checkr runs millions of checks every month, he says the hardest part is to make "all this complexity as simple as we can," [18:09].

q: What advice does Jonathan Perichon have for technical founders starting out?
a: Jonathan advises moving fast, knowing which corners to cut and iterating on customer feedback instead of perfecting the product alone. He said "it's important to be okay with not being 100% perfect and be confident that 90%" [28:45] perfect is still better than existing solutions.

s1-e5-integrating-video-chat-with-childrens-books-alvaro-sabido-caribu

Landscape Forced a Late Redesign: Caribu built its first version in portrait so kids wouldn't cover the camera. Publishers refused to supply content unless it was landscape, forcing a December scramble before the January 14th launch.

Lean, Serverless, One Language: The team started on Parse with OpenTok for video, later moved to Firebase, and rebuilt the app in React Native. That kept things serverless and in JavaScript while adding Android alongside iOS.

Grandparents Were the Paying Users: Product-market fit surveys showed that while Caribu targeted traveling parents, grandparents were the ones paying. The team chose to focus the next quarter on "glammas" aged 50 to 65.

Proposals Need Evidence: Weekly ICE meetings score ideas on impact, confidence and effort. Nothing gets proposed without data or research behind it, and approved items ship in two-week sprint releases.
Name Things for the Future: Sabido warns against calling everything a book when videos, activities or games may follow. An architecture built only around books would mean a huge migration later.

q: How did Caribu get started?
a: Alvaro Sabido developed the concept around his master's at Imperial College, where the team won prize money in a business model competition. They focused on books after asking what "parents miss most when they travel" [09:01].

q: What technology was Caribu built with?
a: The first prototype was an iOS tablet app using Parse as the backend and OpenTok for video, and the team later moved to Firebase and React Native. Sabido said of the Firebase setup, "we kept it 100% serverless all over" [13:30].

q: Who are Caribu's paying customers?
a: Surveys showed Sabido's team that although traveling parents were one target audience, grandparents were driving the relationship with the kids. As he put it, "The people that were actually paying us were the grandparents." [23:05]

q: How does Caribu keep young kids engaged on a video call?
a: Sabido described shared books with page turning and a pointer, activity sheets, and a drawing feature that works in real time on both sides. He said "we've seen pretty much the greatest increase in engagement and retention from this type of content" [29:34], and that calls have multiplied in length.

q: What would Alvaro Sabido do differently with Caribu?
a: Sabido would focus much earlier on what the product was and who it was for, instead of spending well over a year trying to do everything. He admitted, "I think the lack of focus hurt us a lot." [32:59]

s1-e4-an-unconventional-path-to-full-stack-software-engineering-sean-washington

Rewrite Before Launch: With Design Kollective not yet live and no customers depending on it, Sean replaced its Ruby on Rails MVP with a single Elixir and Phoenix codebase, piece by piece, in about two months.

Reconcile Vision With Code: As the first technical hire, Sean studied the founder's original deck, clicked through the app and read the code to find gaps between the features the team perceived and what actually existed.

Too Many Yeses: Sean estimates that maybe 60% of the yeses from his first two years should have been "not now" or "no." Sorting real improvements from convenience tweaks got harder once stores were using the product.

Lean and Stable Platform: Sean says the production app uses under 200 MB of RAM, with median API response times he puts under 50 milliseconds and no caching. The main performance fixes were his own SQL mistakes, such as N+1 queries.
Hiring for Relief: Being the only tech person meant constant on-call stress and less time to ship. Sean hired Paul, his former boss at Octopus, to share support, code reviews and brainstorming.

q: What is Design Kollective and who is it for?
a: Design Kollective is a collection of tools that small businesses, specifically furniture stores, use to sell online. Sean Washington says the goal is to help them compete as larger online players put stores out of business: "we're trying to help brick and mortar businesses stay in business." [26:12]

q: How did Sean Washington become a self-taught developer?
a: Sean studied music and then graphic design, and left college in his senior year to play guitar for a living. Seeing that his design friends wanted freelance work but knew no developers, he gave programming a shot: "So what I did was I started learning how to make WordPress themes." [04:58]

q: Why did Design Kollective move from Ruby on Rails to Elixir and Phoenix?
a: Sean found the Rails MVP hard to navigate and debug, partly because of chains of callbacks, and saw performance issues that needed attention. He had been enjoying Elixir, and he says "that rewrite allowed me to simplify a lot of things" [16:00] while making him intimately familiar with the functionality.

q: How should a solo technical lead handle constant feature requests?
a: Sean Washington had to weigh requests against his 40-hour week and separate real improvements from tweaks that only made someone's life a little easier. Looking back, he admits he agreed too often: "I think the first two years were full of yeses." [18:49] He now sets calendar reminders to step back from the code and think about the platform as a whole.

q: What advice does Sean Washington give developers who are just getting started?
a: Sean's advice is to make rest and self-care a priority, something he says he is still learning after it took a big toll on him. He urges developers to "schedule breaks, scheduled downtime, scheduled time for your brain to not be on all" [40:26] the time. For him, jujitsu classes helped him learn to silence his phone and focus on something else.

s1-e2-scaling-music-licensing-infrastructure-for-creators-tanner-hearne-musicbed
Rewrite, But Respect the MVP: The procedural PHP app was slow and had security gaps, yet it paid hundreds of artists monthly. Tanner patched password storage first, then pushed for a full rewrite.

Framework Over Custom Code: After about four months of research, Tanner chose Laravel. The rebuild with a London company took about eight months and added MVC structure, better password hashing and a data migration.
Manual Before Automated: Musicbed handled parts of payouts and other systems by hand behind an automated-looking experience, then automated once the process was worked out, avoiding costly rewrites.

Claims Cleared in Seconds: SyncID spots a YouTube Content ID claim, checks for an active subscription and tells YouTube to release it. The goal was under 60 seconds; Tanner thinks it now runs under 10.
Hire Through Community: Tanner started Laravel DFW partly to find hires. Of the 15 or 20 people he has hired, maybe two were chosen from resumes; most came from meetups, Twitter or referrals.

q: What is Musicbed and how does its music licensing work?
a: Musicbed is a music licensing platform that represents around 800 artists and licenses their music to filmmakers and creators for TV, commercials, podcasts and more. Tanner Hearne said that for many use cases, "they can check out in like 30 seconds and they have a legal right to use that music" [05:05].

q: Why did Musicbed rewrite its platform in Laravel?
a: The original app was procedural PHP with no framework, and it was hard to manage, slower than it should have been and not as secure as it could have been. After comparing options including Ruby on Rails, Tanner Hearne chose Laravel, recalling, "I basically said, we have to redo the whole thing." [11:49]

q: Should you automate a process before launching a new feature?
a: Tanner Hearne suggests offering the feature with people doing the work behind the scenes at first, so money starts coming in and the process can be refined. His advice is that "over time, automate it once you've worked out exactly how you want the process to work." [20:33]

q: How fast does Musicbed clear YouTube copyright claims?
a: Musicbed's SyncID system watches for claims on uploaded videos, checks whether the filmmaker has an active subscription and tells YouTube to release the claim. Tanner Hearne credited his team, saying "we wanted it to be cleared in under 60 seconds" [36:55], and he thinks they have since gotten it under 10 seconds.

q: How did Tanner Hearne hire his engineering team at Musicbed?
a: Tanner Hearne mostly hired people he met through Laravel DFW, Twitter, friends and employees rather than from resumes. His advice is to "put yourself in places where you'll meet good people" [25:40] instead of relying on them to find you.

s1-e1-building-and-exiting-a-mobile-scanning-app-rylan-barnes-shopsavvy

A Contest Win Opened Doors: After a week off to study the Android SDK and six months of moonlighting, Rylan's app GoCart won first prize in Google's competition. T-Mobile then used it to promote the G1, on condition it be renamed ShopSavvy.

Solving Blurry Barcodes Backwards: Early iPhones had fixed-focus cameras. Instead of sharpening blurry scans, Meatloaf blurred fragments of known barcodes and compared them to the sample, a much faster approach that was also licensed to other companies.

Scanning Was Never the Core: The team expected barcode scanning to be commoditized. It helped win customers and was licensed to Macy's, Sam's Club and others, but ShopSavvy focused on shoppers, backed by wider price coverage and fresher prices.

Founders Can't Delegate Vision: ShopSavvy tried bringing in shopping experts, but the team performed worst when delegation left it without direction and purpose. Heavy experimentation needs founders to set the goals and the problem being solved.

Quiet Builders Beat Self-Promoters: Rylan admits he overvalued people who marketed themselves well, only to see quiet, heads-down teammates usually outperform them. He also warns not to tolerate assholes, who actively hurt the rest of the team.

q: How did ShopSavvy get started?
a: Rylan Barnes first tried phone barcode scanning for price comparison in 2005, but it failed, and he revisited the idea in 2008 as smartphones arrived. As Rylan put it, "I grabbed Android Beta SDK and tried to get an app built" [03:30], which went on to win first prize in Google's Android competition.

q: How did ShopSavvy scan barcodes on early iPhones without autofocus?
a: Rylan built a technology called Meatloaf because early iPhones lacked the computing power to sharpen blurry images in real time. Rylan explained that it took "fragments of known barcodes and then blur them and then compare it piecewise to the sample" [11:37].

q: What did Rylan Barnes learn about leading a startup through pivots?
a: Rylan said running many experiments and pivots is helped by a clear sense of purpose that comes from the top. In his words, there needs to be "a strong core vision from the founders. Vision is not something that you can delegate or outsource" [18:24].

q: What did Rylan Barnes learn about hiring a startup team?
a: Rylan said he used to treat the attention people got as a signal of talent, then completely reversed his view. He found that the obvious, well-marketed picks were usually "outperformed by the people that were just quiet and heads down and just banging it out" [24:30].

q: Who acquired ShopSavvy and why?
a: Rylan said ShopSavvy was sold around December 2015 to Purch, a digital publishing company that writes product reviews and was also drawn to ShopSavvy's large mobile user base. Rylan noted that the product database and "price comparison search engine was a very excellent complement to the work that they" [30:43] were doing.
